->LETTER TO G. VOET<-
<note>Latin: *Epistola ad G. Voetium*. This is a polemical response to Gijsbert Voet (Voetius), a powerful Dutch theologian who accused Descartes of atheism and sought to have his philosophy banned at Utrecht University.</note>

<note>French: *Lettre Apologétique*. Specifically the "Apologetic Letter to the Magistrates of Utrecht" (1648), in which Descartes defended himself against the continued attacks of Voetius and his followers.</note>

<note>Latin: *Notæ in Programma quoddam*. Written in 1647, these are Descartes' critical responses to a broadsheet (a "program") published by his former student, Henricus Regius, who had deviated from Descartes' principles regarding the nature of the mind and body.</note>

# PAUL TANNERY

->AND<-

## THE EDITION OF DESCARTES

Paul Tannery had wished that in Volume V of this edition, the last of the *Correspondence* <note>original: "Correspondance"</note> of Descartes, a comprehensive study would allow the reader to compare the new edition with previous ones, showing what ours contributed in terms of unpublished texts, corrected passages, rectified chronology, and clarifications and information of all kinds. I admit that I shrank from such a task, which would have taken up precious time. But now that Paul Tannery is no longer with us, it is a duty toward him and his family—and perhaps also toward myself—to mark as clearly as possible the share that belongs to him in our joint work, which, in so many respects, must be considered one and indivisible. I can say that for what he himself did for this edition of Descartes, he alone was capable of doing it. He alone could verify, as he did, all the mathematical texts, adding to them such a rich commentary; and his collaboration was by no means limited to that.

Paul Tannery was admirably prepared for an edition of Descartes by his edition of Fermat <note>Pierre de Fermat (1601–1665), a French mathematician famous for his contributions to number theory.</note>, which was then in the process of publication...

since 1891. Furthermore, he had collected in a pamphlet (*The Correspondence of Descartes in the unpublished documents of the Libri collection, studied for the history of mathematics* <note>original: "La Correspondance de Descartes dans les inédits du fonds Libri, étudiée pour l'histoire des mathématiques"</note>, Paris, Gauthier-Villars, 1893) a series of studies on unpublished letters—and not the least important ones—recently returned to the National Library, after an exodus of nearly three-quarters of a century in England <note>The "fonds Libri" refers to manuscripts stolen by Guglielmo Libri in the mid-19th century and later partially recovered from collections in England.</note>. On the other hand, in Rome, he had studied the philosopher's letters on-site in the Boncompagni Collection <note>A significant scientific library assembled by Prince Baldassarre Boncompagni in Italy.</note>, regarding the variants they offer and their scientific interest. Then the discovery and publication of small works by the geometer Beaugrand <note>Jean de Beaugrand (c. 1584–1640), a French mathematician and rival of Descartes.</note>, regarding his quarrels with Descartes, promised an illuminating commentary on many pages that would be obscure to anyone other than Paul Tannery. Finally, the unique knowledge he had acquired of the history of science in the 17th century gave his collaboration an inestimable value.

In the first interviews we had together (October 1894), having been put in touch with one another by the primary promoter of this edition, Mr. Louis Liard <note>A philosopher and influential administrator in the French educational system.</note>, we agreed on the plan to follow. I was of the opinion to start with the most difficult part, that is to say the *Correspondence*, reserving the *Works* for the second part: the correspondence could serve to explain the works much more than the works would serve the correspondence. Paul Tannery agreed. But this correspondence itself, how to publish it? In chronological order, without a doubt. Paul Tannery, who eventually came around to this opinion, had first thought of another plan, which could also be defended. At that time, he was studying the correspondents of Mersenne <note>Father Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), the primary correspondent and scientific facilitator for Descartes and his contemporaries.</note>, whose numerous manuscript letters are found in a muddle in three large folio volumes of our National Library; he would have also willingly studied Descartes' correspondents separately. But the principal among these, by far, being Father Mersenne, the major part of the correspondence would have been published separately, and in what order, if not chronological, to which one inevitably returned. Likewise for the other series: Princess Elisabeth...

->VII<-
->**PAUL TANNERY**<-

Regius <note>Henricus Regius (1598–1679), a Dutch physician and early, though later estranged, follower of Descartes.</note>, Constantijn Huygens <note>A Dutch diplomat and poet, and a close friend of Descartes.</note>, Abbé Picot <note>Claude Picot, the "financial father" of Descartes who helped manage his affairs.</note>, etc., not to mention that for many correspondents, the series would have been reduced to very few letters, sometimes even two or three, or even just one. This idea was therefore quickly abandoned. Paul Tannery had also thought—and this could still be defended—of publishing separately certain polemics <note>Scientific or philosophical disputes.</note> between Descartes and Fermat, Descartes and Beaugrand, and especially Descartes and Roberval <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675), a mathematician who frequently clashed with Descartes over priority and methods.</note>, etc. Many of the philosopher's letters do not, in fact, have a strictly epistolary character; rather, by their length and importance, they constitute true short treatises which could very well have been presented separately. In the end, we preferred to leave each in its place within the correspondence itself; the latter, moreover, almost always deals with scientific and philosophical questions, which gives it a unity of tone from one end to the other—particularly grave and austere—despite a few quips here and there.

Once the chronological order was accepted (and it was necessary for a publication of a purely historical nature), I must say that not only did Paul Tannery adopt it without reservation, but he contributed most ingeniously to ensuring its refinement—that is to say, here, specifically, the page layout. There was, indeed, some trial and error before we agreed on the best arrangement. Each letter, after preparatory work, was accompanied by a multitude of notes that cluttered and overburdened it, and yet I did not want to sacrifice any of them, as they all seemed necessary for the understanding of the letter itself: notes on the date to be restored, notes on the source of the text and its authenticity, notes on many historical and other details within the letter, notes on the connections to be made between it and this or that important passage in the correspondence or the work of a contemporary, etc. We spent some time, as Paul Tannery used to say, "licking our bear into shape," <note>original: "à lécher notre ours." A French idiom referring to the process of painstakingly refining a rough piece of work, based on the old belief that mother bears licked their unformed cubs into the shape of a bear.</note> in order to make it presentable. Finally, he very fortunately hit upon a distribution of the notes which, putting everything in its place...

->VIII<-
->**EDITION OF DESCARTES**<-

offered a well-ordered whole: at the head of each letter, and set in special type, was a prolegomenon <note>A formal introductory essay or set of remarks used to establish context.</note> to fix the date and indicate, where necessary, the nature of the text—whether an authentic autograph <note>A manuscript written in the author's own hand.</note> or a simple copy; immediately below the text were the variants <note>original: "variantes." In textual criticism, these are different versions of the same passage found in different manuscripts or editions.</note>; at the bottom of the pages were the minor notes or brief remarks, those that took up only a few lines; finally, after the letter, and signaled in advance by asterisks, were the clarifications which sometimes required entire pages. Thus, Descartes' text was presented not constricted, but framed and, as it were, enshrined within a continuous border—this border designed specifically to gather and concentrate all the rays of light capable of illuminating it.

Once the agreement was made, the collaborator who had insisted on chronological order <note>Charles Adam himself, who is writing this preface.</note> took on the task of establishing it himself, asking Paul Tannery only to verify the work as it progressed: two safeguards are always better than one. Indeed, one can count the discrepancies between them on this question of dates: they concern only four letters (Vol. I, p. 18 and p. 352; Vol. II, p. 373 and p. 451). Similarly, for the establishment of the text, the variants, the notes, and the clarifications (except for what we shall see later), the copy was always provided by the same collaborator on his own initiative, with Paul Tannery charged with scrupulously revising the proofs regarding typographical correctness and the rest. Consequently, not a page—one might even say literally not a line—was not seen and reviewed, two or three times if not more, by each of the two in turn; it is in this sense that the work is truly one and indivisible.

This having been well established, what is the share that belongs specifically to Paul Tannery in each volume?

Volume I of the Correspondence (April 1622 to February 1638) contains extremely precious notes by him on Descartes and Galileo, regarding the law of falling bodies <note>A fundamental concept in classical mechanics; the editors discuss Descartes' and Galileo's differing mathematical approaches to how objects accelerate downward.</note>,

Volume I ended with the beginning of the great quarrel between Descartes and Fermat. There, Paul Tannery found himself on his own ground: this is clearly seen in the notes on pages 493-495.

Volume II (March 1638 to December 1639) is certainly the one where Paul Tannery contributed the most of his own work, and which, without his assistance, would have remained the most imperfect—let us even say, could not have been put in proper order. It contains, in effect, many mathematical letters, some of which are short treatises; and here one finds precisely the figures long familiar to the editor of Fermat, namely Fermat himself, Roberval, Mydorge, Hardy, Beaugrand, Sainte-Croix, Debeaune, and finally Desargues. Thus, Paul Tannery's annotations become more numerous, more extensive, and some constitute true dissertations. # XI

#### Paul Tannery

We have also printed several items in the Flemish language: the translation is by Paul Tannery, pp. 645-650 and pp. 657-658 (as already seen in volume III, pp. 28-30 and pp. 31-33). It was he alone who published and annotated letter 334 <note>Original: CCCXXXIV</note>, from Mersenne to Descartes, pp. 68-70, and letter 416 <note>Original: CDXVI</note>, pp. 342-344, regarding <note>John Pell (1611–1685), an English mathematician, and Christianus Longomontanus (1562–1647), a Danish astronomer.</note> Pell and Longomontanus. We also owe to him the pages on Roberval and the <term>problem of Pappus<note>A classical geometry problem involving the locus of points whose distances from several lines satisfy certain conditions; it was central to Descartes' development of analytic geometry.</note></term> once again, pp. 364-366; on the <term>center of oscillation<note>Original: "centre d'agitation." In 17th-century mechanics, this refers to the point in a physical pendulum where the period of vibration is the same as that of a simple pendulum.</note></term> and the experiments of <note>Sir Charles Cavendish (1591–1654), a mathematician and patron who facilitated scientific exchange between England and the Continent.</note> Cavendish, pp. 370-371, pp. 388-389, p. 419, p. 428, and especially pp. 597-600; on Torricelli, pp. 556-558, and further on, in the additions, pp. 675-678. Alongside these major pieces, several of which are truly complete dissertations, let us mention for the record the brief scholarly notes on p. 206 a and b, p. 361, and p. 692, as well as minor corrections, rectifications, or even simple reservations on p. 367 a, p. 368 a, p. 392 a, p. 472 (last paragraph), p. 508 a, p. 527 b, p. 553 d, p. 601 a, p. 645, p. 652, p. 655, p. 657, p. 696 a, b, c, and p. 697 a. Finally, to conclude, a small masterpiece, such as only Paul Tannery could write, on pp. 680-683, regarding the <note>Descartes' earliest work, the *Compendium Musicae* (A Compendium of Music), written in 1618.</note> Music.

Volume V (March 1647 to February 1650) contains, among other things, an exchange of letters between Descartes and Carcavi, which was a renewal of the old quarrel with Fermat and Roberval. Paul Tannery's scholarship found further material here to be put to use, to the great benefit of our edition: see especially pp. 367-369, p. 421 c, pp. 422-425, p. 465, and finally pp. 554-555. Let us add to this two letters—one of which was previously unpublished—between Roberval and Torricelli on the <term>quadrature of the cycloid<note>The mathematical challenge of calculating the area under a cycloid curve, a topic of fierce competition among 17th-century mathematicians.</note></term>, pp. 425-428, a few curious short notes on p. 169 c, p. 372 c, pp. 529-530, p. 542, p. 559, and two pieces of information relating to Christiaan Huygens, p. 552, and to Galileo, p. 553. But that of which Paul Tannery was most proud, and rightly so—and of which I was proud alongside him for our fifth volume—is the rich harvest he brought back from the Imperial and Royal Library upon returning from a research trip to Vienna. These include, first of all, four unpublished letters from Le Tenneur to Mersenne, pp. 77-79, p. 102, pp. 103-105, and pp. 120-121, of which several passages provide

## XII

-> EDITION OF DESCARTES <-

new documents on the famous Puy-de-Dôme experiment <note>Conducted in 1648, this experiment proved that atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude, supporting the existence of a vacuum; it was a pivotal moment in 17th-century physics.</note>; plus, a long letter, also unpublished—almost a small treatise—from <note>Jean de Beaugrand (c. 1584–1640), a mathematician and royal official who was a frequent critic of Descartes.</note> Beaugrand to Mersenne, pp. 503-513; finally and above all, seven letters (eight pieces in total) from <note>Florimond Debeaune (1601–1652), a mathematician whose work on "Debeaune's problem" was a significant challenge in the early history of calculus.</note> Florimond Debeaune, including one to Roberval and six to Mersenne, pp. 513-524, pp. 524-529, pp. 530-542; one will understand the joy of Paul Tannery when it is known that not a single line in French had ever been published from this mathematician until now.

One could also credit Paul Tannery with many extracts of letters, or even entire letters, from various correspondents of <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), the friar who acted as the central hub of the 17th-century "Republic of Letters," facilitating communication between Descartes, Pascal, Fermat, and others.</note> Mersenne, published throughout these five volumes: letters from Beeckman, Villiers, Lacombe, Thiébaut, Durel, etc. However, the three large <term>in-folio<note>A book size where the printing sheets are folded only once, creating large-format volumes.</note></term> volumes containing these letters were also combed through by both collaborators. The work of sorting was even more thorough because it was done at leisure in Dijon, where these manuscripts had been sent. Furthermore, it was in Dijon that the laborious sorting of texts for publication took place, distributing them as appropriate and aligning them with the corresponding passages in Descartes’ letters. In fact, this vast correspondence with Mersenne (which does not include Mersenne's own letters) became our shared domain, although Paul Tannery was the first to explore it, and he had even considered extracting a portion of it—itself forming a complete whole—for a local publication he would have titled: *Mersenne and his Bordeaux Correspondents* <note>Original: "Mersenne et ses Correspondants bordelais"</note>. Numerous traces and even sketches of this work were found among his papers.

With the five volumes of Descartes' *Correspondence* finished, the publication of the *Works* was little more than a game in comparison (except for certain parts, as will be seen further on). Nevertheless, the *Essays* that accompany the *Discourse on the Method*, namely the *Dioptrics*, the *Meteors*, and especially the *Geometry*, still had great need—at least for the proofreading—of Paul Tannery's scientific erudition.

XIII

He therefore worked meticulously on this Volume VI, even adding a personal study on <note>A classic geometric problem concerning the path of points relative to multiple lines; it was a central challenge that helped Descartes develop his coordinate geometry.</note> Pappus's problem (pp. 721-725), and preceding the whole work with a *Foreword* signed by him (pp. v-xii).

The last two volumes on which he collaborated, Volumes VII and IX, owe him only his share—always laborious and conscientious to a fault—in the double and triple revision and proofreading, plus a few notes in Volume IX, second part (p. 86 *c*, p. 119 *b* and *c*, p. 154 *a*, p. 223 *c*, p. 235 *b*). Furthermore, Paul Tannery had announced two final studies: one on the <note>Descartes’s attempt to establish mathematical laws for how objects interact when they hit each other; these were some of the earliest, though imperfect, attempts at modern physics.</note> seven rules of the impact of bodies according to Descartes, and another on the <note>The ancient astronomical model placing the Earth at the center of the universe, which was being replaced by the sun-centered Copernican system during Descartes' time.</note> Ptolemaic system. The first remains unfinished (pp. 327-330); the second was never even partially written (p. 330). Sadly, Paul Tannery's work was cut short, in the midst of his labors, by his death.

His collaboration will be missed from now on. Already this Volume VIII was completed without the sense of security he provided to his collaborator—who remained alone at the task—and without the guarantees that a scholar of his caliber assured the public. But how much more will we suffer during the two volumes that still remain! Especially for one where we will present the oldest writings of Descartes, or rather what has been preserved or rediscovered of them, dating from 1618–1619 or 1628. For this, Paul Tannery was essential, and no one will be able to fully take his place. Just recently, a most important discovery was made in Middelburg, Holland: the *Journal* of <note>Isaac Beeckman (1588–1637) was a Dutch scientist and mentor to the young Descartes; their meeting in 1618 is considered a turning point in the history of science.</note> Isaac Beeckman, that old friend to whom the young Descartes had confided his first thoughts. What a joy it would have been for Paul Tannery, and what vivid light his wise erudition would have immediately shed on so many obscure problems! Who will help us now to untangle and resolve them? The same applies to the philosopher’s <term>Posthumous Works<note>original: "Opufcula pofthuma"; minor or smaller writings published after the author's death.</note></term>: they present many difficulties that Paul Tannery had already begun to clear away. He had even published some portions of them, and we have found numerous traces of his work among his papers, which will appear in the

B

### EDITION OF DESCARTES

final volume. But it can be said that he passed away at the very moment when the publication of the *Works of Descartes* still required his assistance and, for certain purely mathematical sections, his direction.

In 1903, the awarding of one of the highest honors available to the <note>The premier learned society of France, established to bring together the nation's scientific, literary, and artistic elite.</note> Institute of France, the <note>A prestigious biennial prize established in the 19th century to reward the most significant contribution to science, letters, or art produced over a five-year period.</note> Jean Reynaud Prize, fell—by virtue of a rotating schedule—to the <note>One of the five academies within the Institute, focused on philosophy, law, and history.</note> Academy of Moral and Political Sciences. The philosophy section first, then the entire Academy, following the report by <note>An influential French philosopher and historian known for his work on the relationship between science and religion.</note> Mr. Emile Boutroux, was unanimous in awarding this prize to the edition of the *Works of Descartes*. The two collaborators were greatly honored by this; they saw in it the validation, by the most distinguished judges, of the work on which they had been working with such enthusiasm for so many years, and which they fully hoped to bring to a successful conclusion together. This final completion would have been the greatest reward for Paul Tannery. He sought no other than the satisfaction of a duty well performed, and the awareness he held, in his heart as a scholar and a Frenchman, of performing a work useful to science and useful to his country.

->CH. ADAM.<-

# NOTICE

Descartes’s *Principles of Philosophy* <note>original: "Principia philosophiæ"</note> were published as many as six times by the Elzeviers <note>A famous dynasty of Dutch printers and booksellers active in the 17th century, renowned for their high-quality scholarly editions.</note> in Holland. Here is the documentation for these six successive editions:

1º **René Descartes’s** *Principles of Philosophy*. (Amsterdam, at the house of Louis Elzevier. Year 1644. With privileges <note>Official legal permissions granted by the government or church to print a work, an early form of copyright.</note>. Printer's mark: *Minerva*. Quarto <note>A book size (In-4) where each sheet of paper is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>, 12 preliminary leaves, 310 pages, 1 blank leaf.)

This small quarto is sometimes found alone. Most often, it is bound in the same volume with the Latin translation of the *Discourse on Method* and the *Essays*, which then forms a second part under this title:

> **René Descartes’s** *Samples of Philosophy: or, a Dissertation on the Method of rightly conducting one's reason, and seeking truth in the sciences: Optics and Meteorology. Translated from the French, reviewed by the author, and corrected in several places.* <note>original: "Specimina Philosophiæ : seu Dissertatio de Methodo rectè regendæ rationis, & veritatis in scientiis investigandæ : Dioptrice & Meteora. Ex gallico translata, & ab auctore perlecta, variisque in locis emendata."</note> (Amsterdam, at the house of Louis Elzevier, 1644. With privileges. Printer's mark: *Minerva*. Quarto, 8 preliminary leaves, 331 pages.)

We have, moreover, reproduced this second part in its proper place—that is, in the same volume as the *Discourse on Method* and the *Essays* of that *Method* in French—in Volume VI of the present edition, pages 517–720.

2º **René Descartes’s** *Principles of Philosophy*. (Amsterdam, at the house of Louis Elzevier. Year 1650. With privileges. Printer's mark: *Minerva*. Quarto, 20 preliminary leaves, 302 pages.)

The preceding bibliographic information clearly shows that the *Principles of Philosophy* <note>original Latin: "Principia Philosophiæ"</note> present no difficulty regarding the establishment of the Latin text. It is sufficient to obtain a copy of the <term>first edition|known as the edition princeps, this is the first printed version of a work authorized by the author.</term>, which is by no means rare, neither in libraries nor even on the market, and to follow it faithfully: all other editions are merely reprints of it. As for the history of the publication and the commentary that the text might require, these are matters we are reserving, as is our custom, for a special chapter on the philosopher's life. — The text only raised problems regarding the French translation of the *Principles of Philosophy*. These can be found examined at length in Volume IX of the current edition, second part, pages VII–XX of the *Notice*.

### TO THE MOST SERENE PRINCESS
## ELISABETH,
### ELDEST DAUGHTER OF FREDERICK, KING OF BOHEMIA,
### COUNT PALATINE AND ELECTOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE.
<margin>5</margin>

->Most Serene Princess^a,<-

I have derived the greatest fruit from the writings I have published until now, in that you have deigned to read them through, and because, having been admitted to your acquaintance by means of them, I have come to recognize your talents to be such that I believe it to be for the benefit of the human race <margin>10</margin> that they be held up as an example for the ages. It would not befit me either to flatter or to affirm anything not sufficiently perceived, especially in this place, in which I am about to attempt to lay the foundations of truth; and I know that the unpretentious and <margin>15</margin> simple judgment of a Philosopher will be more pleasing to your noble modesty than the more ornate praises of more flattering men. For this reason, I shall write only those things...

---

<note>
a. This <term>Dedicatory Letter</term> <note>original: "Epistola dedicatoria"</note> is printed on six unnumbered pages at the beginning of the first edition of the *Principles of Philosophy* <note>original: "Principia Philosophiæ"</note>, immediately following the frontispiece. On the reverse side of that frontispiece is reproduced in full the *Privilege* <note>a legal grant of publishing rights</note> of May 4, 1637 (see Vol. VI, p. 518, of this edition), with this mention at the bottom:

> “Finished Printing on July 10, 1644.”

The *Letter* is followed by 14 unnumbered pages containing the *Index of the Principles of Philosophy* (which we will reproduce not before, but only after the *Principles*, so that we may provide the page numbers). Next come the 310 numbered pages of the *Principles*. On the last page is added an *Errata* of several lines, the corrections of which have been incorporated into our text.
</note>

<summary>In this dedicatory epistle, René Descartes addresses Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, praising her intellect and stating that her engagement with his philosophy serves as a model for humanity. He adopts a tone of "philosophical honesty" rather than courtly flattery to suit her modest and scholarly nature.</summary>

--- Page 32 ---
<meta>This page continues the Dedicatory Letter to Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia. It begins mid-sentence, following Descartes' promise to the Princess that he will only write what he has perceived to be true, rather than using the flowery language of common flatterers.</meta>

### DEDICATORY LETTER.

...which I know to be true by reason or experience, and here in the beginning, just as in all the rest of the book, I shall philosophize.

There is a great difference between true and apparent <margin>5</margin> virtues; and also among the true ones, between those that proceed from an accurate knowledge of things, and those that are joined with some ignorance. By apparent virtues, I mean certain vices that are not very common, which are opposed to other better-known vices; because these are <margin>10</margin> further removed from those vices than the intermediate virtues are, they are therefore more frequently celebrated. Thus, because more people are found who timidly flee from danger than those who recklessly throw themselves into it, rashness <note>original: *temeritas*</note> is opposed to the vice of timidity as if it were a virtue, and is more <margin>15</margin> esteemed by the common people than true courage <note>original: *fortitudo*</note>; so too the extravagant <note>Descartes refers to the "prodigal," those who spend wastefully.</note> are often valued more than the generous; and thus none more easily reach a great reputation for piety than the superstitious or hypocrites.

Among the true virtues, however, many are born not from the knowledge of the right alone, but also from some error: thus <margin>20</margin> goodness often arises from simplicity, piety from fear, and courage from desperation. And these are different from one another, so that they are even designated by different names; but those pure and sincere ones, which flow from the knowledge of the right alone, all have one and the same nature, and are contained under <margin>25</margin> the single name of wisdom <note>original: *sapientia*</note>. For whoever has a firm and effective will to always use their reason correctly, as far as it is in their power, and to carry out everything they know to be best, is truly wise...

---

<note>Editorial note: In the first edition (1644), the word "philosophize" (line 3) did not start a new paragraph. The same applies to "hypocrites" (line 17), "extolled" (page 3, line 8), "is found" (page 3, line 21), and "be snatched" (page 4, line 14).</note>

<summary>In this dedication, Descartes distinguishes between "apparent" virtues (which are actually vices) and "true" virtues, arguing that genuine virtue arises solely from the correct use of reason and wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, wisdom, reason, courage, piety, ethics, Princess Elisabeth, rashness, hypocrisy</keywords>

--- Page 33 ---
<meta>This page continues the Dedicatory Letter to Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia. Descartes is concluding a thought from the previous page, explaining that while "apparent" virtues are often fragmented and flashy, true virtue is a singular, unified expression of wisdom.</meta>

### DEDICATORY LETTER.

...as much as is possible by its own nature; and through this one thing, it possesses justice, courage <note>original: *fortitudinem*</note>, temperance, and all the rest of the virtues, but joined together in such a way that none stands out above the others. For that reason, although <margin>5</margin> these virtues are much more excellent than those marked by some mixture of vice, they are usually not praised as highly because they are less known to the common people.

Furthermore, since two things are required for wisdom as it has been described—namely, the perception of the intellect and the inclination <margin>10</margin> of the will—everyone is capable of that which depends on the will, but some have an intellect much more discerning <note>original: *perspicaciorem*</note> than others. And although it ought to be sufficient for those who are naturally somewhat slow that—even if they remain ignorant of many things—provided they <margin>15</margin> maintain a firm and constant will to omit nothing that might lead them to a knowledge of the right, and to carry out everything they judge to be right, they can be wise according to their own capacity <note>literally: "according to their measure"</note> and most pleasing to God in this regard. Nevertheless, those people <margin>20</margin> are far more excellent in whom, along with a most firm will to act rightly, is found a most discerning mind and the greatest care for knowing the truth.

That this care is at its height in Your Highness is clear from the fact that neither the distractions of the court, nor the customary education which <margin>25</margin> usually condemns young women to ignorance, have been able to prevent you from investigating all the liberal arts and sciences. Furthermore, the supreme and incomparable discernment of your mind is apparent because you have looked most deeply into all the secrets of these sciences and have accurately mastered them in a very short time. <margin>30</margin> and I have a still greater proof of this fact, one peculiar to me: that I have so far found you alone to be the person who...

Next, because in our dreams we daily seem to feel or imagine countless things that are nowhere to be found; and to one who doubts in this way, no certain signs appear by which he may clearly distinguish being asleep from being awake.

<margin>V. Why we may also doubt mathematical demonstrations.</margin>
We shall also doubt the other things which we previously held as most certain; even mathematical demonstrations, and even those principles which we have hitherto thought to be <term>self-evident: truths that are seen immediately by the mind without needing further proof, like "the whole is greater than the part"</term>. This is partly because we have seen some people err in such matters and accept things as most certain and self-evident which seemed false to us; but most of all because we have heard that there is a God who can do all things, and by whom we were created. For we do not know whether perhaps He willed to create us in such a way that we are always deceived, even in those things which appear most clearly known to us. Indeed, this seems no less possible than the fact that we are occasionally deceived, which we noted happening before. And if we imagine that we exist not by a most powerful God, but either by ourselves or by some other source: the less powerful we assume the author of our origin to be, the more credible it will be that we are so imperfect that we are always deceived.

<margin>VI. That we possess free will to withhold assent in matters of doubt, and thus avoid error.</margin>
But meanwhile, from whomever we may ultimately originate, and however powerful or deceptive <note>original: *fallax* — this refers to the famous "evil demon" or "deceiving god" thought experiment</note> they may be, we nevertheless experience this freedom within us: that we can always abstain from believing those things which are not plainly certain and fully explored. Thus, we can take care never to fall into error.

### PART ONE
### 7

<margin>
...be doubted that we exist while we doubt; and that this is the first thing that we know by philosophizing in an orderly manner.
</margin>
In this way we can doubt, and even by imagining things to be false, we easily suppose that there is no God, no heaven, and no physical bodies; we can even suppose that we ourselves have no hands, no feet, nor finally any body at all. But we who think such things are not, for that reason, nothing: for it is a contradiction <note>original: "repugnat enim"</note> to think that something which thinks does not exist at the very same time that it thinks. And therefore this piece of knowledge, *I think, therefore I am* <note>original: "ego cogito, ergo sum"</note>, is the first and most certain of all truths to occur to anyone who philosophizes in an orderly way.

<margin>
VIII.
The distinction between the soul and the body—or between a <term>thinking thing: a mind or soul that lacks physical size</term> and a <term>corporeal thing: a physical object that occupies space</term>—is recognized from this.
</margin>
And this is the best path to recognizing the nature of the mind and its distinction from the body. For by examining who we are—we who suppose everything different from ourselves to be false—we clearly see that no <term>extension: the property of taking up physical space</term>, nor shape, nor local motion, nor anything similar that must be attributed to a body, belongs to our nature. Only thought belongs to it. Therefore, thought is known before and more certainly than any corporeal thing; for we have already perceived thought, but we still doubt the others.

<margin>
IX.
What thought is.
</margin>
By the name of "thought," I understand all those things which occur in us while we are conscious, insofar as there is consciousness of them in us. And thus, not only understanding, willing, and imagining, but even sensing, is the same thing here as thinking. For if I say, *I see, or I walk, therefore I am*; and I understand this to be about vision or walking, which is performed by the body, the conclusion is not absolutely certain; because, as often happens in dreams, I can think that I see or walk, although I do not open my eyes and do not move from my place, and perhaps even although I have no body. But if I understand it as the sensation or consciousness itself of seeing or walking, because it then refers to <note>This sentence continues on the following page.</note>

X.
Things that are most simple and self-evident are made more obscure by logical definitions; such things are not to be counted among the types of knowledge acquired through study.
</margin>
I do not explain here many other terms which I have already used, or will use in the following pages, because they seem to me to be sufficiently known by themselves. I have often noticed that Philosophers <note>Descartes is likely referring to the "Scholastics," the academic philosophers of his time who relied heavily on complex Aristotelian definitions.</note> err in this: they try to explain things that are simplest and self-evident with logical definitions, but in doing so, they only make the things themselves more obscure. When I stated that this proposition, *I think, therefore I am* <note>original: "ego cogito, ergo sum"</note>, is the first and most certain of all to occur to anyone who philosophizes in an orderly way, I did not deny that one must first know what thought is, what existence is, and what certainty is. Likewise, one must know that it is impossible for that which thinks not to exist, and other such things. However, because these are the simplest notions, and because they alone provide no knowledge of any existing thing, I did not think they should be counted [as formal steps of study].

<margin>
XI.
How our mind is better known than the body.
</margin>
Now, in order to know that our mind is known not only earlier and more certainly, but also more evidently than the body, it must be noted that it is very well-known by the <term>natural light: the innate human capacity for reason, independent of sensory experience</term> that nothingness has no attributes or qualities <note>original: "nihili nullas esse affectiones sive qualitates"</note>. Therefore, wherever we detect some qualities, a thing or <term>substance: an underlying reality that supports properties</term> to which they belong must necessarily be found there. Furthermore, the more qualities we detect in a single thing or substance, the more clearly we know it. It is manifest that we detect more things in our own mind than in any other thing, because absolutely nothing can lead us to know something else without that same thing leading us much more certainly to the knowledge of our own mind. For example, if I judge that the earth exists because I touch it or see it, then certainly, from this very fact, I have even more reason to judge that my mind exists. For it could perhaps happen <note>Descartes ends here mid-sentence; he is about to explain that while the "earth" might be an optical illusion, the "judging mind" remains a reality.</note>

<summary>Descartes explains that basic concepts like "existence" are too simple for formal definitions and argues that the mind is more knowable than the body. He introduces the principle that every perception of the outside world simultaneously serves as even stronger evidence for the existence of the perceiver's mind.</summary>

# PART ONE.
<meta>4-5.</meta>
ŒUVRES. III. 2

it can happen that I judge myself to be touching the earth, even though no earth exists; but it cannot be that I judge this, and yet my mind, which is making the judgment, is nothing; and the same applies to everything else.

<margin>XII. *Why this is not equally obvious to everyone.*</margin>
<margin>5</margin>
Those who have not philosophized in an orderly way have seen things differently for no other reason than because they never distinguished the mind from the body with enough accuracy. And although they believed it was more certain to them that they themselves existed than anything else, they did not notice that, in this context, they should have understood "themselves" to mean their minds alone; on the contrary, they instead understood only <margin>10</margin> their bodies, which they saw with their eyes and touched with their hands, and to which they wrongly attributed the power of sensation. This distracted them from perceiving the true nature of the mind.

<margin>XIII. *In what sense the knowledge of all other things depends on the knowledge of God.*</margin>
<margin>15</margin>
When the mind—which knows itself but still doubts all other things—looks around in every direction to extend its knowledge further, it first finds within itself the <term>ideas</term> <note>In Descartes' philosophy, "ideas" are the mental images or representations of things, whether those things exist in reality or not.</note> of many things. As long as it simply contemplates these ideas, and neither affirms nor denies that anything similar to them exists outside itself, it cannot be mistaken. <margin>20</margin> It also finds certain <term>common notions</term> <note>Also called "axioms," these are self-evident truths that the "natural light" of reason reveals to be true, such as "the whole is greater than the part."</note>, and from these it constructs various demonstrations; as long as it focuses on these, it is entirely persuaded that they are true. So, for example, the mind has within itself the ideas of numbers and shapes; it also has among its common notions that *if you add equals to <margin>25</margin> equals, the results will be equal* <note>original: "quòd ſi æqualibus æqualia addas, quæ inde exſurgent erunt æqualia"</note>, and other similar truths. From these, it is easily demonstrated that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles, and so on. Consequently, the mind persuades itself that these and similar things are true, as long as it focuses on the premises from which it deduced them. But because <margin>30</margin> it cannot always focus on those premises, and when it later remembers that it does not yet know whether it was perhaps created with such a nature...

<summary>Descartes explains that people often fail to distinguish the mind from the body, leading to confusion about what is truly "self." He also introduces the idea that while we can be certain of mathematical and logical axioms (common notions) while focusing on them, a deeper foundation is needed for lasting certainty.</summary>

<margin>XIV. From the fact that necessary existence is contained in our concept of God, it is rightly concluded that God exists.</margin>
<margin>10</margin>
Then, considering among the various <term>ideas</term> <note>In Descartes' philosophy, "ideas" are the mental images or representations of things in the mind, regardless of whether those things exist in the physical world.</note> it possesses, it finds one of a supremely intelligent, supremely powerful, and supremely perfect being, which is by far the most important of all. It recognizes in this idea existence—not merely possible and <term>contingent</term> <note>Something is "contingent" if it could either exist or not exist; its existence is not guaranteed by its definition.</note> existence, as in the ideas of all other things it perceives distinctly, <margin>15</margin> but existence that is entirely necessary and eternal. <margin>XV. That necessary existence is not contained in the concepts of other things in the same way, but only contingent existence.</margin>
And it will believe this all the more if it notices that no idea of any other thing can be found within itself in which it perceives necessary existence to be contained <margin>25</margin> in the same way. For from this, it will understand that this idea of a supremely perfect being is not something invented by itself, nor does it represent some <term>chimera</term> <note>A "chimera" refers to a mere fabrication of the mind, like a mythological beast that has no basis in reality.</note>, but rather a true and immutable nature which cannot fail to exist, since necessary existence is contained within it.

<margin>30</margin>
Our mind, I say, will easily believe this if it has first entirely freed itself from <term>prejudices</term> <note>Descartes defines "prejudices" as the unexamined opinions we have held since childhood, which often cloud our clear and distinct reasoning.</note>. <summary>In this passage, Descartes argues that the existence of God can be proven through the mind's idea of a "supremely perfect being," which uniquely includes necessary existence as part of its essence. He compares this logical certainty to the mathematical proofs of geometry, noting that only human prejudice prevents this truth from being obvious to all.</summary>

5 Looking further into the ideas we have within us, we see that insofar as they are certain modes of thinking, they do not differ much from one another; but insofar as one represents one thing and another represents another, they are very different. And the more **objective perfection**

...produced by an efficient and total cause; but also that no idea or image of any thing can exist in us unless there exists somewhere—either in ourselves or outside of us—an **archetype** <note>original: "Archetypus". A primary model or pattern from which copies are made. In this context, it is the "real" thing that the mental idea represents.</note> containing in reality all the perfections that the idea represents. And because we do not find in ourselves those supreme perfections whose <term>idea</term> <note>Latin: *idea*. A mental representation or concept.</note> we possess, we rightly conclude from this very fact that they exist in something different from us—namely, in God—or at least that they once existed; from which it follows most evidently that they still exist.

XIX.
Even if we do not grasp God’s nature, His perfections are known by us more clearly than any other thing.
</margin>

And this is certain and manifest enough to those who are accustomed to contemplating the idea of God and noticing His supreme perfections. For even if we do not **comprehend** them—since it is the nature of the **infinite** <note>original: "infinitum". That which has no limits. Descartes argues that while we can "understand" or "touch" the infinite with our minds, we cannot "embrace" or "grasp" it entirely because our minds are limited.</note> not to be grasped by us who are **finite**—we can nevertheless understand them more clearly and distinctly than any corporeal <note>Physical or bodily objects.</note> things. This is because they fill our thoughts more completely, are simpler, and are not obscured by any limitations.

<margin>
XX.
We are made not by ourselves, but by God, and therefore He exists.
</margin>

However, because not everyone notices this—and because we do not remember the idea of God ever "coming" to us from God (in the same way that someone with an idea of an ingenious machine usually knows where they got it, whereas we have always possessed this idea)—we must further ask: from whom do we ourselves exist, we who possess the idea of God’s supreme perfections? For it is certainly well known by the **natural light** <note>original: "lumen naturale". The innate human capacity for reason and logic which allows us to recognize self-evident truths.</note> that a thing which knows something more perfect than itself cannot have been the cause of its own existence. If it were, it would have given itself all the perfections of which it has an idea; therefore, it cannot have been created by anyone who does not possess all those perfections—that is, by anyone who is not God.

<summary>Descartes argues that the idea of a perfect God in our minds must have been caused by an actual perfect Being, as a finite human could not have invented the concept of the infinite. He concludes that since we are aware of our own imperfections yet possess the idea of perfection, we must have been created by God rather than ourselves.</summary>

# PART ONE

<meta>Sections 8–9.</meta>

<margin>
XXI. 
The duration of our existence is sufficient to demonstrate the existence of God.
</margin>

Nothing can obscure the clarity of this proof, provided we pay attention to the nature of **time**, or the **duration** <note>original: "duratio". Descartes views time not as a continuous flow, but as a series of independent moments that do not naturally lead into one another.</note> of things. The nature of time is such that its parts do not depend on one another and never exist simultaneously. Therefore, from the fact that we exist now, it does not follow that we will exist in the moment immediately following, unless some cause—namely, the same cause that first produced us—continually, as it were, **re-produces** <note>original: "reproducat". This refers to the doctrine of "continuous creation," where God must actively sustain the universe at every instant for it to remain in existence.</note> us; that is, **preserves** <term>conservation</term> <note>Latin: *conservatio*. In this context, it means the ongoing act of keeping something in existence, which Descartes argues requires the same power as the initial act of creation.</note> us. For we easily understand that there is no power in us by which we might preserve ourselves. Furthermore, He in whom there is such great power that He can preserve us (who are distinct from Him) must be even more capable of preserving Himself—or rather, He requires no preservation by anyone and is, finally, God.

<margin>
XXII. 
By our way of knowing God’s existence, all His attributes reachable by the natural power of the mind are known at the same time.
</margin>

There is a great advantage in this way of proving God’s existence—that is, through His idea: we recognize at the same time who He is, as far as the weakness of our nature allows. Looking toward the **idea** innate <note>Something we are born with, rather than learned through the senses.</note> within us, we see that He is eternal, omniscient, omnipotent, the source of all goodness and truth, the creator of all things, and finally, having within Himself all that we can clearly perceive to be an **infinite perfection** <note>original: "perfectio". A quality of being complete or "finished" to the highest possible degree.</note>, or a perfection not limited by any imperfection.

Now, indeed, because God alone is the true cause of all things that are or can be, it is clear that we will follow the best way of philosophizing if we attempt to deduce the explanation of the things created by Him from the knowledge of God Himself, so that we may thus acquire the most perfect science, which is that of effects through their causes. In order that we may undertake this safely enough and without the danger of error, we must use the precaution of always remembering as much as possible both that God, the author of things, is infinite, and that we are altogether finite.

<margin>

</margin>

Thus, if God should perhaps reveal something to us about Himself or others that exceeds the natural powers of our intellect—such as the mysteries of the Incarnation and the Trinity already are—we will not refuse to believe them, even though we do not clearly understand them. Nor shall we wonder in any way that there are many things, both in His immense nature and also in the things created by Him, which exceed our grasp.

### Part One.

<margin>*Matter, the number of stars, etc., are to be considered as indefinite.*</margin>
...infinite, its half would also be infinite; or whether an infinite number is even or odd, and such things: for no one should think about such matters unless they believe their own mind to be infinite. We, however, will not actually affirm that things are "infinite" <note>original: "infinita"</note> when we cannot find an end to them. Instead, we will regard them as <term>indefinite</term> <note>original: "indefinita". Descartes uses this to distinguish between God's absolute lack of limits and the physical world's lack of observable limits.</note><sup>a</sup>. Thus, because we cannot imagine an extension so great that we do not understand there could be one even greater, we will say that the magnitude of possible things is indefinite. And because no body can be divided into so many parts that each of these parts is not still understood to be divisible, we will consider quantity to be indefinitely divisible. Finally, because we cannot imagine a number of stars so large that we do not believe God could have created even more, we will suppose their number to be indefinite; and so it is for all other things.

<margin>**XXVII.** *What the difference is between the indefinite and the infinite.*</margin>
We will call these things indefinite rather than infinite for two reasons. First, so that we reserve the name "infinite" for God alone; for in Him alone do we not only recognize no limits in any respect, but we also positively understand that there are none. Second, because we do not understand other things to lack limits in the same positive way; rather, we only admit negatively that we cannot find any limits they might have.

<margin>**XXVIII.** *That we must examine not the final causes of created things, but their efficient causes.*</margin>
Finally, we will never seek any explanations for natural things based on the <term>final cause</term> <note>A "final cause" refers to the purpose or "goal" for which a thing exists (e.g., "the sun exists to provide light for humans").</note> that God or nature intended in making them. We must not be so arrogant as to think we are participants in His secret plans. Instead, we must consider Him as the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>An "efficient cause" is the actual mechanism or force that brings something about—the "how" rather than the "why."</note> of all things...

# 16 PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 11-12.

However, we must remember, as has already been stated<sup>a</sup>, that we should only trust this natural light so long as nothing to the contrary is revealed by God Himself.

<margin>**XXIX.** *God is not the cause of errors.*</margin>
The first attribute of God to be considered here is that He is supremely truthful and the giver of all light. Therefore, it is completely contradictory to suggest that He would deceive us, or that He could be the proper and positive cause of the errors we experience ourselves falling into. For although the ability to deceive might perhaps seem like a sign of cleverness among us humans, the *will* to deceive certainly never proceeds from anything other than malice, or fear and weakness; consequently, it cannot be attributed to God.

<margin>**XXX.** *It follows from this that everything we clearly perceive is true, and the doubts previously mentioned are removed.*</margin>
And from this it follows that the natural light, or the faculty of knowledge given to us by God, can never reach any object that is not true, insofar as it is reached by that faculty—that is, insofar as it is <term>clearly and distinctly perceived</term> <note>original: "clarè & distinctè percipitur"; a cornerstone of Cartesian philosophy, meaning an idea so sharp and separate from others that it cannot be doubted.</note>. For God would rightly be called a deceiver if He had given us a faculty so warped that it took the false for the true. In this way, that greatest | doubt is removed, which arose from our not knowing whether we might be of such a nature that we were deceived even in those things which seem most evident to us<sup>b</sup>. Furthermore, all the other reasons for doubting that were previously listed<sup>c</sup> are easily removed by this principle.

And if we pay attention to what is clear and distinct in our senses—whether we are awake or in sleep—and distinguish that from what is confused and obscure, we will easily recognize what is to be held as true in any matter. There is no need to pursue these points with more words in this place, since they have already been treated to some extent in my *Metaphysical Meditations* <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "Meditationibus Metaphysicis"; this refers to his 1641 work where he first laid out these arguments in detail.</note>, and a more accurate explanation of them depends on the knowledge that follows.

<margin>
XXXI.
*Our errors, if attributed to God, are merely negations; if to ourselves, they are privations.*
</margin>
But because it still often happens that we are mistaken even though God is not a deceiver, we must investigate the origin and cause of our errors to learn how to guard against them. It should be noted that errors do not depend so much on the <term>intellect</term> <note>the faculty by which we simply perceive or "take in" ideas.</note> as they do on the <term>will</term> <note>the faculty by which we choose, affirm, or deny.</note>. Errors are not "things" that require God’s actual assistance to be produced; rather, when they are referred to God, they are merely <term>negations</term> <note>original: "negationes"; a simple absence of a perfection that was never intended for us.</note>, and when referred to us, they are <term>privations</term> <note>original: "privationes"; the lack of a capability or knowledge that we feel we ought to have.</note>.

<margin>

</margin>
Indeed, all the modes of thinking <note>original: "modi cogitandi"</note> that we experience in ourselves can be reduced to two general categories: one is perception, or the operation of the intellect; the other is volition, or the operation of the will. For sensing, imagining, and pure understanding are simply different modes of perceiving; whereas desiring, feeling aversion, affirming, denying, and doubting are different modes of willing.

</margin>

</margin>
And indeed, the perception of the intellect extends only to those few things offered to it, and is always very finite. The will, however, can in a sense be called infinite, because we never notice anything that could be the object of any other will—even that immense will which is in God—to which our own does not also extend. Thus, we easily extend the will beyond those things which we clearly perceive; and when we do this, it is no wonder that it happens that we are deceived.

</margin>
Nor can God in any way be imagined as the author of our errors simply because he did not give us an all-knowing <note>original: "omniscicium"</note> intellect. For it is in the nature of a created intellect to be finite; and it is in the nature of a finite intellect not to extend to all things.

<margin>

</margin>

### PART ONE

<margin>Yet it happens through our will.</margin>
...that we are deceived, because no one exists who wants to be deceived. But it is one thing to want to be deceived, and quite another to want to <term>assent</term> <note>original: "assentiri"; the act of the will in agreeing that a thought or proposition is true</note> to those things in which it happens that error is found. And although in truth there is no one who expressly wants to be deceived, there is hardly anyone who does not often want to assent to things in which error is contained without them knowing it. Indeed, the very desire to attain the truth often causes those who do not know the right way to find it to pass judgment on things they do not <term>perceive</term> <note>original: "percipiunt"; in Cartesian philosophy, this refers to a mental grasp or understanding rather than just sensory seeing</note>, and therefore they fall into error.

<margin>XLIII. We are never deceived when we assent only to those things clearly and distinctly perceived.</margin>
It is certain, however, that we will never admit anything false as true if we only grant our assent to what we perceive clearly and distinctly. It is certain, I say, because since God is not a deceiver, the faculty of perceiving which he gave us cannot lead us toward the false; nor can the faculty of assenting, when it extends itself only to those things which are clearly perceived. And even if this were not proven by any reasoning, it is so impressed upon the minds of all by nature that whenever we perceive something clearly, we <term>spontaneously</term> <note>without external force or hesitation</note> assent to it, and we cannot in any way doubt that it is true.

<margin>XLIV. We always judge badly when we assent to things not clearly perceived, even if by chance we fall upon the truth; and this happens because we assume those things were previously enough understood by us.</margin>
It is also certain that when we assent to some reasoning which we do not perceive, we are either deceived, or only by chance fall upon the truth, and thus we do not know for sure that we are not deceived. But truly it rarely happens that people assent to things which they notice have not been perceived: because the <term>light of nature</term> <note>original: "lumen naturae"; the natural human capacity for reason and intuition provided by God</note> dictates to us that we should never judge except regarding a thing we have come to know. In this, however, we most frequently err: that we think many things were once perceived by us, and having committed them to memory, we assent to them as if they were fully perceived, though in reality we never perceived them.

### OF THE PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

...Indeed, for a <term>perception</term> <note>original: "perceptionem"; in Cartesian philosophy, this refers to a mental grasp or understanding rather than just sensory seeing</note> upon which a certain and indubitable judgment can rely, it is required not only that it be clear, but also that it be distinct. I call that **clear** which is present and open to the mind when it attends to it; just as we say we see things clearly when, being <margin>5</margin> present to the gazing eye, they move it strongly and openly enough. But I call that **distinct** which, while being clear, is so separated and precise from all others that it contains within itself absolutely nothing else but what is clear.

<margin>XLVI.
The example of pain shows that a perception can be clear even if it is not distinct; but never distinct unless it is clear.</margin>
Thus, when someone feels some great pain, that perception of pain is indeed <margin>10</margin> very clear in them, but it is not always distinct; for people commonly confuse it with their own obscure judgment regarding its nature—for they think there is something in the aching part similar to the sensation of pain, which is the only thing they clearly perceive. And so there can be a clear <margin>15</margin> perception which is not distinct; but no perception can be distinct unless it is clear.

<margin>XLVII.
To correct the prejudices of our early years, simple notions must be considered, and what is clear in each must be noted.</margin>
Indeed, in our earliest years, the mind was so immersed in the body that although it perceived many things clearly, it never perceived anything <margin>20</margin> distinctly; and since it nonetheless made judgments about many things at that time, we have drawn from this many <term>prejudices</term> <note>original: "præjudicia"; literally "pre-judgments" or opinions formed before rational examination</note>, which most people never afterward set aside. To enable ourselves to be free from these, I will here briefly list all the **simple notions** from which our thoughts <margin>25</margin> are composed; and I will distinguish what is clear in each, and what is obscure, or in what way we might be deceived.

Whatever falls under our perception, we consider either as **things**, or as certain <term>affections</term> <note>original: "affectiones"; qualities, properties, or modes of things</note> of things; or as **eternal truths**, having no existence outside our thought. # Part One.

<margin>5</margin> ...substance, duration, order, number, and whatever other things of this sort exist, which extend to all categories of things.

However, I do not recognize more than two supreme categories of things: one is of intellectual or <term>thinking</term> things <note>pertaining to the mind or soul</note>, that is, those pertaining to the mind or to <term>thinking substance</term>; the other is of material things, or those which pertain to <margin>10</margin> <term>extended substance</term> <note>physical matter, which Descartes defines by its "extension" or the space it occupies</note>, that is, to the body. <term>Perception</term>, <term>volition</term>, and all modes of both perceiving and willing, are referred to thinking substance; whereas to extended substance belong magnitude (or extension itself in length, breadth, and depth), figure, motion, <margin>15</margin> position, the divisibility of the parts themselves, and such. 

But we also experience certain other things in ourselves, which should not be referred to the mind alone, nor even to the body alone, and which—as will be shown later in its proper place<sup>a</sup>—arise from the close and <margin>20</margin> intimate union of our mind with the body: namely, the appetites of hunger, thirst, and so on; and also, emotions, or <term>passions of the soul</term> <note>original: "pathemata"; mental states caused by the body</note>, which do not consist in thought alone, such as the movement toward anger, joy, sadness, love, and so on; and finally all the senses, such as pain, titillation, light and <margin>25</margin> colors, sounds, smells, tastes, heat, hardness, and other tactile qualities.

<margin>
XLIX.
Eternal truths cannot be numbered in this way, nor is there a need to do so.
</margin>

And all these things we consider as things, or as qualities or modes of things. But when we recognize that it is impossible for something to be made from nothing, then this proposition: <margin>30</margin> *Nothing comes from nothing* <note>original: "Ex nihilo nihil fit"</note>, is considered not as some existing thing, nor even as a mode of a thing, but as a certain **eternal truth**, which has its seat in our mind, and is called a **common notion**, or an **axiom**.

# THE PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

Of this kind are: *It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time; What has been done cannot be undone; He who thinks cannot fail to exist while he is thinking;* <note>original: "Is qui cogitat, non potest non existere dum cogitat"; this is the logical foundation of Descartes' famous "I think, therefore I am."</note> and countless others, all of which cannot easily be listed, but nor can they be ignored when the occasion arises for us to think of them, provided we are not blinded by any prejudices.

<margin>50. That they are clearly perceived, but not by all people, because of prejudices.</margin>
And indeed, regarding these <term>common notions</term> <note>original: "communes notiones"; these are self-evident axioms or logical rules that the mind naturally knows to be true</note>, there is no doubt that they can be perceived clearly and distinctly; otherwise, they would not be called "common notions." Yet, in truth, some of them are not equally worthy of that name among everyone, because they are not equally perceived by all. I do not think this is because one person's capacity for knowledge is more extensive than another's, but perhaps because these common notions conflict with the preconceived opinions of certain men, who consequently cannot easily grasp them; even though others, who are free from such prejudices, perceive them most evidently.

<margin>51. What substance is, and that this name does not apply to God and to creatures in the same sense.</margin>
Now, as for those things which we regard as things or as <term>modes</term> of things <note>qualities or properties, like "roundness" or "motion," which cannot exist without a "thing" to be round or in motion</note>, it is worth considering each one separately. By *substance*, we can understand nothing other than a thing that exists in such a way that it needs no other thing in order to exist. And indeed, only one substance can be understood as needing absolutely no other thing, namely God. We perceive that all other things can only exist with the help of the <term>concurrence of God</term> <note>the idea that God must continuously "concur" or act to sustain the existence of the universe every moment</note>. Therefore, the name "substance" does not apply to God and to them <term>univocally</term> <note>original: "univocè"; meaning the word has exactly the same meaning in both cases</note>, as is commonly said in the <term>Schools</term> <note>referring to the Scholastic tradition of the university theologians and philosophers of the time</note>; that is, no meaning of that name can be distinctly understood that is common to God and to his creatures.

...accurately distinguish. We can also possess a clear and distinct idea of an uncreated and independent thinking substance—that is, God <note>original: "substantiæ cogitantis increatæ & independentis, id eſt Dei"</note>—provided we do not suppose that this idea adequately represents everything that is in God, nor imagine anything else to be in him. Instead, we should attend only to those things that are truly contained in that idea, and which we clearly perceive to belong to the nature of a <term>supremely perfect being</term> <note>original: "entis summè perfecti"; for Descartes, God's perfection is the foundation of all certainty</note>. Certainly, no one can deny that such an idea of God exists within us, unless they believe there is no knowledge of God at all in human minds.

<margin>
55.
How duration, order, and number are also distinctly understood.
</margin>
*Duration, order, and number* are also very distinctly understood by us, provided we do not attach any concept of "substance" to them. Instead, we should think of <term>duration</term> <note>original: "duratio"</note> as merely the <term>mode</term> <note>original: "modus"; a specific way or state in which a thing exists</note> under which we conceive of a thing insofar as it continues to exist. Similarly, we should understand that neither order nor number are anything different from the things that are ordered and numbered, but are merely the modes under which we consider them.

<margin>
56.
What modes, qualities, and attributes are.
</margin>
Indeed, here we understand "modes" to mean exactly the same thing as what we call "attributes" or "qualities" elsewhere. However, when we consider a substance to be affected or changed by them, we call them *modes*; when we consider that the substance can be described or named based on that variation, we call them *qualities*; and finally, when we look more generally at the fact that these things simply exist within the substance, we call them *attributes*. Because of this, we say that in God there are properly no modes or qualities, but only *attributes*, because no <term>variation</term> <note>original: "variatio"; Descartes argues that because God is perfect and eternal, He cannot change his state</note> is to be understood in him. Even in created things, those properties that never exist in a different way—such as existence and duration in a thing that exists and lasts—should not be called qualities or modes, but attributes.

<margin>...in things, others in thought. And what duration and time are.</margin>
...are said to be modes; others, however, exist only in our thought. Thus, when we distinguish <term>time</term> <note>original: "tempus"</note> from <term>duration</term> <note>original: "duratio"</note> taken in a general sense, and we say that time is the "number of motion," <note>Descartes is referencing the classic Aristotelian definition of time as the "measure of motion."</note> it is merely a mode of thinking. Indeed, we certainly do not understand there to be any different duration in motion than there is in things that do not move. This is clear from the fact that if two bodies are moved for an hour—one slowly and the other quickly—we do not count more time in one than in the other, even though there is much more motion in one. But so that we may measure the duration of all things, we compare it with the duration of those greatest and most uniform motions—those which create years and days—and we call this duration "time." Therefore, time adds nothing to duration taken generally, except for a way of thinking.

<margin>58. That number and all universals are only modes of thinking.</margin>
In the same way, when <term>number</term> <note>original: "numerus"</note> is considered not in any created things, but only in the abstract or in general, it is merely a mode of thinking; as are all other things which we call *universals*.

<margin>59. How universals are formed; and what the five common ones are: genus, species, difference, property, and accident.</margin>
These <term>universals</term> <note>original: "universalia"; these are general categories used to classify specific objects</note> are formed solely from the fact that we use one and the same idea to think of all individuals that are similar to each other. We also apply one and the same name to all things represented by that idea, and this name is "universal." For example, when we see two stones and do not attend to their specific nature, but only to the fact that there are two of them, we form the idea of that number which we call <term>two</term> <note>original: "binarium"</note>. When we later see two birds or two trees, and again consider not their nature but only that there are two of them, we repeat the same idea as before, which is therefore universal; and we call this number by the same universal name, "two." In the same way, when...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 27 regarding how the human mind organizes reality into categories. Specifically, it concludes Section 59 on the "five universals" and begins Section 60, which introduces Descartes' famous theory on the different types of distinctions—how we can tell if two things are truly separate or just different ways of looking at the same thing.</meta>

### PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

...we look at a figure enclosed by three lines, we form a certain idea of it which we call the idea of a **triangle**; and we afterwards use this as a **universal** <note>original: "univerſali"; a general category rather than a specific object</note> to represent to our mind all other figures enclosed by three lines. And when we notice that among triangles, some have a right angle and others do not, we form the universal idea of a **right-angled triangle**. When this idea is related to the previous one (as the more general category), it is called a ***species*** <note>original: "ſpecies"; a sub-category</note>. That "rectitude" or rightness of the angle is the **universal difference** <note>original: "differentia univerſalis"</note> by which all right-angled triangles are distinguished from others. Furthermore, the fact that the square of the base is equal to the squares of the sides is a **property** <note>original: "proprietas"</note> belonging to all of them, and to them alone. And finally, if we suppose that some such triangles are moving and others are not moving, this will be a **universal accident** <note>original: "accidens univerſale"</note> in them. In this way, five universals are commonly numbered: ***genus, species, difference, property, and accident.***

<margin>
60.
On distinctions; and first, on the real distinction.
</margin>

Number, moreover, in things themselves, arises from their **distinction**. This distinction is threefold: ***real, modal, and of reason*** <note>original: "realis, modalis, & rationis"; these refer to things that are truly separate, things that are just "modes" or states of a substance, and things that are only separate in our thoughts</note>. A ***real*** distinction properly exists only between two or more **substances**. We perceive that these substances are mutually and really distinct from one another based solely on the fact that we can clearly and distinctly understand one without the other. For, by acknowledging God, we are certain that He can bring about whatever we distinctly understand. Thus, for example, from the mere fact that we now have an idea of an **extended** or **corporeal substance** <note>that is, physical matter</note>—even if we do not yet know for certain that any such thing exists—we are nevertheless certain that it *can* exist. And if it exists, every part of it that is defined by our thought is **really distinct** from the other parts of the same substance.
