# Part One

<meta>23-24. in top left corner</meta>

...that, from the mere fact that each of us understands himself to be a **thinking thing** <term>res cogitans: Descartes’ famous definition of the mind as an entity whose whole essence is to think</term>, and can through thought exclude from himself every other substance—whether thinking or extended—it is certain that each person, viewed in this way, is **really distinct** from every other thinking substance and from every **corporeal substance** <note>original: "substantiâ corporeâ"; physical or bodily matter</note>. And even if we suppose that God has joined some such corporeal substance to a thinking substance so closely that they could not be more
<margin>5</margin>
tightly joined, and thus formed a single whole from the two of them, they nevertheless remain **really distinct**. This is because, no matter how closely He has united them, He could not strip Himself of the power He previously held to separate them, or to preserve one without the
<margin>10</margin>
other; and those things which can be separated by God, or preserved separately, are **really distinct**.
<margin>15</margin>

<margin>61. On modal distinction.</margin>
### 61. On modal distinction.
**Modal distinction** <note>original: "distinctio modalis"; a distinction between a thing and its qualities, or between the qualities themselves</note> is twofold: one is between a **mode** <note>original: "modum"; a specific state, shape, or way of being</note> properly so called and the **substance** of which it is a mode; the other is between two modes of the same substance. The former is recognized by the fact that we can indeed clearly
<margin>20</margin>
perceive a substance without the mode which we say differs from it, but we cannot, conversely, understand that mode without the substance itself. For example, **shape** <note>original: "figura"</note> and **motion** <note>original: "motus"</note> are modally distinct from the corporeal substance in which they exist; likewise, **affirmation** and **recollection** are distinct from the mind. The latter type, however, is recognized from
<margin>25</margin>
the fact that we can indeed recognize one mode without the other, and vice versa; yet we can understand neither of them without the same substance in which they exist. For instance, if a **stone** <note>original: "lapis"</note> is moved and is square, I can indeed understand its square shape
<margin>30</margin>
without the motion, and conversely, its motion without the square shape; but I can understand neither that motion nor that shape without the substance of the stone.

<summary>Descartes explains that the mind and body are "really distinct" because they can be understood and exist independently through God's power, and introduces "modal distinction" to describe the relationship between a substance and its temporary qualities, like shape or thought.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Section 61 from page 29, which explains how we differentiate between things and their qualities. It concludes the definition of "modal distinction" and begins a new section on "conceptual distinction."</meta>

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 24-25.

However, the distinction by which a **mode** <note>original: "modus"; a specific state or quality of a thing</note> of one **substance** <note>original: "substantiæ"; a thing that exists independently</note> differs from another substance, or from a mode of a different substance—such as the motion of one body differs from another body or from the mind, or as motion differs from duration—seems more properly called **real** rather than **modal**. This is because those modes are not clearly understood without the substances of which they are modes, and those substances are already **really distinct** <note>original: "realiter distinctis"; existing as separate entities in reality</note> from one another.

<margin>
62.
*On the distinction*
*of reason.*
</margin>

Finally, a **distinction of reason** <note>original: "distinctio rationis"; also known as a conceptual distinction, where the mind separates things that are inseparable in reality</note> exists between a substance and any one of its **attributes** <note>original: "attributum"; a fundamental quality</note> without which the substance itself cannot be understood, or between two such attributes of a single substance. It is recognized by the fact that we cannot form a clear and distinct idea of that substance if we exclude that attribute from it. Likewise, we cannot clearly perceive the idea of one such attribute if we separate it from another. For example, because any substance ceases to exist if it ceases to endure, it is distinguished from its **duration** <note>original: "duratione"; the length of time something exists</note> only by a distinction of reason. Similarly, all the "modes of thinking" which we consider as being in objects differ only by reason—both from the objects they are about and from one another within a single object. I remember indeed having elsewhere grouped this type of distinction with the **modal** one—specifically, at the end of my response to the First Objections in the *Meditations on First Philosophy*<insert>a</insert>—but at that time, there was no need to discuss them with such precision, and it was sufficient for my purpose to distinguish both of them from the **real** distinction.

<margin>
63.
*How thought and*
*extension can be*
*distinctly known, as*
*constituting the*
*nature of mind and*
*body.*
</margin>

**Thought** and **extension** <note>original: "cogitatio & extensio"; for Descartes, "thought" defines the mind and "extension" (taking up space) defines physical matter</note> can be viewed as constituting the very natures of **thinking substance** and **corporeal substance**. In this case, they must not be conceived as anything other than the substances themselves...

# PART ONE

...thinking and extended substance, that is, than mind and body; in this way they are most clearly and distinctly understood. Indeed, we understand an extended substance, or a thinking substance, more easily than <margin>5</margin> **substance** <note>original: "substantiam"; something that exists on its own</note> alone, omitting the fact that it thinks or is extended. For there is some difficulty in abstracting the notion of substance from the notions of thought or extension, which indeed differ from the substance itself only by a **distinction of reason** <note>original: "ratione tantùm diversæ"; a conceptual distinction made by the mind rather than a physical separation</note>; and <margin>10</margin> a concept does not become more distinct because we include fewer things in it, but only because we accurately distinguish those things which we do include from all others.

<margin>
LXIV.
*How they are also*
*seen as modes of substance.*
</margin>
**Thought** <note>original: "Cogitatio"</note> and **extension** <note>original: "extensio"</note> can also be taken as **modes** <note>original: "modis"; specific ways or states of being</note> of substance, insofar as one and the same mind can have many <margin>15</margin> different thoughts; and one and the same body, while retaining its same quantity, can be extended in many different ways: now, for example, more in length and less in width or depth, and a little later, on the contrary, <margin>20</margin> more in width and less in length. Then they are distinguished from the substance **modally** <note>original: "modaliter"</note>, and can be understood no less clearly and distinctly than the substance itself—provided they are viewed not as substances, or things separated from others, but only as modes of things. <margin>25</margin> For by the fact that we consider them in the substances of which they are modes, we distinguish them from these substances and recognize them for what they truly are. But on the contrary, if we wished to consider them without the substances in which they exist, by that very act we would be <margin>30</margin> looking at them as **self-subsisting things** <note>original: "res subsistentes"</note>, and thus we would confuse the ideas of mode and substance.

<summary>This page explains that we understand mind and body more clearly through their primary attributes (thought and extension) than as abstract "substance." It further clarifies that thought and extension can be considered "modes" of substance when we look at how a specific mind thinks different things or how a body changes its proportions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of Section 64, which explained how thought and extension can be viewed as "modes" or specific states of the mind and body. Here, Descartes expands on how we perceive different types of these modes, such as specific thoughts and physical shapes, and why we often misunderstand our own sensations.</meta>

### PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

<margin>
LXV.
How their modes are also to be known.
</margin>
By the same reasoning, we will best perceive the diverse **modes of thought** <note>original: "cogitationum modos"; specific ways the mind acts or experiences</note>, such as understanding, imagination, memory, and will; as well as the diverse modes of **extension** <note>original: "extensionis"; the quality of taking up physical space</note>, or those pertaining to extension, such as all shapes, the arrangement of parts, and their motions. We do this by viewing them simply as modes of the things in which they exist. As for **motion** <note>original: "motum"</note>, we should think of nothing but change of place, and we should not inquire into the force that triggers it (though I shall attempt to explain that in its proper place<sup>a</sup>).

<margin>
LXVI.
How the senses, emotions, and appetites are clearly known, even if we often judge them wrongly.
</margin>
There remain the senses, **emotions** <note>original: "affectus"; passions or feelings</note>, and **appetites** <note>original: "appetitus"; physical urges like hunger</note>. These can also be clearly perceived if we take great care not to judge anything more about them than what is precisely contained in our perception—that of which we are intimately conscious. But it is very difficult to maintain this, at least regarding the senses. This is because every one of us, from our earliest years, has judged that all the things we felt were actually things existing outside our own minds, and that they were exactly like the **perceptions** <note>original: "perceptionibus"</note> we had of them. So, for example, when seeing a color, we thought we were seeing something located outside of us that was exactly like the idea of color we were then experiencing within ourselves. Because of this habit of making such judgments, we seemed to see it so clearly and distinctly that we held it to be certain and beyond doubt.

<margin>
LXVII.
That we are often deceived in our judgment regarding pain.
</margin>
The same is true for everything else we feel, even for **tickling** <note>original: "titillatione"</note> and **pain** <note>original: "dolore"</note>. For although we do not believe these sensations exist outside of us, we do not usually view them as being solely in the mind or in our perception; instead, we view them as being in the hand, or in the foot, or in some other part of our body...

<margin>LXVIII. How in these matters what we know clearly is to be distinguished from that in which we can be deceived.</margin>
To distinguish what is clear from what is obscure here, we must most carefully observe that pain and color, and other things of this sort, are clearly and distinctly perceived when they are regarded only as **sensations** or **thoughts** <note>original: "sensus, sive cogitationes"</note>. However, when they are judged to be certain things existing outside our mind, there is no way at all to understand what kind of things they are; it is exactly the same as when someone says they see color in some body, or feel pain in some limb, as if they were saying they see or feel something there, but they are completely ignorant of what it is—that is, they do not know what they see or feel. <margin>LXIX. That magnitude, shape, etc., are known in a far different way than colors, pains, etc.</margin>

### PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY, ARTICLES 28-29.

**70.**
*That we can judge sensible things in two ways: one by which we avoid error, and another by which we fall into it.*
</margin>

It is clear, therefore, that in reality it is the same thing when we say we perceive colors in objects as if we were saying we perceive "something" in the objects, the nature of which we are indeed ignorant of, but which produces in us a very manifest and clear sensation called the <note>original: "sensus colorum"</note> sensation of colors. In our way of judging this, however, there is a very great difference. For as long as we only judge that there is "something" in the objects (that is, in the things, whatever they may ultimately be, from which the sensation comes to us), the nature of which we do not know, we are far from being deceived; rather, we avoid error, because by noticing our own ignorance, we are less inclined to judge rashly about the matter. 

But when we think we perceive colors "in" the objects—even though we do not truly know what it is that we call by the name "color," and we cannot understand any similarity between the color we imagine to be in the object and the color we experience in our senses—we fall into error. Because we do not notice this lack of similarity, and because there are many other things—such as <term>magnitude</term> <note>The physical size or extent of an object.</note>, <term>shape</term> <note>original: "figura"</note>, number, and so on—which we clearly perceive are not felt or understood by us any differently than they actually are (or at least can be) in the objects themselves, we easily slip into the mistake of judging that...

# PART ONE
<note>original: "Pars Prima"</note>

...that which we call color in objects is something entirely similar to the color we feel; in this way, we believe we clearly perceive something that we actually do not perceive at all.

<margin>
**71.**
*That the primary cause of our errors comes from the prejudices of our childhood.*
<note>original: "Præcipuam errorum cauſam à præjudiciis infantiæ procedere."</note>
</margin>

At this point, we can recognize the first and most important cause of all our errors. Specifically, in our earliest years, our **mind** was so closely bound to the **body** that it did not have time for any thoughts other than those by which it felt the things affecting the body. It did not yet refer these feelings to anything positioned outside itself; rather, when something harmful to the body occurred, the mind felt **pain**, and when something beneficial occurred, it felt **pleasure**. When the body was affected without great benefit or harm, the mind had various other **sensations** depending on which parts were affected and how—namely, those we call the senses of **tastes, smells, sounds, heat, cold, light, colors**, and similar things. These sensations actually represent nothing that exists outside of our thought. 

At the same time, the mind also perceived **sizes, shapes, movements**, and the like; these were presented to it not merely as sensations, but as actual things, or <term>modes</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "mode" is a specific way a thing exists or behaves—for example, "squareness" is a mode of a shape.</note> of things, existing outside of thought (or at least capable of existing), even if the mind did not yet notice this distinction between the two types of perception. 

And later, when the **machine of the body** <note>Descartes viewed the physical body as a biological machine governed by mechanical laws.</note>—which is constructed by nature so that it can move in various ways by its own power—tossed itself about randomly, it by chance attained something beneficial or fled from something harmful. The mind, adhering to the body, began to notice that the thing it thus attained or fled existed outside itself. To these external things, the mind attributed not only **sizes, shapes, movements**, and similar properties (which it perceived as things or modes of things)...

<summary>Descartes explains that human error stems from childhood, where the mind is so focused on bodily survival that it confuses internal sensations (like color or pain) with the external reality of objects.</summary>

### THE PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 30-31
<note>original: "PRINCIPIORUM PHILOSOPHIÆ"</note>

...[the mind] perceived, but also tastes, smells, and the rest, noticing that the sensation of these was produced within itself by the body. <note>The 1st edition errata notes that "produced" (effici) should be read as "caused" (causari).</note> And referring everything only to the utility of the body in which it was immersed, the mind believed there was more or less "reality" in each object by which it was affected, depending on how strongly it was affected by it. 

From this, it happened that the mind thought there was much more <term>substance</term> <note>In this context, "substance" refers to the underlying "stuff" or reality that makes up an object.</note>, or <term>corporeity</term> <note>The quality of being a physical, three-dimensional body.</note>, in stones or metals than in water or air; this was because it felt more hardness and weight in them. Indeed, it considered air to be absolutely nothing, so long as it experienced no wind, cold, or heat within it. And because no more light shone from the stars than from the tiny flames of lamps, it represented the stars to itself as being no larger than those flames. 

Furthermore, because the mind did not notice the Earth turning in a circle, nor its surface being curved into a globe, it was more inclined to think both that the Earth was immobile and that its surface was flat. Our mind was imbued from early childhood with a thousand other prejudices of this kind. Later, in youth, it did not remember that these had been accepted without sufficient examination; instead, it admitted them as most true and evident, as if they were known through the senses or implanted by nature itself.

<meta>This page continues René Descartes' analysis of the obstacles to clear human perception. 31-32. PART ONE.

...[even though] <term>astronomical reasoning</term> <note>original: "rationes Astronomicae"</note> now clearly shows us that these [stars] are of the greatest size, our long-held prejudices still carry such weight that it remains extremely difficult for us to imagine them as being any different than we first thought.

<margin>
73.
The third cause [of error] is that we grow weary when paying attention to things not present to the senses; thus, we are accustomed to judging them based on preconceived opinions rather than present perception.
</margin>
Furthermore, our mind cannot focus on any matter without a certain degree of effort and fatigue. It finds it most difficult of all to attend to things that are present neither to the senses nor even to the <term>imagination</term> <note>For Descartes, the "imagination" is a specific faculty of the mind that forms mental pictures of physical shapes, as opposed to the "intellect," which understands abstract concepts.</note>. This may be because of its very nature—being joined to a physical body—or because during our earliest years, when we were occupied solely with sensations and mental images, the mind developed a greater habit and ease in thinking about these physical things than about anything else.

Because of this, many people today cannot conceive of any <term>substance</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "substance" refers to something that can exist independently. Here, Descartes is critiquing the idea that only physical "stuff" counts as real substance.</note> unless it can be imagined, or is physical and perceptible to the senses. They do not realize that only things involving extension <note>The quality of taking up space.</note>, motion, and shape are capable of being "imagined," even though many other things are <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia"; things that can be understood by the pure intellect without needing a mental picture, like the concept of "truth" or "thought."</note>. Nor do they believe anything can exist that is not a physical body; or indeed, that any body exists that cannot be sensed. Since we do not actually perceive any object as it truly is through the senses alone (as will be shown clearly later), it follows that most people perceive nothing but confusion throughout their entire lives.

<margin>
74.
The fourth cause is that we link our concepts to words which do not accurately correspond to the things themselves.
</margin>
Finally, because of the use of speech, we tie all our concepts to the words we use to express them, and we commit them to memory only alongside those words. Since we later remember words more easily than the things they represent, we hardly ever possess a concept of anything distinct enough to be separated from the concept of the word itself. The thoughts of almost all people are concerned with words more than with reality—so much so that they frequently give [their assent] to terms they do not even understand...

<summary>Descartes identifies two major sources of intellectual error: the mind's tendency to tire when thinking about non-physical things, and the way language forces us to associate complex ideas with imprecise words.</summary>

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY
32-33.

...[we give our] assent, because we believe that we once understood those things, or that we received them from others who understood them correctly. While all these matters cannot be treated with total accuracy here—since the nature of the human body has not yet been explained, and it has not yet been proved that any physical body even exists—they nonetheless seem capable of being understood well enough to help us distinguish <term>clear and distinct concepts</term> <note>For Descartes, a "clear" perception is one that is present and accessible to the attentive mind, while a "distinct" one is so precise and different from all others that it contains nothing but what is clear.</note> from those that are obscure and confused.

<margin>75. A summary of what must be observed to practice philosophy correctly.</margin>
Therefore, to philosophize in earnest and to investigate the truth of all knowable things, we must first cast aside all <term>prejudices</term> <note>original: "praejudicia." In this context, Descartes refers to "pre-judgments" or opinions accepted in childhood without critical reflection.</note>; that is, we must take great care not to place any faith in opinions we once accepted, unless we first call them back for a new examination and find them to be true. Next, we must pay attention in an orderly way to the <term>notions</term> <note>Mental representations or basic building blocks of thought.</note> we find within ourselves; only those that we perceive clearly and distinctly while paying such attention are to be judged as true. By doing this, we will first notice that we exist, insofar as we are of a <term>thinking nature</term> <note>original: "naturae cogitantis." This is the foundational realization of his philosophy: that the act of thinking proves the existence of the thinker.</note>; and at the same time, we will see both that God exists and that we depend on Him, and that by considering His <term>attributes</term> <note>The essential characteristics of God, such as being all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly truthful.</note>, we can investigate the truth of all other things, since He is their cause. Finally, we will see that, in addition to the notions of God and our own mind, there is also within us knowledge of many propositions of <term>eternal truth</term> <note>original: "aeternae veritatis." These are self-evident logical axioms.</note>—such as "nothing comes from nothing"—and likewise, knowledge of a certain <term>corporeal</term> <note>Physical or bodily.</note> nature that is extended, divisible, and movable; and also, knowledge of certain senses that affect us, such as pain, colors, and tastes, even if we do not yet know the cause of why they affect us in this way. By comparing these things with the more confused thoughts we had before, we will acquire the habit of forming clear and distinct concepts of all knowable things. And in these few [principles]...

<summary>Descartes provides a definitive summary of his philosophical method, which requires discarding all previous prejudices and using the "thinking self" and the existence of God as the foundations for all clear and distinct knowledge. He lists the primary categories of human knowledge: the mind, God, eternal logical truths, and the properties of the physical world.</summary>

<margin>76. Divine authority is to be preferred over our own perception; but where it is not involved, a philosopher should not assent to anything they have not perceived.</margin>
Above all else, however, we must impress upon our memory as a supreme rule that those things revealed to us by God are to be believed as the most certain of all. And although perhaps the <term>light of reason</term> <note>original: "lumen rationis." A common philosophical metaphor referring to the natural human capacity for logic and understanding, gifted by the creator.</note>, however clear and evident it may be, might seem to suggest something else to us, faith must nevertheless be placed in divine authority alone rather than in our own judgment. But in those matters about which <term>divine faith</term> <note>In this context, Descartes refers to truths specifically revealed through scripture or church teaching, rather than natural observation.</note> teaches us nothing, it is least of all fitting for a philosopher to take anything as true which he has never clearly perceived to be true; it is equally unfitting to trust the <term>senses</term>—that is, the unconsidered judgments of one’s childhood—more than mature reason.

<margin>I.
By what reasons the existence of material things may be known with certainty.</margin>
Even though there is no one who is not sufficiently persuaded that material things exist, this fact was nevertheless recently called into doubt by us <note>original: "a" refers to Part I, article 4, pages 5-6 of the original text.</note> and numbered among the prejudices of our <term>early childhood</term> <note>Descartes argues that many of our "certainties" are actually unexamined beliefs we adopted as children before we could reason properly.</note>. But we feel—or rather, driven by our senses, we <term>clearly and distinctly perceive</term> <note>original: "clarè ac diſtinctè percipimus." The various parts of this matter are endowed with various shapes and are moved by various motions; they also cause us to have various sensations of colors, smells, pain, and so on. If God, acting immediately by Himself, presented the idea of this extended matter to our mind, or even if He only caused it to be presented—

...produced by some thing in which there was nothing of extension, nor of figure, nor of motion: no reason could be devised why God should not be considered a <term>deceiver</term> <note>original: "deceptor." ...how they exist in themselves. For in this way, we will easily set aside the <term>prejudices of the senses</term> <note>original: "praejudicia sensuum." IV. The nature of body consists not in weight, hardness, color, or similar qualities, but in extension alone.
</margin>

By doing this, we will perceive that the nature of matter, or of body considered in general, does not consist in its being a hard, heavy, or colored thing, or something that affects the senses in any other way; but only in its being a thing <term>extended</term> <note>original: "extensa." This is a foundational concept in Cartesian physics: "Extension" refers to the property of taking up space in three dimensions.</note> in length, width, and depth<sup>a</sup>. For, as far as **hardness** is concerned, our senses indicate nothing else to us about it except that the parts of hard bodies resist the movement of our hands when they collide with them. If, indeed, whenever our hands moved toward any part, all the bodies existing there were to move away at the same speed at which our hands approached, we would never feel any hardness. Nor can it be understood in any way that bodies which thus moved away would therefore lose the nature of a body; and consequently, that nature does not consist in hardness itself. By the same reasoning, it can be shown that weight, color, and all other such qualities which are sensed in bodily matter can be taken away from it while the matter itself remains intact; from which it follows that its nature depends on none of these things.

<margin>

</margin>

One is that many people believe that most bodies can be so <term>rarefied</term> <note>original: "rarefieri." To become less dense, as when water turns to steam.</note> and condensed that, when rarefied, they have more extension than when condensed; and there are even some thinkers so subtle that they distinguish the "substance" of a body from its "quantity," and quantity itself from "extension." The other reason is that where nothing else...

But regarding <term>rarefaction</term> <note>original: "rarefactio." The process of a substance becoming less dense or expanding to occupy more space.</note> and <term>condensation</term> <note>original: "condensatio." The process of becoming more dense.</note>, anyone who attends to their own thoughts and refuses to admit anything except what they clearly perceive will not think that anything else happens in these processes except a change of shape. Specifically, "rare" bodies are those between whose parts many intervals exist, which are filled by other bodies. They are made denser only because their parts, by moving toward one another, diminish those intervals or remove them entirely. If this last thing should ever happen, the body becomes so dense that it is impossible for it to be made any denser. Yet, even then, it is not any less <term>extended</term> <note>original: "extensum." This refers to the physical dimensions of the matter itself.</note> than when its parts were scattered from each other and embraced a larger space. This is because whatever extension is contained in the pores or intervals left between its parts must not be attributed to the body itself, but to whatever other bodies fill those intervals. We see this when we observe a **sponge** swelling with water or another liquid; we do not think that each of its individual parts is more extended than when the sponge is squeezed and dry, but only that its pores are wider, and therefore it is spread through a larger space.

</margin>

In the older Aristotelian school of thought, "quantity" was seen as a property that could literally grow or shrink. Descartes argues this is a logical error; matter doesn't "grow," it just moves.</note>, rather than explaining it by this example of the sponge. For even if, when air or water are rarefied, we do not see any of their pores becoming larger,

<summary>Descartes explains that "empty space" is a misconception and defines rarefaction and condensation not as a change in the amount of matter, but as a mechanical change in the arrangement of parts, using a sponge as a primary analogy.</summary>

# PART TWO

...be understood without some <term>extended substance</term> <note>original: "substantiâ extensâ." In Cartesian physics, matter is defined solely by its "extension"—the fact that it takes up space.</note> whose quantity it is, though it can be understood without this specific [substance]. In reality, however, it is impossible for even the smallest amount of this quantity or extension to be taken away without the same amount of substance being removed; nor vice versa, for the slightest amount of substance to be removed without the same amount of quantity and extension being taken away.

<margin>IX. That corporeal substance, when distinguished from quantity, is confusedly conceived as if it were incorporeal.</margin>
And although some people might perhaps say otherwise, I do not believe they perceive anything else regarding this matter; rather, when they distinguish <term>substance</term> <note>The underlying "stuff" of a thing.</note> from extension or quantity, they either understand nothing at all by the word "substance," or they have only a confused idea of an <term>incorporeal substance</term> <note>A substance that does not take up space, such as a soul or a mind.</note>, which they falsely attribute to corporeal substance. They then leave the true idea of this corporeal substance to "extension," which they nevertheless call an <term>accident</term> <note>original: "accidens." A philosophical term for a quality or property that is not essential to a thing’s nature.</note>; and thus, they clearly express one thing with their words while comprehending another in their minds.

<margin>X. What space is, or internal place.</margin>
Furthermore, space—or "internal place"—and the corporeal substance contained within it do not differ in reality, but only in the way we usually conceive of them. For indeed, the extension in length, breadth, and depth which constitutes space is exactly the same as that which constitutes a body. The difference lies in this: in a body, we consider extension as something singular and believe it changes whenever the body changes. In space, however, we attribute to it only a <term>generic unity</term> <note>The idea that "the space" remains the same even if the specific objects inside it are swapped out.</note>; so that, even if the body filling the space is changed, the extension of the space is not thought to change, but to remain one and the same, as long as it stays the same size and shape and maintains the same position relative to certain external bodies by which we define that space.

### PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 38-39.

<margin>
XI.
How extension does not differ in reality from corporeal substance.
</margin>

Indeed, we will easily recognize that the very same <term>extension</term> <note>The quality of taking up space in three dimensions.</note> that constitutes the nature of a body also constitutes the nature of space. These two things do not differ from one another any more than the nature of a genus or species differs from the nature of an individual. To see this, we should focus on the idea we have of some body—for example, a stone—and strip away from it everything that we know is not required for it to be a body. 

First, let us reject hardness; for if the stone is melted or ground into the finest dust, it loses its hardness, yet it does not cease to be a body. Let us also reject color, because we have often seen stones so transparent that they possess no color. Let us reject weight, because although fire is extremely light, it is thought to be no less a "body" because of it. Finally, let us reject cold, heat, and all other such qualities, because either they are not considered in the stone at all, or if they change, the stone is not thought to have lost its nature as a body. 

By doing this, we will notice that absolutely nothing remains in our idea of the stone except that it is something <term>extended</term> in length, breadth, and depth. This is the very same thing contained in the idea of space—not only a space full of bodies, but even that which is called a <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "vacuum." A space entirely empty of matter—a concept Descartes ultimately argues is impossible because space itself is a type of matter.</note>.

<margin>
XII.
How extension differs from substance only in the way it is conceived.
</margin>

There is, however, a difference in the way we conceive them. If a stone is removed from the space or place where it is, we think that its extension is also removed, because we regard that extension as something particular and inseparable from the stone itself. But at the same time, we judge that the extension of the *place* where the stone was remains, and that it is the same extension, even if that place is now occupied by wood, or water, or air, or any other body—or even if it is believed to be empty. This is because in that instance, we are considering extension <note>original: "in genere." Meaning extension viewed as a general category rather than a specific object.</note> in a general sense, and it is judged to be the same...

<summary>Descartes argues that the essential nature of matter is simply "extension" (taking up space). By stripping away a stone's non-essential qualities like color and weight, he shows that only three-dimensional space remains, implying that "body" and "space" are conceptually identical.</summary>

### PART TWO.

...whether it be of stone, wood, water, air, or other bodies, or even of the <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "vacui." A space empty of matter. <margin>XIII. What external place is.</margin>
Indeed, the names of "place" or "space" do not signify anything different from the body which is said to be in a place, but only designate its size, shape, and position among other bodies. And certainly, for that position to be determined, we must look to some other bodies which we regard as motionless; and depending on which different bodies we look toward, we can say that the same thing, at the same time, both changes its place and does not change it. For example, when a ship is carried along at sea, someone sitting on the <term>stern</term> <note>The back part of a ship.</note> remains always in one place, if we consider the parts of the ship among which they keep the same position; and yet that same person constantly changes place if the shores are considered, because they are constantly moving away from some and approaching others. Furthermore, if we assume the Earth moves, and that it moves from the West toward the East exactly as much as the ship is moving from the East toward the West in the meantime, we would say again that the one sitting in the stern does not change their place; because, of course, we would then be determining "place" by certain motionless points in the heavens. But if, finally, we consider that no such truly motionless points are to be found in the universe (as will be shown below <note>See Part III, where Descartes discusses the movement of the heavens.</note>), we will conclude that there is no permanent place for any thing, except insofar as it is determined by our thought.

<margin>XVI. That it is a contradiction for a vacuum to exist, or a space in which there is absolutely nothing.</margin>
<margin>5</margin>
It is manifest that a vacuum, taken in the philosophical sense—that is, a space in which there is absolutely no <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantia." In Cartesian philosophy, substance is that which exists independently; here, he argues that if "extension" exists, a "thing" (substance) must exist to be extended.</note>—cannot exist. This is evident from the fact that the extension of space, or of <term>internal place</term> <note>original: "loci interni." For since we correctly conclude <margin>10</margin> that a body is a substance from the sole fact that it is extended in length, breadth, and depth—because it is entirely contradictory for "nothing" to have any extension—we must conclude the same regarding the space which is supposed to be a vacuum: namely, that since there is extension in it, there must also necessarily be substance in it.

<margin>XVII. That a vacuum, in common usage, does not exclude every body.</margin>
<margin>15</margin>
Indeed, in common usage, we do not typically use the word "vacuum" to signify a place or space in which there is absolutely nothing, but only a place in which none of those things are present which we think ought to be there. Thus, because a pitcher is made to hold water, it is called "empty" <note>original: "vacua."</note> when <margin>20</margin> it is full only of air. Likewise, we say there is "nothing" in a fishpond, even if it is full of water, if there are no fish in it. Similarly, a ship is said to be "empty" <note>original: "inane."</note> if it was intended for carrying merchandise but is loaded only with sand to resist the force of the wind. <note>The "sand" refers to ballast used to stabilize a ship without cargo.</note> Finally, a space is called "empty" <note>original: "inane."</note> in which there is nothing <margin>25</margin> perceptible, even though it is full of <term>created matter</term> <note>original: "materiâ creatâ." # PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 42-43.

...it is customary to say that a jar, in which there is nothing but air, is empty; because of this, we might judge that the air contained within it is not a "subsisting thing" <note>original: "rem subsistentem." <margin>
*XVIII. How we should correct our preconceived notions about the vacuum, taken in an absolute sense.*
</margin>
<margin>5</margin>
Almost all of us have fallen into this error since our earliest years. This happened because, failing to notice any necessary connection between a vessel and the body contained within it, we did not think there was anything to prevent—at least by God's power—the body that fills a vessel from being taken away <margin>10</margin> without any other body succeeding it in that place. Now, however, to correct that error, we must consider that while there is indeed no necessary connection between a vessel and this or that *particular* body contained within it, there is a very great and absolutely necessary connection between the concave shape of the vessel and <margin>15</margin> <term>extension</term> <note>original: "extensione." For Descartes, "extension" is the defining characteristic of matter; if you have length, breadth, and depth, you have matter.</note> in a general sense, which must be contained within that cavity. It is no less of a contradiction for us to conceive of a mountain without a valley than it is to understand such a cavity without the extension contained within it, or to understand this extension without a <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantia." Substance is the "stuff" that possesses properties. Descartes argues you cannot have the property of "size" (extension) without the "stuff" that has that size.</note> that is extended. This is because, as has been <margin>20</margin> frequently stated, there can be no extension of "nothing." Consequently, if one were to ask what would happen if God were to remove every body contained within a vessel and permitted no other body to take the place of what was removed, the answer must be that the sides of the vessel <margin>25</margin> would, by that very fact, become contiguous <note>original: "contigua," meaning they would touch each other.</note>. For when nothing lies between two bodies, they must necessarily touch one another; it is a manifest contradiction for them to be apart, or for there to be a distance between them, and yet for that distance to be "nothing." This is because every distance is a "mode" <note>original: "modus." A mode is a specific way or state in which a substance exists, like "roundness" is a mode of a ball.</note> of extension, and therefore cannot exist without an extended substance<sup>a</sup>.

Moreover, even if we imagine that God wished to make it so that some particle of matter could not be divided into other smaller ones, it still should not properly be called "indivisible." For even if He brought it about that it could be divided by no creatures, He certainly could not take away from Himself the power of dividing it: because it is clearly impossible for Him to diminish His own power, as was noted above<sup>b</sup>. Furthermore, because we commonly think there is <term>action</term> <note>original: "actio." To Descartes' contemporaries, "action" implied an active force or effort.</note> in all motion, but in rest the cessation of action, he is more properly said to be at rest than to be moving, because he feels no action in himself.

Descartes uses this specific word to move away from the idea of "action" or "force" and focus on the geometric change of position relative to surrounding objects.</note> of one part of matter, or of one body, from the vicinity of those bodies which immediately touch it and are viewed as being at rest, into the vicinity of others. # THE PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

### 46.–47.

...of matter, I understand all that is moved together at the same time; even though this itself can again consist of many parts, which have other movements within themselves. And I say that it is <term>translation</term> <note>original: "translatio." In 17th-century physics, this refers to the physical displacement or "carrying across" of an object from one place to another.</note>, not the force or action that transfers it, in order to show that motion is always in the <term>moving object</term> <note>original: "mobili." The thing that is actually in motion.</note>, not in the mover—because these two are usually not distinguished with enough accuracy. Motion is merely a <term>mode</term> <note>original: "modus." A philosophical term meaning a "way of being" or a characteristic. Just as "roundness" is a way for a ball to exist, "motion" is a way for matter to exist; it is not a "thing" you can strip away from the matter and hold in your hand.</note> of the object, not a self-subsisting thing, just as shape is a mode of the shaped thing, and rest is a mode of the resting thing.

<margin>XXVI. No more action is required for motion than for rest.</margin>
Indeed, it must be noted that we suffer from a great <term>prejudice</term> <note>Descartes often uses "prejudice" to mean a "pre-judgment" or a mistaken belief we have held since childhood before we learned to reason properly.</note> in this matter, for we think that more action is required for motion than for rest. We have convinced ourselves of this from our earliest years because our bodies are usually moved by our <term>will</term> <note>Descartes is pointing out that because we "feel" the effort in our muscles when we want to move, we assume "motion" equals "effort."</note> (of which we are intimately conscious), but they stay at rest simply because they are stuck to the earth by <term>gravity</term> <note>original: "gravitatem." In Descartes' time, the cause of gravity was still being debated; he views it here as a force we don't "feel" as an active effort, which tricks our senses.</note>, the force of which we do not feel. And because that gravity, and many other causes unnoticed by us, resist the movements we wish to stir in our limbs and cause us to become tired, we think a greater action or greater force is needed to start a motion than to stop it. We are, in effect, taking "action" to mean that <term>effort</term> <note>original: "conatu." A physical striving or pressure.</note> which we use to move our limbs and, by their help, move other bodies. However, we will easily strip away this prejudice if we consider that we need effort not only to move external bodies, but often also to stop their movements when they are not stopped by gravity or some other cause. For example, we do not use any greater action to push a <term>ship</term> <note>original: "navigium." A common thought experiment in early physics, as a boat on water has very little friction compared to a cart on land.</note> that is resting in still water than we do to suddenly stop it when it is moving; or certainly not much more...

XXXI. How countless different motions can exist in the same body.

Even though each individual body has only <margin>10</margin> one motion proper to itself—since it is understood to move away from only one set of bodies that are contiguous to it and at rest—it can nevertheless also participate in countless other motions if it is a part of other bodies that have other motions. For example, if someone walking on a ship <margin>15</margin> carries a watch in their pocket, the wheels of that watch will be moved by only one motion proper to them, but they will also participate in another motion insofar as, being joined to the walking man, they compose one part of matter with him; and in another insofar as they are joined to the ship <margin>20</margin> tossing on the sea; and in another insofar as they are joined to the sea itself; and finally another insofar as they are joined to the Earth itself, if indeed the whole Earth moves. And all these motions will truly be in those wheels; but because so many cannot easily be understood at once, nor can <margin>25</margin> all of them even be recognized, it will suffice to consider in each body only that single motion which is proper to it.

<margin>
XXXII. How even motion strictly speaking, which is unique in each body, can be taken as several motions.
</margin>

And furthermore, that single motion of each body which is proper to it can be considered as if it were several: as, when in the wheels of carriages we distinguish two different motions—namely, one circular motion around their axle, and another <margin>30</margin> straight motion along the length of the road over which they are carried...

<summary>Descartes explains that while a body has only one "proper" motion relative to its immediate neighbors, it simultaneously participates in multiple motions as part of larger moving systems (like a watch in a traveler's pocket). These other parts would bend in any way necessary and change their shapes so that, when joined with the parts that do not change their shape (but only adapt their speed of motion to the proportion of the space to be occupied), they accurately fill all the corners <note>original: "angulos"</note> that those other parts do not occupy. And although we cannot grasp with our thought how this indefinite division <term>indefinite division: Descartes famously distinguished between the "infinite," which applies only to God, and the "indefinite," which applies to things like space and matter where our minds can find no end or limit</term> occurs, we should not therefore doubt that it happens. This is because we clearly perceive that it follows necessarily from the nature of matter, which is most evidently known to us, and we also perceive that it belongs to the category of things that cannot be grasped by our mind, insofar as it is finite <note>original: "utpote finitâ"</note>.

### Part Two.

<margin>
XXXVI.
That God is the primary cause of motion, and that He always preserves the same quantity of motion in the universe.
</margin>

Having thus observed the nature of motion, we must now consider its cause. This cause is twofold: first, the universal and primary cause, which is the general cause of all the motions in the world; and second, the parti<margin>5</margin>cular cause, through which individual parts of matter acquire motions they did not have before. Regarding the general cause, it seems clear to me that it is none other than God Himself. In the beginning, He created matter along with both motion and rest; and now, by His <margin>10</margin>ordinary concurrence <note>original: "concursum ordinarium"; this is a theological concept suggesting that God does not just "start" the world, but actively sustains its existence and laws at every moment</note> alone, He preserves as much motion and rest in the whole of matter as He placed there at the start. For although this motion is nothing more in the moved matter than a mode <note>original: "modus"; in Cartesian philosophy, a "mode" is a state or quality of a substance—like the shape of a piece of wax—rather than the substance itself</note> of that matter, it nevertheless <margin>15</margin>has a certain and fixed quantity. We can easily understand that this quantity can always remain the same in the whole of the universe, even though it changes in individual parts. For example, we should think that when one part of matter moves twice as fast as another, and this second <margin>20</margin>part is twice as large as the first, there is just as much motion in the smaller as in the larger; and however much the motion of one part becomes slower, the motion of some other part of equal size becomes faster by the same amount. We also understand that it is a perfection in God, not only that He is immutable <note>unchanging</note> <margin>25</margin>in Himself, but also that He acts in a way that is as constant and unchanging as possible. Therefore—excepting those changes which either evident experience or divine revelation makes certain, and which we perceive or believe to happen without any change in the Creator—we ought not to suppose any other changes in His works, lest some inconstancy <margin>30</margin>be attributed to Him. From this it follows that it is most consistent with reason to think

<margin>
**XXXVII.**
*The first law of nature: that each thing, as far as it is able, always perseveres in the same state; and thus, what is once moved always continues to move.*
</margin>
And from this same immutability of God <note>original: "immutabilitate Dei"; this refers to the theological idea that God’s nature and will do not change, which Descartes uses as the foundation for the constancy of the laws of physics</note>, we can understand certain rules or laws of nature, which are the secondary and particular causes of the various motions we observe in individual bodies. The first of these laws is that every thing, insofar as it is simple and undivided, remains—as far as it is in itself—always in the same state, and is never changed except by external causes. Thus, if a certain part of matter is square, we easily convince ourselves that it will remain square forever, unless something arrives from elsewhere to change its shape. If it is at rest, we do not believe it will ever begin to move unless it is pushed to do so by some cause. Nor is there any greater reason, if it is already moving, why we should think it would ever stop that motion of its own accord and without being hindered by anything else. And therefore, we must conclude that whatever is moving will, as far as it is able, always move. However, because we live on the Earth, whose composition is such that all motions occurring near it are quickly halted—and often for reasons that are hidden from our senses—we have frequently judged, since our youth, that those motions which were stopped by causes unknown to us were actually ending of their own accord. We are now inclined to believe the same about all things based on what we seem to have experienced in many cases: namely...

<summary>Descartes introduces the First Law of Nature, known today as the principle of inertia, arguing that objects maintain their state of rest or motion unless acted upon by an external force. <margin>
**XXXVIII. On the motion of projectiles.**
</margin>

And indeed, daily experience regarding <term>projectiles</term> <note>objects thrown or launched into the air</note> entirely confirms our rule. For there is no other reason why projectiles continue in motion for some time after being separated from the hand that threw them, except that once they are moved, they continue to move until they are slowed down by encountering other bodies. And it is manifest that they are usually slowed down gradually by the air, or any other fluid bodies in which they move, and therefore their motion cannot last long. For we can experience with our own sense of touch that the air resists the motions of other bodies if we strike it with a fan; the flight of birds also confirms this. And there is no other liquid that does not resist the motions of projectiles even more obviously than the air does.

<margin>

*The third law: that one body, on encountering another stronger than itself, loses none of its motion; but on encountering a less strong one, it loses as much as it transfers to the other.*
</margin>
The third law of nature is this: where a body that is moving meets another, if it has less force for continuing in a straight line than the other has for resisting it, then it is deflected in another direction and, while retaining its motion, loses only its <term>determination</term> <note>original: "determinationem." Descartes distinguishes between the "quantity of motion" (speed x size) and its direction or "determination." An object can change direction without slowing down.</note> of motion; but if it has a greater force, then it moves the other body with it, and loses as much of its own motion as it gives to the other. Thus we experience that any <term>hard bodies</term> <note>original: "dura corpora." And all the particular causes of the changes that happen to bodies are contained in this third law—at least those that are themselves corporeal; for whether, and what kind of, power <term>human or Angelic minds</term> <note>Descartes is carefully separating the laws of physics from the influence of the soul or spiritual beings, which he intends to discuss in a separate work.</note> have to move bodies, we are not now inquiring, but reserve that for the treatise *On Man* <note>See article 2 above, page 41, note c.</note>.

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 58-59.

...however, there is no cause that might remove or diminish motion itself, because motion is not contrary to motion <note>original: "motus motui non eſt contrarius." Descartes argues that while directions can be opposite, "motion" as a quantity of force only opposes "rest," not other motion.</note>; hence it follows that motion should not be diminished for that reason.

<margin>XLII. Proof of the second part.</margin>
This second part is also demonstrated from the **immutability of God’s operation** <note>original: "immutabilitate operationis Dei." A core Cartesian belief that because God is perfect and unchanging, the laws of physics He established must be constant and mathematically predictable.</note>, who continuously preserves the world by the same action through which He created it in the beginning. Since the universe is completely **full of bodies** <note>original: "omnia corporibus ſint plena." This refers to the concept of the "plenum." Descartes believed a vacuum was impossible; therefore, for one body to move, another must move out of its way in a continuous chain.</note>, and yet the motion of each individual body tends in a straight line, it is clear that from the start of creation, God not only moved the diverse parts of the world in different ways, but also brought it about that some parts should strike others and transfer their motion to them. Thus, by preserving the world now through the same action and with the same laws by which He created it, He preserves motion—not as something always fixed in the same pieces of matter, but as something passing from one piece to another as they collide. In this way, the continuous change found in created things is actually an argument for the unchanging nature of God.

<margin>XLIII. In what the force of each body for acting or resisting consists.</margin>
Here we must carefully note what constitutes the force of any body to act upon another, or to resist another’s action. It consists simply in this: that every single thing tends, as far as it is able, to remain in the same state in which it finds itself, according to the law we first established<gloss>a. Article 37 above, p. 62.</gloss> <note>The "first law" mentioned here is the law of inertia: that objects remain in their state of rest or motion unless acted upon.</note>. From this it follows that something joined to another has some force to prevent it from being separated; that which is separate has force to stay separate; that which is at rest has force to persevere in its rest, and consequently to resist everything that could change it; and that which moves has force to persevere in its motion—that is, in motion of the same...

For Descartes, this isn't just "energy" in the modern sense, but a measure of a body's power to persist in its state.</note> ought to be estimated both from the size of the body in which it is, and the surface area by which that body is separated from another; as well as from the speed of the motion, and the nature and opposition of the manner in which different bodies strike one another.

<margin>XLIV. Motion is not contrary to motion, but to rest; and direction in one way is contrary to direction in the opposite way.</margin>
And it must be noted that one motion is in no way contrary to another motion of equal speed; strictly speaking, only a twofold contrariety is found here. One is between **motion and rest**, or even between the **speed and slowness** of motion, insofar as that slowness partakes of the nature of rest. The other is between the **direction** <note>original: "determinationem." Descartes distinguishes between the "quantity" of motion (speed x size) and its "determination" (the specific vector or path it follows).</note> of motion toward some direction, and the collision of a body in that path which is either resting or moving differently; and according to the proportion of the part in which the body meeting the other is moved, this contrariety is greater or lesser.

<margin>XLV. How it can be determined how much the motion of each body is changed because of the collision of other bodies; and this is through the following rules.</margin>
From these points, so that we might be able to determine in what way individual bodies increase or decrease their motions, or turn them into other directions because of the collisions of other bodies: it is only necessary to calculate <note>original: "calculo subducere." To mathematically account for or deduce.</note> how much force there is in each, whether for moving or for resisting motion; and to establish as certain that the one which is stronger always achieves its effect. And this could easily be calculated if only two bodies were to strike each other, and they were **perfectly hard**, and so isolated from all other things that their motions were neither hindered nor helped by any other surrounding bodies; for they would then observe the following rules ᵃ.

-># OF THE PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 59-60.<-

<margin>XLVI.
First Rule.</margin>
First, if those two bodies, say B and C, were exactly equal and moved with equal speed—B from the right toward the left, and C directly against it from the left toward the right—when they met, they would be **reflected** <note>original: "reflecterentur." In this context, it means they bounce back in the opposite direction from which they came.</note> and would afterward continue to move, B toward the right and C toward the left, without losing any of their speed.

<image-desc>Two rectangular blocks shown in perspective, labeled 'C' and 'B'. Block C is on the left with an arrow pointing right; block B is on the right with an arrow pointing left, indicating they are moving toward each other.</image-desc>

<margin>XLVII.
Second Rule.</margin>
Second, if B were even slightly larger than C, with the other conditions being the same as before <note>i.e., they are moving at the same speed toward each other</note>, then only C would be reflected, and both would move toward the left at the same speed.

<margin>XLVIII.
Third Rule.</margin>
Third, if they were equal in size, but B moved slightly faster than C, not only would both continue moving toward the left, but half of the difference in speed by which B exceeded C would be transferred from B to C. That is, if B previously had six degrees of speed and C only four, after their mutual meeting, each would head toward the left with **five degrees of speed**.

<margin>XLIX.
Fourth Rule.</margin>
Fourth, if body C were completely at rest and was slightly larger than B, then no matter what speed B moved with toward C, it would never move C; instead, B would be repelled by it in the opposite direction. This is because a resting body resists high speed more than low speed, in proportion to the difference between one and the other; therefore, there would always be a greater force in C for resisting than in B for impelling <note>This rule is one of Descartes's most controversial and was later proven incorrect by the laws of classical mechanics. Descartes argued that the "force of rest" in a larger object was insurmountable by a smaller moving object, regardless of its speed.</note>.

-># PART TWO.<-

<margin>50. Fifth Rule.</margin>
Fifthly, if the body **C**, which is at rest, were smaller than **B**, then no matter how slowly **B** moved toward **C**, it would move **C** along with it, transferring such a portion of its motion to **C** that both would afterwards move at the same speed. Specifically: if **B** were twice as large as **C**, it would transfer a third of its motion to **C**; this is because that one third-part would move body **C** just as fast as the remaining two parts would move body **B**, which is twice the size. And so, after **B** had struck **C**, it would move 
<margin>10</margin> **one-third more slowly** than it did before. That is, it would require as much time to move through a space of two feet as it previously required to move through three feet. In the same manner, if **B** were three times larger than **C**, it would transfer a fourth part of its motion to it; and so on for the rest ᵃ.

<margin>51. Sixth Rule.</margin>
<margin>15</margin> Sixthly, if the resting body **C** were exactly equal to body **B** moving toward it, it would be partly pushed by **B** and partly repel **B** in the opposite direction. That is: if **B** approached **C** with four degrees of speed, it would communicate one degree to **C**, and with the remaining three degrees, it would be **reflected** <note>original: "reflecteretur." In Descartes's physics, "reflection" occurs when a body's power to proceed is overcome by the resistance of another, causing it to bounce back.</note> toward the 
<margin>20</margin> opposite direction ᵇ.

<margin>52. Seventh Rule.</margin>

If, however, on the contrary, the excess of speed in **B** were less than the excess of size...

<margin>53. The use of these rules is difficult because every body is touched by many others at the same time.</margin>
But because no bodies in the world can be so divided from all others, and none around us are usually perfectly hard, it is much more difficult to perform a calculation to determine how much the motion of any body is changed by the encounter with others. For at the same time, we must take into account all those things which touch it on every side; and these, in this regard, have very different effects depending on whether they are hard or fluid. Therefore, we must now investigate what the difference between these two states consists of.

<margin>54. What hard bodies are, and what fluid bodies are.</margin>

For whatever shape we suppose it to have, it will always be pushed by exactly as many particles of the fluid from one side as from the other; provided that the fluid itself is not carried more toward one direction than toward the others. And we must suppose that the body B is surrounded on all sides by the fluid DF; and if by chance there is not as great a quantity of this fluid in F as in D, it does not matter: because the fluid does not act upon B with its whole mass, but only with those parts of it which touch its surface. Thus far, indeed, we have viewed B as unmoved; now if we suppose it to be impelled toward C by some force arriving from elsewhere, this force (however small) will suffice—not indeed to move it by itself alone, but to join with the particles of the fluid body FD, and to determine them to also push it toward C, and to communicate to it a part of their motion <note>original: "communicandam". This refers to the Cartesian principle that a body in a fluid is already being buffeted by moving particles; a small external force merely "steers" the existing energy of the fluid.</note>.

<margin>LVII. *Demonstration of the same matter.*</margin>
So that this may be more clearly understood, let us first imagine that the hard body B is not yet in the fluid FD, but that the particles of this fluid *aeioa*, arranged in the manner of a ring, move circularly according to the order of the marks *aei*; and others *ouyao* move in the same way according to the order of the marks *ouy*. For in order for any body to be a fluid, its particles must move in many ways, as has already been said <note>See Article LIV, pages 70-71.</note>. Then let the hard body B rest in this fluid FD between *a* and *o*: what will happen? Namely, the particles *aeio* will be hindered by it, so that they cannot pass from *o* toward *a* to complete the circle of their motion; and likewise the particles *ouya* will be hindered from proceeding from *a* toward *o*; and coming from

added some new force, pushing B toward C. This force, however small, when joined with that by which the particles of the fluid coming from *i* toward *o* also push it toward C, will overcome that force by which those coming from *y* toward *a* push it in the opposite direction. And therefore, it will suffice to change their determination, and to ensure that they are carried along according to the order of the letters *ayuo*, insofar as this is required so as not to impede the motion of body B <margin>Article 60 hereafter, page 76.</margin>: because, when two bodies are determined to move toward parts plainly contrary and mutually opposite to one another, that one in which there is greater force must change the determination of the other. And what I say here concerning the particles *aeiouy* must also be understood regarding all the other particles of the fluid FD which strike against B: namely, that each of those which push it toward C is opposed by just as many others pushing it in the opposite direction.

This illustrates his theory that fluids do not inherently resist motion but rather facilitate it through the redirection of their constituent particles.</summary>

<page-num>75</page-num>
# SECOND PART

...and that a very small force, added to them, is sufficient to change their direction; and that, although perhaps none describe such perfect circles as those represented here by *aeio* and *ouya* <note>original: "ouya"; the first edition reads "oiuy"</note>, nevertheless all undoubtedly move in a circular fashion, or in some ways equivalent to this.

<margin>LVIII.
*If any particles of a fluid move more slowly than a hard body existing within it, the fluid in that part does not function as a fluid.*</margin>
Therefore, once the direction of the fluid particles—which were preventing the body B from moving toward C—has been changed, this body B will begin to move entirely. Indeed, it will move with the same speed with which the external force pushes it, provided we assume that in this fluid there are no particles that do not move faster, or at least as fast, as the body itself. For if any particles are moved more slowly, then, insofar as the fluid consists of them, it does not function as a fluid; nor is the smallest force then sufficient to move a hard body existing in this fluid. Instead, a force great enough to overcome the resistance arising from the slowness of those fluid particles is required. And for this reason, we often see that air, water, and other fluids greatly resist bodies that are moved very quickly within them, yet yield to those same bodies without any difficulty when they proceed more slowly.

<margin>LIX.
*A hard body struck by another hard body does not borrow all its motion from it, but partly also from the surrounding fluid.*</margin>
Furthermore, when body B is moved toward C in this way, it must not be thought that it receives its motion solely from the external force pushing it, but for the most part from the particles of the fluid; specifically, in such a way that those particles composing the circles *aeio* and *ayuo* lose as much of their motion as the particles of the hard body B (which are between *o* and *a*) acquire. This is because those particles of the body now become part of the circular motions *aeioa* and *ayuoa*; although, as they proceed further toward C, they are continually joined by new particles of the fluid.

# THE PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY
## 67-68.

<margin>60.
*That a solid body cannot acquire a greater speed from a fluid than it has received from the force that pushed it.*</margin>

It remains only to be explained here why I did not say a little earlier<note>original: "non dixerim"; referring to the author's previous phrasing on page 74</note> that the direction of the particles in the path <term>ayuo</term><note>These letters refer to specific points in the accompanying diagram illustrating fluid flow</note> is changed absolutely, but rather that it is changed only as much as is required to avoid hindering the movement of body B. Indeed, 

<image-desc>A diagram showing a rectangular solid block labeled 'B' submerged within a fluid medium 'FD'. The fluid is depicted as a series of small particles or paths flowing around the block, constrained by a boundary structure.</image-desc>

this body B cannot move more quickly than it has been pushed by an external force, even though all the particles of the fluid FD often possess much more agitation. This is one of those things that we must especially observe while philosophizing: that we do not attribute to any cause an effect that exceeds its power. Thus, if we suppose a hard body B, previously motionless in the middle of fluid FD, is now pushed with a slow motion by some external force—for example, by my hand—since this impulse of my hand is the sole cause of its movement, it should not be believed that the body moves faster than it is pushed. And although all the particles of the fluid move much faster, it must not be thought that they are directed into circular motions <term>aeioa</term> and <term>ayuoa</term> and the like which are faster than this impulse; rather, insofar as they are driven faster, they continue to be carried in any other directions as before.

<margin>61.
*When a fluid body is carried as a whole toward a certain direction, it necessarily carries with it any hard body it contains.*</margin>

And from this it is clearly perceived that a hard body surrounded on all sides by a fluid and resting in it, exists there as if in <term>equilibrium</term><note>A state of physical balance where opposing forces cancel each other out</note>; and however large it may be, it can always be pushed in one direction or another by the smallest force. This is true whether that force comes from elsewhere, or is situated in the fact that the fluid itself, moving all at once, flows toward some other part.

towards which place it is carried, just as rivers are carried toward the sea, and the entire air, when the East Wind <note>original: "Euro"</note> blows, is carried toward the West. When this happens, it is absolutely necessary that a hard body existing in such a fluid be carried along with it; nor does that fourth rule stand in the way, according to which (as was said a little earlier <note>See Article 49, page 68.</note>) a body at rest cannot be impelled to motion by any other body smaller than itself, no matter how swiftly it is driven.

<margin>62.
*When a hard body is thus carried by a fluid, it is not for that reason "moving."*</margin>
Furthermore, if we attend to the true and absolute nature of motion—which consists in the transfer of a moved body from the vicinity of other bodies contiguous to it, and is equal in both of the bodies that touch each other, although it is not usually named in the same way—we will clearly recognize that a hard body is not so properly said to "move" when it is thus carried by the fluid containing it, as it would be if it were not carried by it; for in the former case, it recedes less from the neighboring particles of that fluid.

<margin>63.
*Why certain bodies are so hard that, although small, they are not easily divided by our hands.*</margin>
There is, however, still one point in which experience seems greatly to oppose the rules of motion delivered a little earlier <note>See Articles 46 to 52, pages 68-70.</note>: namely, that we see many bodies, far smaller than our hands, adhering so firmly to one another that they cannot be separated by any force of the hands. For if their parts adhere to each other by no other "glue" than that each part is at rest next to its neighbors <note>See Article 55, page 71.</note>, and every body at rest can be impelled to motion by another larger than itself which is moving, the reason is not apparent at first glance why (for example) an iron nail <note>original: "clavus ferreus"</note>, or any other body—not large, but very hard—cannot be divided into two parts by the sole force of our hands.

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 68-69.

<margin>LXIV.
I admit no other principles in Physics than those in Geometry or abstract Mathematics, nor do I desire any others, because in this way all phenomena of nature are explained, and certain demonstrations can be given regarding them.</margin>For although we may count each middle part of that iron nail <note>original: "clavi"</note> as a single body, and since that middle part is smaller than our hand, it seems it ought to be able to be moved by the hand's force and thus torn away from the other middle part. But it must be noted that our hands are quite soft, or rather, they approach the nature of fluid bodies more than hard ones; and therefore, they do not usually act all at once upon a body to be moved by them, but only that part of them which, touching that body, presses upon it all at once. Indeed, just as the middle part of an iron nail—insofar as it is to be divided from another middle part—has the character of a single body, so the part of our hand touching it most closely (and smaller than the nail itself), insofar as it can be separated from the rest of the parts of the same hand, has the character of another body. And because it can be more easily separated from the rest of the hand than a part of the nail can from the rest of the nail—and since that separation cannot happen without the sensation of pain—we therefore cannot break an iron nail with the hand alone. But if we arm the hand with a hammer, a file, shears, or another tool <note>original: "malleo, limâ, forfice, aliove inſtrumento"</note>, so that its force is applied to the part of the body to be divided (which is smaller than the body being used to divide it), it will be able to overcome any degree of hardness. I shall add nothing here concerning shapes, nor how from their infinite variety, innumerable varieties of motions also follow, because these things will be sufficiently clear of themselves whenever the occasion arises to treat them. And I suppose my readers already know at least the first elements of Geometry, or at least have a mind sufficiently apt for understanding Mathematical demonstrations. For I plainly profess that I recognize no other matter of corporeal things than that which is divisible in every way,

# THE PRINCIPLES
