## PART THREE.
### *On the Visible World.*

<margin>I. That the works of God cannot be thought of as too vast.</margin>
Having now discovered certain principles of material things, which were sought not from the prejudices of the senses but from the light of reason <note>The "light of reason" refers to clear and distinct intellectual perception, a cornerstone of Cartesian philosophy</note> in such a way that we cannot doubt their truth, we must examine whether we can explain all the phenomena of nature from these alone. We must begin with those which are most universal and upon which the rest depend: namely, the general construction of this entire visible world. In order to philosophize correctly about this, two things especially must be observed. First, that by attending to the infinite power and goodness of God, we should not fear imagining His works to be too vast, beautiful, and perfect; but on the contrary, we must take care lest, if we should perhaps suppose some limits in them not certainly known to us, we might seem to perceive the power of the Creator less magnificently than is fitting.

<margin>II. That we must take care lest, thinking too proudly of ourselves, we suppose the ends which God proposed to Himself in creating the world are understood by us.</margin>
The second is that we must also take care lest we think too proudly of ourselves. This would happen not only if we wished to attach some limits to the world that are known to us by no reason nor divine revelation—as if the force of our thought could reach beyond that which has actually been made by God <column-break/>

### V.
<margin>What the ratio of distance and size is between the Sun, the Earth, and the Moon.</margin>
To us, indeed, at first glance, the Earth seems much larger than all other bodies in the world, and the Sun and Moon larger than the other stars; but correcting the defect of sight with indubitable reasoning, we first notice that the distance of the Moon from the Earth equals about thirty Earth diameters, while that of the Sun equals six hundred or seven hundred. Comparing these distances with the apparent diameters of the Sun and Moon, we easily gather from them that the Moon is indeed much smaller than the Earth, but the Sun is much larger.

### VI.
<margin>What the distance of the remaining planets is from the Sun.</margin>
We also recognize, aided by the method of sight <note>likely referring to telescopic observation or geometric parallax</note>, that Mercury is distant from the Sun by more than two hundred Earth diameters; Venus by more than four hundred; Mars by nine hundred or a thousand; Jupiter by three thousand and more; and Saturn by five or six thousand.

### VII.
<margin>The Fixed Stars cannot be supposed to be too remote.</margin>
As for the Fixed Stars <note>term: Fixed Stars; the stars that appear to maintain a constant position relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets</note>, the phenomena indeed do not allow us to think they are no further from the Sun or Earth than Saturn; but nothing prevents us from supposing them to be removed to any immense distance whatsoever. It is gathered from the motions of the heavens to be explained below <note>original: "infrà explicandis"</note>ª, that they are so distant from us that Saturn, compared to them, appears quite nearby.

Therefore, so that we may compare the parts of the visible world among themselves without prejudice, we must be careful not to judge the Moon, or the Earth, or the Sun to exceed the Stars in magnitude.

<margin>IX. The Sun and the Fixed Stars shine with their own light.</margin>
Moreover, the Stars differ among themselves, not only because some are larger than others, but also because some shine with their own light, while others shine only with borrowed light. Regarding the Sun in particular, there can be no doubt that it possesses within itself the light with which it dazzles our eyes; for it cannot borrow such great light from all the Fixed Stars taken together, since they do not send so much light to us, even though they are no further from us than they are from the Sun; and no other body appears more radiant from which it might receive that light. If such a body existed, it would undoubtedly be visible. The same will easily be believed of all the Fixed Stars by those who consider how vivid the rays are that they vibrate, and how far they are removed from us and from the Sun: for if we were as near to any Fixed Star as we are to the Sun, it is credible that it would appear no smaller, nor less lucid, than the Sun itself.

<margin>X. The Moon and other Planets borrow light from the Sun.</margin>
On the contrary, we see that the Moon shines only on that part which it has turned toward the Sun; from which we know that it is destitute of its own light, and only reflects toward our eyes the rays received from the Sun. The same thing is also observed of Venus by the aid of telescopes <term>perspicillorum: early telescopes or "spyglasses"</term>. And the same is not difficult to conclude regarding Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, from the fact that their light is more obtuse or placid than that of the Fixed Stars.

<margin>XI.
That the Earth does not differ from the Planets in respect to light.</margin>
Finally, we experience the same thing regarding the Earth: for it is composed of opaque bodies which, receiving the Sun's rays, reflect them no less strongly than the Moon; indeed, it is even enveloped in clouds, which although much less opaque than most of its other parts, we nevertheless often see—when they are illuminated by the Sun—to be no less white than the Moon. That the Moon, when it is new, is illuminated by the Earth.</margin>
This is also confirmed by the fact that, when the Moon is positioned between the Sun and the Earth, its face which is not illuminated by the Sun shows a certain faint light. We easily gather that this light reaches it from the Earth, which then reflects toward the Moon the rays it has received from the Sun; for this light gradually diminishes as the part of the Earth illuminated by the Sun turns away from it.

<margin>XIII.
That the Sun can be numbered among the Fixed Stars, and the Earth among the Planets.</margin>
And altogether, if we were to look at the Earth from Jupiter, it would appear smaller to us, but perhaps no less bright than Jupiter appears from here; however, from the nearer Planets, it would appear larger; but from the <term>Fixed Stars</term> <note>Stars that appear to maintain a constant position relative to one another, unlike planets.</note>, because of their excessive distance, it would escape all sight. From which it follows that the Earth can be numbered among the Planets, and the Sun among the Fixed Stars.

<margin>XIV.
That the Fixed Stars always retain the same distance from one another, but the Planets do not.</margin>
The Stars also differ among themselves in that those we call Fixed always preserve the same distance from one another and the same order; the others, however, continually change their position among themselves: whence they are called <term>Planets</term> <note>From the Greek 'planētēs', meaning wanderers.</note> or wanderers.

<margin>Appearances can be explained through various hypotheses.</margin>
When someone looks from one ship at others in the distance that are changing their positions relative to one another, he can often doubt to which of them—and whether even to his own—the motion (from which this change of position proceeds) should be attributed. In the same way, the "errors" <note>The term "errors" here refers to the apparent irregularities or "wanderings" of the planets' paths as seen from Earth.</note> of the Planets, as viewed from the Earth, appear such that it cannot be known from the observations alone to which bodies the motion should properly be attributed. And since these motions are greatly unequal and complicated, it is not easy to explain them unless we choose one specific way, from the various ways they can be understood, according to which we suppose them to occur. To this end, three different hypotheses—that is, positions—have been devised by Astronomers, which are considered not as absolute truths, but only as suitable for explaining the phenomena.

<margin>XVI. Ptolemy's hypothesis does not satisfy the appearances.</margin>
The first of these is that of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), whose geocentric model placed Earth at the center of the universe.</note>. Since this is opposed to many phenomena (especially the waxing and waning of light observed in Venus just as in the Moon), it is now commonly rejected by all Philosophers, and therefore I shall pass over it hereᵃ.

<margin>XVII. The hypotheses of Copernicus and Tycho do not differ insofar as they are hypotheses.</margin>
The second is that of Copernicus, and the third that of Tycho Brahe. These two, insofar as they are only hypotheses, satisfy the phenomena in the same way, and there is no great difference between them, except that the Copernican system is somewhat simpler and clearer. Indeed, Tycho would have had no occasion to change it, were it not that he was attempting to explain not merely a hypothesis, but the actual truth of the matter.

<margin>XVIII. Tycho attributes less motion to the Earth in word, but more in reality, than Copernicus.</margin>
Indeed, while Copernicus did not hesitate to attribute motion to the Earth, Tycho wished to correct this, regarding it as physically absurd and contrary to common human sense. However, because he did not sufficiently consider the true nature of motion, he asserted only in word <insert>that the Earth is stationary</insert>...

<note>original: "a. Voir t. V, p. 386." — See volume 5, page 386.</note>

## 75-76

...that the Earth is at rest, and yet in reality he granted it more motion than the other <note>Descartes is referring to Tycho Brahe, who claimed the Earth was stationary but, in Descartes' view, assigned it motion relative to the surrounding celestial matter</note>.

<margin>XIX.
That I deny the motion of the Earth more carefully than Copernicus, and more truly than Tycho.</margin>
Therefore, I—differing from both only in this respect, that I shall take away all motion from the Earth more truly than Tycho, and more carefully than Copernicus—will here propose that hypothesis which seems the simplest of all, and the most suitable both for understanding phenomena and for investigating their natural causes. Yet, I would wish this to be considered only as a hypothesis, and not as the truth of the matter.

<margin>XX.
The fixed stars must be supposed to be as far as possible from Saturn.</margin>
First, because we are not yet certain how far the fixed stars <term>fixed stars: stars that appear to maintain the same position relative to one another, unlike planets</term> are from us, nor can we imagine them so remote that this would conflict with the phenomena. Let us not be content to suppose them to be just above Saturn, as everyone commonly admits, but let us take the liberty of thinking them to be as much higher as we please. For if we wished to compare their height with the distances known to us here on Earth, that height which is already granted to them by everyone would be no less incredible than any greater height; but if we look to the omnipotence of God the Creator, no distance can be thought so great that it would be less credible than any smaller one. And I shall show belowª that a very great space must be placed between them and the sphere of Saturn, in order to conveniently explain the phenomena not only of the Planets, but also of the Comets.

<margin>XXI.
The Sun, like a flame, consists of very mobile matter, but does not therefore move from one place to another.</margin>
Secondly, because the Sun agrees with the Fixed Stars and with flame in that it emits light from itself, let us think that it also agrees with flame in its motion, and with the Fixed Stars in its position. Indeed, nothing here above the earth...

For we see that it is more mobile than flame; for it dissolves other bodies near which it is placed into small particles and moves them along with itself, unless they are very solid and hard. However, its motion occurs only according to its parts, and the whole mass does not usually migrate from one place to another unless it is carried by some other body to which it adheres. By this reasoning, we can also consider that the Sun indeed consists of a very fluid and mobile matter, which sweeps along all the surrounding parts of the heavens with it; but in this respect, it nevertheless imitates the fixed stars, because it does not migrate from one region of the heaven to another.

<margin>XXII. That the Sun differs from flame because it does not require fuel in the same way.</margin>

Nor should the comparison of the Sun with flame seem inconsistent because we see no flame here on Earth that does not continually require fuel <note>original: "alimento," literally nourishment or food</note>; a fact which is not observed regarding the Sun. For according to the laws of nature, a flame—no less than any other body—once it exists, always continues to exist unless it is destroyed by some external cause. But because it consists of matter that is extremely fluid and mobile, here above the earth it is constantly dissipated by the surrounding matter; and therefore it requires fuel, not so that the same flame which already exists may be preserved, but only so that while it is being extinguished, another new flame is always substituted in its place. However, the neighboring parts of the heavens do not destroy the Sun in this way, and therefore it does not require fuel for its restoration in that manner. But nevertheless, it will be shown below <note>a. Article 69.</note> that new matter is always entering into the Sun, and other matter is gliding out of it.

<margin>XXIII. That all the fixed stars are not located in the same sphere, but each one has a vast space around it.</margin>

And here it must be noted that if the Sun does not differ in its position from the fixed stars, then they are not all located on the circumference of a single sphere, as many suppose,

<margin>XXIV.
*That the heavens are fluid.*</margin>
Thirdly, it must be thought that not only the matter of the Sun and the Fixed Stars, but also that of the entire heavens is fluid or liquid. This is now commonly conceded by all astronomers, because they see that the phenomena of the planets can hardly be explained otherwise.

<margin>XXV.
*That the heavens carry along with them all bodies contained within them.*</margin>
But in this, many seem to me to err: for while they attribute fluidity to the heavens, they imagine it as a space that is plainly empty, such that it does not resist the movements of other bodies, but possesses no power to carry them along with it. However, no such vacuum can exist in the nature of things; and it is common to all fluids that they do not resist the movements of other bodies only because they possess movement within themselves. And because this movement is easily directed in all directions, when it is directed toward one particular part, it necessarily carries along with it all other bodies contained within it which are not held back by any external cause, no matter how solid, stationary, or hard they may be; as is manifest from what was said previously <note>referring to Part II, article 61</note>.

<margin>XXVI.
*That the Earth rests in its own heaven, but is nonetheless carried by it.*</margin>
Fourthly, since we see that the Earth is supported by no columns and hung by no ropes, but is surrounded on all sides only by a most fluid heaven, let us indeed think that it is at rest and has no inclination toward movement, since we perceive none. But let us not think that this prevents it from being carried by that heaven, and following its movements without moving itself.

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 79-80.

<margin>XXVII. *The same must be understood regarding all the Planets.*</margin>
...just as a ship, driven by no winds or oars, and held by no anchors, rests in the middle of the sea, even if perhaps a vast mass of water, gliding down in a hidden current, carries the ship along with it.
And just as the other Planets agree with the Earth in this respect—that they are opaque and reflect the rays of the Sun—we shall not without merit judge them to be similar to it in this also: that each one rests in that region of the sky <note>original: "cœli", referring here to the "heavens" or celestial ether</note> in which it is found; and that every variation of position observed in them proceeds only from the fact that all the matter of the heavens which contains them is in motion.

<margin>XXVIII. *That the Earth, properly speaking, does not move, nor do any of the Planets, even though they are transported by the heavens.*</margin>
And here it is necessary to remember what was said above concerning the nature of motion<gloss>a</gloss>: namely, that (if we speak properly and according to the truth of the matter), motion is only the transfer of one body from the vicinity of those bodies which immediately touch it and are regarded as being at rest, into the vicinity of others. But often, according to common usage <note>original: "ex ufu vulgi", referring to everyday speech as opposed to scientific precision</note>, every action by which a body migrates from one place to another is called motion; and in this sense it can be said that the same thing at the same time moves and does not move, depending on how we determine its location. From this it follows that no motion, properly so called, is found in the Earth, nor even in the other Planets: because they are not transferred from the vicinity of the parts of the heavens that immediately touch them, insofar as those parts of the heavens are considered as unmoved. For to achieve this, they would have to be separated from all those parts at once, which does not happen; rather, because the matter of the heavens is fluid, now some of its particles, now others, are removed from the Planet they touch, and that occurs through a motion which must be attributed to those particles alone, and not to the Planet.

<margin>
## XXIX.
No motion should be attributed to the Earth, even if motion is taken improperly according to common usage; but then it is correctly said that the other Planets move.
</margin>
However, if we take motion according to common usage, it must indeed be said that all the other Planets move, as well as the Sun and the Fixed Stars; but the same can only be said of the Earth in a very inconsistent manner. For the common people determine the locations of the Stars by looking at parts of the Earth as if they were immobile; they judge the stars to move only insofar as they withdraw from the locations determined in this way. This is convenient for the practicalities of life, and therefore consistent with reason. Indeed, from our earliest years, we all thought that the Earth was not a globe but flat, and that "up" and "down" were the same everywhere upon it, as were the cardinal points of the world—East, West, South, and North; we therefore used these to designate the locations of all other bodies. But if a Philosopher <note>In this context, "Philosopher" refers to a natural philosopher or scientist, likely Descartes himself or his contemporaries.</note>, noticing that the Earth is a globe contained in a fluid and mobile heaven, while the Sun and the Fixed Stars always maintain the same position relative to one another, should use these stars as if they were immobile to determine the Earth's location, and therefore assert that the Earth itself moves, he would be speaking without reason. For first, according to the philosophical sense <note>original: "juxta philosophicum sensum"; referring to the strict scientific definition of motion as the transfer of a body from the vicinity of those bodies that immediately touch it.</note>, location should not be determined by very remote bodies, such as the Fixed Stars, but by those contiguous to the thing said to be moving. And secondly, according to common usage, there is no reason why he should consider the Fixed Stars to be immobile rather than the Earth, unless he thinks that beyond them there are no other bodies from which they might be separated, and in respect to which they might be said to move while the Earth remains at rest, in that sense in which...

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 81-82.

...states that the Earth is moved in respect to the Fixed Stars <note>original: "Fixarum"</note>. But to think this is foreign to reason: for since our mind is of such a nature that it acknowledges no limits in the world, whoever attends to the immensity of God and the infirmity of our senses will judge it more equitable to suspect that, beyond all those fixed Stars which we see, there are perhaps other bodies, compared to which the Earth might be said to rest, while all those stars together might be said to move, rather than to suspect that no such bodies can exist.

<margin>XXX.
*That all the Planets are carried around the Sun by the heavens.*</margin>
Thus, with every scruple regarding the Earth's motion removed, let us suppose that the entire matter of the heavens in which the Planets are situated revolves continually, in the manner of a certain vortex <note>A "vortex" here refers to a whirlpool-like motion of fluid matter that Descartes believed filled space and carried the planets along.</note> in whose center is the Sun; and that its parts nearer to the Sun move faster than the more remote parts, and that all the Planets (among whose number is the Earth) always remain among the same parts of this celestial matter. From this alone, without any complex machinery, all their phenomena <note>The observable appearances or movements of the stars and planets.</note> are very easily understood. For just as in those places of rivers where the water, twisted back upon itself, forms a vortex, if various bits of straw lie upon that water, we see them carried along with it; and we see some even turn around their own centers, and complete a full circuit more quickly the nearer they are to the center of the vortex; and finally, although they always strive for circular motions, they nevertheless hardly ever describe perfectly complete circles, but wander somewhat in length and breadth: so we can imagine all these same things regarding the Planets without any difficulty, and through this one explanation all their phenomena are accounted for.

# PART THREE.

<margin>XXXVI.
*On motion in longitude.*</margin>
However, their revolutions around the Sun are called motions in longitude. And these also deviate in that they are not everywhere equally distant from the Sun; but in this age, Saturn is further from it in Sagittarius than in Gemini, by about a twentieth part of its distance; Jupiter is further in Libra than in Aries; and thus other Planets have their Aphelia <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> and Perihelia <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note> in different places. After several centuries, however, all these things will be found to have changed; and each individual Planet, as well as the Earth, will intersect the plane in which the Ecliptic now lies in different places, and will deviate a little more or less from it; and their maximum and minimum distances from the Sun will be found in other signs of the zodiac.

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 85-86.

<margin>XXXVIII.
*According to Tycho’s hypothesis, it must be said that the Earth moves around its own center.*</margin>of the same recession, the phases of the Moon, Eclipses, the stations and retrogradations <note>The apparent slowing down or backward movement of planets in the sky</note> that appear in the Planets, the precession of the equinoxes, the variation in the obliquity of the Ecliptic <note>The angle between the Earth's equator and its orbital path</note>, and similar phenomena: for these will be easily understood by those who have learned even the first elements of Astronomy.

But I will say briefly how, according to the Brahean hypothesis <note>The system of Tycho Brahe, where the Sun orbits the Earth while other planets orbit the Sun</note>—which is now commonly accepted by all those who reject the Copernican system—more motion is attributed to the Earth than by this [my own] theory. First, while the Earth remains immobile according to their opinion, it is necessary that the entire heavens, together with the stars, revolve around it every single day. This cannot be understood without simultaneously understanding that a translation <term>translation: the movement of a body from one place to another</term> occurs of all parts of the Earth, from the vicinity of the parts of the heavens they touch into the vicinity of others. Since this translation is reciprocal <note>original: "reciproca"</note>, as was said above, and exactly the same force or action is required for it in the Earth as in the heavens, there is no reason why, because of this, we should attribute motion to the heavens rather than to the Earth.

Indeed, according to what was said previously, motion should be attributed to the Earth alone: because it occurs along its entire surface, but not in the same way along the entire surface of the heavens, but only along the concave part contiguous to the Earth, which is very small compared to the convex [outer] part. Nor does it matter if they say they do not only think the concave surface of the starry heavens is separated from the earth, but also that the convex surface is separated from another heaven surrounding it—namely, from the crystalline or Empyrean heaven <note>In medieval cosmology, the highest, most refined part of the heavens</note>—and that this is the reason why they attribute that motion to the heavens rather than to the earth. For no argument can be held by which

# PART THREE.

It cannot be proven that such a separation occurs between the entire convex surface of the starry heaven and another heaven surrounding it; rather, they imagine this purely by their own whim. And so, according to their own hypothesis, the reason why motion should be attributed to the Earth is certain and evident; whereas the reason why they attribute it to the heaven, and rest to the Earth, is uncertain and fashioned solely from their imagination.

<margin>XXXIX. And also that the Earth is moved around the Sun by an annual motion.</margin>
According to that same hypothesis of Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), a Danish astronomer who proposed a system where the Sun orbits the Earth while the other planets orbit the Sun.</note>, the Sun, revolving around the Earth in an annual motion, carries with it not only Mercury and Venus, but also Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which are further from it than the Earth is. This cannot be understood—especially in a fluid heaven, such as they suppose—unless the entire intervening matter of the heaven is carried along at the same time, and meanwhile the Earth is separated by some force from the parts of that matter contiguous to it, and describes a circle within it. Therefore, this separation again, which involves the whole Earth and requires a specific action upon it, must be called its motion.

<margin>XL. That the translation of the Earth produces no diversity of appearance in the Fixed Stars, on account of their immense distance.</margin>
However, one scruple still remains in my hypothesis: namely, that if the Sun always maintains the same position among the Fixed Stars, it is necessary that the Earth, which is carried around it, approaches and recedes from them by the entire interval of its orbit. Yet this has not been able to be detected from the phenomena <note>The "phenomena" here refers to stellar parallax, the apparent shift of stars which was not measurable with the instruments of the 17th century.</note> thus far. But this is excused by the immense distance which we suppose to exist between us and the Fixed Stars; a distance so great, in fact, that the entire circle described by the Earth around the Sun, if compared to it, must be regarded as a mere point. I admit that this might seem incredible to those not accustomed to considering the great works of God, and to those who view the Earth as the principal part of the universe and the dwelling place of man, for whose sake all other things were made.

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 87-88.

But to astronomers, who all now know that the Earth, when compared to the heavens, is like a point, this should not seem so strange.

<margin>41. This distance of the Fixed Stars is also required for the motions of Comets, which are now known to be in the heavens.</margin>
And furthermore, Comets—which it is now sufficiently established do not exist in our air, as a too-unrefined antiquity <note>Descartes refers here to the Aristotelian view that comets were atmospheric "exhalations" rather than celestial bodies.</note> believed—require that vast space between the sphere of Saturn and the Fixed Stars <note>term: Fixed Stars (Latin: *Stellae Fixae*). The stars that appear to maintain their positions relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note> to complete all their excursions. For their paths are so varied, so immense, and so different from the stability of the Fixed Stars and the regular orbiting of the Planets around the Sun, that without this space, it seems they could be reduced to no laws of nature. Nor should it move us that Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose precise observations proved comets were further away than the Moon.</note> and other astronomers, who diligently investigated their parallaxes <note>term: Parallax. The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points; used to calculate distance.</note>, said only that they were above the Moon, toward the sphere of Venus or Mercury, but not above Saturn itself. For they could have concluded this from their calculations no less correctly than the former. But since they were arguing against the ancients, who numbered Comets among the sublunary meteors <note>term: Sublunary meteors. Phenomena occurring below the Moon, within the Earth's atmosphere.</note>, they were content to show that they were in the heavens; they did not dare to attribute to them the full altitude which they detected by calculation, lest they be believed less easily.

<margin>42. All things that we see here on Earth also pertain to the phenomena, but it is not necessary to look at everything at the beginning.</margin>
Besides these more general matters, many particular things could still be listed here among the phenomena—not only concerning the Sun, Planets, Comets, and Fixed Stars, but especially also concerning the Earth (namely, all those things we see on its surface). For in order to recognize the true nature of this visible world <note>original: "mundi aspectabilis"</note>, it is not enough to find some causes through which those things we see at a distance in the heavens are explained; but from those same causes, all those things we observe close at hand on Earth must also be deduced. And yet

->### PART THREE<-

...there is no need for us to consider all those details in order to determine the causes of more general things; instead, we shall only recognize that these causes have been correctly determined by us later on, when we notice that not only those things we had in view, but also all other things of which we had not previously thought, can be explained by them.

<margin>XLIII. It is scarcely possible that causes from which all phenomena are clearly deduced should be false.</margin>
And certainly, if we use no principles except those most evidently perceived, if we deduce nothing from them except by mathematical <term>consequences</term> <note>logical deductions following the rigor of geometry</note>, and if in the meantime those things which we thus deduce accurately agree with all the phenomena of nature, we would seem to do an injustice to God if we suspected that the causes of things found in this way were false—as if He had created us so imperfectly that we are deceived even when using our reason correctly.

<margin>XLIV. Nevertheless, I wish for those things which I set forth here to be regarded only as hypotheses.</margin>
However, lest we also seem too arrogant if, in philosophizing about such great matters, we should affirm that their genuine truth has been discovered by us, I would prefer to leave this undecided and propose everything I shall write from now on as a hypothesis. Even if this hypothesis were thought to be false, I shall consider my labor well spent if everything deduced from it agrees with experiments; for in this way, we shall derive as much utility for life from it as we would from the knowledge of the truth itself.

<margin>XLV. And that I shall even assume some things here which are known to be false.</margin>
Furthermore, to better explain natural things, I shall trace their causes further back here than I believe they ever actually existed. For there is no doubt that the world was created from the beginning with all its perfection <insert>a</insert> <note>original: "cum omni suâ perfectione"</note>: so that in it the Sun, the Earth, the Moon, and the Stars existed; and also on the Earth there were not only...

And because I believe I have found such principles, I will briefly set them forth here.

<margin>46. What those things are which I assume here to explain all phenomena.</margin> From what has been said before <insert>a</insert> it is already established that there is one and the same matter for all the bodies in the world, divisible into any parts whatever, and already in fact divided into many parts which move in different ways, and have motions that are in some way circular <insert>b</insert>, and always preserve the same quantity of motion in the universe. But how large these parts of matter are, how quickly they move, and what kind of circles they describe, we cannot determine by reason alone.

The falsity of these suppositions does not prevent the things deduced from them from being true.</margin>
These few things seem to me to be sufficient, so that from them—as if from causes—all the effects that appear in this world may arise according to the laws of nature explained above.

->### PART THREE<-

Confusion seems less consistent with the supreme perfection of God, the creator of all things, than proportion or order; it is also less distinctly perceived by us. Furthermore, no proportion or order is simpler or easier to know than that which consists of total equality. Therefore, I suppose here that all particles of matter were initially equal to one another, both in size and in motion. I leave no inequality in the universe except for that which exists in the position of the Fixed Stars <note>original: "Fixarum"; referring to the stars that appear not to move relative to one another, unlike planets</note>, which appears so clearly to anyone looking at the sky at night that it plainly cannot be denied. And it matters very little what is supposed in this way, because it must afterwards be changed according to the laws of nature. Indeed, hardly anything can be supposed from which the same effect could not be deduced (though perhaps with more effort) through those same laws of nature. For since, by their help, matter successively assumes all the forms of which it is capable, if we consider those forms in order, we can finally arrive at that which is the form of this world. Thus, no error from a false supposition need be feared here.

<margin>XLVIII.
How all the particles of celestial matter became spherical.</margin>

Therefore, to begin showing the efficacy of the laws of nature in the proposed hypothesis, it must be considered that those particles into which we suppose all the matter of this world was initially divided could not, in fact, have been spherical at the start, because many small spheres <note>original: "globuli"</note> joined together do not fill a continuous space. However, whatever their shape was at that time, they could not fail to become round over the course of time, since they had various circular motions. For since they were moved with enough force at the beginning to be separated from one another, that same persevering force was undoubtedly great enough...

<margin>XLIX.
*That around these spherical particles there must be another, more subtle matter.*</margin>
However, since spaces empty of all body <note>original: "spatia omni corpore vacua"; Descartes is arguing against the existence of a vacuum</note> can exist nowhere, and since those round particles of matter, when joined together, leave certain very small intervals around themselves, it is necessary that these intervals be filled by certain other most minute fragments of matter. These fragments must have shapes suited to filling those spaces, and they must perpetually change those shapes according to the requirements of the place they occupy. Namely, while the corners of those particles of matter which are becoming round are gradually worn away, that which is scraped off from them is so minute, and acquires such great speed, that by the sole force of its motion it is divided into innumerable fragments; and thus it fills all the corners which other particles of matter cannot enter.

<margin>L.
*That the particles of this more subtle matter are very easily divided.*</margin>
For it must be noted that the smaller these fragments of other particles are, the more easily they can be moved and further crushed into even more minute pieces. This is because the smaller they are ᵃ, the more surface area ᵇ they have in proportion to their bulk; and they encounter other bodies according to their surface, but are divided according to their bulk ᶜ <note>Descartes argues that smaller objects are easier to break because they have more "handle" (surface) relative to the "stuff" (bulk) holding them together</note>.

# PART THREE.

<margin>Book II. *That there are three elements of this visible world.*</margin>

...they acquire agitation: because, while these are carried through straight and open paths, they expel the others through oblique and narrow ones. For the same reason, we see that from a bellows, even if it is closed slowly, the air nevertheless exits very quickly because of the narrowness of the path through which it passes. And it has already been demonstrated above that some portion of matter must be moved very swiftly and be divided into parts that are in fact indefinite <note>Descartes uses "indefinite" to mean potentially infinite or beyond human measurement</note>, so that various circular and unequal motions can occur without rarefaction <note>The thinning or expansion of matter</note> or a vacuum; and no other matter, besides this, is found to be fit for that purpose.

Now, therefore, we have two very different types of matter, which can be called the first two elements of this visible world. The first is that which has such great force of agitation that, upon encountering other bodies, it is divided into fragments of indefinite smallness, and adapts its shapes to fill all the narrow corners of the angles left by those bodies. The second is that which is divided into spherical particles, very minute indeed if they are compared with those bodies which we can perceive with our eyes; but nevertheless of a certain and determined quantity, and divisible into others much smaller. And a little later we shall find a third, consisting of parts that are either more thick, or have shapes less suited to motion. And we shall show that all the bodies of this visible world are composed of these three: namely, the Sun and the fixed Stars from the first, the Heavens from the second, and the Earth with the Planets and Comets from the third. For since the Sun and the fixed Stars emit light from themselves, the Heavens transmit it, and the Earth, Planets, and Comets reflect it: we shall not be wrong to refer this triple difference, which strikes our sight, to the three elements.

<summary>Descartes defines the first two of his three physical elements—one infinitely fluid and one spherical—and assigns them to the celestial bodies based on how they interact with light.</summary>

### LIV. How the Sun and the Fixed Stars were formed.

In the beginning, the matter of the first element <note>The finest, most fluid matter in Descartes' physics</note> gradually increased, because the particles of the second element <note>The spherical particles forming the bulk of the heavens</note> wore each other down more and more by constant motion; and when there was a <margin>20</margin> greater quantity of it in the universe than was necessary to fill those tiny spaces found between the spherical particles of the second element resting upon one another, whatever residue there was, after those spaces were filled, flowed together toward the centers *S, F, f*; <margin>25</margin> and there it composed certain very fluid spherical bodies: namely, the Sun in center *S*, and the Fixed Stars in the other centers. <margin>55.
*What light is.*</margin>
For it is a law of natureª that all bodies moved in a circle strive, as much as is in them, to recede from the centers of their motion. And here I will explain as accurately as I can that force by which the globules of the second element <note>The "second element" consists of small, spherical particles that make up the heavens.</note>, as well as the matter of the first element gathered around the centers S and F, strive to recede from those centers. For it will be shown belowᵇ that light consists in that force alone; and many other things depend upon the knowledge of it.

<margin>56.
*How the "striving" toward motion in inanimate things is to be understood.*</margin>
When I say that the globules of the second element "strive" to recede from the centers around which they turn, it must not be thought that I am attributing any thought to them from which this striving proceeds; rather, it means only that they are so situated and spurred toward motion that they would truly go in that direction if they were not hindered by any other cause.

<margin>57.
*How different strivings toward diverse motions can exist in the same body at the same time.*</margin>
Because many different causes frequently act simultaneously upon the same body, and some hinder the effects of others, we can say—depending on which causes we consider—that the body at the same time tends, or strives to go, toward different directions. For example, a stone A, rotated in a sling EA around the center E, tends indeed from A toward B if all the causes that contribute to determining its motion are considered together, because it is actually carried in that direction. But if we look only at the force of motion that is within it, we shall say that, when it is at

<margin>LIX.
*How great the power of that striving is.*</margin>
I know indeed that the motion of that ant would be very slow at the beginning, and therefore its striving, if referred only to the start of the motion, might not seem able to be great: but truly it is not entirely nonexistent, and while it achieves its effect, it increases, so much so that the motion resulting from it can be quite swift. For, to use yet another example, if EY were a tube <note>original: "canalis"; a channel or pipe</note> in which a small ball A were contained, in the first moment of time in which that tube is driven in a circle around the center E, the ball A will proceed toward Y only with a very slow motion; but in the second moment it will go a little faster: for it will retain its prior force, and besides will acquire a new one from the new striving to recede from the center E: because, as long as the circular motion lasts, so long does that striving last, and is, as it were, renewed at every moment. And experience confirms this: for if

<margin>LX. *That this striving is found in the matter of the heavens.*</margin>
What has been said here regarding a stone in a sling, or a ball rotated in a tube around center E, is easily understood in the same way regarding all the globules of the <term>second element</term> <note>Descartes' term for the subtle, fluid matter that fills the heavens and forms vortices</note>: namely, that each one strives with a sufficiently great force to recede from the center of the vortex in which it revolves. For it is held back on all sides by other surrounding globules, not unlike the stone by the sling. But furthermore, that force is greatly increased in them because the higher ones are pressed by the lower ones, and all together are pressed by the matter of the <term>first element</term> <note>The finest, most fluid matter that forms the sun and stars</note>, which is gathered in the center of each vortex. And first, so that all things may be accurately distinguished, we shall deal here with these globules alone; nor shall we pay more attention to the matter of the first element than if all the spaces occupied by it were empty—that is, as if they were full of matter that in no way aided or hindered the motions of other bodies. For it is manifest from what was said before<a> that there can be no other true idea of empty space.

<margin>...their poles, to touch the parts of other vortices distant from their own poles.</margin>
...their vortices <term>vortices: large, swirling whirlpools of subtle matter that Descartes believed carried the planets around the sun</term> must now be so arranged among themselves that each one is carried in that direction in which the motions of all the other surrounding vortices are least opposed to it. This is because the laws of nature are such<note>original: "leges naturae"; see Part II, article 40, page 65</note> that the motion of any body can be easily deflected by the encounter of another. Therefore, if we suppose the first vortex, whose center is S, to be carried from A through E toward I, another neighboring vortex, whose center is F, must be carried from A through E toward V, provided no other surrounding vortices interfere; for in this way, their motions will best harmonize with one another. In the same manner, a third vortex—whose center is not in the plane SAFE but stands above it, forming a triangle with centers S and F, and which is joined to the two other vortices AEI and AEV at the line AE<note>The original first edition page 106 is filled by a diagram illustrating these points</note>—must be carried from A through E upward. Given this, a fourth vortex, whose center is *f*, cannot be carried from E toward I to match the motion of the first, because it would then oppose the motions of the second and third; nor from E toward V like the second, because the first and third would resist; nor finally upward like the third, because the first and second would resist. And therefore, it remains that it must have one of its poles toward E and the other in the opposite direction toward B, and it must turn around the axis EB, from I toward V.

<margin>66. The motion of these vortices is deflected in some way so that they harmonize with one another.</margin>

<margin>LXVII.
That the poles of two vortices cannot touch one another.</margin>
Indeed, it seems to me that no other way can be devised by which the motions of these various vortices would less oppose one another. For if we suppose the poles of two vortices to touch each other, they will either both be carried in the same direction, and thus merge into a single vortex; or they will move in opposite directions, and thus most greatly conflict with one another. And therefore, although I do not presume so much as to dare to determine the positions and motions of all the vortices of the heavens, I nevertheless think it can be generally affirmed, and has been sufficiently demonstrated here, that the poles of any vortex are not so near to the poles of other vortices—

<margin>LXVIII. *That these vortices are unequal in magnitude.*</margin>
Furthermore, that inexplicable variety which appears in the position of the **Fixed Stars** <note>original: *Fixarum*; stars that appear to remain stationary relative to one another</note> clearly seems to show that those **vortices** <note>original: *vortices*; in Cartesian physics, these are massive whirlpools of celestial matter that carry planets and stars</note> which revolve around them are not equal to one another. Moreover, I judge it to be manifest from their light that no **Fixed Star** can exist except in the center of some such vortex; for it will be evident, partly from what has already been said and partly from what is to be said below, that light can be explained most accurately through such vortices, and by no other means without them. And since we perceive absolutely nothing else in the Fixed Stars by our senses except their light and their apparent position, we have no reason to attribute anything else to them than what we judge is required to explain these two things. But it is no more required for explaining light that vortices of celestial matter revolve around them, than it is for their apparent position that these vortices be unequal in magnitude. Indeed, if they are unequal, it is necessary that the parts of some that are remote from the **poles** <note>the points at the ends of the axis of rotation</note> touch the parts of others that are near the poles; because similar parts of larger and smaller vortices cannot be applied to one another.

<margin>71.
What is the reason for this diversity.</margin>
Furthermore, it is also necessary to consider that the particles of the second element <note>Descartes' term for the "celestial globules" that transmit light and fill the heavens</note> which revolve around the center L, do not only possess the force of receding from that center, but also of persevering in their speed; these two factors are in some way opposed to each other. For while they gyrate in the vortex L, being confined within certain limits by other neighboring vortices—which must be understood to exist above and below the plane of this figure—they cannot wander toward B without moving more slowly between L and B than they do between L and the other neighboring vortices understood to be outside the plane of this figure. Indeed, they move slower in proportion to how much greater the distance LB is. For, since they move in a circular fashion, they cannot spend more time passing between L and those other vortices than between L and B. And therefore, the force they have for receding from the center L does indeed cause them to wander somewhat toward B, because there they encounter the circumpolar parts of vortex S, which yield to them without difficulty; but on the other hand, the force they have for retaining the speed of their motion prevents them from wandering so far as to reach S. This same restriction does not apply to the matter of the first element <note>The finest, most fluid matter that fills the gaps between globules and forms the sun and stars</note>. For although it agrees with the particles of the second element in this—that by gyrating along with them, it attempts to recede from the centers of the vortices in which it is contained—it differs most greatly in this: it has no need to lose any of its speed when it recedes from those centers, because it finds nearly equal paths everywhere for continuing its motions: namely, in the narrow spaces of the angles that are not filled by the globules of the second element. There is no doubt that the same matter flows out from S toward the <term>vortices</term> <note>whirlpools of celestial matter</note> O and C, and even toward many others, though I define neither their position, size, nor number. Nor do I define whether that same matter immediately returns from O and C to K and L, or whether it instead departs toward many other vortices, more remote from the first heaven, before it completes the circle of its motion.

<margin>72. How the matter that composes the Sun moves.</margin>
But we must consider a little more carefully how the matter moves within the space *d e f g*. Specifically, that part of it which comes from A proceeds in a straight line as far as *d*, where, encountering the <term>globules of the second element</term> <note>the spherical particles that make up the bulk of the heavens in Descartes' physics</note>, it pushes them toward B; and in the same way, another part, which comes from B, proceeds straight as far as *f*, where it meets the globules of the second element, which it repels toward A. And immediately, both the part toward *d* and the part toward *f* are reflected in all directions toward the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the great circle or plane of the sun's path</note> *e g*, and it pushes all the surrounding globules of the second element equally; and finally, it escapes toward M and Y through the passages that exist between those globules around the ecliptic *e g*. Furthermore, while this matter of the first element is carried by its own motion in a straight line from A and B toward *d* and *f*, it is also carried circularly by the motion of the entire vortex around the axis A B, so that its individual fragments describe <term>spiral lines</term>, or lines twisted in the manner of a <term>screw</term> <note>original: "cochleæ"</note>; these spirals, after they have reached *d* and *f*, are then reflected from there on both sides toward the ecliptic *e g*. And because the space *d e f g* is larger than the passages through which the matter of the first element enters or exits it, a certain part of that matter always remains there, composing a most fluid body which perpetually rotates around the axis *f d f e*.

These <term>vortices</term> <note>Descartes' theory that celestial bodies are carried by swirling whirlpools of "subtle matter"</note> are situated in such a way that they send that matter into directly opposite parts. Other vortices, touching the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the apparent path of the Sun</note> of the first heaven, do not regard any certain circle of it (which could be taken for an ecliptic) in the same way. Nor do they admit with equal ease the matter departing from S <note>the Sun</note> through all parts of that circle and others neighboring it. However, no inequalities in the **shape of the Sun** can be argued from this, but only in its **position, motion, and quantity**.

For instance, if the force of the matter of the <term>first element</term> <note>the finest, most fluid matter that forms the Sun and stars</note> coming from pole A toward S is greater than that coming from pole B, that matter will indeed proceed further toward B before it can be repelled by the encounter with the other, than this second matter will proceed toward A. But by proceeding further in this way, its force will be diminished; and according to the laws of nature, both will finally repel each other in that place where their forces are found to be clearly equal, and there they will constitute the body of the Sun. Consequently, the Sun will be further removed from pole A than from pole B.

But the <term>globules of the second element</term> <note>spherical particles that make up the atmosphere of the heavens and transmit light</note> will not be pushed with greater force in part *d* of its circumference than in part *f*, and therefore that circumference will be no less round. Likewise, if the matter of the first element should exit more easily from S toward O than toward C (finding, of course, a more free space there), by this very fact the body S will move somewhat closer toward O. By diminishing the intervening space through that approach, it will finally be halted there where the force is equal on both sides. And so, even if we were to look only at the four vortices L, C, K, and O, and merely suppose them to be unequal to one another, it follows from this that the Sun (S) ought to be neither in the middle of the space between O and C, nor in the middle between L and K. <margin>LXXVI.
*On the motion of the first element <note>The "first element" refers to the finest, most fluid matter that fills the gaps between larger particles</note>, while it is situated among the globules of the second element <note>The "second element" consists of the spherical particles that form the heavens and transmit light</note>.*</margin>

It must then be noted that this matter of the first element, as long as it is situated among the globules of the second, indeed possesses a straight motion from the poles AB toward the Sun, and from the Sun toward the ecliptic YM, as well as a circular motion around the poles common to the entire heaven AMBY; but furthermore, it spends the greatest and principal part of its agitation in constantly changing the shapes of its tiny particles, so that it can accurately fill all the small angles through which it passes. From this it happens that its force, being greatly divided, is weaker; and its individual tiny particles follow the motions of the globules of the second element neighboring them, and are always ready to exit from those narrow spaces in which they are forced into such oblique motions, and to proceed in a straight line toward any direction whatsoever. However, that matter which is gathered in the body of the Sun possesses a great deal of force there, because of the consensus of all its parts in the same very rapid motions, and it spends all those forces in propelling the surrounding globules of the second element in every direction.

<margin>82. That the globules of the second element near the Sun are smaller and move faster than those further away, up to a certain distance; beyond that point, they are all equal in size, and move faster the further they are from the Sun.</margin> It remains to be noted, concerning the globules of the second element <note><term>second element: the celestial matter or "ether" that Descartes believed filled space and formed vortices</term></note>, that those closest to the center of any vortex are smaller and move faster than those a little further away. This continues up to a certain limit, beyond which the higher ones move faster than the lower ones, and as far as size is concerned, they are equal. For example, here in the first heaven, we must imagine that the very smallest globules of the second element are near the surface of the Sun *defg*, and those a little further away are gradually larger up to the surface of the spheroid HNQR, beyond which all are equal. Furthermore, those located on this surface HNQR move the slowest of all; so much so that perhaps the globules at H and Q spend thirty years or even more in completing one circuit around the poles A and B. However, the higher ones toward M and Y, as well as the lower ones toward *e* and *g*, move faster, and both the highest and lowest complete their circuits within a few weeks.

For this follows from what we supposed <note>original: "supposuimus"; see Articles 47 and 48, pp. 101 and 103</note>: that in the beginning all were equal in size (as was fitting, since we had no evidence of their inequality), and that the space in which they are driven in a circle, as if in a vortex, is not perfectly round; then...

<margin>85.

But when it once happens that any globule is so much smaller than those above it, that it is surpassed by them in size more than it surpasses them in speed, it must always thereafter remain lower than them. And even if we suppose these globules to have been made by God <note>original: "à Deo factos fuiffe fupponamus"</note> as accurately equal as possible in the beginning, it nevertheless could not happen, with the passage of time, because of the inequality of the spaces which they traverse and the inequality of their movements...

<margin>86. That the globules of the second element are moved in various ways at once, which results in them becoming perfectly spherical.</margin>

And since these globules are thus agitated not in only one manner, but in many different ways at the same time, it is clearly perceived from this that—whatever shape they may have had in the beginning—they must now be perfectly spherical, not like a cylinder or any spheroid that is rounded on only one side.

### PART THREE

For we have imagined that this [first element] was generated from the fact that the particles of the second element—which were not yet spherical, but angular, and filled the entire space in which they were contained—could not move without their angles being worn away. The tiny fragments separated from them by that friction changed their shapes in various ways, according to the requirements of the different spaces they had to occupy, and thus took on the form of the first element. And now, we still consider in the same way that this first element serves to fill all the narrow spaces found around other bodies. From this, it is manifest that each of its tiny fragments was initially no larger than the angles of the particles from which they were carved out; or rather, no larger than the space that three globules, touching one another, leave in their midst. Therefore, some of these fragments could remain entirely undivided, while others, meanwhile, emerging from narrow spaces whose shapes were changing more and more, had to be divided indefinitely.

->[Diagram of three spheres A, B, and C as described in the image description]<--

Let there be, for example, three globules **A**, **B**, and **C**, of which the first two, **A** and **B**, touching each other at **G**, turn only around their own centers. Meanwhile, the third, **C**, touching the first at **E**, rolls over it from **E** toward **I**, until at point **D** it touches the second at point **F**. It is manifest that the matter of the first element <note>The "first element" refers to the extremely fluid, subtle matter that fills the gaps between larger particles in Cartesian physics.</note> contained in the triangular space **FGI**—whether it consists of several fragments <term>ramentis</term> <note>Latin: *ramenta*, meaning scrapings, chips, or filings produced by friction.</note> or only one—can meanwhile remain unmoved. But that matter which is in the space **FIED** must necessarily move, and no fragment of it between points **D** and **F** can be designated so small that it is not larger than the space <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the geometric proof of the infinite divisibility of matter on the following page.</note>

<margin>88.
*Those minute fragments which have the least speed easily transfer what they have to others and adhere to one another.*</margin>
Thus, in the matter of the first element <note>The "first element" in Cartesian physics refers to the finest, most fluid matter that fills all gaps between larger particles</note>, there are certain fragments less divided than the rest and less rapidly agitated. Since these are assumed to have been carved out from the corners of the particles of the second element <note>The "second element" consists of the spherical globules that make up the heavens</note> when they were not yet rounded into spheres and filled all spaces alone, they cannot help but have very angular shapes, unsuited for movement. From this it happens that they easily adhere to one another and transfer a great part of their agitation into those other fragments which are the smallest and most rapidly agitated. This is because, according to the laws of nature<gloss>a</gloss>, larger bodies (all else being equal) more easily transfer the agitation they possess into smaller ones than they receive any new agitation from those others.

<margin>89.
*Such adhering fragments are found especially in that matter of the first element which is carried from the poles toward the centers of the vortices.*</margin>
And indeed, such fragments are chiefly found in that matter of the first element which moves in straight lines from the poles toward the middle of the heavens. For its least-agitated parts are sufficient for that straight motion, but not for the more oblique and varied movements occurring in other places. Therefore, they are usually expelled from those places into the path of that straight motion, and there they gather into tiny masses, whose shape I would like to be carefully considered here.

<margin>90.

### PART THREE

It is easy to determine this, because it does not seem to depend on any other cause than the abundance of matter from which these small masses are composed; but it is sufficient to conceive of them as tiny columns, hollowed out by three grooves twisted in the manner of screws <note>original: "in modum cochlearum," referring to the spiral shape of a snail shell or a mechanical screw</note>, so that by gyrating they can pass through those narrow passages which have the shape of a curvilinear triangle (FGI), and which are always found between three globules of the second element <term>second element: the medium-sized, spherical particles that make up the heavens and transmit light</term> touching one another. Indeed, from the fact that they are oblong and pass with very rapid motion between these globules of the second element—while in the meantime those globules are rotated by another motion around the poles of the heaven—it is clearly understood that the grooves of <unclear>those particles</unclear> must be twisted in the manner of screws; and indeed more or less twisted, according as they pass through parts more remote from or nearer to the axis of the vortex: because the globules of the second element rotate more quickly in the former than in the latter, as was said before ᵃ.

<margin>91.
*That these particles coming from opposite poles are twisted in contrary ways.*</margin>
And also from the fact that they come toward the middle of the heaven from opposite directions—namely, some from the South and others from the North—while meanwhile the entire vortex <term>vortex: a massive whirlpool of celestial matter carrying planets and stars</term> moves around its own axis in one and the same direction: it is manifest that those which come from the South pole ought not to be twisted in the same direction as those which come from the North pole, but plainly in the opposite way. I consider this very worthy of notice, because the forces of the magnet <note>original: "vires magnetis"</note>, to be explained below ᵇ, chiefly depend on this.

<margin>92.
*That there are only three grooves in them.*</margin>

Namely, if the less agitated matter occupying angle G extends toward D beyond the line FI, it will be pushed out from there by sphere C, and will be diminished to that extent when this sphere C approaches B.

<margin>93.
That among the striated particles and the very smallest ones, there are various sizes of others in the first element.</margin>

<margin>94.
How sunspots are generated from these on the surface of the Sun or the stars.</margin>

But when this matter of the first element reaches the body of the Sun or another star, all its most agitated tiny parts—since they are not hindered by any obstacles from the globules of the second element—strive to harmonize into similar motions. From this it happens that those striated particles, as well as many other slightly smaller ones which (on account of their overly angular shapes or excessive mass) shy away from such great agitation, are separated from the other smallest particles. Easily adhering to one another because of the inequality of their shapes, they sometimes compose very large masses. These masses, being contiguous to the innermost surface of the heavens, are joined to the star from which they emerged; there, they resist that action in which we said above that the force of light consists. <note>original: "vim luminis"; Descartes defines light as a pressure or "action" transmitted through the celestial matter.</note>

<margin>96.
How these spots are dissolved, and new ones generated.</margin>

When, however, these spots <note>original: "maculæ"; Descartes uses this term for what we now call sunspots</note> are dissolved, they do not break away into tiny pieces exactly like those from which they had been composed. Instead, they break partly into thinner pieces that are simultaneously more solid, or possess less angular shapes; for this reason, they are better suited for movement, and thus easily tend toward other vortices <note>Descartes' theory that the universe is composed of massive swirling whirlpools of matter</note> through the passages that exist between the globules of the surrounding heaven. Partly, they break into the thinnest pieces, which are scraped off from the corners of others and are either converted into the purest substance of the Sun or also depart toward the heaven. Finally, they break partly into thicker pieces which, being composed of several striated <note>grooved or channeled</note> or other particles joined together, are expelled toward the heaven. There, since they are too large to pass through those narrow openings which the globules of the second element <note>the medium-sized particles that make up the sky and transmit light</note> leave around themselves, they even enter into the very spaces occupied by those globules; and because they have very irregular and branched shapes, they cannot be moved as easily as those globules.

Yet this ether cannot grow infinitely, even if new particles from the dissolution of spots are always added to it, because the continuous agitation of the globules of the second element through and around it can easily dissolve just as many others, and convert them back into the matter of the first element <note>the finest, most fluid matter that forms the Sun and stars</note>. <margin>101.
That the production and dissolution of spots depend on very uncertain causes.</margin>
But truly, the production or dissolution of spots depends on such minute and uncertain causes that it is not at all surprising if at times none appear on the Sun at all, or if, on the contrary, they are sometimes so numerous that they obscure its entire light. For from the fact that a few shavings <note>original: "ramentis"; the tiny, scrap-like particles of the first element</note> of the first element adhere to one another, the beginning of a single spot is formed; to this, many others are easily joined afterward, which could not adhere to one another unless they lost part of their agitation by striking against those first particles.

<margin>102.
How the same spot can cover an entire star.</margin>
And it should be noted that these spots, when they are first generated, are very soft and thin bodies, and therefore they easily break the momentum of the shavings of the first element that strike against them and join those shavings to themselves. Gradually, however, their inner surface—by the continuous motion of the solar substance to which it is contiguous—is not only worn down and polished, but also condensed and hardened, while meanwhile their other surface, which faces the heavens, remains soft and thin. Therefore, they are not easily dissolved by the fact that the matter of the Sun licks <note>original: "lambat"; a vivid description of the solar fluid brushing against the underside of the spot</note> their inner surface, unless it also flows around and climbs over their edges; but on the contrary, they rather continue to increase as long as those edges, projecting above the surface of the Sun, are not thickened by the encounter with its matter. From this, it can happen that sometimes one and the same spot may extend itself over the entire surface of a star.

<margin>103. Why the Sun has sometimes appeared dimmer; and why the apparent sizes of certain stars change.</margin>
Thus, certain historians report<note>original: "quidam historici"</note> that the Sun has sometimes appeared paler than usual—like the Moon—for several consecutive days, or even for an entire year, providing a dismal light without rays. It can also be noted that many stars now appear smaller or larger than they were formerly described by astronomers. There seems to be no other reason for this than that their light is dulled by a greater or fewer number of spots <note>Descartes uses the term "maculae" (spots) to describe what we now call sunspots or stellar crusts.</note>.

<margin>104. Why some fixed stars disappear, or suddenly appear unexpectedly.</margin>
Furthermore, it is possible for a star <note>term: "fidus" (star/heavenly body)</note> to be enveloped in so many dense spots that it completely escapes our sight: thus, seven Pleiades were once counted, where now only six are seen. Likewise, it is possible for a star previously unseen by us to shine forth with great light very suddenly and in a very short time. Specifically, if its entire body had been covered until then by a vast and thick spot, and it now happens that the matter of the first element <note>term: "materia primi elementi" (the finest, most fluid celestial matter in Descartes' physics)</note>, flowing toward it more abundantly than usual, spreads itself over the outer surface of that spot, it will cover the whole thing in a very short time; and then that star will emit no less light from itself | than if it were involved in no spots at all. Afterward, it can either remain equally bright for a long time or gradually become obscured again. This is what happened at the end of the year 1572, when a certain star, not previously seen, appeared in the constellation of Cassiopeia; it had the greatest light at the beginning, and having been gradually obscured afterward, it disappeared at the beginning of the year 1574. And some others now shine in the sky which formerly did not appear: the cause of these things must be explained more fully here.

<margin>106. What the arrangement of these channels is, and why the striated particles cannot go backward through them.</margin>
Namely, the <term>striated particles</term> <note>Descartes' term for channeled, screw-like particles of the "first element" or subtle matter</note> of the first element, coming not from one single point only, but from the entire region of the heavens which is toward pole A, and tending not toward a single point I, but toward the entire middle of the heavens HIQ, form for themselves channels in the spot *defg*, along straight lines parallel to the axis *fd*, or slightly converging from both sides toward *d*. The entrances of these channels are scattered across the entire half-surface *efg*, and the exits are in the other half *edg*: specifically so that the striated particles, coming from part A, can easily enter them through part *efg* and exit through the opposite part *edg*, but can never return through *edg*, nor exit through *efg*. Because, since this entire spot consists of nothing but the smallest shavings of the first element, which, adhering to one another, compose certain branch-like structures, the striated particles coming from part *f* must have bent the extremities of these branches—which they encountered in those channels—toward *d*; and therefore, if they had to return through the same channels from *d* toward *f*, those extremities of the branches, rising up slightly, would impede their passage. And in the same way, the striated particles coming from part B have hollowed out other channels for themselves, the entrances of which are scattered across the entire surface *edg*, and the exits in the opposite surface *efg*.

<margin>107. Why even those particles coming from one pole do not pass through the same channels as those coming from the other.</margin>
And it must be noted that these channels are also hollowed out like <term>screws</term> <note>original: "cochlearum inftar," referring to the spiral threading of a snail shell or a screw</note>, according to the shape of the striated particles which they admit; and therefore those channels which are open to some are not open to others coming from the opposite pole and twisted in the opposite way.

<margin>114.
*That the same star can appear and disappear by turns.*</margin>
But it can easily happen that the same fixed star may appear and disappear by turns, and in each instance in which it disappears, it is enveloped in a new vortex of spots. For such an alternation is very familiar to nature in bodies that are moved: namely, so that when they are driven by some cause toward a certain limit, they do not stop there, but proceed further until they are driven back toward it again by another cause. Thus, while a weight hanging from a rope descends by the force of gravity from one side toward its perpendicular line, it acquires momentum by which it is carried beyond that perpendicular to the opposite side, until gravity—having overcome that momentum—moves it back toward the perpendicular again, and from there a new momentum arises in it. Thus, when a vessel is once moved, the liquid contained in it goes back and forth many times before it is reduced to rest. And so, since all the vortices of the heavens exist in a certain equilibrium, when the matter of one has once receded from that equilibrium, it can run out many times, now in one direction, now in the opposite, before it rests from that motion.

<margin>115.
*That sometimes an entire vortex, in whose center is a star, can be destroyed.*</margin>

<margin>CXVI.
How a vortex can be destroyed before many spots are gathered around its star.</margin>
And from this it is clear that there is indeed no danger of any <term>vortex</term> being destroyed by its neighbors as long as the <term>star</term> it has in its center is enveloped by no <term>spots</term>; but, when it is covered and overwhelmed by them, it depends only on the position which that <term>vortex</term> holds among the others whether it is absorbed by them sooner or later.
