<margin>CXIX.
How a fixed star is changed into a Comet or into a Planet.</margin>

<note>The diagram illustrates Descartes' theory of "vortices," where space is filled with a fluid matter swirling around stars. Here, multiple smaller vortices (A through T) press against one another, showing the boundaries where one star's influence ends and another's begins.</note>

Now, however, we must consider the manner in which such an opaque and hard globe—composed of a mass of many sunspots <note>original: "macularum"; Descartes believed sunspots were a crust of dark, dense matter that could eventually cover a star entirely</note>—must move as soon as it has been carried away by some neighboring vortex. Specifically, it revolves with the matter by which it is swept along in such a way that, as long as it has less agitation than that matter, it is pushed toward the center around which it revolves. And because all parts of the same vortex do not move with the same speed, nor are they of the same size—but from the circumference down to a certain limit their motion gradually becomes slower, and then from that limit down to the center it gradually becomes faster, and the parts themselves are smaller, as was said above<gloss>See Articles 83, 84, and 85, pages 137, 138, and 140</gloss>—if the globe descending into that vortex is so solid that, before it reaches the limit where the parts of the vortex move most slowly of all, it acquires an agitation equal to the agitation of those parts among which it is situated, it does not descend further. Instead, it passes from that vortex into others, and is a **Comet**. If, however, it has less solidity, and therefore descends below that limit, it thereafter remains always at a certain distance from the star <note>original: "sidere"; here referring to the central sun of that vortex</note> which occupies the center of that vortex, rotating around it; and it is a **Planet**<gloss>See volume 4, pages 461-463</gloss>.

<margin>CXXI. What we understand by the solidity of bodies, and what by their agitation.</margin>
By solidity here I understand the quantity of the matter of the third element <note>In Cartesian physics, the "third element" comprises the large, opaque particles that form planets and sunspots.</note> from which the spots enveloping this star are composed, compared with its bulk and surface area. Indeed, the force by which the matter of the vortex AEIO carries it circularly around the center S must be estimated from the size of the surface according to which the matter meets it; for the larger that surface is, the more matter acts upon it. However, the force by which that same matter drives it toward the same center S must be estimated from the size of the space which is occupied by it. For although all that matter which is in the vortex AEIO strives to recede from S, nevertheless not all of it acts upon the star N, but only that part of it which actually recedes from there when the star approaches; and this part is equal to the space that was occupied by the star. Finally, the force which the same star N acquires from its own motion to persevere in that same motion—which I call its agitation—must not be estimated from its surface,

CXXVIII.
The phenomena of Comets.
</margin>
In the first place, it is observed that they—without any rule known to us—pass through one region of the sky or another, and depart from our sight within a few months or days. They never traverse more than, or certainly not much more than, half the sky, and often much less. Indeed, when they first begin to appear, they usually seem quite large and do not increase greatly afterwards, unless they traverse a very large part of the sky; but when they disappear, they always gradually diminish. At the beginning, or at least near the start of their motion, they seem to move very quickly, but toward the end, they move very slowly. And I remember reading about only one that traveled through about half the sky: namely, the one said to have appeared in the year 1472. How the light of the fixed stars reaches as far as the Earth.

*Whether the Fixed Stars are seen in their true locations: and what the Firmament is.*

Since these locations are not found to have changed since they were first recorded by **Astronomers**, I believe that nothing other than these surfaces should be understood by the name **Firmament** <note>Descartes redefines the "Firmament" not as the whole sky, but specifically as the boundary shell of our solar vortex.</note>.

...the reason why extinguished coals appear black is nothing other than that their entire surface, both internal and external, is covered by those softer particles of the **third element** <term>third element; in Descartes' physics, the densest and largest particles of matter that form the planets and everyday solid objects</term>. <margin>5</margin> When these softer particles are separated from the rest by the force of fire, the coals, which were black, are changed into ashes; these are formed only from hard and solid particles and are therefore white. <margin>134. Concerning a certain refraction on which this tail depends.</margin>
In order that the reasons for all these things may be understood, a new kind of refraction <term>refraction; the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another</term>, which was not discussed in my *Dioptrics* <note>original: *Dioptricâ*; Descartes' 1637 work on optics</note>, because it is not observed in terrestrial bodies, must be considered here. In the same way, if globe F is pushed toward G, when its action reaches H, it is communicated there to globules 7, 8, and 9; these send the primary ray toward G, but also scatter others toward D and B. 

Here, a distinction must be noted which arises from the angle (or obliquity) of incidence of these actions upon the circle CH. Because the action from A to C strikes that circle perpendicularly, it scatters its rays equally on both sides toward D and E. However, the action from F to H, which strikes the same circle at an angle, only scatters its rays toward the center—at least if the angle of incidence is assumed to be 90 degrees <note>Descartes is calculating the angle relative to the tangent of the circle</note>. If the angle is assumed to be smaller, some rays of that action will indeed be sent in the other direction, but they will be much weaker than the others and thus barely noticeable, unless the angle is very small. Conversely, the rays scattered at an angle toward the center of the circle are stronger as that angle is greater.

# PART THREE

<margin>179. On the side directly turned away from the Sun, [the tail] may not always appear straight.</margin>
...in a straight line which passes through the centers of the **Comet** and the **Sun**, sometimes deflecting from it a little; and finally, sometimes wider, sometimes narrower, or even brighter, namely when the lateral rays converge toward the eye. For all these things follow from the irregularity of the spheroid **DEFGH** <note>Descartes uses this term to describe the boundary of the solar system's vortex, which he believes is shaped like an uneven sphere</note>: indeed, toward the poles, where its shape is more compressed, it ought to show the tails of **Comets** as straighter and broader; in the bend that is between the poles and the ecliptic, more curved, and deflecting from the side opposite the **Sun**; and according to the length of that bend, more bright and narrow. Nor do I think anything has been observed concerning **Comets** so far—at least what is not to be considered either a fable or a miracle—the cause of which is not found here.

### CXXXIX. Why such hair-like tails do not appear around the Fixed Stars or the Planets.
<margin>139. Why such hair-like tails do not appear around the Fixed Stars or the Planets.</margin>
It can only be asked why such "hair" <note>original: *comæ*; used here to mean the hazy atmosphere or trailing tail of a celestial body</note> does not also appear around the **fixed stars**, and around the higher planets **Jupiter** and **Saturn**. But the response is easy. First, because they are not usually seen in **Comets** when their apparent diameter is no larger than that of the **fixed stars**, because then those secondary rays do not have enough power to stimulate the eyes. And then, regarding the **fixed stars**, because since they do not borrow light from the **Sun** but emit it from themselves, this "hair" of theirs, if any existed, would have to be scattered in all directions on every side, and be very short; and indeed, such a coma already seems to exist around them. For they do not appear circumscribed by a uniform line, but appear surrounded on all sides by wandering rays; and perhaps we may not wrongly attribute even their **twinkling** <note>original: *scintillationem*</note> (though there can be several other causes for it) to this. As for **Jupiter** and **Saturn**, I do not doubt that, when the air is very pure, short tails also sometimes [appear] on the side [turned away] from the Sun...

### CXL. On the principle of the motion of a Planet.
Now, however, having explained everything pertaining to **Comets**, let us return to the **Planets**. Let us suppose that star **N** <gloss>a. See the figure on page 183 above.</gloss> is capable of less agitation—or possesses less **solidity** <term>solidity: In Descartes' physics, this is a body's capacity to maintain its movement and resist being diverted by the surrounding fluid matter</term>—than the **globules of the second element** <note>Descartes describes the universe as filled with tiny spheres of "celestial matter" that transmit light and form the substance of space</note> that are found toward the circumference of our heaven, yet possesses somewhat more than those which are near the **Sun**. CXLIV.
The fourth.

Fourthly, some motions could have already existed in that Planet from an earlier time, which persist in it for a very long duration, even if other causes oppose them. For just as we see a spinning top<sup>a</sup> <note>original: *turbine*; Descartes uses the analogy of a child's toy—a whipping top—to explain how an object keeps moving once set in motion</note>, from the mere fact that it is spun once by a child, acquires enough force to persist in its motion for several minutes of an hour, and meanwhile completes several thousand rotations, even though it is small in size, and both the surrounding air and the earth on which it stands oppose its motion: so it can easily be believed that, from the mere fact that a Planet was moved when it was first created, it could have continued its circuits from the very origin of the world up to this time without any notable decrease in speed. This is because the span of five or six thousand years <note>Descartes refers to the traditional biblical chronology of the Earth's age common in the 17th century</note> during which the world has stood is much shorter, if compared with the magnitude of a Planet, than the duration of one minute of an hour compared with the mass of a tiny spinning top.

<margin>
CXLV.
The fifth.
</margin>
Fifthly and finally, the force of thus persevering in its motion is much firmer and more constant in a Planet than in the celestial matter <note>original: *materia cœlestis*; the fluid of "globules" or the second element that Descartes believed filled all of space</note> surrounding it; and it is also firmer in a large Planet than in a smaller one. This is because that force in the celestial matter depends on its globules acting in unison <note>original: *conspirent*; literally "breathing together" or moving in the same direction</note> in the same motion; and since they are separate from one another, it can happen from small causes that sometimes more, and sometimes fewer, act together in this way. From this it follows that a Planet is never moved as quickly as the celestial globules surrounding it: for even if it matches that motion of theirs by which it is carried along with them, they meanwhile have several other motions insofar as they are separate from one another. #### On the Earth.

<margin>
I.
*That the false hypothesis which we have already used should be retained, in order to explain the true natures of things.*
</margin>
5      Even though I would not want it believed that the bodies of this visible world were ever created in that way which was described above (as I have already sufficiently warned<sup>a</sup>), I must nevertheless still retain the same **hypothesis** <note>original: "hypothesim". Descartes famously proposed a "fable" of how the world might have formed through mechanical laws, while officially maintaining that God created the world all at once.</note> for explaining those things which appear upon the **Earth**. I do this so that if, as I 10 hope, I show clearly that the causes of all natural things can be provided by this path, and no other, it may be rightly concluded that their nature is no different than if they had been created in such a way.

<margin>
II.
*What the formation of the Earth is, according to this hypothesis.*
</margin>
Let us imagine, therefore, that this **Earth** which we inhabit was once composed solely of the matter of the **first element** <term>primi elementi: The finest, most fluid matter in Descartes' physics, which he believed composed the Sun and stars.</term>, 15 like the **Sun**, although it was much smaller than it; and that it had a vast **vortex** <term>vorticem: A whirlpool of fluid matter that Descartes believed carried planets around a central body.</term> around itself, in the center of which it sat. But, when the **striated particles** <term>particulæ striatæ: Tiny, screw-shaped particles that Descartes believed were responsible for magnetic forces.</term>, and other tiny parts of that matter of the first element (though not the very smallest ones) 20 adhered to each other, and were thus turned into the matter of the **third element** <term>tertii elementi: The coarsest, least agitated matter, which forms solid, opaque bodies like planets and comets.</term>, from these there first arose **opaque spots** <note>original: "maculas opacas". Descartes draws an analogy between sunspots and the crust that eventually formed the Earth's surface.</note> upon the Earth...

### PART FOUR

...closer to the **Sun** than it is now, because of its excessive solidity.

<margin>IV. Description of the second region.</margin>
<margin>5</margin> The middle region **M** is entirely occupied by a very opaque and dense body: for since this body was formed from extremely small particles (namely, those that previously belonged to the **first element** <term>first element: In Descartes' physics, the smallest, fastest-moving particles that form light and heat.</term>), which were joined together, no passages seem to have been left within it, except those so small that they can only provide a path for those **striated particles** <term>striated particles: Screw-shaped bits of matter that Descartes believed passed through the poles of magnets and planets.</term> described above, and for the remaining matter of the first element. <margin>10</margin> And experience testifies to this in **sunspots**, which, although they are of the same nature as this body **M**—except for being much thinner and rarer—nevertheless block the passage of light; they could hardly do this if their passages were wide enough to admit the globules of the **second element** <term>second element: Spherical particles that make up the "ether" or the heavens and transmit light.</term>. <margin>15</margin> For since these passages were initially formed in fluid or soft matter, they would undoubtedly also be straight and smooth enough not to impede the action of light.

<margin>V. Description of the third region.</margin>
<margin>20</margin> But these two inner regions of the **Earth** <note>The "two inner regions" refer to the core (I) and the dense middle layer (M).</note> concern us little, because no living person has ever reached them. Only the third remains, from which we shall hereafter show that all the bodies found here around us can arise. For now, however, we assume nothing else is in it but a large collection of particles of the **third element** <term>third element: The largest, slowest-moving particles that compose solid, earthly matter.</term>, having much **celestial matter** <note>original: "materia coelestis"</note> around them; the inward nature of these particles can be recognized from the way in which they were produced.

<margin>VI. That the particles of the third element in this third region must be quite large.</margin>

### PART FOUR.

...to drive these same particles in many other ways in the meantime. And because, in whichever direction they have begun to move, they continue afterward as much as they can along straight lines, or deviating as little as possible from straight lines: it follows that these **celestial globules** <term>celestial globules: The smooth, spherical particles of the 'second element' that Descartes believed filled the heavens and transmitted light.</term>, mixed among the particles of the **third element** <term>third element: The largest and most irregular particles of matter, which make up the Earth and all solid, tangible bodies.</term> that compose all the bodies of the Earth’s third region, produce various effects in them. <margin>XVI. On the first effect of this first action: that it makes bodies transparent.</margin>

The first effect is that they make all those terrestrial bodies transparent that are liquid and consist of particles of the third element so thin that these globules are carried around them in every direction. For as they move constantly through the passages of these bodies in every direction, and possess the force to change the position of their particles, they easily form straight paths for themselves—or paths equivalent to straight lines—which are therefore suitable for transmitting the action of light. Thus, we find through experience that there is no pure liquid on Earth made of thin particles that is not transparent. Regarding **mercury** <note>original: "argentum vivum." Literally "living silver."</note>, its particles are too thick to admit the globules of the second element everywhere around them. As for ink, milk, blood, and similar substances, these are not pure liquids, but are filled with many tiny dust-like particles of hard bodies. Regarding hard bodies, one can observe that all those are transparent which were transparent while they were being formed and were still liquid, and whose parts retain the same position in which they were placed by the globules of **celestial matter** <note>original: "materiæ cœlestis." The fluid matter of the heavens.</note> while moving around them before they were yet stuck together. Conversely, all those bodies are opaque whose particles were joined and connected by some external force [that resisted] the motion of the celestial globules mixed among them...

<margin>XVII.
How a solid and hard body can have enough passages to transmit rays of light.</margin>

### PART FOUR.

...of liquid terrestrial bodies, they [the celestial globules] continually push out the particles of the **third element** <term>third element: In Descartes’ physics, the largest and slowest particles of matter, which make up solid and liquid bodies on Earth.</term> that they encounter, until they have arranged and ordered them among others in such a way that they no longer obstruct their motions; or, when they cannot be so arranged, until they have separated them from the rest. <margin>XIX. Regarding the third effect: that it makes drops of liquids round.</margin>

The third effect of the **celestial globules** <term>celestial globules: The spheres of the 'second element' that fill the gaps between larger particles of matter and transmit the pressure of light.</term> is that they make drops of water or other liquids hanging in the air (or in another liquid different from them) round, as I have already explained in my **Meteors** <note>original: "Meteoris." For since these celestial globules have very different paths within a drop of water than they do in the surrounding air, and since they always move as much as possible in straight lines, or as close to straight lines as they can manage, it is manifest that those in the air are less hindered in continuing their motions along lines that deviate as little as possible from straight paths by the presence of a water drop if that drop is perfectly **spherical** than if it took on any other shape. For if there is any part on the surface of that drop that protrudes beyond a spherical shape, the celestial globules running through the air will strike it with greater force than the other parts, and will therefore push it toward the center of the drop. Conversely, if any part of its surface is closer to the center than the rest, the celestial globules contained within the drop itself will [push] it away from [the center] with greater force...

Descartes argues the circle is the most "natural" curve because its deviation from a straight line is uniform at every point.</term>, which is the only way a circular line differs from a straight one, is smaller than any angle made of straight lines, and is equal at every point in no curved line except a circle: it is certain that a straight line can never be bent more equally, and less at each of its points, than when it transitions into a circular one.

<margin>
XX.
Explanation of the second action, which is called gravity.
</margin>
The **force of gravity** <note>original: "Vis gravitatis."</note> does not differ much from this third action of the **celestial globules** <term>celestial globules: The fast-moving, spherical particles of the 'second element' that Descartes believed filled the space between planets and transmitted light and pressure.</term>. For just as those globules, through their own motion alone—by which they are carried indiscriminately in every direction—press all the particles of every drop equally toward its center, and thus make the drop round: so through that same motion, being hindered by the mass of the whole Earth from traveling in straight lines, they propel all its parts toward the center; and in this, the gravity of terrestrial bodies consists.

<margin>
XXI.
All parts of the Earth, if considered alone, are not heavy, but light.
</margin>
To understand the nature of gravity perfectly, it must first be noted that if all the spaces around the Earth not occupied by the Earth's own matter were a **void** <term>void: An empty space or vacuum. Descartes used this as a thought experiment, though he famously argued that a true vacuum was physically impossible because "space" is itself a form of matter.</term>—that is, if they contained nothing except a body that could neither hinder nor help the motion of other bodies in any way—and if, meanwhile, this Earth turned on its axis by its own motion in a period of twenty-four hours, all those parts of it that were not very firmly bound to one another would fly off in every direction toward the heavens. This is the same way we see that when a **spinning top** <note>original: "turbo."</note> rotates, if sand is thrown upon it, the sand immediately recedes from it and is scattered in all directions; and thus the Earth should be called not heavy, but rather **light** <note>original: "levis." In this context, "lightness" (levitas) refers to the centrifugal tendency of an object to move away from the center of rotation.</note>.

<margin>
XXII.
*In what the lightness of celestial matter consists.*
</margin>

Descartes argued that space is a "plenum," entirely filled with matter, and that "empty" space is a logical impossibility.</note>, and the Earth is not moved by its own internal drive <gloss>a. However, the celestial matter—insofar as it all moves together in the same motion that carries the Earth—possesses no force of gravity or **lightness** <note>original: "levitatis." But insofar as its parts have more agitation than they spend on this motion, and are therefore always hindered by encountering the Earth from continuing their motions in straight lines, they always recede from it as much as they can; and in this, their lightness consists.

*How all parts of the Earth are pushed downward by this celestial matter, and thus become heavy.*
</margin>

Ibid., page 173.</gloss> in the particles of terrestrial bodies, whenever they have some of those terrestrial particles above them, they must exert that force of theirs upon them. And thus the **gravity** <note>original: "gravitas."</note> of each terrestrial body is not properly produced by all the celestial matter flowing around it, but precisely only by that part of it which—if that body descends—immediately ascends into its place, and therefore which is of a size—

How much gravity is in any given body.

These being subtracted from both sides, whatever celestial matter remains in that volume of air acts upon whatever remains of the terrestrial parts in body **B**; and in this alone does its **gravity** <note>original: "gravitatem." ### PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

For example, in vessel ABC, water droplet 1 is not pressed by the others—2, 3, and 4—existing above it. This is because if these were to be moved downward, other droplets, such as 5, 6, and 7 or similar ones, would have to <margin>5</margin> ascend into their place; and since these are equally heavy, they prevent the others from descending. However, these droplets 1, 2, 3, and 4, with their forces joined together, do press upon part of the bottom, B. <margin>10</margin> This occurs because, if they cause the bottom to descend, they will also descend themselves, and in their place, parts of air 8 and 9—which are lighter than the droplets—will ascend. Yet, no more droplets press upon that same part of the vessel B than these 1, 2, 3, and 4, or others equivalent to them; this is because, at that moment in time <margin>15</margin> when this part B can descend, no more can follow it. And from this, it is very easy to explain countless experiments concerning the weight of bodies, or rather, if I may speak this way, **gravitation** <note>original: "gravitationem." Descartes is distinguishing between the static property of "gravity" and the active force or process of "gravitation."</note>, which seem miraculous to those who philosophize poorly. <margin>20</margin>

# PART FOUR

...causes can be imagined; but whether their effect is so great as to be perceived by the senses is not yet certain to me.

<margin>
XXVIII.
*Concerning the third action, which is light; how it moves the particles of air.*
</margin>

The power of light, insofar as it spreads from the Sun and the stars into all parts of the heavens, has already been sufficiently explained above <note>See Part III, article 55 and following, page 108.</note>. It remains only for us to note here that its rays, descending from the Sun, agitate the particles of the Earth in various ways.

Indeed, although light, considered in itself, is nothing other than a certain **pressure** <term>pressure: For Descartes, light is not a traveling particle but a mechanical "push" transmitted instantaneously through the fluid matter of space.</term> which occurs along straight lines extending from the Sun to the Earth, this pressure is not applied equally to all particles of the **third element** <term>third element: The largest, slowest-moving particles that form solid bodies like Earth, as opposed to the faster "celestial" elements.</term> that compose the Earth’s uppermost region. Instead, it hits now some particles and then others, and even hits one end of a single particle at one moment and the other end at another. Because of this, it is easy to understand how various motions are excited within these particles.

For example, if **AB** is one of the particles of the third element composing the uppermost region of the earth, resting upon another particle **C**, and many other particles such as **D**, **E**, and **F** lie between it and the Sun: these intervening particles will sometimes block the Sun's rays **G**, **G** from pressing on the end **B**, but they will not block them from pressing on end **A**. In this way, end **A** will be pushed down, while the other end **B** will be lifted up.

->[Diagram showing rays of light labeled G descending toward a cluster of particles. Particles D, E, and F are positioned above a long particle AB. Particle AB is balanced on a smaller particle C. The rays G hit end A but are blocked from end B by the particles above it.]<-

And because these particles are constantly changing their positions, a little later they will be positioned so that they block the Sun's rays tending toward **A**, but not those tending toward **B**. Thus, end **A** will be lifted back up, and **B** will be pushed down.

<margin>
XXIX.
*Concerning the fourth action, which is heat; what it is, and how it persists when the light is removed.*
</margin>

Now, this agitation of terrestrial particles—whether it arises from light or from any other cause—is called **heat**, especially when it is greater than usual and affects the senses; for the name "heat" refers specifically to the sense of touch <note>original: "caloris enim denominatio ad sensum tactûs refertur"</note>. It should also be noted that each of these terrestrial particles, once set in motion, continues to move afterward according to the laws of nature<gloss>See Part II, article 37, page 62.</gloss> <note>Descartes refers here to his principle of inertia: an object in motion stays in motion unless acted upon by an outside force.</note> until it is stopped by some other cause. Therefore, the heat produced by light remains for some time after the light itself has been removed.

<margin>
XXX.
*Why heat penetrates deeper than light.*
</margin>

It should furthermore be noted that the terrestrial particles, when struck by the Sun's rays in this way, agitate other nearby particles that the rays themselves do not reach; and these in turn agitate others, and so on in succession. Since half of the entire Earth is always illuminated by the Sun, so many particles of this kind are moved at once that, although the light itself stops at the first opaque surface it hits, the heat generated by it must reach all the way to the innermost parts of the Earth’s middle region.

<margin>
XXXI.
*Why it causes almost all bodies to expand.*
</margin>

Finally, it should be noted that these terrestrial particles, when they are agitated by heat more than usual, generally cannot be contained in as narrow a space as they occupy when they are at rest or moving less. This is because they have irregular shapes which take up less room when they are joined together in a certain way at rest than when they are separated by constant motion. From this it follows that heat **rarefies** <term>rarefy: To expand or become less dense. Descartes imagines particles as physical shapes that need more "elbow room" to vibrate or spin than they do when sitting still.</term> almost all terrestrial bodies, though some more and others less, according to the various positions and shapes of the particles of which they are composed.

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 214-216.

...by the particles which, moved daily by the force of heat, rose toward **B** during the day and descended again at night, always following one another and filling those passages <term>passages: 'meatus'—microscopic channels or pores within the solid crust</term>. However, when the volume of body **D** <gloss>original: 'mole imminuto' — reduced in mass or size</gloss> later decreased, its particles no longer occupied all the passages of body **E**; <margin>5</margin> other smaller particles, coming from **B**, took their place. Since these did not sufficiently fill the passages of body **E**, and because a vacuum does not exist in nature, celestial matter <gloss>original: 'materia cælestis' — the subtle, fluid substance Descartes believed filled all space that appeared empty</gloss>—which alone is capable of filling all the tiny gaps <margin>10</margin> found around the particles of earthly bodies—rushed into them. This matter altered their shapes and exerted force to pull some apart in such a way that neighboring passages were made narrower. From this, it easily happened that, as certain parts of body **E** were disconnected from one another, <margin>15</margin> fissures <note>original: 'fissuræ' — cracks or splits</note> formed within it, which then grew larger and larger over time. This occurred in exactly the same way we see many cracks open in the earth during summer when it is dried by the Sun; the earth gapes more and more the longer the drought <margin>20</margin> persists.

<margin>**XLII.**
*How the crust itself was broken into various parts.*</margin>
Furthermore, since there were many such cracks in body **E**, and these were constantly increasing, eventually its parts adhered so little to each other that it could no longer be supported in the manner of an arch between **F** and **B**. Therefore, the whole structure, <margin>25</margin> shattered, collapsed by its own weight onto the surface of body **C**. And since this surface was not wide enough to receive all the fragments of the crust lying flat against each other while maintaining the positions they previously held, some of them had to tilt to the <margin>30</margin> side and lean upon one another. <margin>XLV. What the nature of air is</margin>
And the inward natures of all these things can be drawn from what has already been said. For first, we know from these things that air must be nothing other than a mass <note>original: "congeriem"</note> of particles of the **third element** <term>third element: Descartes categorized matter into three types: the first (light/fire), the second (the transparent heavens), and the third (the dense matter of planets and Earthly objects)</term>, so thin and so separated from one another that they follow any of the motions of the **celestial globules** <term>celestial globules: the spherical particles of the second element that Descartes believed filled all space and transmitted light</term>; and therefore, air is a body that is very rare, fluid, and transparent, and can be composed of tiny bits of any shape. Indeed, unless its particles were entirely separated from one another, they would have long ago adhered to body **E** <note>the Earth's crust</note>; and since they are separated, each one moves independently of its neighbors and occupies that entire small sphere which it requires for circular motion around its own center, and it expels all its neighbors from that space. For this reason, it does not matter what shape they may be.

<margin>XLVI. Why it is easily rarefied and condensed.</margin>
Furthermore, air is easily condensed by cold and rarefied <note>expanded</note> by heat; for since almost all its particles are flexible, like **soft feathers** or thin strings, the faster they are driven, the wider they extend themselves, and therefore they require a larger sphere of space for their motion. It is known from what has been said <sup>a</sup>, that by heat, nothing else is to be understood here than an acceleration of motion in those particles, and by cold, a reduction of the same.

<margin>XLVII. Concerning its violent compression in certain machines.</margin>
Finally, air, when violently compressed in some vessel, has the power of springing back <note>original: "resiliendi"</note> and immediately extending itself through a wider space. From this, machines are made which, by the power of air alone, throw water upwards like fountains; and others which shoot projectiles with great force, like bows.

He explains that heat expands air by accelerating these particles, while compression allows air to store mechanical energy, as seen in air-powered fountains and weapons.</summary>

## PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

And the cause of this is that when air is so compressed, each of its particles does not have for itself alone that tiny spherical space which it requires for its movement, but other neighboring particles enter into it; and since, meanwhile, the same heat, or the same agitation of these particles, is maintained by the motion of the **celestial globules** <term>celestial globules: spherical particles of the "second element" that Descartes believed filled all space and transmitted light and heat through their constant motion</term>, which are constantly flowing around them, they strike one another with their extremities and drive each other from the spot, and thus all together make an effort to occupy a larger space.

<margin>XLVIII. On the nature of water: and why it is easily turned now into air, now into ice.</margin>
As for water, I have already shown <note>original: "oſtendi^a"; See footnote *a*</note> why only two types of particles are found in it, of which some are flexible and others inflexible; and if they are separated from one another, the latter compose salt and the former fresh water. And because I have already explained all the properties of both salt and fresh water at length, based on this single foundation, in the *Meteors* <note>original: "Meteoris^b"; referring to Descartes's 1637 work *Les Météores*</note>, there is no need to write more about them here. But I would only wish it to be noted how aptly everything fits together, and how it follows from such a generation of water that there must also be a proportion between the thickness of its particles and the thickness of the particles of air; likewise between them and the force with which the globules of the **second element** move them, so that when these globules act a little less than usual, they change water into ice and air particles into water <note>Descartes is describing condensation</note>; but when they act a little more strongly, they turn the thinner particles of water—namely those that are flexible—into air <note>Descartes is describing evaporation</note>.

There remains another regular movement of the water, by which twice a day in every location it rises and falls, and meanwhile always flows from East to West. To explain the cause of this movement, let us place before our eyes that small **vortex** <term>vortex: in Cartesian physics, a "vortex" is a large circling whirlpool of fluid celestial matter that carries planets and moons along in its current, as Descartes did not believe in a vacuum or gravity as an attractive force</term> of the heavens which has the Earth at its center, and which, along with the Earth and the Moon, is carried within a larger vortex around the Sun. Let **ABCD** be that small vortex <gloss>a</gloss>;

### PART FOUR

<margin>...that they flow from East to West.</margin>
...toward F and G, or from West to East, the bulge of water <note>original: "tumorem". Descartes visualizes the tide as a physical "swelling" or "bulge" caused by the Moon's pressure.</note> 412, and likewise the bulge of air 856, which presently weigh upon part E of the Earth, gradually migrate to other more Westerly parts; so that after six hours they weigh upon part H of the Earth, and after twelve hours upon part G. **54.**
Why at the same latitude, regions that have the sea to the East are more temperate than others.
</margin>
This flow, although it is not very fast, is nevertheless clearly detected by the fact that long voyages are much slower and more difficult toward the Eastern parts than toward the Western; and because in certain narrows of the sea, the water always flows toward the West; and finally because, all other things being equal, those regions that have the sea to the East, such as **Brazil**, do not feel the heat of the Sun as much as those which have long tracts of land to the East and the sea to the West, such as **Guinea**; because the air which comes from the sea is cooler than that which comes from the land.

Why there is no ebb and flow in lakes and ponds: or why it occurs at different hours on different shores.

Finally, it should be noted that the entire Earth is not actually covered by the sea, as we assumed just a moment ago ᵇ; nevertheless, because the **Ocean** spreads through its entire circumference, the same thing must be understood of it, regarding the general motion of the waters, as if it involved the whole. However, **lakes** and **ponds**, whose waters are separated from the Ocean, undergo no such motions: because their surfaces are not so wide that the <term>celestial matter</term> <note>original: "materiâ cælesti". In Descartes's physics, this is the subtle, fluid substance that fills all space and transmits pressure from the Moon to the Earth's oceans.</note> would press significantly more on one part than on another due to the Moon's presence.

How the specific causes of these variations on individual shores are to be investigated.

The particular causes of all these variations can be deduced from what has been said ᵃ <note>original: "ex dictis". Descartes refers to the principles established in Articles 50, 51, and 52 on pages 234-236.</note>, if we consider that the waters of the Ocean—when the Moon is new or full—are at their highest at six o'clock (both morning and evening) in places far from the shores toward the Ecliptic <note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky; Descartes uses it here to describe the central belt of the Earth's surface.</note> and the Equator, and therefore they flow toward the shores. Depending on whether the shores are near or far, and whether the waters reach them through paths that are straight or winding, wide or narrow, deep or shallow, the waters are carried to them sooner or later, and in greater or lesser volume. Furthermore, because of the greatly varied and uneven windings of these shores, it often happens that waters heading toward one shore meet those coming from another, so that their course is changed in various ways. Finally, various winds—some of which are regular in certain places—push these waters in different ways. Indeed, I do not think anything is observed anywhere regarding the ebb and flow <term>fluxum & refluxum; the rising and falling of the tide</term> of the sea whose causes are not contained within these few principles.

...are, such as the particles of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury</note>, salt, and fresh water, and any others contained in its larger channels <note>original: "meatibus"; Descartes uses this term to describe the pores or passages within solid matter</note>; but also those which are the hardest of all and adhere most firmly to one another. <margin>5</margin> It is not that these are completely separated from each other; but in the same way that we see the branches of trees shaken when driven by the winds, and the spaces between them made now larger, now smaller, even though the trees are not thereby uprooted: so we must think that the thick and branch-like particles of body <margin>10</margin> C <note>Body C refers to the Earth's crustal layer in Descartes' cosmology</note> are so connected and intertwined that they are not usually completely disjoined from each other by the force of heat, but are only shaken a little bit, opening the channels left around them now more, now less. <margin>61. *Concerning sharp and acidic juices, from which vitriol, alum, etc., are made.*</margin> <note>original: "atramentum sutorium"; literally "shoemaker's ink," a historical term for ferrous sulfate or green vitriol</note>

And since meanwhile these <margin>25</margin> particles, driven by the force of heat, creep here and there through these channels, dashed against and rubbed by their hard walls, they are sharpened like little swords, and thus turned into certain sharp, acidic, corrosive juices: which juices, afterwards growing together with metallic matter, form vitriol; <margin>30</margin> with stony matter, alum; and thus many other things.

<margin>LXII. *Regarding the oily matter of bitumen, sulfur, etc.*</margin>

<margin>LXIII. *Concerning the principles of the Chemists; and how metals ascend into mines.*</margin>
And so we have three things here <gloss>a</gloss> <note>referring to Articles 58, 61, and 62</note> which can be taken as the three common principles of the Chemists: salt, sulfur, and Mercury. I might have described each of these individually <margin>15</margin> in this place if I had been permitted, up until now, to perform the various experiments required for a certain knowledge of them. <margin>20</margin>

Since there are large cavities full of water beneath the plains and mountains, there is no doubt that many vapors—that is, water particles separated from one another and moved rapidly by the force of heat—daily reach the outer surface of the plains and the highest ridges of the mountains. <margin>5</margin> For we see that many such vapors are lifted even higher, all the way to the clouds. They rise more easily through the passages of the earth, where they are supported by its solid particles, than through the air, whose fluid and mobile particles cannot support them in the same way. <margin>10</margin> However, after these vapors have ascended in this way, they become sluggish when cold follows; losing their form as vapor, they turn back into water. This water cannot descend through those same passages through which the vapor ascended, because they are <margin>15</margin> too narrow; instead, it finds somewhat wider paths in the gaps between the crusts or shells <note>Descartes envisioned the Earth's exterior as a series of collapsed layers or "crusts"</note> from which the entire outer earth is formed. These paths lead the water down at an angle, following the slope of the valleys and plains. And where these subterranean water-paths terminate at the <margin>20</margin> surface of a mountain, valley, or plain, springs gush forth. Many of their streams, gathered together, form rivers, which flow down through the lower parts of the earth's outer surface into the sea.

<margin>LXV. Why the sea does not increase despite the rivers flowing into it.</margin>
Although much water flows steadily from the mountains <margin>25</margin> toward the sea, the cavities from which they ascend can never be exhausted for that reason, nor can the sea increase. For this outer earth could only have been generated in the manner described a little earlier <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "a", referring to Article 42, p. 228</note>—namely, from the fragments of bodies...

<meta>This page continues Part IV of René Descartes' Principles of Philosophy. <page-num>246</page-num>
<header>PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY 231-232.</header>

By <term>spirits</term> <note>In 17th-century science, "spirits" were not ghosts, but the most volatile, active, and fast-moving particles of a substance, often associated with acids or alcohols.</note> I mean particles of sharp juices, as well as volatile salts, which are separated from one another and move so quickly that the force with which they persist in moving in all directions outweighs their weight. By <term>exhalations</term>, however, I mean branched, very thin particles of oily matter, moved in the same way. Indeed, in waters and other juices and oils, the particles only crawl; but in vapors, spirits, and exhalations, they fly.

<margin>LXXI. How various types of stones and other fossils arise from their different mixtures.</margin>

And indeed, spirits fly with greater force and more easily penetrate all the narrow passages of the earth; when they are trapped by these passages, they stick more firmly and thus produce harder bodies than exhalations or vapors. Since there is a very great diversity among these three types, according to the diversity of the particles from which they are composed, many types of stones and other non-transparent <term>fossils</term> <note>original: "fossilium." In Descartes' time, a "fossil" referred to anything "dug up" from the ground, including minerals and ores, not just the remains of prehistoric life.</note> also arise when they remain trapped in the narrow passages of the earth and are mixed with its own particles. Many types of transparent fossils and gemstones also arise when they first collect into juices in the cracks and cavities of the earth, and then gradually, as their most slippery and fluid particles depart, the remaining ones cling to one another.

<margin>LXXII. How metals reach the outer earth from the inner earth, and how minium is made.</margin>

In this same way, the vapors of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi," literally "living silver," the old name for mercury.</note>, by crawling through the small cracks and larger passages of the earth, leave behind particles of other metals mixed with them, and thus impregnate the earth with gold, silver, lead, and others. Because of their extraordinary slipperiness, the mercury particles then proceed further, or slide back down; or they even occasionally stick there when the passages through which they might return are blocked by sulfurous exhalations. And then the particles of quicksilver itself, by the very minute [particles] of those exhalations...

<margin>LXXIV. *Why they are found primarily at the roots of mountains, facing South and East.*</margin>

<margin>15</margin> those parts of the mountains that face the midday Sun <note>The South</note> or the East more than in others, because the heat is greater there, and it is by the force of this heat that they are lifted. For this reason, these are the primary places where miners typically search for them.

<margin>LXXV. *That all mines are in the outer earth; and that one can never reach the inner earth by digging.*</margin>
Nor should it be thought that by any persistence in digging, one could ever
<margin>20</margin> reach the inner earth: partly because the outer earth is too thick when compared to human strength; | but especially because of the intervening waters, which would leap out with all the greater force the deeper the place where their
<margin>25</margin> veins were first opened, and they would overwhelm all the miners.

<margin>LXXVI. *Regarding sulfur, bitumen, clay, and oil.*</margin>
The thinnest particles of exhalations, such as those described a little earlier <gloss>a</gloss> <note>Article 70, pages 245-246.</note>, compose nothing but pure air when they are alone; but they easily join with the thinner particles of spirits...

<summary>Descartes explains that metals and minerals rise from the Earth's interior through fissures to settle in mountain roots, particularly in sun-warmed southern or eastern slopes. He also asserts that human mining is limited to the Earth's outer crust because deep-seated water reservoirs would flood any attempt to reach the planet's core.</summary>

<margin>**LXXIX.** Why several shocks usually occur in an earthquake: and thus it sometimes lasts for several hours or days.</margin>

<margin>**LXXX.** On the nature of fire, and its difference from air.</margin>
But here it remains for me to say how a flame can be lit in those cavities, and at the same time to explain the nature of fire. Earthly particles, of whatever size or shape they may be, take the form of fire when they individually follow the motion of the <term>first element</term> <note>In Cartesian physics, the "first element" is the finest, most fluid matter that fills all gaps between larger particles; it is the primary source of light and heat.</note>; likewise, they take the form of air when, flying among the globules of the <term>second element</term> <note>The "second element" consists of spherical particles that fill the heavens and transmit light through their pressure.</note>, they imitate their agitation. Thus, the first and primary difference between air and fire is that the particles of the latter are agitated much more quickly than those of the former. For it has already been sufficiently shown above that the motion of the matter of the first element is much faster than that of the second. But there is also another very great difference: although the coarser particles of the <term>third element</term> <note>The "third element" consists of the largest, slowest-moving particles that form solid bodies like the Earth.</note>, such as those composing the vapors of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi." Mercury.</note>, can take the form of air, they are not necessary for its preservation; on the contrary, air is purer and less subject to corruption when it consists only of the smallest particles. For the coarser ones, unless they are continuously agitated by heat, sink downward by their own weight and spontaneously lose that form. Fire, however, without somewhat thick bod- <note>The text cuts off mid-word (corporibus) and will continue on the next page.</note>

<margin>**81.** How fire is first ignited.</margin>
For since the globules of the <term>second element</term> <note>original: "secundi elementi." In Descartes’s physics, these are spherical particles that fill most of space; they are larger than the first element and responsible for the transmission of light.</note> occupy all the intervals around the Earth that are large enough to receive them, and they all lean upon one another in such a way that one cannot be moved without the others (except perhaps circularly around its own axis); although the matter of the <term>first element</term> <note>original: "primi elementi." The finest, most fluid matter that fills the tiny gaps between the larger spherical globules.</note>, filling all the small angles left by those globules, moves within them as rapidly as possible, yet if it has no more space than what is contained in those angles, it cannot have enough force there to carry away the earthly particles—which are all supported by each other and by the globules of the second element—and thus it cannot generate fire. But for fire to be first ignited in some place, the <term>celestial globules</term> <note>original: "globuli coelestes." Another name for the second element particles.</note> must be expelled by some force from the intervals of several earthly particles; these particles, then separated from one another and floating in the matter of the first element alone, are carried away by its swiftest motion and driven in every direction.

<margin>**82.** How fire is preserved.</margin>
And so that this fire may be preserved, those earthly particles must be sufficiently thick, solid, and fit for motion, so that, being thus impelled by the matter of the first element, they have the strength to repel the celestial globules from the place where the fire is, and into which they are ready to return; and thus they prevent those globules from again occupying the intervals left to the first element, thereby breaking its strength and extinguishing the fire.

<margin>**83.** Why it requires fuel.</margin>
And furthermore, the earthly particles, striking against those globules, cannot be hindered by them from proceeding further; and by exiting from that place in which the first element exerts its forces, they lose the form of fire,

<summary>Descartes explains that fire is created when earthly particles are separated from one another and caught up in the rapid motion of the fine "first element," provided they are strong enough to keep larger "celestial globules" at bay. This mechanical model describes fire not as a substance, but as a state of motion among particles of different sizes.</summary>

### PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

...rigid, if they are struck by another hard body, the spaces lying between many of their particles—which are usually occupied by the <term>globules of the second element</term> <note>original: "globulis secundi elementi." In Descartes’s physics, these are spherical, medium-sized particles that fill the space between solid objects and the finer "first element."</note>—become narrower than usual. Consequently, these globules are forced to leap out, leaving nothing but the <term>matter of the first element</term> <note>original: "materiam primi elementi." The most subtle, fluid, and fast-moving substance that fills all gaps in the universe.</note> around those particles. Then, because these particles of flint are <term>brittle</term> <note>original: "friabiles," meaning easily crumbled or broken into small pieces.</note>, as soon as they are no longer pressed by the blow, they spring apart from one another. Thus, floating in the matter of the first element, which alone is found around them, they compose fire.

So, if **A** represents the flint whose front particles still contain visible globules of the second element, **B** will represent the same flint when it is struck by some hard body; its <term>pores</term> <note>original: "meatus." The tiny channels or passages within a solid body.</note>, having become narrower, can no longer contain anything except the matter of the first element. Finally, **C** shows the same flint after it has been struck, when some of its particles have been separated from it and, having only the matter of the first element around them, are turned into sparks of fire.

<margin>
**85.**
How fire is produced from dry wood.
</margin>

If wood, no matter how dry it may be, is struck in this same manner, it will not emit sparks. This is because wood is not particularly hard; the first part of it that meets the striking body bends toward the second part and touches it before this second part even begins to bend toward the third. In this way, the globules of the second element do not depart from many of their intervals all at once, but rather successively—now from one gap, now from another. However, if this wood is rubbed for a long time and with enough force, the unequal agitation and vibration of its particles caused by that <term>friction</term> <note>original: "frictio."</note> can shake out the globules of the second element from several of their intervals. This simultaneously disjoins the particles from one another and thus changes them into fire.

<summary>Descartes provides a mechanical explanation for the creation of fire, arguing that sparks result from the sudden expulsion of air-like globules from the pores of a brittle stone, while wood requires sustained friction to achieve the same separation of particles.</summary>

# Part FOUR.

<margin>**86.** How fire is produced by the collection of the Sun's rays.</margin>
Fire is also ignited by means of a concave mirror or a convex glass, which directs many rays of the Sun toward the same location. For although the action of those rays has the <term>globules of the second element</term> <note>original: "globulos secundi elementi." In Cartesian physics, these are the medium-sized particles that make up the heavens and transmit light.</note> as its subject, it is nevertheless much more violent than their ordinary motion. Since this action proceeds from the <term>matter of the first element</term> <note>original: "materiâ primi elementi." The finest, fastest-moving substance, of which the Sun and stars are composed.</note>—from which the Sun is formed—it possesses enough speed to excite fire. Furthermore, so many rays can be gathered together at once that they also possess enough force to agitate the particles of <term>terrestrial bodies</term> <note>original: "corporum terrestrium." The coarse, solid matter of the Earth.</note> with that same speed.

<margin>**87.** How fire is produced by violent motion alone.</margin>
Indeed, it does not matter by what cause the terrestrial particles first begin to move very quickly. Even if they were previously without motion, if they merely float in the matter of the first element, they immediately acquire from this alone a very rapid agitation. This happens for the same reason that a ship, if not tied down by any ropes, cannot be in a <term>torrent of water</term> <note>original: "aquâ torrente." A fast-moving stream or current.</note> without being carried along with it. And even if those terrestrial particles do not yet float in the first element in this way, if they are simply agitated fast enough by any other cause, by this very fact they will shake themselves and the <term>globules of the second element</term> placed around them so much that they immediately begin to float in the first element; and thereafter, they will be maintained in their motion by it. For this reason, any very violent motion is sufficient to excite fire. Such motion is commonly found in <term>lightning</term> and <term>whirlwinds</term>, namely when a high cloud, rushing down into another lower one, explodes the air trapped between them, as I explained in the *Meteors* <note>original: "in Meteoris explicui." This refers to Descartes' scientific essay *Les Météores*, specifically Discourse VII.</note>.

<margin>**88.** How fire is produced from a mixture of different bodies.</margin>
To be sure, that motion alone is hardly ever the sole cause of fire in such cases; for <term>exhalations</term> <note>original: "exhalationes." Dry, earthy vapors thought to be highly flammable.</note> are almost always mixed with the air, and their nature is such that they are easily turned either into a flame or at least into a luminous body. And—

<margin>89. *On lightning and shooting stars.*</margin>
And indeed in thunderbolts or lightning flashes, the cause that drives many exhalations together at once is obvious, due to the fall of one cloud onto another. In still air, however, when one exhalation has been thickened and stilled by the cold, another—arriving from a warmer place, or consisting of particles more suited for motion, or even pushed by some gentle wind—easily makes an impact into its pores, and expels the second element from them. And since the particles of the former exhalation are not yet so tightly joined together that they cannot be separated by this impact from others, they break out into flame by this very action: in which way I believe <term>shooting stars</term> <note>original: "stellas trajicientes."</note> are ignited.

92.
On those things which grow hot and do not glow: such as in enclosed hay.

That indeed the particles of some spirit or liquid, by entering the passages of a hard or even liquid body, can sometimes excite fire, is shown by damp hay shut up in some place, <term>lime</term> <note>Calcium oxide, which reacts exothermically (releases heat) when mixed with water.</note> sprinkled with water, all fermentations, and not a few liquids known to Chemists, which heat up when mixed together, and sometimes even catch fire. If these plants are meanwhile shut up in a narrow place, the particles of those juices, migrating from some plants into others, find many passages in those plants which are already beginning to dry out. These passages are slightly too narrow for the juices to enter them along with the <term>globules of the second element</term> <note>Medium-sized spherical particles that Descartes believed filled the atmosphere and transmitted light.</note>; therefore, as they flow through them, they are surrounded only by the matter of the first element. Being very rapidly driven by this matter, they acquire the agitation of fire.

# 242-243. PART FOUR. 257

5 ...of the drying [hay], which these same particles 1, 2, and 3, upon entering, can no longer have the <term>second element</term> <note>The "second element" consists of medium-sized, spherical globules that Descartes believed filled the atmosphere and transmitted light.</note> around them, but only the <term>first element</term> <note>The "first element" is the finest, most fluid material in Descartes's universe, making up the sun and fire; it fills the tiniest gaps where larger particles cannot fit.</note>. It is clear that between points B and C, they must follow the moderate motion of the second element, but between D and E, they must follow the very fast motion of the first. It does not matter that only a very small quantity of this first element is found around them. For it is enough that they float entirely within it: just as we see a ship 10 drifting down a river, following its course no less easily where the water is so narrow that it almost touches the banks on both sides, as where the river is at its widest. Moved so quickly, these particles have much more power to strike and shake the particles of the surrounding bodies than the first element does on its own: just as a ship, when 15 striking a bridge or some other obstacle, shakes it more strongly than the water of the river that carries it. And therefore, by rushing into the harder particles of the hay, they easily separate them from one another, especially when many particles rush together from different sides toward the same point. When they disconnect and carry 20 away enough particles in this manner, fire is created; however, when they only shake them, and do not yet have the power to disconnect many at once, they only slowly heat and decay the hay.

<margin>
**XCIV.**
*How fire may be ignited in the cavities of the earth.*
</margin>
By all these same means, fire can be ignited not only on the surface of the earth but also within its cavities. For in those places, sharp <term>spirits</term><note>Highly active, volatile, or corrosive particles capable of penetrating other substances.</note> can penetrate the passages of thick exhalations in such a way that they ignite a flame within them. Furthermore, fragments of rock or flint—worn away by the secret flow of water or other causes—may fall from the arches of these cavities onto the ground below. In doing so, they can violently expel the trapped air or strike fire through the collision of the flints. Once a single body has caught fire, it easily communicates that flame to other neighboring bodies suited to receive it. The particles of the flame, meeting the particles of those bodies, set them in motion and carry them away with them. However, this pertains less to the *generation* of fire than to its *preservation*, which must be discussed next.

# PART FOUR

...[of the] <term>second element</term><note>Descartes’s "second element" consists of spherical "globules" that fill the heavens and transmit light. They are larger than the first element but smaller than the third.</note>, but both these and those float in the matter of the <term>first element</term> in such a way that they are carried along by its motion; and although they often touch and push one another, they do not support [the flame] from every side, as they usually do in other places where there is no fire.
<margin>5</margin>

<margin>**XCVI. How fire is preserved within it.**</margin>
The matter of the first element, which is found in great abundance in this flame, is always striving to exit the place where it is because it moves so rapidly; and indeed, it strives to move upward—that is, to move away from the center of the Earth—because, as was said above <margin>a. Articles 22 and 25, pp. 213 and 214.</margin>, it is lighter than the <term>celestial globules</term><note>Another term for the "second element" particles that make up the air and sky.</note> that occupy the passages of the air. Therefore, both these globules and all the <term>terrestrial particles</term><note>The "third element," consisting of larger, slower-moving pieces of matter that form the Earth and solid objects.</note> of the surrounding air strive to descend into its place; they would thus immediately smother the flame if it consisted of the first element alone. But the terrestrial particles, continually exiting from the <term>wick</term><note>original: "ellychnio"</note> FG, as soon as they are immersed in the first element, follow its course. Upon meeting those air particles that were ready to descend into the space of the flame, they repel them, and in this way, the fire is preserved.

...placed: because, since they are carried toward the fire by their own weight alone, there is no danger that the fire might be extinguished by the particles situated below it. Thus, the flame of an inverted candle is overwhelmed by the liquid <note>original: "liquore"; here referring to the melted wax or oil</note> which otherwise preserves it; and on the contrary, other fires can occur in which the terrestrial particles are so solid, so numerous, and vibrated with such great force, that they repel even water poured upon them and cannot be extinguished by it.

<margin>CI. What is required for a body to be suitable for nourishing a fire.</margin>
The second thing required for the preservation of fire is that it adhere to some body from which new matter can reach it to replace the smoke that is departing. Therefore, that body must contain many particles that are sufficiently thin—relative to the type of fire being maintained—and these must be joined to one another (or to other thicker particles) in such a way that they can be separated by the impulse of the fire's particles and the neighboring <term>globules of the second element</term><note>Descartes theorized that the universe was filled with three types of matter. The "second element" consists of perfectly round, fluid globules that transmit light.</note>, and thus be converted into fire.

<margin>CII. Why a flame from spirit of wine does not burn linen.</margin>
I say that the particles of this body must be sufficiently thin in proportion to the fire being maintained; for example, if <term>spirit of wine</term><note>original: "vini spiritus"; an early term for distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note> is sprinkled on a linen cloth and catches fire, this very thin flame will indeed consume all the spirit of wine, but it will not touch the linen—which another fire would easily burn—because the linen's particles are not thin enough to be moved by such a delicate flame.

<margin>CIII. Why spirit of wine burns so very easily.</margin>
Indeed, spirit of wine feeds a flame very easily because it consists only of very thin particles, and because these particles have certain "branches" <note>original: "ramuli"</note> that are so short and flexible that they do not stick to one another (for if they did, the spirit would turn into oil); instead, they are shaped such that they leave many tiny spaces around themselves, which are not [filled] by globules...

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

...of the <term>second element</term><note>Descartes believed the universe was filled with three types of matter. The "second element" consists of fluid, round globules that transmit light.</note>, but can be occupied by the matter of the <term>first element</term><note>The "first element" is the finest, most agitated matter that fills the gaps between globules and makes up the sun and fire.</note> alone.

<margin>CIV.
Why water [extinguishes fire] with such difficulty.</margin>
On the other hand, water seems very opposed to fire because it consists of particles that are not only somewhat thick but also smooth and slippery. This means that nothing prevents the globules of the second element from surrounding and following them from all sides. Furthermore, because water particles are flexible, they easily enter the <term>meatus</term><note>original: "meatus"; refers to the internal pores or passages within a solid body.</note> of bodies that are burning. By keeping the fire particles away from those bodies, they prevent others from catching fire.

<margin>CV.
Why the force of large fires is increased by water or salts thrown into them.</margin>
Nevertheless, some bodies are of such a nature that water particles sent into their passages actually help the fire; because by rebounding from there with force, they themselves become ignited. For this reason, <term>smiths</term><note>Blacksmiths and metalworkers.</note> sprinkle <term>coal</term><note>original: "carbones fossiles"; literally "dug-up coals," referring to mineral coal rather than charcoal.</note> with water. Similarly, a small amount of water thrown into massive flames increases them. Salts perform this even more powerfully: for since their particles are rigid and long, like spikes, they are vibrated in the flame and, striking other bodies, have great power to shake their tiny parts. This is why salts are commonly added when melting metals.

<margin>CVI.
What kinds of bodies are easily burned.</margin>
Now, those materials commonly used for nourishing fire, such as wood and similar substances, consist of various particles. Some of these are very thin, others a little thicker, and others thicker still by degrees. Most of them are branched, and large passages lie between them. Consequently, when the particles of fire enter these passages, they first set the thinnest particles in motion, then those of medium size, and with their help, they very quickly move the thicker ones. In this way, they shake out the celestial globules—first from the narrower intervals and then from the rest—and carry almost all of them away (except for the very thickest ones, from which <term>ashes</term><note>original: "cineres"</note> are made).

<summary>Descartes explains the mechanical reasons why water typically extinguishes fire by blocking pores, but notes that small amounts of water or salt can intensify large fires by adding momentum to the particles. He also describes wood as a fuel composed of branched particles of varying sizes that are easily agitated by fire.</summary>

### Part Four

<margin>
**107.**
Why some things catch fire, and others do not.
</margin>

When the particles that emerge from a burning body are so numerous that they have the power to expel the **celestial globules** <note>The "second element," or round particles that fill the sky and transmit light.</note> from a space of nearby air, they fill that space with **flame**. However, if there are fewer of these particles, **fire** occurs without flame. This fire either creeps slowly through the **meatus** <term>passages</term> <note>original: "meatus"; the internal pores or channels within a solid body.</note> of its **tinder** <note>original: "fomitis"</note> as it finds matter it can consume, such as in those ropes or wicks used in war to ignite the **gunpowder** <note>original: "tormentorum pulverem"; literally "powder for engines of war."</note> of cannons.

<margin>
**108.**
Why fire is preserved for some time in embers.
</margin>

Certainly, if it has no such fuel around it, fire is not preserved unless it is enclosed within the pores of the body it inhabits. It requires time to dissolve all the particles of that body so that it can free itself from them. This can be seen in **glowing coals** <note>original: "carbonibus accensis"</note>, which, when covered by ashes, retain fire for many hours. This happens solely because that fire resides in certain thin and branching particles that are entangled with other thicker ones; although these thin particles are moved very rapidly, they can only escape one after another. Perhaps before they can exit in this way, they must be worn down by their long motion and divided into several smaller parts.

<margin>
**109.**
Concerning gunpowder made from sulfur, saltpeter, and charcoal; and first, concerning sulfur.
</margin>

Nothing, however, catches fire more quickly, nor preserves it for a shorter time, than **gunpowder** made from sulfur, **saltpeter** <note>original: "nitro"</note>, and charcoal. Indeed, even sulfur alone is highly flammable because it consists of particles of sharp juices which are wrapped in such thin and dense branches of **oily matter** <note>original: "materiæ oleagineæ"</note> that many passages remain open between those branches only to the **first element** <note>The finest, most agitated form of matter that constitutes fire and the sun.</note>. For this reason, sulfur is considered "very hot" even for medicinal use.

Saltpeter, however, consists of particles that are oblong and rigid...

### Part FOUR

<meta>249-250. This likely refers to the section or paragraph numbers in standard editions of the Principles.</meta>
->WORKS. III.<-
->34<-

In charcoal, there are many pores: both because many existed previously in the bodies <note>meaning the wood or organic matter from which the charcoal was made.</note> from which it was produced by burning, and also because, as those bodies were being burned, a great deal of smoke escaped from them. Only two types of particles are found within it: one consists of the thicker particles which, when separated, make up the ashes; the other consists of thinner particles which catch fire easily because they have already been stirred by the force of fire. However, because these are entangled with long and multiple branches <note>Descartes's mechanical physics explains solidity through "branched" or "hooked" particles that physically interlock.</note>, they cannot be separated without some force: this is evident from the fact that while other particles turned into smoke during the previous burning, these remained behind.

<margin>**115.** On the grains of this powder, and in what its primary power consists.</margin>

Thus, sulfur and saltpeter easily enter the wide pores of the charcoal, where they are enveloped and held fast by its branched particles; this is especially true when they are moistened with liquid and compacted into grains, or tiny pellets, and then dried. The purpose of this process is to ensure that the particles of saltpeter are ignited not just one after another, but many at once, in one and the same moment. For when fire brought from elsewhere first touches the surface of a grain, it does not immediately inflame and dissolve it; rather, it needs a certain amount of time to travel from the surface to the interior parts. Once there, having first ignited the sulfur, it gradually agitates the particles of saltpeter. Eventually, these saltpeter particles gather enough force—and require more space to describe their rotations <term>gyros</term> <note>Descartes believed that heat is the rapid circular motion or vibration of particles; as they move faster, they need more "room" to spin, causing expansion.</note>—that they snap the charcoal's bonds and shatter the entire grain. And although this time is extremely short if measured in hours or days, it must be noted that it is quite long when compared to the incredible speed with which the bursting grain spreads its flame through all the surrounding air.
