<margin>5</margin> remaining there alone and always rotating very rapidly as if in a certain tiny star, repelled from itself on all sides the <term>globules of the second element<note>The "second element" consists of larger, spherical particles that fill the sky and transmit the pressure of light.</note></term>, for which alone, among the particles of the surrounding <term>soot<note>original: "fuliginis."</note></term>, a passage still lay open, and thus it would diffuse light through the whole vault: small
<margin>10</margin> indeed and somewhat dim, but which could easily regain its strength from the movement of the external air when the place was opened, and, the soot having been dispersed, show a burning lamp.

<margin>CXVII.
On the remaining effects of fire.</margin>
Now let us come to those effects of fire which could not yet be recognized from the ways in which it arises and is preserved. For it is already clear from what has been said how it shines,
<margin>15</margin> how it heats, and how it dissolves all bodies by which it is nourished into many particles; and also how, from these bodies, first the extremely thin and slippery particles emerge, and then others, perhaps not thicker than the former, but more
<margin>20</margin> branchy and entangled—namely those which, adhering to the walls of chimneys, compose soot; and how the thickest of all particles remain as <term>ashes<note>original: "cineres."</note></term>. But it remains for us to show briefly in what way, by the force of the same fire,
<margin>25</margin> some of the bodies by which it is not nourished melt and boil, others are dried and hardened, others evaporated, others converted into <term>lime<note>original: "calcem." A powdery residue (calx) produced by heating minerals.</note></term>, and others into glass.

<margin>CXVIII.
Which bodies melt and boil when brought near to it.</margin>
All hard bodies, composed of particles that are separated from their neighbors with no more difficulty than others,
<margin>30</margin> and can be disjointed by some force of fire, melt while undergoing that force. For a liquid is nothing other...

...than to consist of particles separated from one another and which are in some state of motion. And since the motion of these particles is so great that some of them are turned into air or fire—and thus, requiring more space for their motion than usual, they expel others—these liquid bodies effervesce and boil.

<margin>CXIX. Which things are dried and hardened.</margin>
Furthermore, bodies in which there are many thin, flexible, and slippery particles, interwoven with other thicker or branch-like ones but not very firmly attached, exhale those thin particles when moved near fire, and by this very process, they are dried. For to be dry is nothing other than to lack those fluid particles which, when gathered together, compose water or some other liquor. And these fluid particles, when enclosed in the <term>passages<note>original: "meatibus." Descartes imagines matter as having tiny pores or channels through which smaller particles flow.</note></term> of hard bodies, dilate them and agitate other particles of those bodies by their motion; this removes or at least diminishes their hardness. But once they have exhaled, the others that remain are usually joined more closely and bound more firmly, and thus the bodies harden.

<margin>CXX. On ardent, insipid, and acid waters.</margin>
And indeed, the particles that are exhaled in this way are distinguished into various kinds. For first—to pass over those which are so mobile and thin that they alone can form no body except air—the thinnest of all after those, and which are most easily exhaled, are those which, when caught in the accurately closed vessels of the <term>chemists<note>original: "Chymicorum." This refers to early modern experimentalists and alchemists who studied the properties of substances through distillation.</note></term> and collected together, compose <term>ardent waters<note>original: "aquas ardentes." Literally "burning waters," referring to flammable spirits or high-proof alcohol.</note></term>, or spirits, such as are usually drawn from wine, wheat, and many other bodies. Next follow sweet or <term>insipid waters<note>original: "insipidæ." Waters that lack a strong taste or medicinal "spirit," typically resulting from standard distillation of plants.</note></term>, such as those distilled from plants and other bodies. In the third place are corrosive and acid waters, or sharp juices; which are extracted from salts not without great force of fire.

### Part Four

<margin>121. Concerning sublimates and oils.</margin>
Certain thicker particles—such as those of <term>mercury<note>original: "argenti vivi," literally "living silver."</note></term> and various salts—cling to the tops of vessels and harden into solid masses. These require a significant amount of force to be lifted upward into the air. <margin>5</margin> However, oils are the most difficult of all substances to extract from hard, dry bodies; this must be achieved not so much through the brute force of fire as through a specific skill. Because the particles of oils are thin and branch-like, too much force would break and tear them apart before they could be drawn out of the <term>passages<note>original: "meatibus." Descartes envisions matter as containing microscopic pores or channels through which smaller particles travel.</note></term> <margin>10</margin> of those bodies. Instead, a large amount of water is poured over them; the smooth and slippery particles of the water permeate these passages, gradually coaxing the oil particles out intact and carrying them away.

<margin>122. That the effect of fire changes when its intensity is varied.</margin>
In all these processes, the degree of heat must be carefully observed, for when the intensity is changed, the result is always <margin>15</margin> altered in some way. For example, many bodies, when exposed first to a slow fire and then gradually to a stronger one, dry out and release various particles. They would not release these same particles if they were subjected to intense heat from the very beginning; instead, the entire substance would likely melt.

<margin>123. Concerning lime.</margin>
<margin>20</margin> The method of applying fire also changes its effect. Some things will melt if they are heated all the way through at once; but if a strong flame merely "licks" their surface, it transforms that surface into <term>lime<note>original: "calcem." In early chemistry, "calx" refers to the powdery residue—typically a metallic oxide—left after a substance has been roasted or "calcined."</note></term>. Indeed, any hard bodies that are reduced to a very fine powder by the action of fire alone <margin>25</margin>—specifically by the breaking or expulsion of the thinner particles that once bound the rest together—are commonly said by the <term>chemists<note>original: "Chymicos." This refers to practitioners of the chemical arts in the 17th century.</note></term> to be turned into lime. There is no difference between ashes and lime other than this: ashes are the remains of bodies where a <margin>30</margin> large portion of the material was consumed by the fire, whereas lime is formed from those substances that remain almost entirely intact after the burning is complete.

<margin>124. Concerning glass, and how it is made.</margin>
The final effect of fire is the conversion of <term>lime<note>original: "calcis." In early modern science, "calx" referred to the powdery residue left after a substance had been thoroughly burned or oxidized.</note></term> and ashes into glass. After all the thinner particles have been torn away and cast off from the bodies being burned, the remaining parts—which persist as lime or ashes—are so solid and thick that they cannot be lifted upward by the force of fire. These particles have shapes that are mostly irregular and angular; because of this, when they rest upon one another, they do not cling together, nor do they even touch, except perhaps at certain very tiny points. However, when a strong and long-lasting fire continues to exert its power over them—that is, when the thinner particles of the <term>third element<note>Descartes categorized matter into three types based on size and motion; the "third element" consists of the largest, slowest particles that form solid macroscopic bodies.</note></term>, together with the <term>globules of the second element<note>original: "globulis secundi [elementi]." These are the fluid, spherical particles that Descartes believed filled the heavens and transmitted light.</note></term>, are swept along by the <term>matter of the first element<note>The "first element" is the most fluid and agitated matter, filling the gaps between larger particles.</note></term> and move very rapidly in all directions around those ash particles—their angles are gradually worn down and their surfaces are smoothed. Perhaps some of them are even bent. Thus, as they slide and flow over one another, they touch not just at points, but across certain small surfaces; in this way, being joined together, they compose glass.

<margin>125. How its particles are joined together.</margin>
Indeed, it must be noted that when two bodies whose surfaces have some width meet each other in a straight line, they cannot come so close to one another that some space does not remain between them, which is occupied by the globules of the second element. But when one is drawn <insert>See volume V, page 174.</insert> obliquely over another or slides across it, they can be joined much more closely. For <note>original: "exempli causâ," abbreviated as "ex. ca." in the first edition.</note> example, if bodies B and C meet each other along the line AD, the <term>celestial globules<note>original: "globuli cælestes." Another term for the particles of the second element that make up the sky and space.</note></term> at their surfaces...

<summary>Descartes explains the formation of glass as a mechanical process where intense fire wears down the jagged angles of ash and lime particles, smoothing them until they can slide together and bond across wider surfaces. He distinguishes this close bonding from the loose contact of irregular particles, which always leave gaps for "celestial globules" to pass through.</summary>

<margin>126. Why it becomes liquid when it is red-hot, and easily takes on all shapes.</margin>
For glass, while it is still red-hot, is liquid, because <margin>15</margin>its particles are easily moved by that force of fire, by which they have already been smoothed and bent. But when it begins to cool, it can take on any shape. This is common to all bodies liquefied by fire; for while they are still liquid, their parti-<margin>20</margin>cles do not find it difficult to accommodate themselves to any shapes, and when they later <term>harden<note>original: "concrescunt"; literally "grow together" or congeal.</note></term> through cold, they retain the same shapes they last assumed. It can even be stretched into threads as thin as hair, because its particles, already beginning to harden, flow more easily <margin>25</margin>over one another than they are separated from one another.

<margin>**127.** *Why it becomes very hard when it is cold.*</margin>
When the glass has then cooled completely, it is very hard, but at the same time also very fragile—and all the more fragile the more quickly it cooled. The cause of this hardness is simply that it consists of particles that are quite thick and inflexible, which cling to one another not through an intertwining of "branches" <note>Descartes often uses the analogy of microscopic hooks or branches—*ramuli*—to explain how matter stays together.</note>, but by immediate contact. Indeed, most other bodies are soft because their particles are flexible, or at least end in certain flexible branches that join them together by being mutually hooked. No adhesion of two bodies can be firmer than that which arises from their immediate contact; that is, when they touch each other in such a way that neither is in motion to be separated from the other. This happens to the particles of glass as soon as they are removed from the fire, because their thickness, their closeness <note>original: "contiguitas"</note>, and the inequality of their shapes prevent them from being maintained by the surrounding air in that motion by which they were previously being separated from one another.

<margin>**128.** *Why it is very fragile.*</margin>
Nevertheless, glass is very fragile because the surfaces along which its particles touch one another are very small and few. Many other softer bodies are more difficult to break because their parts are so interwoven that they cannot be separated without many of their branches being broken and torn away.

<margin>**129.** *Why its fragility is reduced if it is cooled slowly.*</margin>
Glass is also more fragile when it has cooled quickly than when it has cooled slowly. Its <term>pores<note>original: "meatus"; the internal channels or passages between particles.</note></term> are wide enough while it is red-hot, because at that time much matter of the <term>first element<note>In Descartes’s physics, the "first element" consists of the finest, most mobile matter that fills all gaps.</note></term>, together with the <term>globules of the second element<note>The spherical particles that Descartes believed composed the heavens and transmitted light.</note></term>, and perhaps even some of the thinner particles of the <term>third element<note>The largest and least mobile particles that form solid terrestrial bodies.</note></term>, pass through them. However, when the glass is cooled naturally, these pores are made narrower, because the globules of the second element alone, passing through them, require less space; and if the cooling is too rapid— <note>The text ends mid-sentence as the original Latin breaks off with "cele-".</note>

<summary>Descartes explains that glass is hard due to the direct contact of inflexible particles and fragile because those contact points are few. He also introduces the idea that slow cooling allows the internal "pores" of the glass to settle more stably than rapid cooling.</summary>

But if the glass is first moved toward a slow fire, and then gradually toward a more powerful one, so that it heats up equally in all its parts, it will not break; this is because all its pores will be loosened equally and at the same time.

<margin>**131.** How it becomes colored.</margin>

It takes on various colors according to how these harder particles block its pores <note>original Latin: "meatus," referring to the internal channels or passages between particles of matter</note>, more or less and in various ways.

<margin>**132.** Why it is rigid like a bow; and generally, why rigid things, when bent, spontaneously return to their original shape.</margin>
Finally, glass is rigid: so much so that it can be bent somewhat by an external force without breaking, but afterward it springs back with force, like a bow, and returns to its previous shape. This is clearly seen when it is drawn into very thin threads. This property of springing back generally applies to all hard bodies whose particles are joined by immediate contact rather than by an intertwining of branches <note>Descartes distinguished between materials held together by hooked or "branch-like" particles and those, like glass, held together by the simple pressing together of smooth surfaces.</note>. Consequently, the particles of matter accustomed to passing through them find the paths less convenient than usual and push against the walls of the pores to restore them to their original shape. For instance, if the pores in a relaxed bow through which the globules of the second element <note>The "second element" in Cartesian physics consists of small, spherical particles of celestial matter (ether) that fill the spaces between larger bits of terrestrial matter.</note> usually pass are circular, we must assume that in a taut or bent bow, they become...

These channels are hollowed out to the exact measure of those particles, such that those which receive the striated particles coming from the South Pole can in no way <margin>5</margin> receive those coming from the North Pole; nor, conversely, can those which receive Northern particles admit Southern ones. # PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

...are more angular than those of others, and are therefore more firmly bound to one another. It is no objection that some of its lumps <note>original: "glebae"</note> melt quite easily the first time they are exposed to fire; for then their fragments <note>original: "ramenta"</note>, not yet joined to one another but separated from <margin>5</margin> each other, are easily moved by the force of heat. Furthermore, although iron is harder than other metals and less easy to melt, it is nevertheless also one of the least heavy, and is easily destroyed by rust or eaten away by "strong waters" <note>A term used in early chemistry (aqua fortis) for nitric acid or other corrosive acids.</note>: all of which are indications that its particles <margin>10</margin> are not more solid than the particles of other metals, even though they are thicker, but rather that many passages <note>original: "meatus"</note> are contained within them.

<margin>
CXXXVII.
In what manner these channels also exist in its individual fragments.
</margin>

However, I do not wish to assert here that there are complete holes, twisted in the manner of screws, within the individual fragments of iron through <margin>15</margin> which the striated particles <note>original: "particulae striatae." These are the screw-shaped particles Descartes believed were responsible for magnetism.</note> pass; nor do I wish to deny that many such holes may be found in them. But it will suffice here if we consider the halves of such channels to be so engraved upon the surfaces of the individual fragments that, when these surfaces are properly joined together, they form complete holes. And it can easily be believed that those <margin>20</margin> thicker, branched, and porous particles of the inner earth from which iron is made, were so divided by the force of spirits or sharp juices <note>Likely referring to acidic vapors or volatile liquids within the Earth.</note> permeating them, that those halved channels remained on the surfaces of the fragments that were separated from them; and <margin>25</margin> that these fragments afterwards gradually ascended into the mines through the veins of the outer earth, pushed along both by those spirits and also by exhalations and vapors.

<margin>
CXXXVIII.
How these passages are made fit to admit the striated particles coming from either side.
</margin>

And it must be noted that as they ascend in this way, they cannot always be turned in the same direction because they are angular, <margin>30</margin> and they encounter various inequalities in the veins of the earth; and since the striated particles, which from the inner earth...

<summary>Descartes explains that iron's unique properties—its hardness yet low density and susceptibility to rust—stem from its thick, branched particles containing "halved" screw-like channels. These fragments were formed in the Earth's interior and pushed upward into mines by underground vapors and acidic fluids.</summary>

# Part Four.

...coming with force, seeking paths for themselves through the whole exterior [of the earth], they find the passages of these fragments <note>original: "ramenta"; these are the microscopic shavings or pieces that Descartes believes make up the structure of metals.</note> so situated that, in order to continue their movement in straight lines, they try to enter through those openings through which they were previously accustomed to exit. There they encounter those very tiny tips of the branches <note>Descartes envisions the channels as having microscopic "hairs" or "branch tips" that act like one-way valves.</note> which, as was said before<sup>a</sup>, stand out among the coils of the passages and rise up against the returning striated particles <note>original: "particulis striatis"; these are screw-shaped particles that Descartes theorized were responsible for magnetic force.</note>. At first, these branch tips resist them, but being pushed by them very often, they are all eventually bent in the opposite direction, or some are even broken. When these channels later change their position along with the fragments they are in, and present their other openings to the striated particles, these particles again encounter the branch tips rising in the channels and gradually bend them back the other way. The more often and the longer this is repeated, the easier the bending of these branches in either direction becomes.

<margin>
CXXXIX.
What the nature of the magnet is.
</margin>
And indeed, those fragments which have often ascended in this way through the veins of the outer earth, being turned now one way and now another—whether they are gathered together by themselves or embedded in the passages of other bodies—compose a lump <note>original: "glebam"</note> of iron. However, those fragments which either always retained the same position, or at least, if they were forced to change it a few times to reach the mines, remained there unmoved for many years afterward, firmly embedded in the channels of a stone or another body, make a magnet. Thus, there is almost no lump of iron that does not in some way approach the nature of a magnet, and there is no magnet at all in which there is not some iron.

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

...be contained; even if perhaps sometimes that iron adheres so closely to certain other bodies that it can more easily be destroyed by fire than be extracted from them.

<margin>
140.
How steel and any kind of iron are made by melting.
</margin>
Now when lumps <note>original: "glebæ"</note> of iron are brought to a fire and melt, so that they may be turned into iron or steel, their fragments <note>original: "ramenta"; Descartes uses this term to describe the tiny, fundamental pieces of metal</note>, agitated by the force of heat and separated from foreign <note>original: "heterogeneis"</note> bodies, twist themselves about here and there until they apply themselves to one another along those surfaces in which it was said a little earlier that half-channels <note>original: "dimidiatos meatus"</note>, suitable for receiving striated particles <note>Descartes' theory of "striated particles"—screw-shaped matter—was his mechanical explanation for magnetic and metallic properties</note>, were carved; and also until the halves of those channels match so fitly that they form whole channels. When this happens, immediately the striated particles—which are found no less in fire than in other bodies—flowing through them more freely than through other places, prevent the tiny surfaces (from whose fit positioning and conjunction the channels arise) from changing their position as easily as before; and their contiguity, or at least the force of gravity which presses all fragments downward, prevents them from being easily separated. And while meanwhile the fragments themselves continue to move because of the agitation of the fire, many of them join together <note>original: "conspirant"; literally "breathe together" or move in concert</note> in the same movement, and the whole liquid melted from them is distinguished into various little droplets or lumps <note>original: "grumulos"</note>: in such a way, clearly, that all those fragments which move together make up one droplet, as it were, which droplet immediately smooths and polishes its own surface by its motion. For by the encounter with other droplets, whatever is rough and angular in the fragments from which it is composed is pushed away from its surface toward the interior parts, and thus all the parts of each little droplet are joined together as tightly as possible.

<summary>Descartes provides a mechanical explanation for the smelting of iron and steel, suggesting that heat allows microscopic fragments to align their internal channels to accommodate the flow of "striated particles," eventually forming cohesive droplets.</summary>

# PART FOUR. 281

<margin>
141.
Why steel is very hard, rigid, and brittle.
</margin>
And the whole liquid, once separated into droplets or lumps <note>original: "grumulos"; refers to the small clusters or granules of metal forming in the melt</note> in this way, if it cools quickly, solidifies into steel that is exceedingly hard, rigid, and brittle, much like glass. It is hard because it consists of fragments <note>original: "ramentis"; Descartes uses this to describe the tiny, microscopic pieces of matter</note> joined very closely to one another. It is rigid—meaning that if it is bent, it returns of its own accord to its previous shape—because during that bending, the tiny surfaces of its fragments are not pulled apart; instead, only the shapes of the channels <note>original: "meatus"; the microscopic pathways through which Descartes believed "striated particles" flowed to create magnetism and cohesion</note> are altered, just as was said earlier regarding glass <sup>a</sup>. Finally, it is brittle because the droplets or lumps of which it is composed do not stick to each other except through the contact of their surfaces, and this contact can only be direct in very few and very small places.

<margin>
142.
The difference between steel and other types of iron.
</margin>
However, not all lumps of ore <note>original: "glebæ"</note> are equally suited to be turned into steel; and even those same lumps from which the best and hardest steel is usually made produce only common iron when they are melted by an unsuitable fire. For if the fragments of the ore are so angular and jagged that they stick to one another before they can fitly align their surfaces and be separated into droplets; or if the fire is not strong enough to divide the liquid into droplets and squeeze the fragments composing them together; or conversely, if the fire is so strong that it disturbs the proper positioning of those fragments: the result is not steel, but iron that is less hard and more flexible.

However, it is softened because all its particles are shaken by the heat; and if it is then cooled slowly, it does not regain its previous hardness, nor its rigidity, nor its brittleness, but becomes flexible like cheaper iron. For while it is cooled in this manner, the angular and jagged
<margin>5</margin> fragments <note>original: "ramenta"; Descartes' term for the tiny, microscopic pieces of matter that make up a body</note>, which had been pushed from the surfaces of the lumps <note>original: "grumulorum"; the small clusters or granules of metal forming in the melt</note> into their inner parts by the force of the heat, stretch themselves outward. Tangled with one another, like tiny hooks,
<margin>10</margin> they join certain lumps to others. Consequently, these fragments are no longer so tightly packed within their own lumps, and the lumps no longer adhere to each other through direct contact, but rather as if bound by certain hooks or barbs. Thus, the steel
<margin>15</margin> becomes not particularly hard, nor rigid, nor brittle, but soft and flexible. In this respect, it does not differ from common iron, except that if steel is heated to a glow again and then cooled quickly, its former hardness and rigidity are restored—but not in iron, or at least not to the same degree. The
<margin>20</margin> reason for this is that the fragments in steel are not so far removed from the position suited for maximum hardness that they cannot easily resume it by the force of fire and retain it during very rapid cooling. However, since they never had such a position in iron, they never resume it.
<margin>25</margin> Indeed, to cool glowing steel or iron very quickly, it is usually plunged into water or other cold liquids; conversely, it is put into oil or other fatty substances so that it cools more slowly. And because the harder and more rigid it becomes, the more brittle it also turns, so that swords, saws, files, or other
<margin>30</margin> instruments may be made from it, it should not always be quenched in the coldest liquids, but in temperate ones, according to...

**144.**
**What the difference is between the channels of a magnet, steel, and iron.**
</margin>
As for the <term>channels</term><note>original: "meatus"; the microscopic pores or passages within a solid body through which Descartes believed subtle matter flowed</note> suitable for receiving <term>striated particles</term><note>original: "particulis striatis"; screw-shaped particles that Descartes theorized were responsible for magnetic force</note>, it is clear enough from what has been said <gloss>See Articles 134-140, pages 276-280.</gloss> that there must be many of them both in steel and in iron. It is also clear that these channels are more complete and perfect in steel, and that the ends of the small branches <note>original: "ramulorum"; the tiny, bristle-like protrusions within the metal's pores</note> protruding into their coils,
<margin>10</margin> once they have been bent in one direction, cannot be as easily bent back in the opposite direction—though even in steel, they are more easily bent than in a magnet. And finally, in all these channels—whether in steel or other iron—unlike in a magnet, their openings do not naturally turn in one direction to receive the striated particles
<margin>15</margin> coming from the <term>South</term><note>original: "Austro"</note>, and in the opposite direction to receive those coming from the <term>North</term><note>original: "Borea"</note>. Instead, their positions must be varied and uncertain, because they are disturbed by the agitation of fire. And in that very brief pause during which this
<margin>20</margin> | agitation of fire is stopped by the cold, only as many of those channels can be turned toward the South and North as there are striated particles coming from the Earth's poles seeking a path through them at that time. And because these striated particles do not match all the channels of the iron in
<margin>25</margin> number, all iron indeed receives some <term>magnetic force</term><note>original: "vim magneticam"</note> from the position it held relative to the parts of the Earth when it last cooled from a glow, or even from the position in which it has stood unmoved for a long time, if it has stood unmoved in that same position for a long duration. Yet,
<margin>30</margin> compared to the multitude of channels it contains, it could possess an even greater force.

<summary>Descartes explains that steel and iron contain internal channels for magnetic particles, but unlike a natural magnet, their orientation is disorganized by heat and only partially aligned by the Earth's magnetic field during cooling.</summary>

Meanwhile, however, as many new particles always arrive from the parts of the heavens <note>original: *cœli*; in Descartes's physics, this refers to the subtle matter of space</note> E and F, just as many depart through other parts of the heavens G and H, or are scattered on their journey and lose their shapes; not indeed by passing through the middle region of the Earth: because there they have passages <term>meatus</term> carved out to their specific measure, through which they flow most rapidly without any obstacle; but by returning through the air, water, and other bodies of the outer earth...

<margin>
149. What the poles of a magnet are.
</margin>
And just as in the Earth, so in the magnet: the middle point of that part in which are the openings of the passages through which the striated particles coming from the Southern part of the heavens <note>original: *Australi cœli parte*</note> enter, we shall call the **Southern pole**; and the middle point of the other part, through which these striated particles exit, and others coming from the North enter, we shall call the **Northern pole**. Nor are we concerned that others commonly call the pole we call "Southern" the "Northern"; for the common people—who alone have the right to authorize through frequent use names that are poorly suited to things—are not accustomed to speak of this matter.

But when the spheres merge into one, it is then primarily easier for the striated particles coming from O toward S to proceed straight as far as P—taking the place of those which were returning from T through X to S and *b*—than to be reflected toward V and R (where those coming from X proceed without difficulty). It is also easier for those coming from P toward S to proceed as far as O than to be reflected toward X (where those coming from V also proceed without difficulty); and thus these striated particles pass through these two magnets O and P just as if they were a single magnet.

Furthermore, it is easier for the striated particles proceeding straight from O to P, and from P to O, to expel the **intermediate air** <note>original: *aërem intermedium*</note> from S toward R and T into the place [previously occupied by] magnets O and P, and thus to cause these magnets to approach each other until they touch at S, than to struggle through all that air from A to *b* and from V to X; these two paths become shorter as these two magnets [approach] each other...

<margin>154. Why they occasionally repel one another <sup>a</sup>.</margin>
However, the like-named poles <note>original: *poli cognomines*; meaning North-to-North or South-to-South</note> of two magnets do not approach each other in this way; instead, if they are moved too close, they move apart. This happens because the **striated particles** <term>striated particles: Descartes imagined these as tiny, screw-threaded bits of matter that can only pass through channels turning in one specific direction</term> coming from the pole of one magnet, which faces the other magnet, cannot enter this second one. They require some space between these two magnets through which they may pass, so that they can return to the other pole of the magnet from which they first exited. Specifically, those exiting from O through pole A, since they cannot enter into P through its pole *a*, require some space between A and *a* through which they may pass toward V and B. By the same force with which they moved from B to A, they push magnet P; likewise, those exiting from P push magnet O—at least when their axes BA and *ab* are in the same straight line.

<margin>155. Why the parts of magnetic segments that were joined before cutting also repel each other <sup>a</sup>.</margin>
And from this, it is very easily understood why, if a magnet is cut by a plane parallel to the line drawn through its poles, and a segment is freely suspended above the magnet from which it was cut, it spontaneously turns itself and seeks a position opposite to the one it had before. Thus, if parts A and *a* were previously joined, and likewise B and *b*, afterward *b* turns itself toward A, and *a* toward B. This is because, previously, the **Southern** <note>original: *Auſtralis*</note> part of one was joined to the **Southern** part of the other, and the **Northern** <note>original: *Borealis*</note> to the **Northern**. After the division, however, the **striated particles** <term>striated particles: Descartes imagined these as tiny, threaded bits of matter that can only pass through channels turning in one specific direction, like a screw through a nut</term> exiting through the Southern part of one must enter through the Northern part of the other; and those exiting through the Northern part must enter through the Southern.

<margin>156. Why two points that were previously contiguous in one magnet become poles of different power in its fragments <sup>b</sup>.</margin>
It is also manifest why, if a magnet is divided by a plane cutting the line drawn through the poles at right angles, the poles of the segments that touched each other before the cutting—such as *b* and *a*—are of opposite power. This is because the **striated particles** that exit through one of those poles must enter through the other.

<margin>158. Why a magnet communicates its force to iron brought near it <sup>a</sup>.</margin>
Nor is it surprising that iron, when brought near a magnet, acquires magnetic force from it. For it already possesses passageways <note>original: *meatus*</note> suitable for receiving the **striated particles**, and nothing is lacking for it to acquire that force, except that certain tiny ends of the "branches" from which its filaments consist protrude here and there in those passageways. These must all be bent toward one and the same direction in those channels through which the **striated particles** coming from the **South** <note>original: *Auſtro*</note> can pass, and toward the opposite direction in others. But when a magnet is brought near, the **striated particles**, rushing into the passageways of the iron with great force and in great abundance—like a torrent—bend these ends of the "branches" in this manner; and thus they give the iron everything that was required for magnetic force.

<margin>159. Why iron receives magnetic force in different ways, according to the various modes in which it is applied to the magnet <sup>b</sup>.</margin>

**160.**
Why oblong iron only receives this power along its length.<sup>a</sup>
</margin>
One might only ask why these **striated particles**, entering the part S of the iron from the magnet's pole A, do not continue straight toward E, but are instead reflected here and there toward R and T; and why this iron receives magnetic power along its length rather than its width. But the explanation is straightforward: they find much more open and easy paths within the iron than in the air, and they are therefore reflected back from the air toward the iron.

<margin>
**161.**
Why a magnet loses nothing of its power, even though it communicates it to iron.<sup>b</sup>
</margin>
The answer is also easy if one asks why a magnet loses nothing of its power when it communicates it to iron. For no change occurs in the magnet simply because the **striated particles** exiting it enter iron rather than any other body—except perhaps that, by passing more freely through iron than through other bodies, they exit the magnet even more abundantly when iron is joined to it. Thus, far from its power being diminished, it is actually increased.

<margin>
**162.**
*Why this power is communicated to iron very quickly, but is strengthened by the passage of time.* <note>original Latin: "Cur hæc vis celerrimè ferro communicetur, sed diuturnitate temporis in eo confirmetur"</note>
</margin>
This power reaches the iron in a very short time because the **striated particles** <term>striated particles: Descartes' theoretical "screw-shaped" particles that flow through magnetic channels</term> flow through it with great speed; however, it is strengthened within the iron by a long duration, because the longer the ends of the small "branches" <term>branches: microscopic protrusions Descartes imagined within iron that act like one-way valves</term> have remained bent in one direction, the more difficult it is for them to be bent back in the opposite direction.

<margin>
**163.**
*Why steel is more suited to receiving this power than common iron.* <note>original Latin: "Cur chalybs ad eam recipiendam aptior sit, quàm vilius ferrum"</note>
</margin>
Steel receives this power more strongly than common iron because it contains more numerous and more perfect passages suited for receiving the **striated particles**. It also preserves this power more consistently because the ends of the "branches" protruding into those passages are less flexible <note>meaning they are stiffer and hold their new shape better than those in soft iron</note>.

<margin>
**164.**
*Why a greater power is communicated to it by a more perfect magnet than by a less perfect one.* <note>original Latin: "Cur major ei communicetur à perfectiore magnete quàm à minùs perfecto"</note>
</margin>
A greater power is communicated to the iron by a larger and more perfect magnet for two reasons: first, because the **striated particles** rush into the iron's passages with more force and bend the ends of the internal branches further; and second, because many particles rushing in at once open more of these passages for themselves. It should be noted that there are actually more of these passages in steel—which consists entirely of iron filings—than in a magnet, which contains a great deal of stony matter in which the iron filings are embedded. Therefore, when only a few **striated particles** from a weak magnet enter the iron, they do not open all the passages, but only a few—specifically those that were closed by the most flexible ends of the branches.

**165.**

</margin>
From this it follows that even common iron—in which the ends of these branches are very flexible—receives power from the Earth itself. The Earth is indeed the largest magnet, but it is quite de- <note>The text ends mid-sentence; "de-" likely begins "debilis" (weak) or "demissior" (lower/fainter) in reference to the Earth's magnetic intensity compared to a concentrated lodestone.</note>

But I am easily convinced that the **declination** <note>the angle at which a compass needle deviates from true north</note> is not entirely the same, nor perhaps even as great, in a magnet positioned this way as in one whose poles are equally distant from the Earth. For the **striated particles** <term>striated particles: Descartes’ theoretical "screws" of matter that create magnetic force by flowing through specific channels</term>, in this upper region of the Earth, do not only return from one pole to another through lines equally distant from its center, but also everywhere (except under the equator) some ascend from its inner parts; and the rotation of a magnet held upright above the poles depends on these latter [ascending particles], while the declination depends chiefly on the former [returning particles].

<margin>**171. Why the magnet attracts iron.ᵇ**</margin>
Furthermore, the magnet attracts **iron**, or rather, the magnet and the iron move toward each other; for there is no actual "pulling" occurring there, but as soon as the iron is within the **sphere of activity** <term>sphere of activity: the "field" or range of a magnet's influence</term> of the magnet, it borrows power from it. The **striated particles**, emerging from both, expel the intervening air; this causes both to approach each other just as two magnets do. Indeed, iron moves even more freely than a magnet, because it consists only of those fragments in which the striated particles have their passages, whereas a magnet is weighed down by much stony matter.

**175.**
How and why the force of one magnet increases or diminishes the force of another.ᵃ
</margin>

The force of a single magnet is increased or diminished in various ways by the approach of another magnet or piece of iron. But there is one general rule in this matter: whenever these magnets are positioned so that one sends **striated particles** <term>striated particles: microscopic, grooved particles shaped like screws that Descartes theorized were the cause of magnetic attraction</term> into the other, they assist each other; conversely, if one draws those particles away from the other, they hinder each other. This is because the more quickly and abundantly these particles flow through each magnet, the greater the **virtue** <note>original: "virtus," referring to the inherent power or magnetic strength</note> in it; and more particles, more highly agitated, can be sent from one magnet or piece of iron into another than can be sent from the air, or any other body placed in its stead, when the magnet is absent. Thus, not only when the **South pole** <note>original: "polus Australis"</note> of one magnet is joined to the **North pole** <note>original: "polo Boreali"</note> of the other do they help each other to support iron hung from their other poles, but also when they are separated and the iron is placed between them both. For example <note>original: "Exempli gratia"</note>, magnet C is assisted by magnet F in holding the iron DE joined to it;

and vice-versa, magnet F is assisted by magnet C in supporting the end E of this iron in the air. For the iron could be so heavy that it could not be supported by magnet F alone if the other end D were resting on any body other than magnet C.

<margin>**177.** Why a weak magnet, or a piece of iron, can pull iron away from a stronger magnet when in contact with it.ᶜ</margin>
From this, it is clear why a weak magnet, or even a small piece of iron, often pulls another piece of iron away from a stronger magnet. It must be noted that this never happens unless the weaker magnet touches that iron which it is pulling from the stronger one. Indeed, when two magnets touch an oblong piece of iron with their opposite poles—one at one end and the other at the other—and then these two magnets are moved away from each other, the iron in between does not always stick to the weaker one, nor always to the stronger one. Instead, it sticks sometimes to one, sometimes to the other; and I believe there is no reason why it should stick to one rather than the other, except that it touches the one it sticks to over a larger surface area than it does the other.

### PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

...so that only the weak **magnetic power** <note>original: *vis magnetica*</note> of the entire Earth is felt here among us.

<margin>181. Why no other body placed in between hinders this power.</margin>
But besides iron or a magnet, no other body can be placed in the position of the plate **CD** that would prevent the magnet **AB** from exerting its power on the **needle EF**. For in this outer Earth, we have no body—no matter how solid and hard—that does not contain many **pores** <note>original: *meatus*. Descartes envisions these as tiny channels or passages within matter.</note>. These pores are not specifically shaped to the measure of the **striated particles** <note>Descartes’ "striated particles" are screw-shaped pieces of matter that he believed were responsible for magnetic attraction by fitment into specific channels.</note>, but are much larger, as they also receive the **globules of the second element** <note>In Cartesian physics, the "second element" refers to the subtle, fluid matter that fills the solar system and carries light.</note>. Therefore, these striated particles can pass through those pores no less freely than through the air, in which they also encounter those same globules of the second element.

<image-desc>A schematic diagram of a magnetic experiment. A central rectangular block marked A and B is enclosed by an upper boundary marked C and E, and a lower boundary marked D and F. A base or ground level is marked G and H. The space between the boundaries contains horizontal and shaded lines representing the orientation of magnetic particles.</image-desc>

<margin>182. Why an unsuitable position of the magnet gradually diminishes its strength.</margin>
If iron or a magnet is held for a long time in a different orientation toward the Earth (or toward other neighboring magnets) than it would naturally turn itself if nothing hindered its motion, it gradually loses its strength by this very fact. This is because the **striated particles** coming from the Earth or other nearby magnets encounter its pores at an oblique or reverse angle, and thus gradually change and corrupt the shapes of those pores.

<margin>183. Why rust, humidity, and position also diminish it, and intense fire completely removes it.</margin>
Finally, magnetic power is greatly diminished by humidity, **rust** <note>original: *rubigo*</note>, and position; and it is completely destroyed by a powerful fire. For rust, blooming out from the **iron filings** <note>original: *ramentis*. These are tiny scrapings or fragments of the metal.</note>, blocks the openings of the pores; moisture in the air and the positioning of the object do the same, as they are the beginnings of rust. The agitation of **fire**, however, completely disturbs the position of those filings. And I think nothing—

<margin>185. What the cause of this attraction in glass might be.</margin>
Indeed, from the manner in which it was said to be generated <a> <note>original: *Art. cxxv, p. 270*. Referring to Article 125, page 270.</note>, it is easily gathered that, besides those larger intervals through which the **globules of the second element** <term>globuli secundi elementi; in Descartes’ physics, the "second element" consists of spherical particles that make up the sky and air and transmit light</term> can pass in all directions, many **oblong cracks** <note>original: *rimulas*</note> are also found between its particles. Since these are too narrow to receive those globules, they grant passage only to the **matter of the first element** <term>materia primi elementi; the most fluid and finest matter which fills the gaps between all other particles</term>. It must be thought that this matter of the first element, accustomed to taking on the shapes of all the passages it enters, is formed into certain thin, wide, and oblong **ribbons** <note>original: *fasciolas*</note> as it passes through those cracks. Since these ribbons do not find similar cracks in the surrounding air, they keep themselves within the glass, or at least do not wander far from it; instead, being wound around its particles, they flow from some of its cracks into others in a kind of circular motion. 

For although the matter of the first element is extremely fluid, because it nonetheless consists of tiny parts agitated unequally—as I explained in articles 87 and 88 of the third part <b> <note>original: *Ci-avant p. 142 et 144*. Referring to pages 142 and 144 earlier in the volume.</note>—it is consistent with reason to believe that many of its most violently stirred bits constantly migrate from the glass into the air, and others return from the air into the glass in their place. However, since those that return are not all equally stirred, those with the least agitation are expelled toward the cracks (for which no corresponding passages exist in the air). There, clinging to one another, they compose those ribbons; as a result, these ribbons acquire their shapes **over the course of time** <note>original: *successu temporis*</note>...

# PART FOUR

...fixed shapes, which they cannot easily change. However, because they do not find such easy paths there, they immediately return to the glass, bringing with them the smaller bodies in whose passages they have become entangled.

<margin>186. That the same cause for this attraction appears to exist in other things as well.</margin>
Moreover, what we have noted here regarding glass must also be assumed for most other bodies: namely, that certain gaps are found between their particles. Since these gaps are too narrow to admit the **globules of the second element** <term>globuli secundi elementi; in Cartesian physics, these are spherical particles that make up the sky and air and transmit light</term>, they receive only the **matter of the first element** <term>materia primi elementi; the finest, most fluid matter that fills the spaces between all other particles</term>. Because these gaps are larger than those in the surrounding air that are open only to this first element, they become filled with its less agitated fragments. These fragments, joined to one another, form particles with various shapes according to the diversity of those gaps; for the most part, they are thin, wide, and oblong like **little ribbons** <note>original: *fasciolarum*</note>. Thus, by winding around the particles of the bodies they inhabit, they can move continuously. For the gaps from which they take their shape must be very narrow to exclude the globules of the second element; unless they were oblong like cracks, they could hardly be larger than the spaces between air particles not occupied by those same second-element globules. Therefore, although I do not deny that another cause of attraction previously explained <a> <note>original: *Art. clxxxiv, p. 311*. Referring to Article 184, page 311.</note> might perhaps take place in some bodies, because it is not so general and this attraction is observed in a great many bodies, I think there is no other cause in them than...

Furthermore, I would like it to be noted here that those particles in the **pores** <term>meatus; the microscopic channels or passages within a solid body</term> of earthly bodies, formed from the **matter of the first element** <term>materia primi elementi; the finest, most fluid matter that fills the spaces between all other particles</term>, can be the causes not only of various attractions, such as those seen in amber and in the magnet, but also of innumerable other and marvelous effects. For the particles that are formed in each individual body have something unique in their shape, by which they differ from all others formed in different bodies. Since they retain the intense agitation of the first element, of which they are parts, it can happen for the smallest of reasons that they either do not wander outside the body in which they are contained, but only run back and forth within its pores; or, on the contrary, they may depart from it very quickly and, pervading all other earthly bodies, reach places however remote in the shortest time. There, finding matter suitable for receiving their action, they may produce some rare effects. 

And indeed, whoever considers how marvelous the properties of the magnet and of fire are, and how different they are from those we commonly observe in other bodies; how a huge flame can be kindled from a tiny spark in a moment of time, and how great its power is; to what an immense distance the **fixed stars** <term>stellae fixae; the distant stars that appear stationary relative to each other, unlike planets</term> spread their light in every direction; and the rest, whose causes, in my judgment, I have deduced with sufficient evidence from principles known to and admitted by all—namely, the **shape, size, position, and motion** <note>These are the fundamental mechanical properties Descartes uses to replace spiritual or magical explanations of nature.</note> of the particles of matter—will easily persuade themselves that there are no powers in stones or plants so **occult** <note>original: *occultas*; referring to "hidden" qualities that medieval philosophers could not explain</note>, and no instances of **sympathy or antipathy** <term>sympathia and antipathia; traditional terms for the mysterious attraction or repulsion between objects, like a magnet and iron</term>...

...affects the mind with a certain sense of cheerfulness; and any other causes that move those small nerves in the same way also produce that same sense of joy. Thus, the imagination of enjoying some good does not contain the sense of joy in itself; instead, the spirits <note>original: "spiritus"; Descartes refers to "animal spirits," which he envisioned as a very subtle wind or flame that traveled through the nerves to transmit signals</note> are sent <margin>5</margin> from the brain to the muscles into which those nerves are inserted. With their help, the openings of the heart are expanded, and its small nerves are moved with that specific motion from which the sensation of joy must follow.

So, when pleasant news is heard, the mind first judges it and rejoices with that **intellectual joy** <note>original: "gaudio intellectuali"</note> <margin>10</margin> which occurs without any commotion of the body. Because of this, the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that held that a wise person should be governed by reason and remain unmoved by physical passions</note> said that such joy could exist in the "wise man" <note>the idealized Stoic sage who is free from irrational emotions</note>. By the same reasoning, when blood is too thick and flows poorly into the chambers of the heart, not expanding sufficiently there, it creates a different motion in those same nerves of the heart's region. When this motion is communicated to the brain, it produces <margin>20</margin> a sense of **sadness** in the mind, even though the mind itself may not know why it is sad. Many other causes can produce the same effect.

Furthermore, other motions of those small nerves produce other **affections** <term>affectus: translated here as "affections" or "passions," referring to states where the mind is being acted upon by the body</term>, such as love, hate, fear, anger, and so on. This is true insofar as they are <margin>25</margin> merely affections or "passions of the soul" <note>original: "animi pathemata"; from the Greek 'pathos', meaning something one undergoes or suffers</note>—that is, insofar as they are certain **confused thoughts** that the mind does not produce by itself alone, but which it experiences because it is intimately joined to the body. For the **distinct thoughts** that we have regarding things to be embraced, or <margin>30</margin> desired, or avoided, are entirely different in kind from these affections. There is no different explanation for the **natural appetites**, such as hunger and thirst, which [arise] from the nerves of the stomach...

<margin>191. On the external senses: and first, on touch.</margin>
As for the external senses, five are commonly counted, based on five different kinds of objects that move the nerves serving them. These movements excite an equal number of types of **confused thoughts** <note>original: "cogitationum confusarum"; in Descartes's philosophy, "confused thoughts" refers to sensory perceptions like color or pain, which feel vivid but do not provide a clear mathematical understanding of the object itself</note> in the soul. First, the nerves ending in the skin over the entire body can be touched by any physical objects. Through the skin, these nerves are moved as a whole: in one way by an object’s hardness, in another by its weight, in another by heat, and in another by humidity. In as many different ways as the nerves are moved (or hindered from their ordinary movement), they excite just as many different sensations in the mind. From these, the various qualities of touch are named. Furthermore, when these nerves are shaken more violently than usual, but not so much that the body is harmed, a sensation of **tickling** <note>original: "titillatio"</note> occurs. This is naturally pleasing to the mind because it signals the strength of the body to which the mind is so closely joined. But if some injury results from that movement, the sensation of **pain** is produced. From this, it is clear why physical pleasure and pain—though opposite as sensations—differ so little in their physical cause.

<margin>192. On taste.</margin>
Next, other nerves are spread through the tongue and nearby areas. These are moved in different ways by the particles of bodies that have been separated from one another and are floating in the saliva within the mouth. Depending on the different shapes of these particles, they produce the sensations of different flavors.

This is how we gain the sense of light and colors, as I have already explained sufficiently in my works *Optics* and *Meteorology*.

# PRINCIPLES OF PHILOSOPHY

...the nerves that extend from the external limbs to the brain <note>original: "illud," referring back to the brain mentioned on the previous page</note> are obstructed, the sensation of those limbs is likewise lost. And finally, this is proven by the fact that pain is sometimes felt as if it were in certain limbs where there is no cause for pain, but rather the cause is in other parts through which the nerves pass as they stretch from the limbs to the brain. This last point can be demonstrated by countless experiments, but it will suffice to provide one here. 

There was a certain girl who had a hand affected by a serious disease. Her eyes were covered whenever the **Surgeon** <term>Chirurgus; at this time, surgeons were distinct from physicians, focusing on manual operations and amputations</term> approached, so that she would not be disturbed by the sight of the surgical equipment. After a few days, her arm was **amputated** <note>original: "amputatum"</note> up to the elbow because of **gangrene** <term>the death of body tissue due to a lack of blood flow or a serious bacterial infection</term> spreading within it. Cloths were substituted in place of the arm so that she was completely unaware she had lost it. Meanwhile, she complained of feeling various pains, sometimes in one finger of the hand that had been cut off, and sometimes in another. This certainly could not have happened for any other reason than that the nerves, which previously descended from the brain to the hand and were now terminated in the arm near the elbow, were being moved there in the same way they had been moved before when they were in the hand, in order to impress upon the **soul** <note>original: "animæ"</note> residing in the brain the sensation of this or that aching finger.

<margin>
197.
That the mind is of such a nature that various sensations can be excited in it by bodily motion alone.
</margin>

It is proven next that such is the nature of our **mind** <note>original: "mentem"</note> that, from the mere fact that certain motions occur in the body, it can be driven toward any **thoughts** <note>original: "cogitationes"</note> whatsoever, even those that bear no likeness to the motions themselves; and specifically toward those confused thoughts called **senses** or **sensations** <note>original: "sensationes"</note>. For we see that words, whether uttered by the mouth or merely written, excite all kinds of thoughts and emotions in our minds. On the same paper, with the same pen and ink, if only the tip of the pen [is moved] in a certain way...

### PART FOUR

...if [the pen] is drawn across the paper, it will carve out letters which will excite thoughts of battles, storms, and furies, as well as feelings of indignation and sadness in the minds of readers. But if the pen is moved in another, almost similar way, it will produce very different thoughts of tranquility, peace, and pleasantness, and the entirely contrary feelings of love and joy. It will perhaps be answered that writing or speech does not **immediately** excite feelings or images of things in the mind, but only various **understandings** <note>original: "intellectiones"</note>; and it is only upon the occasion of these understandings that the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note> then forms images of various things within itself. 

But what shall be said regarding the sensation of **pain** <note>original: "doloris"</note> and **tickling** <term>titillatio; used here to describe a light, pleasant, or irritating physical sensation</term>? A sword is applied to our body and cuts it: from this alone follows pain, which is surely no less different from the **local motion** <term>motus localis; the physical movement of an object from one place to another</term> of the sword or the body being cut than color, or sound, or smell, or taste. And therefore, since we clearly see that the sensation of pain is excited in us by the mere fact that some parts of our body are moved locally by the contact of some other body, we can conclude that our mind is of such a nature that it can experience the affections of all other senses from certain local motions.

That there exist insensible particles of bodies.

But I consider many particles in individual bodies which are perceived by no sense: a fact that perhaps those who take their own senses as the measure of things knowable <note>Descartes is critiquing the narrow view that only things we can see or touch are "real" or "knowable."</note> do not approve of. Nor do I think any person using reason would deny that it is far better to judge—by the example of those things we perceive by sense to happen in large bodies—about those things that happen in minute corpuscles (which escape the sense only because of their smallness), than to explain these...

### PART FOUR ###

...to devise some new things, I know not what, which have no resemblance to those things that are perceived by the senses.

<margin>
202.
That the philosophy of Democritus differs no less from our own than from the common view.
<note>original: "Democriti Philosophiam non minùs differre à nostrâ, quàm à vulgari."</note>
</margin>
Yet Democritus also imagined certain <term>corpuscles</term> <note>Small physical particles; the building blocks of matter in mechanical philosophy.</note> having various shapes, sizes, and motions, from whose accumulation and mutual collisions all sensible bodies arose; and yet his way of philosophizing is commonly rejected by everyone. But no one ever rejected it because it considered certain bodies so small that they escaped the senses, which were said to have various sizes, shapes, and motions; because no one can doubt that many such things truly exist, as has just been shown. But it was rejected, first, because he supposed those corpuscles to be <term>indivisible</term> <note>The word "atom" literally means "uncuttable." Descartes disagreed, arguing that because matter is extension, it can always be mathematically divided further.</note>, on which account I also reject it; secondly, because he imagined there to be a <term>vacuum</term> <note>An empty space containing no matter. Descartes believed the universe was a "plenum," entirely filled with matter.</note> around them, which I demonstrate cannot exist; thirdly, because he attributed gravity to them, which I understand as belonging to no body when viewed alone, but only insofar as it depends on the position and motion of other bodies and is referred to them; and finally, because he did not show how individual things arose from the collision of corpuscles alone, or if he did show it for some, his explanations were not all coherent with one another: at least as far as can be judged from those things recorded of his opinions. Whether, however, those things which I have written so far on Philosophy are sufficiently coherent, I leave for others to judge.

</margin>

He argues that his system is more coherent because it explains gravity and the formation of objects through the relative motion of particles.</summary>

...recognize. To which I respond: that I have first considered, in a general way, from the simplest and most well-known principles—the knowledge of which is implanted in our minds by nature—what the principal differences might be between the sizes, shapes, and positions of bodies which, because of their extreme smallness, are imperceptible to the senses; and I have considered what sensible effects would follow from their various encounters.

<margin>5</margin> And then, whenever I noticed similar effects in things perceived by the senses, I judged that they arose from a similar encounter of such bodies; especially since it seemed that no other way of explaining them could be devised.

<margin>10</margin> In this, man-made objects have helped me not a little: for I recognize no difference between them and natural bodies, except that the operations of things made by art <note>In this context, "art" refers to human craft, technology, and engineering.</note> are, for the most part, carried out by instruments

<margin>15</margin> large enough to be easily perceived by the senses—for this is required so that they can be fashioned by human hands. On the other hand, natural effects almost always depend on certain mechanisms so minute that they

<margin>20</margin> escape all our senses. And certainly, there are no rules in <term>Mechanics</term> <note>original: "Mechanicâ"; the study of the motion of objects and the forces that act on them.</note> that do not also belong to <term>Physics</term> <note>original: "Physicam"; at this time, "physics" referred broadly to the study of the natural world.</note>, of which it is a branch or a species. It is no less natural for a

<margin>25</margin> clock, composed of these or those wheels, to indicate the hours, than it is for a tree, arising from this or that seed, to produce its particular fruits. Therefore, just as those who are practiced in examining <term>automata</term> <note>original: "automatis"; self-moving machines, like clockwork statues or mechanical birds.</note>, when they know the purpose of a machine and see some of its parts, can easily guess from those parts how the other parts they cannot see were made; in the same way, from the sensible effects and visible parts of natural bodies, I have endeavored to investigate what their causes and their imperceptible particles are like.

<margin>30</margin>

<page-num>329</page-num>
<header>Part Four</header>
<sig>42</sig>
<meta>310. Works Vol. III.</meta>

...that external things can be sensed, unless some <term>local motion</term> <note>original: "motus localis"; Descartes refers to the physical movement of matter through space, arguing that sensations like light or heat are caused by particles physically striking our nerves.</note> is excited by them in our nerves. <margin>**207.** *But I submit all my works to the authority of the Church.*</margin>
Nevertheless, mindful of my own insignificance, I affirm nothing. Instead, I submit all these findings both to the authority of the Catholic Church and to the judgments of those more prudent than myself. I would not wish for anything to be believed by anyone unless they are persuaded of it by evident and invincible reason.

<meta>This page serves as the editorial introduction to the second part of Volume VIII of the works of René Descartes. It follows the publication history of his polemical writings against Gisbertus Voetius.</meta>

# NOTICE

The second part of this volume VIII contains, as we announced in volume VII, pages xi–xii of the Preface, the following three pieces by Descartes:

1. *Letter to the Most Celebrated Man, Mr. Gisbertus Voetius* <note>original: "Epistola ad Celeberrimum Virum D. Gisbertum Voetium"</note>;
2. *Letter of Defense, or Apologetic Complaint* <note>original: "Lettre Apologétique, ou Querela Apologetica"</note>;
3. *Notes on a Certain Broadside, etc.* <note>original: "Notæ in Programma quoddam"</note>.

The first of these three pieces appeared in the month of May 1643; the second bears the dates of June 16, 1645, and February 21, 1648; the third is from the end of 1647. Let us examine all three in succession.

## I

The first edition of the *Letter to Voet* appeared simultaneously in Latin and Flemish:

1. *Letter of <term>RENÉ DESCARTES</term> to the most celebrated Man, Mr. Gisbertus Voetius. In which are examined two books, recently published together at Utrecht on behalf of Voetius: one regarding the Brotherhood of Mary, the other regarding Cartesian Philosophy.* <note>original: "Epistola RENATI DES-CARTES, Ad celeberrimum Virum D. Gisbertum Voetium..."</note> (Amsterdam, Published by Louis Elzevir, <term>1643</term> <note>original: CIƆ. IƆC. XLIII. This is an older form of Roman numeral notation where CIƆ represents 1,000 and IƆC represents 600.</note> Printer's mark: Minerva. <term>Small duodecimo</term> <note>original: "Pet. in-12," a book size where each sheet is folded into twelve leaves, roughly 5 by 7 inches.</note>, 6 preliminary leaves, 282 pages, 3 blank leaves.)

2. *Letter of <term>RENÉ DESCARTES</term> to Mr. Gisbertus Voetius. In which are considered two books, recently published for the same Voetius at Utrecht, the first...* <note>original: "Brief van RENÉ DES CARTES, aen D. Gisbertus Voetius..."</note>

<summary>This preface outlines the publication history of three of Descartes' polemical works from the 1640s, focusing specifically on his written defense against the Dutch theologian Gisbertus Voetius.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, Gisbertus Voetius, Louis Elzevir, Utrecht, 1643, bibliography, polemics, Letter to Voet</keywords>

--- Page 382 ---
<meta>This page continues the bibliographic description of the early editions of Descartes' Letter to Voet, specifically detailing the Flemish version and the subsequent Latin reprints included in the Meditations.</meta>

# NOTICE

...entitled *The Confraternity of Mary* <note>original: "Confraternitas Mariana"</note>, and the other, *Cartesian Philosophy* <note>original: "Philosophia Cartesiana"</note>. (At Amsterdam, by Rieuwerdt Dircksz. van Baardt, in the year 1643. <term>Quarto</term> <note>original: "In-4," a book size where each sheet is folded into four leaves.</note>, 8 preliminary leaves, and 160 pages.)

The Latin text was reprinted, starting from 1650, in the same volume as the *Meditations*, in an *Appendix* with separate pagination. This appendix first included the 5th and 7th Objections and Replies, followed by the *Letter to Father Dinet*. It can be found there in the five successive editions by the Elzeviers in 1650, 1654, 1663, 1670, and 1678; and from 1685 onward, in the editions by the Blaeus in Amsterdam. (See our volume VII, pages viii–x of the *Notice*, and page xxiv.)

The Flemish text appeared in the same place in the Flemish editions of the *Works of Descartes*, translated by Glazemaker. This text, moreover, was itself only a translation, according to a note in Descartes' own hand. This note was written, it is true, regarding the *Apologetic Letter* mentioned below, but it undoubtedly applies equally to the *Letter to Voet*:

> "I have had this writing translated into Flemish; but because it is a language that I understand very little, I pray those who read it to have regard principally for the French, for which alone I can answer." (See volume V, page 125, lines 3–6.)

We are therefore sufficiently authorized not to include the Flemish translation in the present edition, but only the original, which is here in Latin.

This text, in all successive editions from 1650 onwards, is identical to the 1643 printing. We therefore only had to obtain this <term>first edition</term> <note>original: "édition princeps"</note>, which is quite rare (there is a copy in the City Library of Nancy), and reproduce it: no difficulty arose in the reconstruction of the text.

As for the date and all the circumstances surrounding the publication of the *Letter to Voet*, this is not the place to recount them in this *Notice*. They can be found in many parts of the *Correspondence* (letters from December 7, 1642, March 23, April 23, May 30, June 6, 9, and 28, 1643, etc., in volume III, pages...

## II

The *Letter of Apology to the Magistrates (or Vroedschap)* <note>A Dutch term for the council of elders or city regents who governed the municipality.</note> *of Utrecht* presented first of all a difficulty regarding the text. Which text should one choose, indeed?

We know that the papers, for which this inventory was prepared, were transported from Stockholm to Paris and finally placed in the hands of <term>Clerselier</term> <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the primary editor of Descartes’s posthumous works and a devoted follower of his philosophy.</note>. (See volume I, pages xvii–xviii of the *Introduction*.) One can therefore be certain that the French text, published by him in 1667, is perfectly authentic. Clerselier, moreover, judged it to be of great importance himself; consequently, he gave it the first place in volume III of the *Letters* and specifically highlighted it to the Reader in the *Preface* to that volume. (See volume V, page 652, lines 17–26, of the present edition.) We shall therefore follow it with complete confidence.

However, this *Apologetic Letter* seems to have been written first in Latin. Documents retrieved from the <term>Archives of Utrecht</term> and published by us previously (volume IV, page 226) state this in explicit terms:
> "June 13 (New Style, June 23), 1645. — *Read a Latin Letter from Descartes to the Burgomasters and <term>Town Council</term> <note>The "Vroedschap" was the governing council of Dutch cities, composed of wealthy and influential citizens.</note> of this City (Utrecht), dated at Egmond the 16th of this month, New Style, which the Secretary is to translate.*" <note>original Dutch: "Gelesen een Latijnse Missive..."</note>

Later, thinking of leaving the Netherlands, perhaps never to return, Descartes again addressed the *Apologetic Letter* to the Council of Utrecht, but this time in French and Flemish:
> "Tuesday the 14th (New Style, 24th) of March 1648. — *Received and read a letter from Monsieur Descartes dated at Egmond the 21st of February last, by which he sends to the Honorable Town Council two written copies, one in French and one in Dutch.*" <note>original Dutch: "'s Dynsdachs den XIIIIen..." Note that in the 17th century, the term "Duyts" was often used to refer to the local Dutch/Flemish language.</note> (See our volume V, page 125.)

it can still be seen, but with an additional note in <term>Descartes’s</term> hand, which we reproduced above on page IV, line 19: this text is only a translation, and not the original; and furthermore, it is a translation for which Descartes himself admits he cannot answer. We are therefore fully authorized to exclude this Flemish version from our edition and to retain only the two texts, Latin and French.

The simplest approach would be to consider both as being equally by Descartes, and to print them using the typeface reserved for the philosopher’s authentic texts. They would be placed side-by-side, and the reader could refer, at their discretion, to the Latin or the French for their greater convenience. However, this would implicitly admit two things: first, that the French text, published by <term>Clerselier</term> in 1667, is indeed the original that he found among the papers sent back from <term>Stockholm</term> (O); and second, that the Latin text, published in <term>Amsterdam</term> in 1656 and subsequently reproduced starting in 1683, is perfectly consistent with the other original found in those same papers (L). Now, while we can be certain regarding the French text, a doubt remains concerning the Latin text. The text published in Amsterdam in 1656 is, in fact, preceded by a *Preface* (which is unsigned, incidentally), where one reads this declaration (hereafter, p. 280, l. 6):

> "When he was about to set out for Sweden, <term>Descartes</term> <note>Original Latin: *Cartesius*.</note> (or, as the author of the *Preface* calls him, **our Hero** <note>Original Latin: *noster Heros*.</note>) left in these lands this Apology which we give to you, written by himself in French <note>Original Latin: *Gallicè*.</note> and translated into Latin <note>Original Latin: *Latinè*.</note> by a Friend, with the intention of publishing it if his private efforts proved unsuccessful."

This testimony is formal: Descartes, on the eve of his departure for Sweden, had left his *Apologetic Letter* in Holland, written in French, and it was a friend who translated it into Latin. The text published in 1656 would therefore be only a translation. Perhaps it differs very little from the Latin original, which also existed. Perhaps (the author of the *Preface* having been mistaken) it is that very original itself. But, for lack of being able to—
