Indeed, the *Apologetic Letter*, like the *Letter to Voet* <note>The *Letter to Voet* (Epistola ad Voetium) was Descartes's public defense against Gisbertus Voetius, a powerful Dutch theologian who accused him of atheism.</note> before it, requires—on almost every page, and often several times on the same page—clarifications borrowed from the pamphlets of the two <term>Voets</term> <note>Gisbertus Voetius and his son Paulus.</note>, father and son, of <term>Schoock</term> <note>Martinus Schoock, a student of Voetius who published the "Admiranda Methodus," a scathing critique of Descartes.</note>, of <term>Desmarets</term> <note>Samuel Des Marets (Maresius), another contemporary theologian involved in the controversy.</note>, and so on. Would they have appeared twice, in the corresponding places of the French and Latin texts? What a complication! We preferred to annotate only the main text, that is, the French text. The Latin text is printed without notes, but with cross-references, page by page, to the pagination of the preceding French text, and consequently to its commentary. # PREFACE <note>original: "ARGUMENTUM"</note>

Since I published certain specimens <note>Descartes refers here to the *Discourse on the Method* and its accompanying essays on optics, meteors, and geometry published in 1637.</note> of that Philosophy which I consider to be true and especially useful for human needs, many among the learned—and indeed, particularly those who are regarded <margin>5</margin> by everyone as exceptionally gifted and scholarly—have urged me to cultivate it further and to publish it in its entirety. But although I attribute much weight to their judgment, some others appear to offer an even more certain testimony in its favor: those nourished <margin>10</margin> on the controversies of the Schools <term>the Schools: Scholasticism, the traditional system of philosophy and theology based on Aristotle that dominated universities at the time.</term>, who labor with the greatest zeal to overwhelm it with curses and to extinguish it, as it were, in the blade <note>original: "in herbâ"; a metaphor for destroying something in its infancy or before it can bloom.</note>. For it has always been so free to philosophize, and so many have hitherto erred harmlessly regarding the knowledge of natural things, that if I were to be mistaken after all the others, no danger <margin>15</margin> to the human race need be feared from it; but if by chance I have found the truth, a great utility is to be expected. And therefore, it is possible that those who love the truth, on account of a slender and doubtful hope of finding it in my writings, might invite me to publish them. But there seems to be no cause why others <margin>20</margin> should attack my opinions with such bitterness, except...

->EPISTLE<-

...that they firmly persuade themselves that their own opinions are true, and they fear that, if the truth were known, no more honor would be given to those scholastic controversies <note>Scholasticism was the traditional system of philosophy and theology taught in universities, which Descartes sought to replace with a more certain, reason-based method.</note> in which their learning consists.

<margin>5</margin>Since, however, these men attack me not with reasons but only with slanders, I am not accustomed to answer them. But one of their number, Gisbertus Voetius <note>Gijsbert Voet (1589–1676), a Dutch Calvinist theologian and a fierce opponent of Descartes.</note>, not content, like the others, to accuse me of error and ignorance, invents such atrocious crimes against me, and <margin>10</margin>exercises his malice toward me in such indirect ways, that I judged his injuries should not be kept silent by me. And when, last year, he published a certain judgment in the name of the University of Utrecht <note>original: "Academiæ Vltrajectinæ"</note>, of which he was then Rector, in which he condemned my *Philosophy* <note>original: "Philoſophiam"</note> on the pretext that he imagined various false and absurd opinions <margin>15</margin>*to follow from it, conflicting with orthodox Theology*<gloss>Judgment of March 17, 1642, the text of which is reproduced in the *Letter to Father Dinet*, volume VII of the present edition, p. 590. See especially p. 593, lines 4-8.</gloss>: he forced me to include that judgment in a certain writing, which I then happened to have in press, adding a refutation of it, and at the same time a brief description of Voetius’s "virtues": so that, because <margin>20</margin>he attacked me not with reasons but only by authority, I might make known to all how much his authority should be worth, and compel him to produce those *false and absurd opinions, conflicting with orthodox Theology, which he had said follow from my Philosophy*. For although it is not permitted to ask the reason for a judgment from <margin>25</margin>those who exercise supreme power: certainly if he who has dared to condemn another, over whom he has no jurisdiction, [fails to provide] the causes of that condemnation to one asking...

### TO G. VOET.

...provides none, by this very fact he declares himself a slanderer.

Therefore, I was expecting some response from Voet, by which he might show us those opinions clashing with orthodox theology, and free himself from the suspicion of slander, when a lengthy book was published on his behalf, the title of which is *Cartesian Philosophy, or the Admirable Method of the New Philosophy of René Descartes* <margin>5</margin> ᵃ: but it appeared under the name of one of his disciples, who is a Professor of Philosophy at Groningen ᵇ, and no reasons were contained in it to prove or excuse what was previously written, but <margin>10</margin> only new slanders more atrocious than the earlier ones. For besides the insolence and cheapness of the insults worthy only of camp-servants <note>original: "calonibus" — refers to low-ranking servants or drudges, implying the language used was beneath a scholar</note>, nothing milder is asserted about me in that book than that *I deceitfully and quite secretly teach Atheism* ᶜ; and <margin>15</margin> of such an insolent and criminal curse no other proof is offered than that I wrote against Atheists, and many judge that I have solidly refuted them: so much so that nothing could ever be written in which a more evident and more inexcusable slander is found.

<margin>20</margin> This imposed on me the necessity of refuting it in this writing, and of publicly imploring the help of the Magistrates to restrain such a troublesome slanderer. Since indeed he enjoys public stipends for [teaching] youth—

### LETTER

...virtue is to be established, and he is a Professor of the Academy, if so atrocious and so notable a crime of his were to remain unpunished, it would seem to be supported, in a way, by the authority of those who permit him to hold that office. And it can never be attributed <margin>5</margin> as a disgrace to any College or any Republic that someone in it is guilty; for laws and Magistrates are held everywhere for the reason that guilty people can exist everywhere; but those are worthy of the greatest praise among whom no crimes are tolerated once they have been clearly <margin>10</margin> revealed.

When, however, a few months ago, I received from Utrecht <term>Ultrajectum</term> 144 pages, or the first six gatherings <note>original: "folia" — referring to the printed sheets of a book before binding</note> of that slanderous book, where I heard its publication was being overseen by Voet, I responded to them during my leisure in successive hours. And when <margin>15</margin> that publication was subsequently interrupted for a while on account of the book on the *Marian Confraternity* ᵃ, whose printing by the same publisher Voet was urging more strongly, so that it might appear before the time of the Gallo-Belgic Synod <note>A gathering of the Walloon (French-speaking Protestant) churches</note>, recently held at The Hague ᵇ, in which regarding the matter he attacked in it—

---

a. *Marian Confraternity* <note>original: "Confraternitas Mariana"</note> is the title reproduced at the top of the pages. The title appearing at the head of the volume is much longer: *A Specimen of Assertions, partly ambiguous or slippery, partly dangerous, excerpted from a treatise very recently written for the purpose of establishing or restoring Sodalities of the Blessed Virgin Mary among the Reformed, titled "Defense of Piety and Sincerity," etc., which is offered to the Belgian Churches and their faithful pastors and elders for consideration by GISBERT VOET, Professor of Theology in the Academy of Utrecht...* (Utrecht, From the Workshop of Joannes van Waefberge, Year 1642.) — See below, p. 79, note a.

b. This Synod of the Walloon Churches took place at The Hague on April 15, 1643. ¶ The Church of 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original: "Bois-le-Duc"</note> sent Samuel Desmarets and Otto Copes as deputies there. "Meanwhile, the Synod is convoked at The Hague for April 15, and in the name of the Church of 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original: "Sylvae-Ducensis"</note>, which had requested this final duty from me, with the Most Honorable Master Copes, then an Elder, joined to me, I am delegated to the Synod." (SAMUEL DESMARETS <note>Latin: "Maresii"</note>, *Ultimate Patience, etc.*, 1645, pp. 358-359.)

<meta>This page continues Descartes’ explanation of why he has decided to respond to the personal attacks of Gijsbert Voetius. ### TO G. VOETIUS

...he thought it was to be dealt with, I believed it my duty to examine this book as well, as soon as it was published. I did this not insofar as it deals with questions pertaining to a religion different from my own <note>Descartes was a Catholic, while Voetius was a leader of the Dutch Reformed Church</note>—which I have avoided <margin>5</margin> with the greatest care, lest I give the adversary any occasion to make an outcry—but insofar as I could most clearly demonstrate from it his malice and his license for lying. For since Voetius does not come out against me except in a mask <note>original: "personatus" — referring to Voetius' habit of publishing attacks under his students' names</note>, sending out <margin>10</margin> now one of his disciples, now another, so that he is not bound to stand by what they have written; yet meanwhile, he confirms those words with his authority among those who—considering that he is a Minister of the Church <term>Ecclesiæ Ministrum</term> and therefore ought to be a man of integrity and not at all a liar—will not believe he would have permitted his <margin>15</margin> disciples, writing for him and with his awareness, to charge me with such unspeakable crimes unless I were indeed guilty. I therefore thought it necessary to diminish <note>original: "elevare" — meaning to weaken or debunk</note> all that authority which he so badly misuses, by exposing some of his deeds, teaching, and merits, both so that I <margin>20</margin> can free myself from the persistence of his slanders, and also for the public good, because he is troublesome in this matter not to me alone.

Nor do I heed the foolish complaints <note>original: "ineptas querelas"</note> with which, as I know his character, he will undoubtedly try to stir up hatred against me, by saying that in his person I am also attacking other <margin>25</margin> theologians, and passing judgment on the controversies of his religion. For no one who deigns to read this writing will fail to recognize that such a claim is utterly false, and that I have most accurately abstained from both. Furthermore, when I heard in these days it being boasted by his friends that <margin>30</margin> something had recently been judged in his favor in the Gallo-Belgic Synod <note>The assembly of French-speaking Protestant churches in the Netherlands</note>, I diligently inquired into the matter, lest I might perhaps have something in this writing—

<summary>Descartes explains that he is attacking Voetius’ personal character and "license for lying" rather than his theology, arguing that Voetius uses his status as a minister to make his slanders appear credible.</summary>

Article 25<a>, refers its decision to the general national Synod, although it had been requested by the Church of 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original Latin: "Ecclesiâ Sylvæducensi"</note> to deliver a judgment. From which it is manifest that the Synod can in no way approve that Voetius,

The Church of 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original French: "Boisleduc"</note>, having read to this Company its instructions regarding the matter of the Brotherhood of the Virgin <note>A religious society that became a flashpoint for conflict because it included both Catholics and Protestants</note>, and having asked for a regulation for our Churches regarding those who belong to the aforementioned Brotherhood—as it is reformed in said place—as to whether they can and should be admitted to the offices of Elders and Deacons, and if they should be admitted to the Holy Supper of the Lord: the Company, having distinctly considered in this proposal what is lawful <note>original: "licite"</note> versus what is expedient; as for what is lawful, has referred it to the National Synod; and for what is expedient, advises the Consistory not to admit in the future to the offices of Elders and Deacons those who belong to the aforementioned Brotherhood, due to the scandal <note>In this context, "scandal" refers to an action that causes others to stumble in their faith or creates public offense</note> caused to some; and for those who currently belong to this Brotherhood and hold the offices of Elders and Deacons, they may remain there until their term has expired. And as for other Colleges or Societies bearing the name of saints, which might exist in any city, about which the aforementioned Church has made a similar request to us, the Company having no occasion to enter into deliberation on this matter, has also determined nothing upon it. » (*Synodal book, etc., vol. I had been informed for some time that you were preparing a certain book against me, and now, look, I have at last received its first six <term>folios</term> <note>In 17th-century printing, a "folio" or "sheet" refers to a large piece of paper folded to create multiple pages. # | *On the Introduction of the book which is falsely titled "Cartesian Philosophy."*

## PART ONE.

I do not yet have that sheet which will contain the full title, since it has not yet been printed, and <margin>5</margin> perhaps, as is usually the case, it will be printed last of all; but because in the headings of the pages I see you call your book *Cartesian Philosophy*, I fear that some might think you have done this to defraud the readers. Since they expect from me a book with a not dissimilar title but a very different <margin>10</margin> argument <note>original: "argumenti." Descartes is likely referring to his own *Principles of Philosophy*, which he was preparing at the time</note> <gloss>a</gloss>, your book might be sold to them in place of mine. ...they assert, unjustly; and they say that nothing gave rise to this story except that, in naming a certain species of hellebore <note>A plant used in antiquity to treat madness; here it is the center of a pedantic dispute over naming.</note>, he followed Dodonaeus <gloss>a</gloss>, and some smatterer or other, having found another name for the same herb in another book, therefore thought he was in error. # EPISTLE
## 8-10.

You think you can stir up great resentment against me because I stated in that very letter that *no solution to any question has ever been given, through the power of principles peculiar to Peripatetic <note>This refers to Aristotelian philosophy, which was the standard academic curriculum in European universities at the time.</note> Philosophy, which I cannot prove to be invalid and false* <sup>a</sup>. But here I find your judgment lacking; for you betray the cause you defend and confirm my words, since you present no such solution that I could not prove false, but instead, as your entire rebuttal, you merely call me a "shady character" <note>original: "tenebrionem," literally a creature of the shadows, often used for a trickster or one who avoids the light of truth.</note> and a fool. People know well enough that you have always been most generous in challenging others and in posing questions. [In the same way, on page 88 below, you repeat those same words of mine and "refute" them with nothing but insults.]

And from this, those who are less learned will surely discover the poverty of common <note>Traditional Scholastic or Aristotelian philosophy.</note> philosophy. Although they may have often heard it being disparaged by others, they surely never suspected it to be so bankrupt that it does not contain the certain knowledge of even a single thing—despite the fact that you and your colleagues market it as the "knowledge of things divine and human" and the foundation of all other sciences.

You know them to be highly learned, and yet even they have remained silent on this matter until now. As for those who are more learned, they have known for a long time that absolutely no demonstration can be built upon the specific principles of Peripatetic philosophy. ### 10-12. TO G. VOETIUS.

...reasoning resting on the principles of Aristotle is sold as a true demonstration, and I am there to point out its flaws, they will certainly not find me guilty of excessive arrogance. Nor will they doubt that I can easily perform what I have promised there. For the solution to a question does not consist in the conclusion alone, but most especially in the premises; unless the conclusion is properly derived from these, even if it happens to be true by chance, the solution will nevertheless be illegitimate and false.

<margin>10</margin> You say later, on that same page 8, that I dare to thrust my Philosophy partly upon certain idle people of no study and no erudition, and partly upon certain statesmen <sup>a</sup>. You add, on page 9, that I—who am at other times more timid than a deer <note>original: "damâ timidiorem"</note> and only bold in the shadows of my own den—have recently worked in earnest to introduce my sterile and abortive trifles, as if they were true and pure Philosophy, through a certain Physician <note>This refers to Henricus Regius, a professor of medicine at Utrecht and early supporter of Descartes.</note> into a new but nonetheless famous Academy <note>The University of Utrecht, founded in 1636.</note>, after having supposedly driven out all ancient Philosophy.

And then you attack that Physician, so that you may reproach him for the naming of the herb I mentioned a little while ago <sup>b</sup>. And finally, you conclude regarding me as follows: *It has been decided to expose, in a few words, the Philosophy of this charming man—who is foolish to the point of laughter—for the sake of the youth (who ought not to be ignorant of the battles now begun, in which their dear Aristotle is being attacked), and indeed for the sake of others (whom this most lying man labors to deceive and to sell smoke to)* <sup>c</sup> <note>To "sell smoke" (original: "fumos vendere") is a Latin idiom meaning to sell empty promises or to deceive people with worthless things.</note>. ### LETTERS 12-14.

...ever to have thrust my thoughts on Philosophy [upon anyone].
"We know," you say on page 12, "what power lies in the charms of nimble hands <note>original: "agilium manuum"</note> and a flattering tongue." You, of course, might know this, because you preach and teach; I, however, live in the country, and <margin>5</margin> as much as I can, I remove myself from the crowd of men. I have never laid snares for anyone's ears, I have never had any disciples, I have sought none—but rather, I have fled from them. Furthermore, Regius had already been made a Professor for some time, and was teaching those things which you say I wanted to introduce into your <margin>10</margin> Academy <note>The University of Utrecht</note> through him, before I had ever even spoken to him<sup>a</sup>; and therefore, if he held anything of mine, he had drawn it all from my previously published writings; | and he did so by his own singular strength of mind. For I did not explain [my whole] Philosophy in those works, but <margin>15</margin> only proposed some samples of it, so that everyone could judge from them whether it would be to their advantage to learn the rest of my thoughts; and so that in this way, if I could be of benefit to no one, I might at least harm no one, and deserve well of all. (As can be seen on pages 5 and 6 of the *Discourse on the Method* <note>original: "Dissertationis de Methodo"</note>, and in <margin>20</margin> the end of the letter to Father Dinet<sup>b</sup> <note>Pierre Dinet was a Jesuit provincial and former teacher of Descartes.</note>.) I point these things out precisely here so that you may know there is no other way to attack <margin>25</margin> my opinions than if they are examined in the writings already published by me, and it is shown that something is contained in them that is evil or false. There is no place here for deception or trickery; those writings are in the | hands of men; anyone can examine and criticize them at their leisure. But if someone should imagine other [opinions]...

# TO G. VOETIUS.

I only ask that you consider what is contained in this part of your writing—in which you have striven to depict me, and to enumerate, if not all, then certainly my chief vices, and which is entirely transcribed here—from
<margin>5</margin> which a prudent reader might judge whether those epithets with which you saw fit to adorn me a moment ago actually suit my person. Truly, in inquiring into my vices, you have found nothing else except that
*I am French by birth, born of honorable parents, not entirely devoid of talent, and that I live as a bachelor, and supported by*
<margin>10</margin> *whatever mastery of Mathematics I possess, I meditate on a new Philosophy, for which some already hold good hope.* Yet, you call
me a *scoundrel, a shyster* <note>original: "tenebrionem," literally one who operates in darkness or a swindler</note>, *a fool, more timid than a deer,*

And since all these things are found in the first two pages in which
<margin>15</margin> you began to deal with me, it is likely that still more and perhaps even more unworthy things will be found in the following pages. If these things had been babbled by a drunken woman or an angry innkeeper, they would be laughed at; but when they have been written and
committed to print by a Theologian, a Pastor of his Church, who
<margin>20</margin> wishes to appear most religious and most pious, and who ought to lead others by his example—I will not say of gentleness, humility, patience, or charity, lest perhaps you despise these virtues of the ancient Church—but at least of moderation, clemency, and gravity, I do not see by what reasoning they can
<margin>25</margin> be excused.

# EPISTLE
## TO G. VOETIUS

...should its author be torn apart with the most atrocious insults? Philosophy, as it is usually sought by me and all others who study it, is nothing other than the knowledge of those truths which can be perceived by the **natural light** <note>In 17th-century philosophy, the "natural light" refers to human reason, as opposed to "divine light" or revelation</note>, and which are of use to
<margin>5</margin> human needs; so much so that no study could be more honorable, none more worthy of man, and none even more useful in this life. However, that common philosophy which is taught in schools and academies is only a certain collection of opinions, for the most part
<margin>10</margin> doubtful—as is apparent from the continuous disputes by which they are typically shaken—and useless, as long experience has now shown: for no one has ever converted anything from **primary matter**, **substantial forms**, **hidden qualities** <note>These are technical terms from Scholasticism—the medieval school of thought based on Aristotle—which Descartes believed were empty labels that explained nothing about the physical world</note>, and such things, into their own use. 
<margin>15</margin> Therefore, it is in no way consistent with reason that those who have learned these opinions, which they themselves admit to be uncertain, should hold others in hatred because they are trying to find more certain ones. It is indeed hateful to wish to innovate anything regarding Religion: because since everyone says they believe that the religion they embrace
<margin>20</margin> was instituted by God, who cannot err, they consequently believe that nothing in it can be changed without it being an evil. But regarding Philosophy, which everyone freely admits is not yet sufficiently known by men and can be increased by many excellent discoveries, nothing is more
<margin>25</margin> praiseworthy than to be an **Innovator** ᵃ. Perhaps you will say that you...

### | *Regarding the deeds of Voetius, from which I first began to know his virtues.* <note>Descartes uses "virtues" ironically here to describe Voetius's hostile behavior</note>

## PART TWO.

Because men are not usually accustomed to attack others so violently without cause—lest I should perhaps seem to have given you cause through some fault of mine—<margin>15</margin> I will briefly recount everything that has passed between me and you until now. I have never, as far as I know, spoken to you, nor am I yet known to you by face; and I was thinking no more of you than of those who are not yet born, when it was first announced to me that you were in the habit of <margin>20</margin> counting me among the **Atheists** <term>Atheist: In the 17th century, this was a devastating legal and social accusation, often leveled at anyone who questioned traditional Aristotelian science</term>; and that you were attacking Professor **De Roy** <note>original: "De Roy"; Henricus Regius (1598–1679), a Dutch doctor and early proponent of Cartesian science at Utrecht</note>—whom people knew taught many things that agreed with my opinions—with the most unjust machinations...

---

What of the crowd of **Lullists** <note>Followers of Ramon Llull’s logical system</note> and **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of the medical and chemical theories of Paracelsus</note>, and the chimerical throng of the **Brothers of the Rose Cross** <note>The Rosicrucians, a secret society of mystics and philosophers rumored to possess hidden knowledge</note>? If you except **Ramus** <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572), a famous critic of Aristotelian logic</note> alone, the rest have either two followers or none at all: and some adhere to him, not because he overthrew **Aristotle** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose works formed the basis of the university curriculum (Scholasticism)</note> (although he tried), or obscured his philosophy with his own light; but because he seems to have indicated a method by the aid of which one can successfully progress through the vast estates of the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: A name for the followers of Aristotle, referring to his habit of walking while teaching</term>. » (Page 6-7.) # LETTER
<center>### TO G. VOETIUS</center>

...to be attacked. This indeed drove me to inquire more diligently into the truth of the matter: what kind of man you were, and what could have moved you to | this behavior. As far as the facts were concerned, there was no doubt: your theses against Regius <note>original: "in Regium"; referring to Henricus Regius, a professor at Utrecht and a disciple of Descartes whose defense of "new philosophy" was attacked by Voetius</note> were already in circulation <gloss>a</gloss>, and your <margin>5</margin> remarkable judgment against the <term>new Philosophy</term> <note>referring to Cartesianism and the scientific revolution it sparked</note> was published shortly thereafter <gloss>b</gloss>. As for your character, however, I heard that you were quite diligent and tireless in performing all the duties of your ministry and profession; that you preached, taught, and debated more frequently than the <margin>10</margin> rest of your colleagues; and that through your expression, your voice, and your gestures, you displayed a superior piety. You appeared to burn with such zeal for defending the truth and purity of your religion that you would condemn with the greatest severity not only the slightest of vices—especially those of the powerful—but even those things which many do <margin>15</margin> not consider to be vices at all. Furthermore, you would debate and declaim most vehemently against all those who disagreed with you. These reports indeed | would have driven me to look up to you as if you were one of the Prophets or Apostles, if there had not remained in me a doubt arising from the fact that I knew <margin>20</margin> I was most unjustly numbered among the **Atheists** by you. But because even good men, when poorly persuaded by others or judging with insufficient prudence, can sometimes be deceived, I thought one of two things must be true: either you were in reality a most holy man, though perhaps not sufficiently prudent; or (forgive me <margin>25</margin> for finding no milder word to express the truth of the matter) a **hypocrite**. For I judged that with those talents I heard you possessed, there could be no middle ground between virtue and vice. Which of these two was true, became more evident...

<page-num>37</page-num>
<header>TO G. VOETIUS</header>
<meta>42-44.</meta>

not a single word is found concerning forgetting <note>original: "oblivione"</note>, but only regarding the removal of prejudices <note>original: "præjudiciis tollendis"; Descartes refers to the process of clearing the mind of unverified assumptions</note>, just as in no other place in my writings. From this, the reader will easily recognize how much credit should be given to your citations. For it is one thing to set aside prejudices—that is, opinions rashly accepted beforehand—which means to cease giving them one’s assent <note>Assent (assensum) is a key Cartesian term: the intellectual decision to accept something as true</note>, an act that depends solely on our will and is absolutely required for laying the first foundations of Philosophy; it is quite another thing to forget them, which is almost never within our power. But since the first theses that you ever published in your Academy dealt with prejudices, and in many other places you have confessed that they must be rejected, it was not fitting for me to be rebuked by you for having written the same. Therefore, you preferred to invent something else to attribute to me, which would provide more abundant material for your accusations.

As for what remains in this chapter, it is not worth reporting, nor does it prove anything other than that you fail to make sufficient use of your prudence and your natural logic—just as you lack faith and honesty—when you attribute absurdities to a man whom you previously called "ingenious"<sup>a</sup>, absurdities that could not be believed of him. This is also true of your citation on page 22 of the words from the Epistle of the Apostle Jude, verse 10, *concerning those who slander the things they do not know*<sup>b</sup>.

> *Nevertheless, René Descartes, as he himself said and testified to several most trustworthy men, was occupied for twenty full years in this task: that he might be able to forget all those things which he had ever learned. Indeed, he earnestly warns that this must be done in the Method published in French in the year 1637, pages 16 and 17, and he acknowledges this as his own doctrine in the response to the seventh set of Objections, page 32 of the Elzevir edition. Let pages 7, 21, 23, and 24 of the same Response also be consulted. Hence, in his school, the first mark of a future disciple is whether he can forget all that he has learned from others. » (The Admirable Method, p. 17-18.)* <note>Voetius’s book was titled *Admiranda Methodus* (The Admirable Method), which was a satirical and critical attack on Descartes's *Discourse on Method*.</note>

For no one, seeing in what way you attack my Philosophy, would not immediately turn those same attacks back upon you; for since you have never seen it—insofar as I have not yet published it—you clearly cannot know it.

...which from this you would have known should be touched upon only very sparingly and cautiously.

The first category is that of the wicked and the frivolous <note>original: "improborum & nugacium"; Descartes refers to authors who lack moral weight or intellectual seriousness</note>, whom I join together: for there is scarcely anyone who is purely frivolous without some
<margin>5</margin>mixture of wickedness. However, no book was ever written by an Atheist, or a Libertine <note>In the 17th century, a "libertine" was often a free-thinker who rejected religious or social norms</note>, or a frivolous Kabbalist <note>A follower of Jewish mysticism; here used dismissively to suggest occult nonsense</note>, or a Magician, or any other impostor, which you do not wish to appear to have read through. And you correctly show this regarding certain ones: for you interweave their entire arguments into your own writings.

<margin>10</margin>The second category is that of the contentious <note>original: "contentioforum"; those who write specifically for the sake of argument and conflict</note>, whose authors often think it a matter of piety to tear each other apart with insults due to partisan zeal. You are accustomed to cite so many of this kind that, if you have read even a fourth part of them, you must have spent the primary
<margin>15</margin>time of your life among quarrels and brawls. I do not indeed affirm that all books of this sort are bad: for those who defend the truth and only attack vices are to be praised; but nonetheless I think they should not be read too much, because such is the weakness of our nature that many are often incited
<margin>20</margin>to love vices by the very prohibition of them. Neither do I say that it is never useful for Theologians or others to see bad books, namely when it is their duty to refute or correct them; but this happens only rarely. And just as no one ever visits those suffering from the plague merely for the sake of
<margin>25</margin>their own amusement: so no pious man is accustomed to read bad books repeatedly just to hunt for the reputation of having read much; for they are indeed contagious. Indeed, I am even now experiencing this myself: for since it has been necessary to read through <note>original: "evolverem"; literally to unroll a scroll, meaning to examine or study a text</note> some of your writings to write this letter,

### 49-51. TO G. VOETIUS. 41 ###
<sig>50</sig>
<meta>Works. Vol. III.</meta>

A certain roughness has affected my style because of this, which I can scarcely correct; and for this reason I ask for your pardon, for speaking here somewhat more harshly than is my habit.

<margin>5</margin> The third category of books consists of **commonplaces** <note>Reference books where a writer collects useful quotations or passages under general topics for easy retrieval</note>, **commentaries**, **compendiums**, **indices**, and the like, which are compiled from various sayings of other authors. Even if I do not think them bad, nor entirely to be looked down upon, I admit no other
<margin>10</margin> use for them than that they sometimes help to recall to memory those things which we previously learned from the **primary books** <note>Descartes refers to original source texts or foundational works by great thinkers</note> from which they were excerpted. For indeed, those who neglect the original sources and approach only these little streams draw nothing but murky waters from them, nor do they
<margin>15</margin> achieve any true learning. For whatever is exceptional in the writings of great minds is not contained in this or that sentence which can be copied out, but arises from the entire body of the work. Nor is this something we grasp immediately upon the
<margin>20</margin> first reading; rather, we learn it gradually through frequent and repeated study, almost without noticing, as we digest it and transform it into our own *lifeblood* <note>original: "succum," literally "juice" or "sap," implying the way the body internalizes nutrients</note>. It is clear from your writings, in which you cite them quite often, that you are very well-practiced in paging through such commonplaces, commentaries, and dictionaries. But I
<margin>25</margin> cannot similarly detect that you have a great familiarity with those primary books upon which all true learning—that which can be acquired by reading—depends. For although you occasionally call upon them as witnesses, you usually do so inappropriately, and
<margin>30</margin> you mix them indiscriminately with other authors of far lesser quality.

You do not seem to have read them, but merely to have their words from some transcriber. And furthermore, just as those who often lie among **scented cushions** <note>original: "odoratos pulvillos"</note> cannot help but retain something of their fragrance, so it seems difficult to me <margin>5</margin> for the **scholarly works** <note>original: "lucubrationes," literally "work by candlelight," implying deep late-night study</note> of great men to be read extensively by anyone, and yet afterward find nothing similar to their style in that person's own writings. But forgive one who speaks the truth candidly: I have read many of your writings, and yet I have never found in them any reasoning, or any thought, that was not humble or common; nothing <margin>10</margin> that savored of an ingenious or erudite man.

I say **erudite**, not **learned** <note>Descartes distinguishes between "eruditum" (refined/cultivated) and "doctum" (well-read/trained)</note>: for if by the name of **learning** you wish to include everything that is learned from books, the bad as well as the good, I will gladly admit that you are most learned. For I see that you have sufficiently read the fables of the **Leviathan** <margin>15</margin> <note>See note a</note>, and the impious trifles of some **Bonaventure des Périers** <note>See note b</note>, and many such things. By **erudite**, however, I understand only the man who, through study and cultivation, has polished his mind and his character. And such erudition is acquired not by the <margin>20</margin> promiscuous reading of any books whatsoever, but only by the reading of the best ones—and that frequently and repeatedly—and likewise through the conversation of those who are already erudite, when we are permitted to enjoy them.

<meta>This page continues Descartes’s critique of Voetius’s intellectual habits. On the previous page, Descartes began defining "erudition" not as mere book-learning, but as a refinement of the mind. He now explains that true wisdom comes from investigating truth and virtue, rather than relying on snippets, summaries, and logical shortcuts used by those he considers pedants.</meta>

<page-num>43</page-num>
<header>53-55. TO G. VOETIUS.</header>

...and finally, I am convinced that erudition is acquired through the diligent contemplation of virtues and the investigation of truth. But as for those who seek knowledge only in **commonplace books** <note>original: "locis communibus" — reference books where students collected useful quotes and arguments</note>, indices, and dictionaries, they can indeed <margin>5</margin> fill their memory with many things in a short time, but they do not become any wiser or better because of it. On the contrary, since these books contain no chain of reasoning, but instead decide everything either by authority or, at most, by brief **syllogisms** <note>formal logical arguments consisting of two premises and a conclusion</note>, those <margin>10</margin> who seek their learning from them become accustomed to believing the authority of all writers equally. They exercise no choice among them except insofar as partisan interests move them. Thus, little by little, they unlearn how to use their natural reason correctly, and they substitute an <margin>15</margin> artificial and **sophistical** <note>clever but false or misleading reasoning</note> reasoning in its place. For you should know that the true use of reason—in which all erudition, all **good sense** <note>original: "bona mens," Descartes's term for the capacity to judge well and distinguish truth from error</note>, and all human wisdom consist—does not lie in disjointed syllogisms. Rather, it consists only in the careful and accurate gathering <margin>20</margin> together of everything required for the knowledge of the truths being sought. And since these things can hardly ever be expressed in syllogisms unless many are linked together, it is certain that those who use only disjointed ones almost always omit some part of those things which should be viewed <margin>25</margin> together. In this way, they become accustomed to thoughtlessness and unlearn their "good sense." And while they consider themselves very learned because they hold in their memory many things written by others and believe them, they acquire from this a most foolish and truly **pedantic** <margin>30</margin> <note>original: "pædagogicam," referring to the narrow-minded or arrogant style of a schoolmaster</note> arrogance. And if, moreover, they devote much time to reading wicked, trifling, and contentious writings, even if nature did not make them bad or entirely destitute of talent...

<summary>Descartes argues that true wisdom and "good sense" come from the holistic investigation of truth rather than the memorization of snippets from reference books or the use of isolated logical formulas. He warns that relying on such shortcuts leads to intellectual arrogance and the loss of natural reasoning abilities.</summary>

Though indeed, it must be admitted that nature also contributes much to this; for those types of books <margin>5</margin> which I have distinguished are usually mixed together. Often, within one and the same author, some things are found to be bad, some trifles, some good and devised by the author himself, and others copied from elsewhere. But according to the different **natural disposition** <note>original: "ingenio" — the innate character or intellectual temperament of a person</note> of the readers—just as bees and spiders <margin>10</margin> do from flowers—some extract only honey from them, while others extract only poison. From this it happens that through the study of letters, those who are inclined toward the good become better and wiser; however, those inclined toward evil become worse and more foolish. The former are distinguished from the latter by this most certain sign: that <margin>15</margin> each person is more frequent in leafing through those books in which they can find more things suited to their own nature. But they also differ greatly in their character: for just as the ill-bred tend to be arrogant, stubborn, and quick to anger, so on the contrary, the truly learned are never prideful. <margin>20</margin> For they are conscious of human weakness, and they do not value highly what they know, but consider that there are far more things of which they are ignorant. And for that reason they are also candid and teachable, and always ready to learn truths not yet known to them; and finally, accustomed to bending their **mind** <note>original: "ingenium"</note> to various things, <margin>25</margin> they cannot help but be mild, kind, and humane. And these people indeed, since they understand that true erudition does not depend on books alone, they also busy themselves in acquiring it through private **meditation** <note>original: "meditatione" — here meaning disciplined, focused reflection on a subject</note>, or through the various experiences of business, and the friendship of excellent men. They are not <margin>30</margin> always occupied among books; whence it happens that by the unskilled...

These are the three things they almost always notice in those who are badly learned. <page-num>47</page-num>
<header>61-63. TO G. VOETIUS. 47</header>

...[arguments] such that no one even examines whether they are good, which is what usually happens with yours. Finally, he is a man who rises up against all those who oppose him in even the smallest matter, or who simply do not applaud him, as if they were his most bitter enemies; he <margin>5</margin> strives to make them as infamous as possible through his sermons <note>original: "concionibus" — public religious discourses or sermons</note> and writings. By this path, you have forced many to keep silent about you, or even to praise you against their will. It is no wonder that such a man reaches the highest reputation for learning <note>original: "eruditionis" — scholarly knowledge acquired through study</note> and the greatest authority among his own people; <margin>10</margin> nor is it a wonder that he preserves it, as long as his tricks <note>original: "artes" — here meaning deceptive skills or "dark arts" of rhetoric</note> are detected by no one. But when, perhaps blinded by his excessive power, he hurts so many people that some think it worthwhile to expose those very tricks; and when he commits such inexcusable errors that they are easily recognized even by the unlearned; <margin>15</margin> it would be very strange if he did not finally fall from that unmerited reputation and power. For even if such a man is very pleasing to most of his listeners in the church and his disciples in the Academy <note>The University of Utrecht, where Voetius was a professor</note>, if they once notice how much harm they should fear from him, they will turn away from him <margin>20</margin> with the greatest intensity.

I see indeed that I am drifting further and further from my intended discourse, which was only about the use of books. But perhaps you will not object to this, because after I have added a few more things about sermons and the instruction of students, <margin>25</margin> you will have everything here in one place that seems to me worth noting regarding your scholarship. Therefore, the sermons of that Doctor whom I have just described usually please the people; for it is the nature of all men to delight in being moved not only to cheerfulness, but especially <margin>30</margin> to any sad emotions of the soul <note>original: "affectus animi" — a technical term in 17th-century philosophy for the passions or emotions</note>. Hence, tragedies please us no less than comedies...

For these [better preachers] set forth what is displeasing to the listener; whereas that man sets forth only what is pleasing. And indeed, it is a great comfort to the crowd—not <margin>20</margin> wicked, but unlearned—that they can at times be piously moved, piously angry, and piously scornful of the powerful: for whatever they do by such a man's persuasion or example, they think it pious. They hear from his disciples how many books he writes and what great victories he reports over whatever adversaries in his <margin>25</margin> disputes <note>original: "disputationibus"</note>; they cannot doubt that he is most learned, for they do not know how to distinguish such things. So too they think his vehemence in preaching, and his freedom in rebuking the nobility, proceed from an extraordinary holiness <note>original: "sanctitate"</note> and a kind of prophetic zeal <note>original: "zelo"</note>. For these reasons, the crowd <margin>30</margin> accepts him as their chief leader and exhorter, if by chance they must ever resist the powerful or fight against the adversaries of their religion; and whatever he...

Whether it is actually useful for the <term>Commonwealth</term> <note>original: "Reipublicæ" — the state or organized society</note> for such a preacher to be active within it is not for me to inquire. <margin>5</margin> Those who have care of it know well enough what is expedient. Neither do I examine whether it is good for unlettered men to hear many minute details of controversies, which they could ignore without any detriment to their salvation; nor whether they can learn them accurately enough from sermons; <margin>10</margin> nor whether they are rightly taught by those who do not so much explain reasons as hurl insults at people; nor whether it is pious and humane to hate some men because they disagree with us in religion. But I only affirm that every disturbance of the mind toward anger, hatred, <margin>15</margin> and brawling, however just its cause might be, is always extremely harmful to the very person who is so moved. For we are so constituted by nature that through even small practice we acquire a great inclination toward wicked passions; and whoever has allowed himself to be moved to anger even once for a just <margin>20</margin> cause is, by that very fact, much more ready to be angry another time even for an unjust one. <note>Descartes is applying his theory of habit and "passions of the soul" here: repeated emotional states create physical "traces" in the brain that make those emotions easier to trigger later.</note> Simple women <note>original: "mulierculæ" — a diminutive term used here to characterize the uneducated female laity</note> in the church hear a man—whom they consider the wisest and most holy—declaiming, disputing, and hurling insults against other men. <margin>25</margin> Most of the time, they do not understand the matter he is discussing; and they have nothing better to do than to imitate all his disturbances with pious affection, and to excite similar ones in themselves. Thus it happens that later, having returned home, they bicker over every minor cause. Nor do the men <margin>30</margin> reap any better fruit from this, especially those who, though understanding these controversies to some extent, cannot...

The second art, which I notice in your writings, is that by the help of which you compose books on any proposed subject, which the unskillful judge to be most full of learning. Even
<margin>5</margin>your disciples, without any real erudition, are able to imitate it, provided they only look at the indexes of various books, especially those in which many other books are cited. After they have gathered indiscriminately everything they find in those sources regarding the matter they have undertaken to treat,
<margin>10</margin>of whatever quality they may be, they arrange them according to the order of **commonplaces** <note>original: "locorum communium" — a traditional rhetorical method of organizing arguments or information under general headings or "places" like "causes," "effects," or "definitions."</note>, adding the names of all the authors from whom they have taken something, as well as others who are praised by those authors. Thus, for example, if they wish to write about **Atheism**, whatever
<margin>15</margin>they find in their collections regarding the meaning of that name, they will write in the first place; in the second, its synonyms; in the third, its types or degrees; and so consequently: its causes, effects, adjuncts, signs, contraries, etc. By this method, they will not have excerpted even the
<margin>20</margin>smallest word from any author for which they do not find some place in their own work. For they will also be able to review there all the men whom they know have been called **Atheists** <note>original: "Atheos" — a grave accusation in the 17th century, often used to silence intellectual or religious rivals.</note> by others, and, if they happen to have read any of those authors’ very trifling and wicked books, they can copy out their entire arguments, and also
<margin>25</margin>recount any **little stories or fables** <note>original: "historiolas aut fabellas"</note> of no importance about them. Furthermore, if they secretly wish someone ill, they will be able to freely number among the signs or causes of Atheism everything that they think is true of him, or believe is thought of him by others. It does not matter if these things are
<margin>30</margin>praiseworthy, or as far removed from such a suspicion as possible; for they will easily add some evil of their own, by reason of which, in a bad...

# LETTER
<meta>76-78</meta>

...men endowed with the most outstanding talent are usually **Atheists**; they provide various examples of them, and teach their primary arguments while never refuting them. But they must observe only one thing, which is easiest for the unskilled to observe: <margin>5</margin> namely, that they should produce nothing exceptional—neither from themselves nor copied from other authors—by which the reader might be rendered more learned. They may indeed, when some question of no importance arises that could be resolved in few words, dispute it at great length, and consume all their **Dialectic** <note>original: "Dialecticam"—the formal art of logical reasoning and debate</note> <margin>10</margin> in entangling the matter. They can also recount many other such things. But as for the most important matter, which is the **existence of God**, they might admit it should not be omitted, nor proven solely by the authority of **Sacred Scripture** <note>original: "sacræ Scripturæ"</note>, but most especially by <margin>15</margin> philosophical reasons. Yet let them be carefully on guard never to attempt to do so anywhere; and rather, like bad **Physicians** who, being ignorant of true and simple remedies, are accustomed to fatigue their patients with a great multitude of either useless or harmful drugs: so, when it comes time to address the matter, they say <margin>20</margin> that very much is required to resist **Atheism**, and that, besides *an accurate knowledge of the sacred letters*, one must possess *a universal science of universals, especially Metaphysics, Pneumatics* <note>original: "Pneumaticam"—in this context, the study of spiritual beings or the soul</note>, *Physics, general Astronomy, Geography, Optics, and speculations on sounds, <margin>25</margin> weights, etc.; likewise a knowledge of particulars, whether ancient or modern history*; and finally, they prepare a long library against the **Atheists**, into which they even place some of those very authors whom they previously denounced as suspected of **Atheism**. If they observe all these things, <margin>30</margin> they will compose writings very similar to yours, as will be manifest to those who [read] your four small books on that matter, <note>Descartes refers here to Voetius's "Disputationes Selectae," where Voetius attacked Descartes's philosophy.</note>

<margin>10</margin> ### PART FIVE.

For who does not know that by "thing" is understood a real being <term>Real being: Latin "ens reale," referring to an actual entity rather than a mere figment of the mind.</term>, and that "being" is named from *being* or existing <note>Descartes is pointing out the etymological link between the Latin "ens" (being) and "esse" (to be).</note>, and that the very natures of things are called by philosophers *essences* <note>original: "essentias"</note>, because we cannot conceive of them except as <margin>15</margin> | beings or existing things? And it is absurd what he adds next, namely that *God is thought of as a deceiver*. For although, in my first Meditation <note>Descartes's "Meditations on First Philosophy" (1641), where he famously doubts everything, even proposing a "malicious demon" to test his certainty.</note>, I spoke of some supremely powerful deceiver, nevertheless the true God was by no means conceived of there, because, as he himself says, it cannot be that the true God is a <margin>20</margin> deceiver. And if he were asked how he knows that this is impossible, he must answer that he knows it from the fact that it implies a contradiction in the concept—that is, from the fact that it cannot be conceived; so that this very point, which he used to attack me, is sufficient to defend <margin>25</margin> me.

could not be prevented, since their liberty had been guaranteed in the terms of surrender, those to whom the protection of that city was committed thought it very useful—both for preventing suspicions and for fostering peace and harmony among the citizens—that they themselves be admitted into that same Confraternity <margin>10</margin>
alongside the Roman Catholics, but on the condition that nothing should thereafter be done in it that was foreign to their own religion. And this could not be refused by the others, because since, according to the laws of surrender, all ecclesiastical property was to be turned over to the public <margin>15</margin>
treasury, they had reserved the administration of the goods of that Society for themselves on no other grounds than that it was not spiritual or ecclesiastical, but only civil. Thus, therefore, the most illustrious governor of the city, and 13 others from the more honorable citizens<sup>c</sup>,

---

a. <note>original: "Confrérie de Notre-Dame"</note> The Confraternity of Our Lady, founded in Bois-le-Duc in 1318, and reorganized by Erard de la Marck, Bishop of Liège, by an ordinance of January 18, 1518; Bois-le-Duc was then part of his diocese.
b. Bois-le-Duc was taken from the Spaniards by the Dutch, commanded by Prince Frederick Henry, in 1629, after a siege that lasted from May 1st to September 17th.
c. The governor of the city was Johan Wolphaert van Brederode. Here are the names of the thirteen others: Lord van Thienen, H. Bergaigne, Henrick Kuysten, G.-W. Pieck, Andries de Fresnes, A. Ploos van Amstel, R. Tullekens, J. van Casteren, Otto Copes, J. Ruysch, Pieter Lus, Johan Gans, and Lazarus van Zonst. — <note>original: "Erant inter illos Optimates..."</note> "There were among those <term>leading men: members of the social elite or ruling class, referred to as 'Optimates' in Latin</term> who were private individuals and had never held a magistracy. There were also military commanders, over whom the governor had no more authority than any citizen or preacher might be called a hired soldier of the garrison. But someone might object that some of those leading men—indeed, most of them—were in part <term>aldermen: local magistrates or judges, known as 'scabini' in Latin</term> (in whose hands the ordinary and daily administration of the city's policy lies there)."

Doubtless, one should read: May 16 (New Style). Voet gives neither the name of the place (*Given at N.*) nor that of the signer (*N. N.*) here. But, on June 27, 1642, in a letter to Godefroy Udemans, a pastor like himself, he wrote:
> "...I, overwhelmed by academic colleges and other labors, do not publish books so frequently now. Lately, however, having been given the opportunity, I pushed out this one which you see, *on Indirect Idolatry*: into which you will see inserted the determination of the case proposed to me by Mr. Lemann, pastor of 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original Latin: "Sylvæ-ducensi"</note>, regarding the Fraternity of the Rosary or of Mary. I would wish you to weigh it carefully, and grieve with me over the blindness and love of worldly vanity <note>original Greek: φιλοκοσμίαν (philokosmian)</note> of those who, in that city and in the sight of adversaries, do not blush to give their names to such an idolatrous Fraternity..."
(See A. C. Duker, *Gisbertus Voetius*, second volume, first part, 1904, Appendices, p. xxxiv.)

And elsewhere Voet provides the following explanations as well: "*Since I neither wished nor was able to refuse the request of this Reverend brother and fellow-minister* <term>symmista; a colleague in the ministry or fellow-initiate</term>, *yet had scarcely the leisure or spirit to write much to him, I used the opportunity, which was then convenient, and as if sparing effort, I proposed this case along with the disputation on Indirect Idolatry (almost all the material of which the public lectures on commonplaces <note>standard theological topics</note> had explained a few days before), with an application made through inclusion and logical consequence.*" (*Marian Confraternity*, p. 4.)

Voet divided his theses *On Indirect and Shared Idolatry* into three parts, which were defended on May 21 (*part one*), May 28 (*second*), and June 14, 1642 (*third*). See his collection *Selected Disputations*, vol. III, p. 234, 285, and 347. Voet could therefore send them to his colleague Udemans on June 27.

a. Desmarets, a pastor at Bois-le-Duc <note>The French name for 's-Hertogenbosch.</note> since 1636, recounts how 
things happened as follows: “When someone among the Officials shared these conditions (see below, p. 93-94, 
note a) with me and asked what I felt about this whole matter, I frankly declared that I saw nothing in it 
that could be justly rebuked or accused of religious communion with idolaters.” (*Ultima patientia*, 1645, p. 95.) 
— And again: “Therefore they sent a formal deputation to me, and asked that, since they were being 
attacked publicly by a celebrated theologian, beyond what is right and lawful, in a public

right and sincere intention in conducting it.” (*Ibid.*, p. 96.) — 
“I therefore prepared that writing, which, having been read and re-read in their full assembly 
and approved by the common vote of all, was afterwards published

> "And since the public accusation of your Theses required a public excuse for our people, it is better that it was entrusted to me, who am most devoted to you in all things, than to someone else who might have respected you less and poured more vinegar than oil into his speech." <note>original: "plus aceti quàm olei." b. Desmarets said, in effect:
> "Nor therefore ought I to resist the opinion of the Distinguished Voetius regarding the thesis: by the grace of God, there is agreement between us on that. Voetii ſententiæ, quoad theſim, debebo reluctari..." from *Defense*, p. 11.</note>
Desmarets targets Lemann here, and even more so in the following passage:
> "But the chief fault lies with whoever it was who, contrary to law and right, deceived this most candid man of ancient sincerity, and was the author of emitting these half-baked things to the public... The fault of excessive credulity of this distinguished man falls back upon the sycophant, who, having abused his ease and candor, exposed him to this complaint and entangled him in an unnecessary controversy." <note>original: "Sed præcipua culpa eſt penes eum... Credulitatis nimiæ culpa..." from *Ibid.*, p. 12 and 13.</note>
See previously, page 67, note a, for Lemann's letter to Voet.

One can understand from the Ministers of the Word <note>A common term for Protestant clergy.</note> how it happened. Thus, this 
Minister was dragged onto the stage by you so that, as

<header>LETTER</header>

So now, you have already been remarkably and publicly beaten in 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original: "Sylvæducis"; the Latin name for the city of 's-Hertogenbosch in the Netherlands.</note> under a false persona, but this did not break your spirit. Not even when the most noble and most distinguished Senate of that city—having learned that another book on the same subject, namely this *Marian* <note>Referring to the Virgin Mary.</note> Confraternity, was being prepared by you—wrote letters to the Illustrious Estates of the Province of Utrecht and the renowned Senate of the city, and even to you yourself, to prevent its publication, as you yourself boast on page 421. For, neglecting all these things, you yourself finally with your *Con-*
<margin>5</margin> <note>This is a catchword, a common printer's device where the first syllable of the next page is printed at the bottom of the current one.</note>

...cousin of Constantin Huygens <note>A prominent Dutch diplomat, poet, and scientist who was a friend of Descartes.</note>, sharply blames the Aldermen <note>original: "Echevins"; the municipal magistrates.</note> of the city, and (without naming C. Lemann <note>Lambertus Leeman, a minister in 's-Hertogenbosch whose anti-Catholic writings caused a major controversy.</note> elsewhere), he thus takes up his defense:

> "...Some of them attack the honor of the most virtuous, condemning them unheard; not content with this, they have ordered the Consistory <note>The governing body of a local Reformed church.</note> to proceed with the suspension from office of the most zealous and upright Minister of all. But, seeing that the Consistory did not wish to condemn a good man without having seen an accusation, nor before having heard the accused in his own defense, they desired and effected, through threats, that the Consistory find it acceptable that this faithful Minister should not take the Lord's Supper with them; I say nothing yet of the threats made to use the military hand against the Consistory. To verify all this, I could, if necessary, obtain an extract from the books of the said Consistory of the Flemish Church, where everything is recorded. This Minister has gone to make his complaints to the Synod of Gelderland, convened at Harderwijk, to which our Consistory is subject, where he will produce the opinion of the Faculty of Law at Leiden, approved by the entire Academic Senate, declaring that his Writing—which these nine Aldermen, five or six of whom were formal parties [to the dispute], had decried (the author neither cited nor heard) at the crossroads of every street as an infamous libel—contains nothing defamatory or calumnious. This Writing, in any case, as a work composed by an Ecclesiastical man and dealing with religious matters, ought to have been examined and judged by Ecclesiastics. The said Minister will also produce at the Synod the opinions of the Theological Faculties of the Academies and Illustrious Schools of Leiden, Utrecht, Franeker, Harderwijk, and Deventer (of which I have copies) on the matter of the Sodality of the Virgin Mary, which has caused so much trouble in this City and Church; all the said opinions, based on an infinity of passages from Holy Scripture cited therein, carry the view that it is not permitted for members of the Reformed Church to be brothers or members of the said Idolatrous Sodality, even on the condition of not binding themselves to anything contrary to the Reformed Religion..." (*Manuscript, University Library, Amsterdam.*)

The Synod of Harderwijk, of which Zuerius <note>The Latinized name for Boxhorn or another associate of Huygens involved in the legal defense.</note> speaks, was held from the 23rd to the 29th of August.

-> ### TO G. VOETIUS. <-
<meta>Top left margin: 109-110.</meta>

...you enter the arena with your *Marian Confraternity* <note>original: "fraternitate Mariana"; a controversial work by Voetius attacking a local religious society in 's-Hertogenbosch.</note>. I have read this entire book at my leisure; but to tell the honest truth, I found no part of it that could be read without indignation and disgust. I cannot force myself to speak mildly here; you display in it excessive malice, absurdity, injustice, arrogance, and stubbornness—vices that are, of all things, the most hateful. Your malice appears in the fact that | you have collected so many things and written such a thick book <note>original: "tam crassum librum scripseris"</note>, not so much to [serve the] cause...

7 *Not a new paragraph (first edition).*

1643. The following year, the Synod of Guelders was held at Zutphen, from August 28 to September 2, 1644, and Cornelis Lemann <note>Lambertus Leeman, the controversial minister.</note> went there as a deputy from 's-Hertogenbosch, accompanied by Jacob Zuerius, one of the "elders" (*seniores*) of the Reformed Church. This Zuerius or Suerius had, moreover, been personally involved in the whole affair (see above, p. 8, note *b*), and it is indeed him that Desmarets <note>Samuel Desmarets, a rival theologian who often sided with Descartes against Voetius.</note> seems to target in a passage of his *Apologetic Letter* (see below, p. 82, note *a*):

> "And although in the *Specimen* <note>Referring to Voetius's book *Specimen assertionum*.</note>, page 419, he [Voetius] defends the Schism and Donatism <note>A reference to a 4th-century heresy; here it implies that Zuerius was being divisively radical and separating from the mainstream church.</note> of that former Elder who separated himself from the Church, on the sole pretext that his Pastor judged the Nobles to be immune from that foul Idolatry of which they were accused (which man, moved not by zeal or piety, but by hatred and malice—may God forgive him—stirred up this whole tragedy)..." (*The Final Patience* <note>original: "Ultima patientia"; a work by Samuel Desmarets.</note>, p. 99-100.)

a. The *Specimen Assertionum etc.*, or *Marian Confraternity*, contains no fewer than 511 pages (it is a small 12mo volume, it is true, but with very small text, 36 lines per page). — As for the exact date of the publication of this book, here it is, according to Desmarets:

> "Already toward the end of September in the year 1642, the first three leaves of his *Specimen* had been seen by some." (*The Final Patience*, p. 318.)

Voetius himself wrote to André Rivet <note>A prominent French Huguenot theologian living in the Netherlands.</note> on October 26, 1642:

> "I was quite concerned about the reputation of the patron of the Marian Confraternity as soon as I inspected that infamous and smoky little book... The dispute between me and him will be easily settled; but my writing, which is now being printed, neither can nor should be suppressed by that settlement. ... You have two quires <note>A "quire" or "quaternio" is a set of folded leaves of paper for a book.</note> of our *Specimen*." (Acquoy and Rogge, *Archive for Dutch Church History*, IV, 293 and 295.)

— Voetius explains the composition of his book thus:

> "I had initially decided to issue only a preliminary work, and to reserve a proper response for a greater necessity and a better opportunity. But various rumors spread far and wide along with the book, and other things that occurred after our Preface with the excerpts had already been printed, forced me—having changed my plan and my printer alike (for the former could not finish the work he had begun)—to [write] somewhat more at length..."

# TO G. VOETIUS.

55

That "martyr" of yours <note>Descartes is likely referring to Jean Le Maire (Lemannus), a colleague of Voetius whose name was attached to a pamphlet, though many suspected Voetius was the true author.</note> deserves little from you; it was under his name that the *Rebuttal* <note>original: "Retorsio"; a polemical response to Samuel Desmarets.</note> appeared, yet on page 416 you portray him as completely unskilled. You mention the rumor that he is not its author, suggesting he did not possess enough Latin for the task. And then, 
<margin>5</margin>responding coldly with these words: *Regarding the Minister’s command of Latin, and his studies of the arts, languages, and theology, I feel nothing ordinary; I speak from experience.* <note>original: "nihil vulgare." Voetius uses a double-edged Latin phrase. While it could mean "extraordinary," in this context Descartes argues it implies the man didn't even have "common" or basic knowledge.</note> From this, one is naturally led to conclude that he does not even possess an ordinary knowledge of Latin or theology. It seems more 
<margin>10</margin>believable that he lacks basic skills than that he possesses "more than ordinary" ones. You were so scrupulous that you preferred to use an ambiguous word rather than tell a lie—even though, by doing so, you confirm that you are the true author of that notorious *Rebuttal*<sup>a</sup>. Nor do you seem to me any 
<margin>15</margin>more respectful toward the other pastors of the Netherlands <note>original: "Belgii pastores"; referring to the Reformed clergy in the Dutch Republic.</note> when, in addressing them on page 27, you write: *I will show in fact that this will be no less pleasing to me than when you add courage to me and provoke me to attempt similar or even greater things—both in person and so frequently, and even through collective letters—with your shouts of encouragement and approvals (I will add no more, lest I seem 
<margin>20</margin>foolish, or lest envy should hear this).* It is as if they had ever provoked you to publicly criticize the Nobles and Magistrates of the cities in your theses, and in this way to stir up disturbances—something I do not believe any of them would ever do. I could note countless other examples, but I do not wish...

->## LETTER<-

to undertake a full examination of your book; those parts I leave to Desmarets <note>original: "Maresio"; referring to Samuel Desmarets (1599–1673), a French Protestant theologian and a major opponent of Voetius.</note>; for he has already given such a specimen of talent, prudence, and learning in his *Defense* that I do not doubt he will perform excellently in this matter, and it will be well worth the effort<sup>a</sup>. Meanwhile, I will only briefly remind you of those points that occur to my memory.

I have noted absurdity in all those things you propose in place of arguments, and at the same time a most hateful unfairness: for nowhere do you use reasoning correctly, and everywhere you violate the rule: *Whatever law a person establishes for another, they should be bound by that same law themselves* <note>original: "Quod quisque juris in alium statuerit, ut ipse eodem jure utatur." Thus, on page 24, you quote these words of Desmarets: *I would certainly have wished that, content with a general inquiry, you had not designated 's-Hertogenbosch* <note>original: "Sylvamducis"; the Latin name for the Dutch city 's-Hertogenbosch.</note> *and our people by name*<sup>b</sup>.

->### TO G. VOETIUS.<-

To which you respond thus: "And I, along with others who love the true religion, piety, and the peace of the church, would have much more wished that he <note>Referring to Samuel Desmarets, the pastor of 's-Hertogenbosch.</note> had not attacked those *Theses on Idolatry*, for the sake of such a cause, especially at this time, and in such a book."
<margin>5</margin> For if lectures, corollaries, and *Academic Theses*—not only those of adversaries, but even of friends, members of your own circle, neutral parties, and anonymous authors—had to be harangued in idle and<gloss>a</gloss> hateful books, what end would there be, and what would the state of affairs look like?
No response could be imagined more absurd or unfair than this.
<margin>10</margin> For you believe it was permissible for you to name 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original: "Sylvam-ducis"; a city in the Netherlands where Voetius’s rigid Calvinist views caused significant political and religious friction.</note> in your academic positions, and by slandering its Magistrate and Nobles, to disturb the church's peace there as much as you possibly could. Meanwhile, you find fault with Desmarets, their pastor, because he dared to contradict those "sacred" theses of yours in order to protect the
<margin>15</margin> innocence of his people and to look after the ecclesiastical peace in his own city. Similar examples of such unfairness appear everywhere in your book, and indeed often they are so absurd that they remind me of the madness of Fimbria. After he had wounded Quintus Scaevola <note>Gaius Flavius Fimbria and Quintus Mucius Scaevola were figures from Roman history; Fimbria was a violent partisan who attempted to assassinate Scaevola, a respected jurist.</note>,
<margin>20</margin> intending to kill him, he actually tried to summon Scaevola to court afterward because he "had not received the whole blade into his body." <gloss>b</gloss>

Perhaps such unfairness could be tolerated if it were not joined with such arrogance. But those who see how insolently and proudly you always play the part of the accuser
<margin>25</margin> or the judge—when in reality you are the one accused—will see that you are guilty of a crime which cannot be denied, and which requires only a humble plea for pardon and a demonstration of repentance...

And indeed, there are none in a commonwealth more worthy of condemnation, none to be afflicted with greater punishments, than those who, by speaking ill of its rulers, give the common people an occasion to respect and observe them less, and thus to withdraw themselves all the more freely <margin>15</margin> from their authority. But one must think very differently about your own reputation—or even, through you, the reputation of your religion and profession—than about that of the political Magistracy. For even if you had the best cause, it would still be more honorable for you, and more <margin>20</margin> conducive to the praise of your religion, if you freely submitted yourself to the <term>Synod|A formal assembly of church delegates</term> and allowed yourself to be judged—or even condemned <note>original: "ipsa"; the footnote indicates the first edition mistakenly used "ipso"</note>—by it, rather than so stubbornly opposing other theologians and <term>consistories|synedriis; local church councils</term> and refusing the judgments of the synods. Furthermore, this would be a <margin>25</margin> credit to your profession: that you did not, as the ignorant usually do, wish to seem as if you could never err; and certainly in a <term>Theologian|A scholar of religious doctrine</term> nothing can be more worthy of praise and respect than if, by submitting his judgment to the judgments of others, and by candidly confessing <margin>30</margin> and correcting his errors (as we are all human), he provides others with examples of Christian piety and humility.
