You may mock me as a rustic and unlearned man because I call you back to those common virtues of simpler folk. Nothing is to be expected from you except that to which you are bound by strict law. <margin>5</margin> Come then; was it not at least fair, after both you and <term>Maresius|Samuel Desmarets, a prominent Reformed theologian and rival of Voetius</term> had written once, that you should refrain from further writing and wait for the judgment of the Synods? Or do you think anyone will believe that you feared the truth would be so shrouded in false prejudices by Maresius that, even if supported by your patronage, it could not be <margin>10</margin> recognized in a Synod by the learned theologians who would examine it there? Did you really hope it would be more easily discovered by any others who read your *Confraternity* <note>original: "Confraternitatem"; referring to Voetius's work "De Fraternitate et Confraternitatibus"</note> far and wide? It is certainly much more likely that you do not wish to commit your cause to <margin>15</margin> the Synods because you know it is so clearly bad that it could not even be excused by your own brethren. And because you offer no reasons for your writing except those I have reviewed here, it must be concluded from your own words that you *are stubborn, and unseasonably contentious, and* <note>original Greek: ἄτακτον (*ataktos*), meaning disorderly, rebellious, or lawless</note> disorderly, <margin>20</margin> giving neither the due honor to the <term>Magistrates|Optimates; the leading citizens or city officials</term> nor reverence and authority to the ecclesiastical assemblies.

But perhaps all these things could be overlooked if you had anything in your whole book from which it appeared that you believed the action of the Magistrates of <term>'s-Hertogenbosch|Sylva-Ducis</term> deserved to be <margin>25</margin> censured, or at least, if you used any true or honest reason to defend or excuse those things you wrote previously. However, although I have paid close attention to these two points, I have found that neither has been provided by you in any way.

# TO G. VOETIUS.
<meta>132-133.</meta>

Nor do you press this part of your argument very much, but you immediately pass to a dispute about the name, which you extend over many pages right to the end of the book, asserting that this name is idolatrous, and <margin>5</margin> producing many <term>commonplaces|Standard rhetorical or theological arguments used to support a general point</term> on the subject; yet from all of them you only conclude that, if the name is kept, at least some shadow of superstition is retained. Thus, your entire dispute—so burning | and so fervent—finally dissolves into a shadow. It is entirely <margin>10</margin> manifest that you had absolutely no other pretext for attacking this <term>Sodalitas|A brotherhood or religious society</term> than the fact that it is named after the Virgin <term>Deipara|A Latin theological term meaning "God-bearer" or Mother of God</term>, and not, as your books are titled, after *Thersites* or *Tertullus*$^a$ <note>original: "Thersite vel Tertullo." Thersites was a famously ugly and scurrilous character from Homer's Iliad; Tertullus was the orator who prosecuted the Apostle Paul. Voetius used these names in the titles of his polemical attacks.</note>. I say pretext, not cause or reason. For you know that in these regions there are <margin>15</margin> very many churches that still commonly retain the names of the Saints given to them in ancient times; and that in your own city <note>Utrecht</note> there is a college of Canons called Saint Mary's$^b$; nor do you think yourself overshadowed by any idolatry simply because you received the first name Gysbert from Saint Gysbert, <margin>20</margin> and indeed following the custom of the Roman Church in baptism—

---

a. Titles of two works. See earlier, p. 63, note *a*, and p. 75, note *c*.
b. <term>Desmarets|Samuel Desmarets (Maresius), a collaborator and friend of Descartes</term> insists on this reason in his *Apologetic Letter* (see earlier, p. 82, note *a*), p. 23:
> "No city of the United Netherlands has more societies of this kind than the one in which the Distinguished Man (*Voetius*) teaches (*Utrecht*). There are Colleges there that are not only purely civil, such as the Merchants of *St. Nicholas*, the Smiths of *St. Joseph*, etc., but also several others that are purely pious in use and specifically intended for works of mercy and offices of charity, such as *St. Job*, the *Holy Cross*, and similar ones; indeed, there are many of purely spiritual and religious foundation which, under these same names, have been transformed into purely political ones, like this one in 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original: "Sylvæducenſe"</note>—such as the Canons of both sexes, which are named after *St. Mary*, *St. John*, and others. Nor has it ever been heard said that the Reformed [Protestants], when joining and constituting these Colleges, were accused of the crime of any idolatry because of their superstitious and faulty origin, or their customary naming after Saints." (*Ultima patientia*, page 101.) See also page 10 earlier, note *a*.

Thus, it is clear that you had absolutely no reason of any weight to disapprove of the action taken by the <term>Optimates|The "best men" or leading magistrates and citizens</term> of <term>'s-Hertogenbosch|The city of 's-Hertogenbosch, known in Latin as Sylva-ducis or "the Duke's wood"</term>; yet you did have a reason <margin>5</margin> for wanting to disapprove of it: namely, because it had been approved by others. # LETTER
<meta>137-139.</meta>

[...not] a single word, nor anything spoken against his own conscience, nor against the truth—as you so often call <term>Maresius|Samuel Des Marets (1599–1673), a Protestant theologian and ally of Descartes</term> and myself—then he clearly slanders in a shameful manner, and the infamy of it rebounds upon himself. When, however, someone clearly demonstrates that another has said something not only false, <margin>5</margin> but also that the speaker knew perfectly well was false, then if he wishes to speak candidly and freely as an honest and noble man, he ought to say that the other is lying. And if he catches that person in such lies frequently, he ought to say that he is a <note>original: *mendacissimum*; a most habitual or "lyingest" liar</note> most habitual liar. <margin>10</margin> Moreover, because nothing is more disgraceful or more shameful for noble men than to lie, he who lies most frequently and most openly must be called utterly impudent.

And yet, it is indeed not only false that you imputed no crimes to the <term>Optimates|The leading magistrates</term> of <margin>15</margin> <term>’s-Hertogenbosch|A city in the Netherlands, referred to in Latin as *Silva Ducis*</term>, as you write here; but it is also perfectly clear that you know this well. For you could not have forgotten the words that are read in your own <note>original: *thesibus*; these were academic arguments published for public debate</note> theses; they were brought back to your memory quite sufficiently by Maresius, and you yourself repeat them several times in your own book. Furthermore, on page 306, <margin>20</margin> you ridiculously pretend that these were the jibes of the <term>Papists|Descartes uses the term *Pontificiorum*, referring to Roman Catholics</term>, and not your own. Therefore, when you deny that you wrote them, it must be admitted that you are lying. Since you lie so often in this manner, [it must be said] that you are a most habitual liar; and finally, that you are most impudent, because that kind of lie is of all <margin>25</margin> types the most manifest. For you appeal to your own theses, which were committed to print and are held by many, and from which it is perfectly clear that you are lying.

Indeed, there is that incredible audacity by which you not only appeal to an inspection of your theses—from which you well know you must be condemned—<margin>30</margin> but you even [attack] Maresius, who wrote nothing about you that is not most clearly seen to be true, as if [he were caught] in a mani[fest lie...]

# To Gisbertus Voetius.

...to establish your dogmas, you create confusion, not only to show that you disagree with Maresius<note>Samuel Desmarets (1599–1673), a Protestant theologian and rival of Voetius.</note> on this thesis—which he, for the sake of pleasing you, had previously denied<gloss>a. > If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love <note>original: *Charitatem*. While often translated as "charity," in this context it refers to the theological virtue of selfless, divine love.</note><sup>a</sup>, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. ...badly, but, as much as is in our power, let us do good to our friends. And because nothing is better than to be free from vices, therefore no one ever bestows a greater benefit upon another than when he attempts to recall him from some vice by appropriate means. <margin>5</margin> But I add, *by appropriate means*: for if someone rebukes another untimely, or too severely for a slight fault, or in the presence of others when it is not necessary, or if he attributes false crimes to him, and thus seems to seek not so much his improvement <note>original: *emendationem*</note> <margin>10</margin> as his disgrace and his own glory, he will be hateful and troublesome. But it is almost always permissible to admonish one's friend modestly in private, with no one else knowing; and if this is not sufficient, and the fault is serious, it is also permissible to persist and rebuke; and then to ensure the same is done by his other friends—one, two, or all of them. <margin>15</margin> If all these things do not help, and his sin is such that it makes him unworthy of the friendship of an honest man, we may indeed withdraw ourselves from his familiarity and no longer count him among our friends. But certainly, as long as we love him, we must never <margin>20</margin> reproach him publicly before everyone, including strangers and those unknown to him; for in this way we would not procure his good, but rather his harm—namely, infamy <term>infamy: a public loss of reputation or disgrace</term>. And this is to be understood not only regarding hidden vices, but also public ones: for those who sin publicly are accustomed <margin>25</margin> to glory in their sins, and do not care that it is known they commit such things; but they grieve that they are blamed for it. And it must be noted that it is the fear of infamy that most strongly draws men back from vices, and not infamy itself, which once it has been inflicted on someone, is no longer <margin>30</margin> feared by him. And therefore those who do not listen to the private rebukes of friends, do not even [listen] to public reproaches...

<margin>15</margin> sins*, but there is added *against you* <note>original: *in te*</note>. And since we have more right to rebuke someone when he has affected us ourselves with an injury, than when we merely see that he has done some other evil: there is no doubt that here are contained all the ultimate remedies which one is permitted to use to rebuke one’s
<margin>20</margin> neighbor when he has committed some sin of great importance. Nor are all the sins of the neighbor brought back to this principle under any other name than because it is supposed that there is such great zeal in pious men that they take it no less poorly that someone sins against God—or, because God cannot
<margin>25</margin> be harmed by men, that he who sins (and whom they love as a neighbor) harms himself by sinning—than if he were to inflict an injury upon them. ...[authori]ty and the command of the legislator. Therefore, I will also subjoin some things about these matters here.

And first, indeed, as for the censures that are made without any right of condemning, and are properly called **accusations**: it is certain that <margin>5</margin> these are permitted in every well-ordered republic, provided they are true, and even sometimes commanded, as in the case of high treason <note>original: *crimine majestatis*</note>. And generally, those who disparage others but say nothing false about them are not condemned by the laws. For it is expressly held <margin>10</margin> in Book 18 of the <term>Digests</term> <note>The *Digesta* or Pandects: a massive compilation of Roman juristic writings ordered by Emperor Justinian</note> regarding insults and libelous pamphlets: *that it is not good or fair for a person who has defamed a guilty party to be condemned for that reason; for it is both necessary and beneficial for the sins of the guilty to be known* <sup>a</sup>. 

But nevertheless, there are various reasons why certain accusations are less honorable and just for some than for others. For <margin>15</margin> surely, no one ever honorably accuses defendants who are humble and ready for repentance, unless he is a <term>Praetor</term> <note>A Roman magistrate or judicial official</note> or is compelled to do so by some other cause; because it conflicts with the charity <note>original: *charitate*; referring to the theological virtue of selfless love</note> which we all ought to show one another, to desire that <margin>20</margin> someone who is a suppliant and asks for pardon should be punished. But if someone who is arrogant and obstinate commits those acts by which the peace and harmony of the Republic can be disturbed, and who, having been warned privately by friends and even by Magistrates, refuses to correct or acknowledge his sins; who becomes so <margin>25</margin> vehement in attacking others, so bold in slandering, so persistent in persecuting, that hardly anyone dares to resist him; who, finally, has so many escapes, so many deceits for concealing his vices, and such great impudence in denying them, that although they can easily be understood...

### LETTER

...by those who <column-break/> examine the case, yet it is not so easy for just anyone to demonstrate these things to everyone. It is certain that he who is able and dares, and who is not appointed to any public office <note>original: *publico munere*</note>, acts rightly if he accuses such a defendant. Indeed, he cannot honorably refrain from accusing <margin>5</margin> if he has been provoked by that person and harmed by atrocious slanders <note>original: *calumniis*</note>, lest he seem either faint-hearted or neglectful of matters pertaining to the public good and his own reputation.

However, I have excluded those who perform public duties, not because none of them may accuse others—for some <margin>10</margin> are compelled to do so by their office—but because for those whose office requires no such thing, it is less honorable than for private citizens. For they must take care lest, when they cannot be judges, they appear to want to abuse the authority <margin>15</margin> of their office to crush someone’s innocence.

Indeed, private individuals accuse at their own peril, and unless everything they have said is true, or at least unless they had just causes for believing them to be true, they are punished as slanderers. But those established in authority often cause harm with greater impunity. <margin>20</margin>

But certainly, of all those who hold any public office, for none is it more unbecoming to accuse others than for **Preachers** <note>original: *Concionatoribus*; those who deliver public sermons</note>, **Professors of Theology**, and **Pastors of the Churches**. For since, by reason of their office, they are regarded as men exceptionally pious, learned, and burning with the zeal of **charity** <margin>25</margin> <note>original: *charitatis*; refers to the theological virtue of selfless love</note>, they weigh down the cause they attack with a great prejudice <note>The author uses "prejudice" (*praejudicium*) to mean the unfair weight their holy reputation gives to an accusation before facts are even proven</note>. And, should they wish to be wicked, they have many opportunities to slander with impunity. But even if it were perhaps sometimes granted to them to accuse others, to avenge injuries done to them, and <margin>30</margin> to indulge private hatreds: <column-break/> yet never truly...

For, as for sermons <note>original: *conciones*; public religious discourses</note>, no one doubts that they were established for teaching the truth regarding matters <margin>5</margin> pertaining to religion, and at the same time for discouraging men from sins and urging them toward virtue, but not for bringing disgrace <note>original: *ignominia*</note> upon anyone, nor for displaying examples of malice, nor for usurping any jurisdiction over individual men. For since he has been publicly chosen to speak the truth from that pulpit, <margin>15</margin> he adds public authority to his private testimony, <column-break/> and thus abuses the dignity of his office to defame his neighbor. Next, because every public reproach of specific persons, no matter how true and just it may be, nevertheless exceeds the limits of charity <note>original: *charitatis*; in this context, the Christian duty of love and kindness toward others</note> and invites hatred toward one's neighbor; therefore <margin>20</margin> it sets the worst possible example in a sermon. <column-break/> Finally, because under the pretext of denouncing vices, one can easily commit this crime with impunity—namely, reproaching specific persons by not naming them, but by describing them with such characteristics that although they are certainly recognized <margin>25</margin> by the listeners, the speaker can still pretend he was not thinking of them. Therefore, those who are truly pious, and who do not attempt to usurp any unlawful authority over civil authorities and others by that route, are accustomed to take the greatest care lest the same thing ever be said of them that you boast of yourself, <margin>30</margin> on page 331: namely that, <column-break/> *by your usual method, you [mention] specific deeds in your sermons not infrequently...*

...was instituted for the good of those who are accused, but for the rest who, through fear of a similar accusation, shrink more from vices, as has already been said. But listen to Blessed James <note>Referring to the Epistle of St. James 4:11</note> saying in chapter 4: *He who speaks against a brother, or who judges* <margin>5</margin>*his brother, speaks against the law, and judges the law.* <note>original Latin: *Qui detrahit fratri, aut qui judicat fratrem suum, detrahit legi, & judicat legem.*</note> For it is granted to you—indeed, it is even commanded to you as a preacher <term>concionatori (preacher): one who delivers public sermons or addresses a congregation</term>—to rebuke vices and to try to recall men from them. If you indeed do this, you speak against the law and you judge the law; that is, you claim more for your own judgment <margin>15</margin>than for the law. For the purpose of determining what is legal, you have, I believe, your Synods <note>original: *Synodos*; assemblies of church leaders meant to reach collective decisions on doctrine and practice</note>, in which judgment is rendered by the common opinion of all; and for punishing the deeds of men, there are the Magistrates <note>original: *Magistratus*; civil authorities who hold the legal power to punish crimes, distinct from the church</note>. I am not easily persuaded that your fellow ministers <note>original: *symmystas*; literally "fellow-initiates," referring here to his colleagues in the clergy</note> will bear it with equanimity that <margin>20</margin>you alone, by your own authority, should so decide on questions not yet determined among you, that although other theologians and even entire consistories <term>synedria (consistories): the governing councils or courts of the Reformed Church</term> disagree with you, you nevertheless wish your single decree to be valued more than the opinions of all others—unless perhaps they <margin>25</margin>appoint you as the head of their Church. I would not dare to advise against that, lest I be suspect to them, or deserve poorly of our own people. But truly, if even the Magistrates were to allow you to judge the specific deeds of men in sermons or academic theses, and thus to freely <margin>30</margin>assault the reputation of all men, I would be greatly astonished.

For this reason, they were not believed unless they gave credit to their words through great and indubitable miracles. And so that you may understand that their right was so immense that no similar right could easily be granted to you, <margin>20</margin>see how God describes it in Jeremiah 1: *Behold,* he says, *I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to root out and to pull down, and to waste and to destroy, and to build and to plant.* <note>original Latin: *Ecce, inquit, constitui te hodie super gentes & super regna, ut evellas, & destruas, & disperdas, & dissipes, & ædifices, & plantes.* Descartes quotes the Vulgate Bible, Jeremiah 1:10.</note> Now he who was thus set over nations and kingdoms was a man alone, having no <margin>25</margin>visible counselors with whom he might deliberate on what was to be done, and also having no civil power. Therefore, it would not have been reasonable for Kings and peoples to submit themselves to him voluntarily, unless he had shown by evident miracles that he had truly been <margin>30</margin>sent by God, the Lord of kings. You, indeed, imitate those extraordinary Prophets best in this: that you [criticize] the [lives] of other men...

<page-num>125</page-num>
<header>TO G. VOETIUS.</header>
<meta>187-189.</meta>

...whether you disregard advice and, as if you were accustomed to speaking with God, you draw your decrees from your own heart; but miracles have so far been lacking to you, and I have learned from your own writings that in this age, according to your religion, <margin>5</margin> no such Prophets are recognized in the Church—specifically, those who would perform miracles and who ought to be believed in all things.

And for that reason, there will be no need for me to examine what might be conceded to our side or to others who disagree with you on this matter. It is enough that it be understood that you are neither <margin>10</margin> immune from the danger of error, nor do you have any privilege over all the other Ministers of your religion. For it follows from this that if it were permitted for you to rebuke the actions of the <term>Magistrates|The civil authorities and city officials who governed the Dutch Republic.</term> before the people on your own authority, it would also be permitted to all others; and since <margin>15</margin> you are able to err, and there are "as many opinions as there are men," <note>original Latin: *quot homines tot sententiae*; a famous Roman proverb suggesting that everyone has a different viewpoint, leading to inevitable disagreement.</note> no other fruit is to be expected from such a practice than turmoil and confusion. Everyone knows that such evils in a Republic so powerful, consisting of so many members, and whose entire safety depends on harmony, must be <margin>20</margin> guarded against as diligently as possible. But lest we meanwhile forget Charity <note>original: *Charitas*; in this context, the Christian virtue of selfless love and goodwill toward one's neighbor.</note>, just as we are accustomed to forgive friends for whatever they may do against us as long as we judge them to be truly our friends—whereas we are more angry with those who we recognize are faking friendship in order to <margin>25</margin> harm us than with those who are openly injurious—so, if ever a truly pious <term>Theologian|A scholar of divinity; Descartes is distinguishing between sincere religious scholars and those who use religion as a political weapon.</term>, who is clearly led by no other feeling than Charity, should exceed the limits of his office, he could easily be excused. But if anyone, while feigning piety in his face and words, shows by his very deeds nothing other than malice and a <margin>30</margin> lust for power <note>original: *dominandi lubidinem*; a strong critique of religious leaders seeking to dominate the state.</note>, he must be completely restrained.

6 <note>original French editor's note: *Non à la ligne* (1st edition); meaning the text did not start a new paragraph in the original 1643 printing.</note>

<summary>Descartes argues that since Voetius cannot perform miracles to prove divine inspiration, he has no right to publicly attack government officials. He warns that allowing every minister to claim such authority would lead to political instability and social "confusion."</summary>

You thought you could gain no small amount of authority for yourself from this: that your academic students, and all others to whom the fame of your deed might reach, seeing that you had dared to condemn such men and so famous a city for <margin>5</margin> a deed done by them for the good of the state <note>original: *reipublicæ*, referring to the public welfare or the Commonwealth of the Netherlands.</note> and approved by other theologians, and that you had done so with impunity, would revere your power. But it happened quite inconveniently for you that Maresius <note>Samuel Maresius (1599–1673), a French Protestant theologian and rival of Voetius.</note> showed, in a public writing,<sup>a</sup> the innocence <margin>15</margin> of his people and the injustice of your rebuke; and then also, that the Magistrates of 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original: *Sylvæducis*.</note> and others tried, through various letters, to ensure that you would abstain from further writing and wait for the judgment of the next Synod <note>a regional council of the Reformed Church.</note>, to which those you had accused <margin>20</margin> declared they were willing to submit. For in this situation, it was impossible for you not to either openly cast off the mask of piety and charity by not complying with their most just petition, or to lose a great part of your hope for dominance if you allowed yourself to be brought to order by the Synods. <margin>25</margin> Which of these you preferred, you show by the publication of the book *On the Marian Confraternity* <note>original: *de Confraternitate Marianâ*; a reference to a specific religious society in 's-Hertogenbosch that Voetius attacked.</note>: for in it, you fight for victory with no weight of reasons and no honest pretext, but by sheer stubbornness and the audacity of slandering.

And the entire artifice of that book consists in this alone: that you made it so long and so tedious that no man's patience could endure reading it in its entirety; and in it you so frequently accuse, rebuke, and condemn Maresius <note>Samuel Maresius (1599–1673), also known as Samuel Des Marets, a French Protestant theologian who became a bitter rival of Voetius.</note> along with

<margin>10</margin> of yours are explained on the other pages which they have not read. However, you found the material to forge such a thick volume by collecting many empty stories with which you try to make the Sodalities of the Blessed Virgin <note>Religious lay associations or confraternities. ...clearly recognize that this audacity of yours must necessarily be restrained. For nothing can more openly lead toward civil discord <note>Descartes emphasizes that Voetius’s behavior is a political threat, not just a religious one.</note> than if someone, protected by the authority of a single city, should condemn in a public writing the actions of another city—and indeed, actions not of a trivial sort, but undertaken for the good of the state <term>reipublicæ</term>—and should attack them not so much with arguments as with insults.

Perhaps you take it ill that I write these things; but what was I to do? What is at stake here is the common safety and peace of these regions where I, no less than you, have lived for many years. Nor is there any question here about the fairness of the matter you criticized. There is no need to wait for any synod <note>A formal meeting of church leaders to decide on points of doctrine or discipline.</note> to determine whether it is permissible for your associates to enter into some society with Roman Catholics named after the Blessed Virgin <note>original: "B. Virgine"; referring to the "Sodality of Our Lady," a point of major contention where Voetius attacked the city of 's-Hertogenbosch for its religious tolerance.</note>, in which nothing is done contrary to your religion (a matter in which I think great difficulty would be found). Rather, the only question here is whether it is permissible for the theologian of one city, by his own authority, to condemn another city and, as far as he can, to defame <term>infamare</term> it; and whether it should be thought that his lords, given the fairness and prudence they possess, will not take action against him. Especially since they have already experienced how stubborn you are, such that unless you are restrained in time, you will easily reach an intolerable level of audacity; and nothing else can be expected if you are spared this time, than that perhaps in the future—having become not better, but more cautious—you will indeed refrain from naming cities, but in the meantime, by that method you boast is *usual* <note>original: *uſitatâ*; Descartes is likely mocking Voetius’s specific scholastic or polemical style of attacking opponents indirectly.</note> to you, you will continue to defame the actions of those you wish...

# LETTER
<page-num>134</page-num>
<header>LETTER</header>
<meta>Marginal reference in header: 204-206.</meta>

...you describe them in such a way that they can easily be linked back to the people themselves; thus, you will do no less harm, but perhaps there will be less occasion to punish you.

I will not set forth here other reasons why I believe your superiors, both political and ecclesiastical, cannot excuse you, <margin>5</margin> lest I should seem to want to teach them—by warning you—those things which they can know better than I, and which they undoubtedly already know. But there is one thing more which I do not think should be omitted for the sake of the common people. <margin>10</margin> I have heard that this is always observed in your religion <note>Descartes, a Catholic, is referring here to the Dutch Reformed Church to which Voetius belonged.</note>: if any Preacher <term>Concionator</term> <note>original: "Concionator"; a public speaker or minister in the Reformed tradition.</note> is caught in some shameful sin <term>peccatum</term>, for example, if he has committed adultery, theft, or homicide, he is to be stripped of his office. And not without cause: for although those who do not live well <margin>15</margin> may still give good advice to others, their words are never granted as much trust as they would be if the speakers were thought to be upright and blameless. But surely no sin is more shameful for a Preacher, none provides better grounds for his words to be disbelieved, and none therefore renders him <margin>20</margin> more unworthy of his office, than if he should very frequently and most openly lie, speak evil, and slander. For other sins are committed outside the sermon <term>concionem</term> and are excused due to human frailty. Indeed, we ought to believe out of charity that those who have committed them <margin>25</margin> have set aside the will to persist in them before they begin to preach; and therefore, they are to be heard no less than if they had previously been blameless. There is no danger at all that anyone would provide examples of homicide, or adultery, or <margin>30</margin> theft within the sermon; but | on the contrary, if someone, incensed by anger, kills a man, or by some other impulse of the mind...

<note>In the 1st edition, line 3 did not begin a new paragraph.</note>

<summary>Descartes argues that while sins like theft or murder disqualify a preacher, the act of lying and slandering from the pulpit is a far greater betrayal of the office's purpose. He suggests that Voetius’s habitual dishonesty makes him more unworthy of his position than those who commit "fragile" human sins.</summary>

# TO G. VOETIUS.
<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>TO G. VOETIUS.</header>
<meta>Marginal reference in header: 206-208.</meta>

...prompted by impulse, has committed other sins, he often later repents of them so much that he can more effectively and powerfully call others away from them than one who has never fallen into them. But the license for lying, speaking evil, and slandering
<margin>5</margin> can be exercised nowhere more easily than in a sermon <term>concione</term> <note>original: "concione"; referring to the public delivery of a sermon or religious address from the pulpit.</note>, and nowhere is it more deserving of blame. For sermons are established for the purpose of teaching the truth; the people expect it from that place, and therefore no vice in a preacher is greater than being a liar. Furthermore, 
<margin>10</margin> since sermons are also established to provide examples of Christian piety and charity <note>original: "pietatis & charitatis"; here, Descartes appeals to the fundamental virtues of the Christian faith which Voetius, as a theologian, should uphold.</note>; and since, among the various kinds of lies, none are more foul, nor more foreign to charity, than those which tend toward the harm of one's neighbor and are called "evil-speaking" and "slander": 
<margin>15</margin> then none are more blameworthy in a preacher. That you have been caught in such lies not just once, but quite often in your book, has already been sufficiently shown above. There is no need for men to take my word for it: I have asserted nothing that is not manifest from your own 
<margin>20</margin> publicly edited writings. Or certainly, if there are some who wish neither to unroll your writings, nor think it fair to believe me when I affirm it—rather than you, their pastor, who strenuously denies the same—they still cannot excuse you unless they condemn Maresius <note>Samuel Maresius (1599–1673), also known as Samuel Desmarets, was a prominent theologian who was at times a colleague and at other times a bitter rival of Voetius.</note>, your 
<margin>25</margin> fellow-minister. For it cannot be denied that you often accuse him in your book of lying and slander. In this matter, if you are speaking the truth, then he is unworthy to preach; but if you speak falsely, then certainly in this very act of accusing him of slander, you yourself are slandering. And because 
<margin>30</margin> there can be no suspicion regarding him, I think no excuse remains for you.

<summary>Descartes argues that while a preacher might recover from other sins, chronic lying and slander are uniquely disqualifying because they violate the core purpose of the pulpit. He uses the conflict between Voetius and his colleague Samuel Maresius to trap Voetius in a logical contradiction: either Voetius is a slanderer or his fellow minister is a liar.</summary>

### PART EIGHT.

Next come reflections on the private conduct of Descartes, to which he does not respond here (he had already done so in advance, p. 22, lines 5-15): "What kind of morals he possesses in his life, someone could hardly explain: for who could track all his hiding places and his dwellings, changed more often than is the custom of the Wagon-dwellers <note>original: "Hamaxobiis"; a term for nomadic tribes</note>? Now he is said to live in West Friesland, now in Guelders, again in Holland or Overijssel, or the Diocese of Utrecht, so that one might not wrongly suspect at first glance that he has emerged from the Society of the Brothers of the Rosy Cross <note>the Rosicrucians, a secret mystical society</note>, whose boastful voice Germany could indeed hear not so many years ago, though they themselves, however diligently sought, were difficult to find. I would not be unwilling to agree with this suspicion, if I did not know that this most ambitious man wants his name (which the aforementioned Brothers took care to suppress in silence) | to be sung through every corner of the world with open pipes. He also does not seem to have bound himself by the vow of the Anchorites <note>religious hermits</note>: for those men or women whom he loves to visit, he visits and greets at high noon; and although he can hardly bear the name of the ancient Philosophers, following their example he is said to be a revived Satho <note>likely a reference to a lewd or satirical figure</note> with his Phrynes <note>Phryne was a famous ancient Greek courtesan; the author implies Descartes keeps mistresses</note> whom he is said to hold dear and embrace closely. But for me to freely profess what I judge of the man, I believe him either to be driven by the stings of a bad conscience, perhaps because he touched a sacred-taboo <note>original: "bidental"; a place struck by lightning, which was religiously forbidden to touch</note> somewhere (God knows); or to be from the lineage of Timon or some other gloomy misanthrope <note>original: "μισανθρώπου"; a hater of mankind</note>; or finally to be deluded by a pleasant madness. But what has not yet been brought onto the stage, I cannot go on to detect more fully before the day. However it may be, this at least is most true: the man is tirelessly impudent, proud, fastidious, slanderous, and a common reviler, who seems to have no regard for what he says. To pass over other evidence of this matter, even the single Letter to Dinet <note>Descartes's published letter to Father Dinet, where he defended himself against similar charges</note> teaches this abundantly." (Pages 14-17.)

And the same phrase returns: "The theologian... against those in power... displaying [zeal]."

Since he wanted to burden the tail of his book with this unhappy ballast <note>original: "infelici faburrâ"</note> to persuade the unlearned that his philosophy—which for a few years had been taught by the Doctor at the University of Utrecht—had been proscribed and eliminated through injustice, he labors to persuade the incautious and those ignorant of the facts that this was importunately procured by a single Theologian, at that time the Rector Magnificus. In doing this, one can detect almost as many crimes of the man as there are words: for he belches out such crude and thick lies in nearly every line that he could have written with equal right and breath that the Theologian, the Rector Magnificus of the previous year, wanted to betray the country, attempt parricide against the Prince, consecrate this city to Vulcan <note>A classical way of saying "to burn the city down"</note>, lead a band of robbers and rebels, or introduce Turkism <note>original: "Turcismum," referring to Islam</note>, Socinian heresies, or Judaism—and what not? To come to the point: our man [Descartes] quite craftily, and clearly according to the method of false politicians and false pragmatists, labors to discharge all his bile on one Theologian, or the Rector Magnificus, by pretending that what was a decree established by the entire College of Professors was done by him alone. He does this either to set the Theologian at odds with his colleagues, or to find greater favor with the Fathers of the Society of Jesus <note>The Jesuits</note>, to whom the Theologian is more hated than others because he once drew his pen against certain dogmas of the Roman Church. But if it had pleased Descartes to consult his Doctor, or rather if the Doctor had been pleased to worship the truth and respect his conscience, he could not and should not have hidden that it is false: that the Theologian was either hasty or importunate in proscribing the figments of the new philosophy. Rather, various other Professors, colleagues of the Doctor, wished for these dreams and figments to be crushed in the bud <note>original: "in ipsâ herbâ," literally "in the blade of grass"</note>, and often complained to their Rector Magnificus that those things were being tolerated too long, which would eventually disturb the academic peace; they argued that a muzzle should be put on those hungering for novelty, and every occasion for heresy should be swept far away. But the Rector—that is, the Theologian himself—often turned away the weapons aimed at the Doctor’s throat, hoping that with leniency and long-suffering he could be recalled to duty in due time. Indeed, if either the Doctor or Descartes himself had considered these things, which are more certain than those things thought up in the Holy Office <note>original: "apud Sagram," likely referring to the Sacred Congregation of the Inquisition</note>, he would have decreed a different reward for the Rector's indulgence and moderation; nor would he have [written] against him...” (Pages 38-42.)

<note>
a. This entire passage from the Preface is worth citing, because the words of Regius, which Schoockius recalls, are precisely those that Descartes himself had advised, if not dictated, to his disciple in January 1642 (see volume III, pp. 494-495). Here it is in full:
> "Where is your shame!
> "Has a theologian ever attempted such a thing? Let the Physician (*Regius*) himself be heard, so that the whole world may recognize that Descartes is most worthy of the scepter of the Cretans <note>original: "Crætensium sceptro"; a classical allusion to the Cretans being notorious liars.</note>.
> "Thus he speaks in the Preface to the Reverend Theologian’s theses: *Honorable Rector, having seen your most learned and subtle theses, which you recently saw fit to propose for discussion regarding <term>substantial forms</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, the "substantial form" was the essence that gave a thing its specific properties; Descartes rejected this in favor of mechanical explanations.</note> and other physical matters, to others and also to the Professors of Medicine and Philosophy in our Academy, among whom I also play some part: I was certainly filled with the greatest joy, both because so great a man wished to exercise his style, his talent, and us in such material, since I do not doubt that you have used the strongest possible arguments for defending your opinion, so much so that after yours, if anyone expected stronger ones, he should rightly be considered to be in vain; and also because, since the greatest part of them [the theses] diametrically opposes the dogmas I have been accustomed to teach before now, you seem to have aimed primarily at me in your preface, and wished to invite me to respond, and thus to incite me to a certain honorable rivalry of inquiring more curiously into the truth. And certainly, I should boast greatly of this assault: for even if I were inferior in the contest itself, it would be glorious for me even to be defeated by such a great adversary. I therefore give you huge thanks for this, and I add this to the pile of the greatest benefits with which you have previously bound me to you, while in my medical profession and in my <term>problematic province</term> <note>original: "provincia problematica"; refers to the academic duty of presiding over public debates or "problems."</note> you always showed me the readiest assistance, and in many other things you were perpetually a supreme patron, supporter, and friend to me. Which one should I believe? The man [Descartes] accustomed to lying, who declares that the Theologian labored to circumvent and overthrow the innocent Physician through slander? Or the Physician himself, who, after the theses were published, proclaims and acknowledges the Theologian as his supreme patron, supporter, and friend? For I prefer to believe the Physician, my fellow countryman and formerly also my colleague, rather than René [Descartes]; for he does not seem to have been made for slandering and lying in the same way.*" (Pages 46-49.)

It should be remarked that Regius’s text is the word-for-word Latin translation of the draft response that Descartes had sent him in French. The last sentence was even already in Latin in Descartes's letter (vol. III, p. 495, lines 16-19); except that Regius went further than the text, adding "supreme friend" to the simple word "supporter." — As for the two functions mentioned by Regius (*Medical Profession and problematic province*), see vol. # LETTER
## 233-234.

...the dictates of Regius <note>Henricus Regius (1598–1679) was an early supporter of Descartes whose lectures on "New Philosophy" caused great controversy in Utrecht.</note>, you have attacked not indeed with any reasons, but with the most foolish chatter. Which chatter certainly could have been applied no less to any of my own writings; but because Regius's dictates have not been published, you hoped by <margin>5</margin> this means it would be less easily detected, and by fewer people, how closely your malice is joined with incredible ignorance.

Since, however, already above, in the 3rd and 5th parts of this letter <note>original: "epistolæ"</note>, I have discussed the first two sections of your book more than enough, there is no need for me to say anything <margin>10</margin> more about them. Nor indeed about the rest; for I know well enough that no one of any talent will read them without utterly despising them and recognizing them as the most impudent and foolish slanders. But nevertheless, lest I omit anything <margin>15</margin> that might seem to pertain to me, I will yet run through the remaining two sections.

In the third [section], after a ridiculous equivocation regarding the name of Theology <note>Descartes refers to his opponent's confusing or misleading use of the term "Theology" to frame philosophical disputes as religious heresy</note>, you begin to seem to want to say something specific...

## *Concerning the fourth section of the book on Cartesian Philosophy, and at the same time concerning the merits of its Authors.*

### THE FINAL PART.

After you have shown by those "remarkable" examples with what firm reasons and with how mature a judgment <margin>5</margin> you disapprove of my opinions, you add one more section for the conclusion, divided into four chapters, which contains nothing but four notorious slanders.
<margin>10</margin> In the first chapter, on page 245, *you assert that my method of philosophizing paves the way to Skepticism* <gloss>a</gloss>, *and that I remain stuck in the position of the Skeptics* <gloss>b</gloss>. You offer reasons for this: *That I seemingly thunder against Skeptics of the first <margin>15</margin> rank; that I boast of the most certain and evident knowledge of various things; and finally, that I spread around new criteria of truth—namely, those which cannot be applied to any science by any man, whoever he may be, through the aid of nature.* And you cite no other "new criteria" than that I wish to embrace as true only those things which are so clear that no...

<margin>5</margin> most solid and celebrated Theologian: he refutes all the arguments used by <term>Saint Thomas<note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval philosopher and theologian whose "Five Ways" for proving God's existence were standard in Catholic teaching.</note></term> to prove the existence of God and shows them to be invalid; and other serious and pious theologians have done the same, so much so that by those who speak in your fashion, it could be said of Saint Thomas

<gloss>a</gloss> Gregory of Valentia, born in March 1551 at Medina del Campo (Old Castile), entered the novitiate of the Society of Jesus on November 23, 1565. <margin>5</margin> you have nevertheless produced in them not even the slightest argument to prove the existence of God or to attack Atheism; on the contrary, you have testified that doing so is extremely difficult. Clearly, you were afraid that someone might compare you to Vanini <note>Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619) was an Italian philosopher burned at the stake for atheism. Voetius uses him as a "bogeyman" to suggest that public piety can mask secret heresy.</note>, because you had heard that he himself wrote against atheists and yet was burned because of Atheism. But you ought to have noted that he was not burned because of his public writings (which, though they contained only weak arguments and were perhaps prepared for the sake of deception, created no danger for him), but because of private deeds and words proved by witnesses. Yet you care so little for what you say, provided only that you can slander me, that we might rightly believe you have never even read Vanini's books. For everywhere you write "Vaninium" instead of Vanini <note>Descartes is pointing out a "typo" in Voetius's Latin—writing *Vaninium* instead of the correct *Vaninus*—as evidence that Voetius is citing authors he hasn't actually read.</note>; and since this same error is found everywhere in your pamphlets *on Atheism*<sup>a</sup>, as can be seen on pages 7, 9, and the rest, many will perhaps judge that this *Cartesian Philosophy* <note>original: *Philosophiam Cartesianam*. This refers to a specific anonymous attack titled "The Admirable Method of Cartesian Philosophy," which Descartes suspected Voetius of ghostwriting for his student Martin Schoock.</note> was written by you. I do not wish to persuade the reader of this, however, for it is enough that it was written on your behalf and published with your knowledge and consent, so that I have no less right to bring a legal action for defamation <note>original: *injuriarum actio*. A formal legal claim under Roman law for injury to one's reputation or person.</note> against you than against the one who claims to be the author.

---

a. Theses defended on June 22 and 29, and July 6 and 13, 1639. See volume III of this edition, pages 604–605.

<page-num>183</page-num>
<header>TO G. VOETIUS.</header>

In the final chapter, on page 268, you assert that my Method *produces not so much philosophers as madmen and lunatics* <sup>a</sup> <note>original: "non tam Philosophos quàm deliros phreneticosque gignere"</note>; and you prove this with a single reason: namely, because I wrote that *the mind must be led away from the senses to understand divine things* <sup>b</sup> <note>original: "mentem abducendam esse à sensibus ad res divinas intelligendas"</note>. Thus, as I see it, you good men never wish to meditate, nor to think about God, for fear that you might become lunatics.

And now there is no need for me to ask where the false rumors arise—the ones I hear are usually spread about the students of Regius <note>Henricus Regius (1598–1679) was a professor of medicine at Utrecht and an early, though later estranged, disciple of Descartes.</note> after they left Utrecht <note>term: Ultrajectum (the Latin name for Utrecht)</note>—namely, that they have fallen into madness. You indicate this clearly enough on page 269, saying you do not wish to collect examples of those who recently, from being priests of *Wisdom* <note>original: "Sophiae"</note>, were transformed by that *Philosophy* either into initiates of *Folly* <note>original: "Moriae," likely an allusion to Erasmus's "The Praise of Folly"</note> or *priests* of madness.

Naturally, you do not wish to name them, lest the falsehood of your slanders become too apparent; but meanwhile you want it believed that some have lost their wits, because although you lack any pretext for speaking ill, you still have the rage for slandering. And I find this to be the power of my philosophy: it can drive to insanity not those who cultivate and approve of it, but the envious and malicious who snarl at it.

And yet I do not complain that you recall men from embracing my philosophy by striking into them a fear of madness and enthusiasm <note>In the 17th century, "enthusiasm" referred to a state of irrational religious delusion or supposed private revelation.</note>; I care little that you call it ridiculous, inept, and utterly false. If I am unskilled, if I am deceived, if through imprudence I have committed something bad to writing, whatever it may be—since I have never forced it upon anyone, nor recommended it with any artifice, but have only laid it out plainly so that everyone might use it at his own risk—it cannot be so harmful...

b. See vol. VI, p. 37, l. 4-5, and p. 561, l. 12.

<margin>20</margin> gravely wounded by your academic judgment, I dared to speak back, and did not receive the entire weapon in my body. But because I am most fond of peace and quiet, I have never summoned anyone to court until now, and I am so ignorant of legal matters that even now I do not yet know to which judges such a case belongs; 
<margin>25</margin> and because offenses which are publicly known are usually punished by public authority, even if no one in particular complains of them, I will be content this time to make your slanders so well-known and famous that they will not easily be ignored by those whose duty it is to inquire into them.

<header>LETTER</header>

...he can, which have not yet been set forth there, by which he might show that to be true: there is no doubt that I ought to be punished most severely, and I ask for no favor or pardon. But if he has no reasons better than those he has already set forth, as <margin>5</margin> I am certain he has none; and if from these nothing else can be concluded but that he calumniates most impudently and atrociously, as I trust all fair judges will very easily recognize: I ask them, as much as I can, to decide once and for all whether no calumnies <note>In this context, "calumny" refers to a malicious and false accusation intended to damage a person's reputation, which was a serious legal matter in the 17th century.</note> are ever to <margin>10</margin> be punished in these regions. For this one is so atrocious, so inexcusable, and so public, that it cannot go unpunished without all others seeming to be permitted by this very fact.

I know indeed that the inhabitants of these Provinces <note>The United Provinces of the Netherlands, known for their relative religious and intellectual tolerance.</note> enjoy <margin>15</margin> great liberty; but I am persuaded that this liberty consists in the security of good and innocent men, not in the impunity of the wicked. And since good men can never be safe where the wicked are given the liberty of harming them, I consider this Republic <margin>20</margin> free specifically on this account: that all in it enjoy equal rights, and that incorrupt judgments are made, by which injuries brought by anyone against anyone else, if not harshly and cruelly, are certainly punished accurately and as often as is necessary. Perhaps lighter and more obscure calumnies <margin>25</margin> can sometimes be overlooked; but none can be more grave or more evident than this. To kill a father, to set fire to or betray one’s country, are lighter things than to craftily teach atheism. And it should be noted that you do not assert that I am an **Atheist**, lest perhaps in this I be believed to be ignorant rather <margin>30</margin> than wicked; but that *I craftily and secretly [teach] atheism* <note>original: "me subdole atque occulte Atheismi [doctrinam spargere]" — Descartes is highlighting that Schoock isn't just calling him an unbeliever, but a conspirator who hides his true views to corrupt others.</note>

And indeed, you do an injury to your Academy, Republic, and Church, in that you wish your private vices to be considered a part of them—and indeed a more secret or sacred part—into which it would be a sin for a foreigner to inquire. And you have several times <margin>20</margin> reproached Maresius <note>Samuel Des Marets (1599–1673), a French Protestant theologian who often clashed with Voetius.</note> with this same crime of *curiosity* by the same right, namely that he had dared to examine your "blessed" theses: but you, for your part, were not "too curious" in someone else's Republic when, in those very same theses, you accused the magistrates of 's-Hertogenbosch <note>original: "Sylvæducenses"; referring to the leaders of the city of 's-Hertogenbosch (Bois-le-Duc) in the Netherlands.</note> of idolatry. ...to persuade [others] that the power of a Professor of Theology in your new University <note>The University of Utrecht, which had recently been elevated from a gymnasium to a university in 1636.</note> ought to be so great that he may, at his whim and without reason, condemn anyone else in public judgments; and that those he has so condemned <margin>5</margin> are not allowed to mutter a word in response, lest they immediately be accused of excessive curiosity <note>original: "curiositatis"; here meaning meddling or interference</note> in a foreign Republic, and be said to be snooping into the sacred matters of Theology and your ecclesiastical Politics, and *to be plotting the disturbance of Churches and Universities*. Indeed, you bestow a great honor upon your Church if you wish its affairs <margin>10</margin> and sacred things to consist of your slanders, to such an extent that no one dares complain about them without being accused of plotting the disturbance of your Churches.

It will also not benefit you to call me a *foreigner and a Papist* <note>original: "Pontificium"; a derogatory term used by Protestants for Roman Catholics</note>. Nor is it necessary for me to say that the treaties <margin>15</margin> of my King <note>King Louis XIII of France</note> with the Lords of these regions <note>the United Provinces of the Netherlands</note> are such that, even if I had only landed here today for the first time, I should still enjoy the same rights as the natives; and I have lived here for so many years, and am so well known to all the most honorable people, that even if I had come from the side of the enemy, I should <margin>20</margin> no longer be considered a foreigner. Nor is it even necessary for me to appeal to the religious freedom granted to us in this Republic. But I simply affirm that such wicked lies, such scurrilous insults, and such atrocious slanders are contained in your book, that not <margin>25</margin> even an enemy against an enemy, or a Christian against an infidel, could use them without declaring himself to be wicked and criminal. I add that I have always experienced such courtesy among this people, have been so kindly received by everyone with whom I have associated, and have found all others to be so kind <margin>30</margin> and helpful, and so far removed...

...[be safe] from that boorish and insolent freedom of yours to harass anyone, no matter how unknown or innocent they may be. Indeed, I do not doubt that your own countrymen turn away from you far more than they would from any foreigners.
<margin>5</margin>
Finally, *the character of the inhabitants of the Netherlands is so well known to me* <note>original: "Belgii"; in the 17th century, "Belgium" was commonly used in Latin to refer to the Low Countries, specifically the United Provinces of the Netherlands.</note> that I believe those who govern others often imitate God Almighty <note>original: "Deum Opt. Max.", an abbreviation for "Deo Optimo Maximo," meaning "To God, the Best and Greatest."</note> in this regard: they are quite slow and hesitant to demand punishment from the guilty. Yet, once the audacity <margin>10</margin> of the wicked has reached the point where they judge it must be restrained, these same rulers cannot be corrupted by any favor, nor deceived by any empty words. And as for you, who have so poorly served the honor of your profession <note>Referring to his status as a Professor of Theology.</note> and your religion by publishing books devoid of charity or reason—filled only with slanders—beware. They <margin>15</margin> may judge that they cannot properly protect that honor unless they take action against you <note>original: "animadvertant"; in this legal context, it implies a formal punishment or judicial censure.</note>. Farewell.

## I

Among the letters of Regius—or rather the extracts for which Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706) was a French scholar and biographer of René Descartes. He translated and summarized many documents that are now lost in their original form.</note> provides the translation—we have omitted one (the 25th), which contains an interesting passage regarding the affair of Bois-le-Duc <note>Also known as 's-Hertogenbosch, a city in the southern Netherlands.</note> (see above, p. 64-107). Here is the entire paragraph where it is mentioned:

> "The defamatory pamphlet by the so-called Minister of Bois-le-Duc against the book by Desmarets <note>Samuel Maresius (1599–1673), a French Protestant theologian who often clashed with Voetius.</note> was merely the forerunner of a substantial volume that Voetius undertook in haste to attack the Brotherhood of Our Lady of Bois-le-Duc <note>A religious and social fraternity. Voetius, a strict Calvinist, attacked this group for what he perceived as Catholic or "idolatrous" tendencies.</note>. The Magistrates of that city were informed of this; and having assembled to deliberate on the means to repress the insolence of this troublemaker, they wrote as a body to the States of the province of Utrecht and to the Magistrates of the city. Voetius even boasted since <gloss>(in the margin: Page 421 of [the work regarding] the Marian Brotherhood)</gloss> that they did him the honor of writing to him privately to make the pen fall from his hands; but it was in vain. For, even though the Magistrate of Utrecht had stopped the printing of this new book <gloss>(in the margin: Letter 25 of the manuscript of Regius)</gloss>, and had forbidden Voetius to continue it in order to satisfy the orders of the States of the province, he did not cease to act secretly <gloss>(in the margin: The Argument of the Letter to the celebrated Voetius)</gloss> during the months of November and December. He was content to change the printer and the format of the book, which from an octavo <note>A book size where the printer's sheet is folded three times to make eight leaves.</note> became a duodecimo <note>A smaller book size where the sheet is folded into twelve leaves.</note>: so that he might show it to the Gallo-Belgic Synod <note>A regional gathering of French-speaking Reformed churches in the Low Countries.</note> which was to assemble at The Hague in 1643 <gloss>(in the margin: Volume 2 of the letters of Descartes, page 541. — Letter 25 of the manuscript of Regius)</gloss>. By exempting himself from the obedience he owed to the secular magistrates through the ecclesiastical authority of the Synod—to which the gentlemen of Bois-le-Duc had been willing to refer for the decision on their brotherhood—he hoped to find a way to make his cause triumphant there. The gentlemen of Bois-le-Duc were warned of the lack of submission he showed toward his superiors. Some were indignant at it, and among others Mr. Brederodius <note>Johan Wolfert van Brederode (1599–1655), a high-ranking Dutch nobleman and military leader.</note>, a Protestant and a person of high rank who was a member of the brotherhood, who had Voetius threatened with being given the lash— <note>The text ends mid-word with "étri-", likely "étrivières" (lashings/whipping with leather straps).</note>

<summary>This page provides historical background on Gijsbert Voetius’s defiance of civil authorities in Utrecht and Bois-le-Duc, detailing how he secretly printed a banned book by changing its format to circumvent a legal injunction.</summary>

## BY MR. DESCARTES, <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher and mathematician whose work "Meditations on First Philosophy" sparked intense debate in Dutch universities</note>

# TO THE MAGISTRATES

## OF THE CITY OF UTRECHT <note>The "Vroedschap" or city council of Utrecht, which had the power to ban books and initiate legal proceedings against individuals deemed a threat to public order or religion</note>

### Against Messrs. Voetius, Father & Son. <note>Gisbertus Voetius, the influential Rector of Utrecht University and a staunch defender of Reformed Orthodoxy, and his son Paul Voet. They accused Descartes of atheism and subverting the youth</note>

<meta>This page contains the opening of a formal letter from René Descartes to the authorities in Utrecht. It establishes the historical context of his long-running dispute with Gisbertus Voetius, a Dutch theologian. The footnotes provide crucial bibliographic details regarding the letter's transmission in Latin, French, and Flemish.</meta>

# TO THE MAGISTRATES<gloss>a</gloss>

## OF UTRECHT

->[JUNE 16, 1645 & FEBRUARY 21, 1648<gloss>b</gloss>.]<-

Gentlemen<gloss>c</gloss>,

<margin>5</margin>Those who are aware of the continual insults I have received for the past four years from the Voetius family, find

<gloss>a</gloss> “**To the Magistrates.**” These are the terms used by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier, the first editor of Descartes' letters</note>, and they correspond to the Latin text: **To the Magistrate.** <note>original: "Ad Magistratvm." See hereafter, the *Apologetic Complaint* (Querela Apologetica).</note> In reality, this letter was addressed to the **Vroedschap** <term>Vroedschap: The city council or "Body of the City" that governed early modern Dutch towns</term> of Utrecht. (See p. viii above, *Foreword*.) The **Vroedschap**, or *City Body*, in Utrecht included: *two mayors, two treasurers, twelve aldermen*, and *twenty-four councilors*, totaling forty members, as seen above (p. 155, note *a*) in a passage from the Preface of the *Admirable Method* <note>original: "Admiranda Methodus"</note>. (Information provided by Dr. S. Muller, Archivist at Utrecht.)

<gloss>b</gloss> The date of February 21, 1648, is the one found written in Descartes' own hand at the end of a Flemish translation of this letter, preserved in the Utrecht Archives. (See our volume V, p. 125, and above, pp. iv and ix, *Foreword*), with a note, also in Descartes' hand, declaring that he vouches for the French text only. However, the same letter had been sent a first time to the Vroedschap, in Latin, on June 16, 1645 (see our volume IV, p. 226, and above p. viii, *Foreword*). This first date, June 16, 1645, corresponds perfectly with Descartes' statement below (lines 5-6): *the continual insults I have received for the past four years from the Voetius family*. And likewise again below, p. 271, line 9 and p. 272, line 5, on two occasions: *for four years*. The attacks by Voet <note>Gisbertus Voetius, a staunch critic of Descartes</note> did not, in fact, begin seriously until 1641. — And this alone would suffice to prove that the French text of February 21, 1648, conforms to the Latin text of June 16, 1645.

Thus, Gentlemen, you can see that they boast of having obtained from you the condemnation of a writing in which they themselves can find no grounds for complaint. And so that you may know <margin>5</margin> that, when they describe the details of this condemnation—claiming that G. Voetius <note>Gijsbert Voetius (1589–1676), a powerful Dutch theologian and rector of Utrecht University, was Descartes’s primary antagonist.</note> neither solicited nor procured it, that he was never heard by your deputies, that he himself gave the declarations of the witnesses to one of them (who were also never <margin>10</margin> heard), and several other similar things—it is not to do you honor, nor to persuade those who read their writings of their innocence or my crime. For it is well known that, if I had committed the slightest wrong, I would have been called before my legitimate judges, and <margin>15</margin> that G. Voetius and yourselves, if you wished to take up his cause, would have had enough influence to obtain justice from them without following such extraordinary paths. Rather, it is instead to glory in the power they hold over you, and to make themselves formi-<margin>20</margin> dable to those who are your subjects, knowing that the awareness of their crimes will henceforth make them contemptible to the rest of the world. I pray you to consider that, in the same book where the younger Voetius <note>Paul Voet (1619–1667), the son of Gijsbert Voetius, who defended his father's positions.</note> writes all these things about you, and fur-<margin>25</margin> ther in another titled *Unjust Tribunal* <note>original Latin: "Tribunal iniquum." ...one is in danger of one's life, as in the combats of the theaters <note>Likely referring to staged gladiatorial fights or dramatic tragedies where "blood" is expected, unlike the "bloodless" intellectual debates of a university.</note>; or rather like the disputes held over theses in your Academy <term>Academy: The University of Utrecht, where the controversy began.</term>, without any shedding of blood, and even without becoming at all angry, when those who <margin>5</margin> dispute are men of honor. Now, the younger *Voëtius* <note>Paul Voet (1619–1667), son of the theologian Gijsbert Voetius.</note> cannot be excused for the reproaches he makes against the Gentlemen of *Groningen* <note>The university authorities in Groningen who had ruled that Martin Schoock was guilty of libeling Descartes.</note>, on the grounds that his father is not within their jurisdiction, and that he was not summoned, nor the case debated with him. For his father was neither plaintiff nor defendant in this matter, <margin>20</margin> and nothing at all was judged against him; they only received the depositions of *Schoock* <note>Martin Schoock, the professor who initially published attacks on Descartes but later confessed that Gijsbert Voetius had pressured him into doing so.</note>, as is done in all criminal trials, when these depositions can serve to excuse the crime of the one who is accused. For example, if a complaint is made against someone <margin>25</margin> for having received from him a payment in counterfeit money, and this person, to excuse himself, says that he did not know | this money was counterfeit, and that it was not he who made it, but that it was given to him by another; if this other person is not from the same <margin>30</margin> jurisdiction, his Judges do not have the right to summon him, nor to bring him to trial; but they cannot for that reason [prevent themselves from judging the case...]

...in the year 1642, according to his custom, (Schoock) had traveled to Utrecht during the dog days <note>The "dog days" (*ferias caniculares*) refer to the hottest period of summer, usually July and August, when universities were often in recess.</note> to visit friends, and was received by Master Voëtius together with the most illustrious Professors of that Academy, and some other honorable men, at a feast that was altogether sumptuous and magnificent. 
<margin>5</margin>At this gathering, once the tables were already cleared, the most illustrious Mr. Dematius and others brought up the mention of Descartes's Letter to Dinet <note>Descartes's *Letter to Dinet* (1642) was a public defense of his philosophy where he complained about the attacks coming from Utrecht.</note>, in which Master Voëtius, his teacher, was quite severely lashed; and he was asked and urgently invited by Mr. 
<margin>10</margin>Voëtius to draw his pen <note>To "draw his pen" (*calamum... stringeret*) is a metaphor for beginning a written attack, akin to drawing a sword for battle.</note> against Descartes on behalf of himself, his teacher. <note>original Latin: "anno 1642, more ſuo (Schoockius) per ferias caniculares Vltrajectum ad viſendos amicos excurriſſet... vt pro ſe, Præceptore ſuo, calamum in Carteſium ſtringeret."</note>

Is it not a remarkable thing, that something done so publicly, at feasts, in the presence of several people who ought to care for their conscience and their honor (for I do not wish to believe 
<margin>15</margin>that everyone who associates with Voëtius becomes like him), and which is in itself so probable that even those who judge only by conjecture do not doubt that it is true—namely, that Voëtius solicited Schoock to write against me; is it not, I say, a remarkable 
<margin>20</margin>and surprising thing that this very event was chosen by him to be denied before the Judges, and to serve as the foundation for a sentence by which he intended to ruin me? and there is no reason to doubt the truth of this deposition <term>deposition|A formal statement or testimony given by a witness for use in a legal proceeding.</term> made by Schoock before his Judges; 
<margin>25</margin>for it was not even contradicted by his adversaries in their lawsuit against him, where they stuffed in so many other irrelevant and less important matters, that they certainly would not have omitted that one if they had not been afraid of being convicted by the 
<margin>30</margin>testimonies of those who were present at that feast.

<meta>This page provides an explanatory note on a Dutch manuscript copy of the preceding letter, continuing the historical context of Descartes’ dispute with the authorities at Utrecht.</meta>

# CLARIFICATION

---

In the Utrecht Archives, a Dutch translation of this same letter is preserved in a manuscript notebook of 90 and a half pages. The handwriting is that of a copyist, but Descartes reviewed it, adding a few annotations in his own hand here and there. For instance, he corrected *Dinet* <note>original: "Dinet"; referring to Father Jacques Dinet, a Jesuit and former teacher of Descartes</note> (p. 222, l. 1), where the copyist had written *dient* <note>original: "dient", a Dutch word meaning "serves"</note>; a few lines lower, he added the word *rules* <note>original: "regulen"</note> (ibid., l. 10), which had been left blank. He added, in the margin, <margin>Piety toward a parent <note>original: "Pietas in parentem"</note></margin> (p. 230, l. 15), which was omitted in the translation; and he did the same for other section titles: *Unjust Tribunal* <note>original: "Tribunal iniquum"</note> (p. 234, l. 17-18, and p. 240, l. 25), *Rebuttal of Calumnies* <note>original: "Retorsio calumniarum"</note> (p. 235, l. 7), and *Admirable Method* <note>original: "Admiranda Methodus"</note> (p. 258, l. 24). He also added a forgotten proper name, *Dematius* <note>Hendrik Dematius, a notary in Utrecht</note> (p. 234, l. 11), as well as two quotations, also omitted: *wicked hand* <note>original: "scelerata manus"</note> and *to serve the scene* <note>original: "scenæ servire"; a phrase meaning to adapt to circumstances or play a part</note> (p. 245, l. 15). Finally, he restored the word *Method* <note>original: "Methodum"</note>, which the copyist had skipped in the quotation from the *Sacred to Good Faith* <note>original: "Bonæ fidei Sacrum"; a polemical work written against Descartes</note> (p. 249, l. 2), and he reinstated this word *Method*, which had been translated into Dutch as "the order" <note>original: "de ordre"</note> (p. 258, l. 18, 19, etc.). But what matters most is that Descartes himself signed this translation, adding these words, in his own hand, on the last page:

->Gentlemen<-
->Your Excellencies<-
->Very humble<-
->and obliged<-
->servant<-
->DESCARTES.<-
->Written at Egmond,<-
->the 21st of February<-
->1648.<-

# CLARIFICATION

And on the same page, in the little space remaining, he added this handwritten note:

> I have had this writing translated into Flemish <note>original: "Flamend"; here referring to the Dutch language</note>; but because it is a language that I understand very little, I pray those who will read it to have regard primarily for the French, for which alone I can be responsible.

Descartes had first sent his letter *in Latin* on June 16, 1645. But of the forty members of the Utrecht City Council <note>original: "Vroedschap"; the traditional name for the council of regents in early modern Dutch cities</note> (see above, p. 201, note *a*), how many understood that language? It is even probable that not all of them understood *French* equally well. This is why Descartes judged it safer to send them a *Flemish* translation on February 21, 1648.

# TO THE READER

*Just as something new always comes out of Africa <note>original: "Ut ex Africâ semper aliquid novi"—a classical proverb from Aristotle and Pliny the Elder, here used to imply that the University of Utrecht is a source of strange and dangerous ideas.</note>, so every day some monster emerges from the Voetian workshop: so persistent is that theological hatred of* Gisbert Voet, *that it seems to surpass the eternal flames of Mount Etna and Vesuvius. For a long time now, our Hero <note>Referring to René Descartes, who died in Stockholm in 1650.</note> had departed to join the majority in Sweden; the dispute between Schoock and Voet <note>Martinus Schoock and Gisbert Voet were involved in a famous legal and academic battle over the philosophy of Descartes.</note> had fallen silent for several years after Schoock's appeal; a truce in polemical writings had been arranged by public authority between* Voet and Maresius <note>Samuel Maresius (Desmarets), a theologian at Groningen who was often at odds with Voet.</note>, *as theologians of the same party; when suddenly there appeared, like a most horrific ghost, Voet’s* **REFORMED NATURAL THEOLOGY**^a, *filled partly with the silliest nonsense, and partly stitched together with the most atrocious slanders and insults against* Maresius, Schoock, *and the <term>renowned</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸν πάνυ" (ton pany), an honorific meaning "the great" or "the celebrated."</note>* **DESCARTES**, *the Glory and Leader of Philosophers. It is so composed that in truth, instead of a reformed natural theology, it presents to its reader a mere, most deformed moral "devil-ology"*^b.

*Indeed, that witless book displeased all wiser men, and, as we hear, it was marked for censure by certain Synods in the Netherlands; but since these judgments remain within private walls, something ought to have been publicly set against it, lest its author triumph unpunished over the Truth and Innocence of others, and congratulate himself on his malice all the more because he is said to have received a grander reward from the* Magistrates of Utrecht *for its dedication*^c. *What those from Gronin[gen]*—

---

(Utrecht, | From the Workshop of Johannes à Waesberge, Bookseller. | 1656, in-quarto, 614 pages, plus two unpaginated indices of 34 pages.)
</note>

<note>
b. No new paragraph in the 1st edition. The same remark applies to the following paragraphs, until "Plura potuissent" etc. (Page 281, end.)
