# APOLOGETIC COMPLAINT

*...regarding the people of Groningen, it is not yet clear to us, except for what we have heard by rumor, that Maresius <note>Samuel Desmarets (1599–1673), a French Protestant theologian active in the Netherlands and a rival of Voet.</note> wrote something on his own behalf as a sort of appendix to some other theological treatise; whether this is true, and whether Schoock <note>Martinus Schoock, a former student of Voet who later turned against him.</note> will remain silent, time will tell.*

*In truth, we did not think our Hero <note>Referring to René Descartes.</note> could be better defended than by himself: as he was about to set out for Sweden, he had left in these lands this Apology which we now give to you—written by himself in French and translated into Latin by a friend—with the intention of publishing it if private efforts achieved nothing. But since he was prevented by death <note>Descartes died in Stockholm in 1650.</note> and could not complete what he had intended, we are now compelled by the persistence of his adversaries to bring it to light. We do this so that the pleasure they took in slandering a dead man may be lost as they hear the truth about themselves from his own mouth, and so that in the future these weak little hares might cease to pluck the beard of a dead lion. If you compare what this greatest of men wrote for his own defense—clearly, judiciously, and vigorously, as is his habit in all things—with what is contained in the "Reformed Natural Theology" (reformed in the style of Voet, that is) from page 253 to 264 inclusive<gloss>a</gloss>, you will see all those arguments so crushed and reduced to dust by the Cartesian thunderbolt that nothing remains for the Voetians but to seriously repent—if they have any conscience left—at the unexpected crowing of this French cock <note>original: "Galli"—a pun on "Gallus," which means both "a Gaul/Frenchman" and "a rooster."</note>, and to exchange the bitterness of their unwashed mouths for the bitter tears of penance.*

*We could have added several other things to this Cartesian Apology that have been seen until now, which would have been more than enough to blunt the old slanders that the "Reformed Natural Theology" serves up again. But there was no need to sew these old rags onto the new purple robes of our Descartes, since his work stands well enough on its own; those other pieces can be reprinted separately and bound into a single volume of documents relevant to the Cartesian cause, should Voet and his followers drive us to it. In the meantime, accept this list of several small works particularly relevant to this matter, which we would wish to be highly recommended to you alongside this Apology:*

**THE TRIUMPH OF THE SACRED WAR**, or the sentence passed on May 31, 1649, by the most noble and most excellent Magistrate of Utrecht, between Gisbert Voet, the plaintiff, and Carolus Dematius, his associate, both Doctors of Sacred Theology and Professors of the same faculty in the University of Utrecht, on one side, and Martin Schoock, Master of Liberal Arts and Professor of Philosophy in the University of Groningen...

# APOLOGETIC COMPLAINT <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "Querela Apologetica." In the 17th century, an "apology" was not an admission of guilt, but a formal legal and philosophical defense of one's conduct and reputation.</note>

->To the Most Noble and Honorable Lords,<- <note>Addressing the Magistrates (the city government) of Utrecht.</note>

Those who know of the continuous injuries I have endured for four years from the Voetius family <note>Referring to the powerful theologian Gisbertus Voetius and his son, Daniel.</note> wonder why I have not attempted to seek redress until now. It is not that I consider their speeches or books worthy of my attention—except where they abuse your authority to harm me—but because they build all their slanders against me upon a sentence they claim you passed. Thus, I am widely believed to be obligated to defend my honor and my name. I feel the same way myself; however, the reason for my delay was both the legal matter I had with Schoock <note>Martin Schoock, a former associate of Voetius who became entangled in the dispute.</note> and the conflict that arose between him and Gisbertus Voetius. Meanwhile, I have endured all the insults of these men, who injuriously portray me as a "deserter of the cause" and provoke me regarding your city, as if I were interdicted from water and fire <term>aquâ & igni interdictum</term> <note>A Roman legal phrase meaning "banished" or "outlawed," essentially stripped of all civil rights.</note> within its walls. Furthermore, they threaten me with some unknown legal action they claim to be keeping in reserve, to be prosecuted at a suitable time; thus they compel me, even against my will, to defend myself.

But, to proceed in order and to satisfy at least the rest of the world (if not also yourselves), and to make it clear to everyone that I have never failed in my duty nor in my courtesy—which should have earned me a very different treatment from you than what I have received—I shall here briefly set before you the justice of my cause and the unfairness of my adversaries. I do this so that, if possible, I may through you avenge the injuries they have done; or, if that cannot be achieved, that you might at least deign to inform me of the nature of the lawsuit instituted against me in | your city, who the judges were that sat upon it, and what motives they relied upon. For as of yet, I have learned nothing of it, except through the writings of the Voetius family or through rumors spread in their favor, which I cannot believe with any certainty.

In March of the year 1639, Mr. Emilius <note>Antonius Aemilius (1589–1660), a professor at Utrecht and a friend of Descartes.</note>, in your Academy <note>original: "Lyceo." Referring to the University of Utrecht.</note> Pro-

# COMPLAINT <note>original: "Querela."</note>

---

[Master Aemilius] <note>Antonius Aemilius (1589–1660), a professor of history and eloquence at Utrecht and a supporter of Descartes.</note>, a professor and a principal ornament of that place, delivered a funeral oration for Master Reneri <note>Henricus Reneri (1593–1639), the first professor at Utrecht to teach Cartesian philosophy.</note>, who had also greatly honored your Academy. Among many things concerning Reneri's honor, Aemilius devoted the largest part of his speech to praising him for the friendship he had cultivated with me; he bestowed upon me such great tributes that my modesty does not allow me to repeat them. I will only include here the title and conclusion of the Elegy which he added to that oration when it was printed. The title was: *To the spirit of the deceased, who lived in the closest union with the most noble René Descartes, the Atlas and unique Archimedes of our century, having been taught by him to penetrate the secrets of nature and the furthest reaches of the heavens.* And in the conclusion, he addressed the deceased thus:

> *And the new things he taught, now discovered, lie open to you,*
> *And all things are manifest in the clear light of day;*
> *So that you may rightly doubt whether they are clearer to you*
> *By his skill, or now by your own state as a blessed spirit.* <note>The poem suggests that Reneri, now dead, can see the truths of the universe clearly—and it is a toss-up whether Descartes' philosophy or the afterlife itself provided more clarity.</note>

These praises pleased the more honorable citizens of your city, as was shown by the fact that it seemed appropriate for them to be published by your Academy's printer. Nor was there any suspicion of flattery in them, since at that time Master Aemilius knew me only by reputation and my writings. Nor had I sought them out myself; on the contrary, when certain poems concerning the same subject, composed by him and sent to me for my review, were later requested back because he had no other copy and wished to commit them to the press, I politely excused myself from returning them. It was not that I did not take pleasure in being praised by such a great man, but because I knew that one can hardly be elevated with the highest praise by the most esteemed men without offending those who wish to be thought of as such but are not; it was enough for me to know what he thought of me, and I did not desire it to be made public by him.

Shortly after, specifically in June of the same year, Gisbertus Voetius <note>The influential and conservative head of the Utrecht theology department and Descartes' primary antagonist.</note> wrote extensive theses *on Atheism*. And although he did not explicitly name me in them, those who know me can clearly perceive that he laid there the foundations of that persistent slander in which he has ever since persevered. For he mixed into the characteristics of Atheism everything he knew from public rumor was attributed to me, even though nothing in those things was anything but good and worthy of praise<sup>a</sup>. And what is most worthy of note is that he, too, knew me only by reputation and my writings; so much so that from those very qualities which had been the material for Aemilius’s praises, Voetius brewed the poison of his own malice.

---

a. "And worthy of praise" addition. See p. 205, l. 4.

<summary>Descartes contrasts the high praise he received from Professor Aemilius, who compared him to Archimedes, with the subsequent "theses on Atheism" published by Gisbertus Voetius. He argues that Voetius maliciously twisted the very same intellectual qualities praised by others into evidence of religious subversion.</summary>

### DEFENSE <note>original: "APOLOGETICA"</note>

<margin>Reference to pages 205-207.</margin>

I will not say how many testimonies from honorable men have confirmed to me since that time that he has tried to persuade everyone that I am an **Atheist**, and how he has spread this poison everywhere throughout these provinces. Indeed, he would want this to be proven to him, yet as long as he holds such power, there is no one who wishes to testify against him. I shall be satisfied to observe that, in the following year, he went searching through the very monasteries of France for one of the most fervent defenders of the Roman Religion, with whom he might conspire against me as if against a public enemy of the human race. I will repeat here certain parts of the letter which he wrote to that man, of which I have sent you an exact copy made from the original <note>original: "αὐτόγραφον" (autographon)</note> in my possession. These are his words:

> *You have doubtless seen certain philosophical works <note>original: "Philosophemata," likely referring to the Discourse on Method and its essays.</note> of **René Descartes** published in French in quarto. That man is striving—though too late, in my opinion—to establish a **new sect**, never before seen or heard of in the nature of things; and there are those who admire and adore him as if he were a **new God fallen from heaven**. And a little later: His discoveries <note>original: "εὑρήματα" (heurēmata)</note> ought to be subjected to your judgment and censure. They could be struck down by no **Physicist** <term>Physico: a natural philosopher or scientist</term> or **Metaphysician** more successfully than by you; for you excel in that part of **Philosophy** in which he is believed to be most powerful—namely, in **Geometry** and **Optics**. Certainly, this labor is worthy of your erudition and subtlety. The Truth, asserted by you thus far and shown in the reconciliation of **Theology** and **Physics** and **Metaphysics** with **Mathematics** <note>original: "Mathesi"</note>, requires you as its champion, etc.*

Here I would like it noted that while it is not a sin to cultivate friendship with men of another religion and to write to them (otherwise you yourselves would be implicated in a great crime because of the treaty with our King), yet in this "holy Reformed man"—who frequently calls me a **Jesuit-lover** <note>original: "Jesuitastrum," a pejorative term implying a secret or low-level Jesuit agent.</note> and uses no argument more frequently to traduce me before you than that which he takes from my religion—this is a most certain sign that he does not observe the rules he usually prescribes for others. Nor is he of such great scrupulosity, provided he believes none of this will reach the common people, that he cannot solicit the goodwill of one of our monks and recognize him as a champion of truth, saying: *The Truth asserted by you and shown in the reconciliation of Theology, etc.*, if only he can harm me in some way through him.

And to show that he attempted to publicly traduce me as the author of some **new heresy**, not because he thought anything in my opinions ought to be corrected (which he cannot even grasp, as they exceed his capacity), but out of pure malice, by saying: *That man is striving for a new sect, etc. And there are those who adore him as a God, etc.*: I will relate what that prudent and learned monk replied to him: *Namely, that he would gladly write against my opinions if he had any reasons to attack them; he asked, therefore...*

<summary>Descartes exposes the hypocrisy of his accuser, Gisbertus Voetius, who secretly sought an alliance with a Catholic monk to discredit Descartes' philosophy while publicly attacking Descartes for his Catholic ties.</summary>
<keywords>Atheism, Jesuitastrum, Geometry, Optics, Sect, Metaphysics, Voetius, Religious hypocrisy</keywords>

# COMPLAINT <note>original: "QUERELA"</note>

<margin>Reference to pages 207-209.</margin>

I told Voetius that I would be willing to share my own thoughts with him, or those that my friends had suggested, and that I would investigate them on my part as well. But Voetius never sent any, even though the men he had entrusted with that investigation were named to me. He felt it was enough to have written out his comparison of me to Vanini <note>Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619) was an Italian philosopher executed for atheism; Voetius frequently used this comparison to imply Descartes was a secret atheist.</note>—which holds the place of honor among his slanders—and to have spread the rumor that this Monk was going to write against me <gloss>a</gloss>.

Furthermore, to make it clear that I do not fear my literary or scientific opinions being challenged, and that I do not take offense at such things so long as slanders against my character are avoided: I will add here that this wise religious man <note>Descartes refers here to a member of a religious order, likely Marin Mersenne.</note> sent his open response to me. He left it to my judgment, and I myself faithfully ensured it was delivered to Gisbertus Voetius after I had read and sealed it. There was no deception or collusion in this: that religious man truly intended to do what he promised. Indeed, if Voetius, along with the entire rabble of his conspiratorial faction, could have suggested even the smallest argument against me to him, that man would undoubtedly have put it on paper. This would have been most welcome to me, as was made clear later when he did put other arguments into writing, which I myself took care to publish under the title of the **Second Objections** against my **Meditations**.

I shall pass over what happened during those two years regarding Mr. Regius <note>Henricus Regius, a professor of medicine and early supporter of Descartes at Utrecht University.</note>, who was thought to be teaching my philosophical opinions and who risked the first martyrdom because of them. However, I later saw in the book to which he attached his name that he was more innocent in this regard than I had supposed. For he placed nothing in that book concerning matters that can be referred to Theology which is not diametrically opposed to my own views.

Nevertheless, I am bound to say that, on the occasion of a single little word in his theses—which was of no importance, nor did the sense in which he interpreted it conflict with the accepted opinion—Voetius issued contrary theses which were debated for three days. In that dispute, I was also named, so that there could be no doubt that he considered me the author of those opinions. He praised those views by saying that those who admitted them were **Atheists** or **beasts**; and as if I were the **leader** <note>original: "ἀρχηγὸς" (archêgos)</note> of some new sect of heretics, or had sold myself as a Prophet, he said of me mockingly, "**Elijah will come**" <note>A biblical reference used to mock the "arrival" of a predicted teacher or messiah.</note>. Indeed, he came very close to branding Mr. Regius with the mark of **heresy** in the name of his own Theological Faculty. He would have done so had not a leading man of your order <note>Likely a reference to a high-ranking magistrate or university official.</note> prevented him; and finally, a judgment was issued in the name of your University by which my opinions were condemned under the title of "**new and presumptive Philosophy**."

# 209-211. DEFENSE <note>original: "APOLOGETICA"</note>. 287

After these events, nothing else remained for him but to misuse his Faculty of Theology—which, as became clear later, was entirely at his whim—to defame me before the Magistrate <note>The civil government of Utrecht.</note> as the author of a doctrine so pernicious that it had infected one of your own Professors <note>Henricus Regius, an early supporter of Descartes at the University of Utrecht.</note> with heretical rot.

Once all this became known to me, it would have been the height of imprudence not to oppose this man’s machinations. I could not have taken a more honorable, just, or gentler<gloss>a</gloss> path—and one about which he could find less reason to complain—than the one I followed. I was content, on the occasion of a writing that I was then preparing for the press, to recount in a few words the injuries I had received from him. My only intent was to uncover his secret tunnels <note>Descartes uses the term "cuniculos," referring to underground mines or tunnels used in siege warfare to topple walls, symbolizing Voetius’s hidden plots.</note> and to blunt the force of his malice, signaling to those who might hear his words that they should not be accepted without proof, since they came from a sworn enemy.

I mention these things to inform those whom this "upright" man persuaded that I was the first to attack him. It will help them to know that, besides the foul talk I heard from all sides that he was spreading about me—in his lectures, disputes, | sermons, and elsewhere—and the letters written in his own hand (the originals of which I keep), in one of which he compares me to Vanini <note>Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619), an Italian philosopher executed for atheism; this was the most dangerous accusation one could face at the time.</note>, a comparison upon which the most atrocious and filthy of his slanders rests; I can list seven different printed works by which he strove to harm me before I had said, written, or done anything against him. Specifically: four different works on Atheism; a fifth, which he called *Corollaries added to the theses on the Jubilee*; a sixth, which was an *Appendix to those Corollaries, or Theses on substantial forms*; and finally, for the seventh, the *Judgment of the University of Utrecht*. I do not wish to take anything away from the part his colleagues claim for themselves in this last work; but since he was their Rector <note>The head of the university.</note> at the time, they will not deny that the greater part of it is owed to him. It will perhaps be said that I was not named in the majority of those printed works; but neither was he named in my writing—indeed, neither was your University nor your City mentioned. The only difference was that because the things I wrote about him were true, they offended him far more than the things he wrote about me offended me, since his words lacked not only truth, but even the appearance of probability.

In truth, this writing of mine stung him so much that I learned shortly afterward that he was discussing plans | to bring a legal action for injury against me and was composing various writings against me. He wished to strike me and drag me into court at the same time, so that the one who had already been beaten would be fined on top of it.

# 211-213. COMPLAINT <note>original: "QUERELA"</note>. 288

And indeed, I was forewarned from various places that he was itching to write against me; the matter was so widely known that reports were even written to me from France. Several strange details from his writings against me were also reported, which now appear partly in the *Preface* of the book attributed to Schoock <note>Martinus Schoock, a former student of Voetius who served as a "front" for his attacks on Descartes.</note>, and partly in the *Historical* narrative that bears the name of your Academy <note>The University of Utrecht.</note>. I was also informed that he was deliberating over who, at his instigation, would write against me—that is, who would publish his own compositions under their names, adopting his style as their own and adding what they could of their own. I was told that in the company of many people, someone suggested these roles should be entrusted to his son, but the mother intervened, replying that her son was too young to risk his reputation in this way; the husband should write instead, if anyone had to write. At that time, there was still no mention of Schoock; yet many already knew what would be in that book which later appeared under his name. I note this so that you may consider how improbable it is that Voetius could persuade anyone—against the conscience of the infinite number of people who knew exactly what I knew—that he would be | <column-break/> free from blame for the books published against me<gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "in me"</note> for his own defense. At the same time, you may see that I had just cause, when I received the first six pages of such a book (which did not yet have an author's name printed on it), to address the response I was preparing to Voetius.

But what most moved me to write that response was not the atrocity of the insults I found in those pages; they were so absurd and hardly credible that they seemed more worthy of contempt than of offense and anger<gloss>b</gloss> <note>original: "et irâ"</note>. Instead, three other more serious reasons drove me. The first of these was the public utility and the peace of these Provinces <note>The United Provinces of the Netherlands.</note>, which my fellow Frenchmen have always desired and promoted with more care than many of the locals. For although I would not wish to say that I wrote to Voetius about any crime, I thought I would perform a useful service for this Republic by revealing to simpler folk those truths I had discovered about him—doing so in exactly the same way, but with far better right<gloss>c</gloss> <note>original: "eodem... jure"; the French text notes this was done "to reward him."</note>, as he himself was spreading many lies about me, pretending that he did so to warn the studious youth. My second reason was that I knew specifically that I would be doing something pleasing to many of your citizens—not indeed to those who recoil from your sacred rites, as he absurdly tries to persuade others (for I believe there is no one among them who does not so | <column-break/> despise him that they would wish everyone who defends those rites to become like him and...)

# APOLOGETICA <note>Apologetic Works / Defense</note>. 289

Thus, having prepared my second writing so that it could both sufficiently protect itself and defend the previous one, and having sent certain copies of it to your two Consuls <note>The presiding mayors of Utrecht</note> serving at the time, which were presented to them most honorably in my name by two of your leading and most respectable citizens: I was not a little struck when, some weeks later, I received your Edict, promulgated on June 13, 1643. Not that I was not greatly pleased by what it contained regarding Voetius: for I read there a manifest condemnation of him, in that you pronounced him useless—indeed, highly harmful to your City—if the things I had written about him were true; for I was certain of their truth. But I wondered that I had been summoned by You to prove these things, as if any jurisdiction over me belonged to You; I also wondered that this summons had been made with such an uproar, and to the sound of a bell, as if I were a criminal; and finally, I wondered that for this purpose you had pretended not to know my residence, when your Consuls could have been informed of it (unless they were already aware of it) by asking those who [delivered] the book...

However, since this way of proceeding could admit various interpretations, and because I thought I had earned not your hatred, but your favor, I believed your intention was not to harm me, but only to make the whole matter public. In this way, the man who was guilty and subject to your jurisdiction could be punished with the approval of the entire world.

For this reason, I also committed my response to your Edict <term>Edictum: an official public decree issued by the city magistrates</term> to print. In that response, after giving thanks that you deigned to undertake an examination of the character of the man by whom I had been wronged, I also asked that you might take the opportunity to inquire whether he had been an accomplice and participant in the book published under the name of Schoock <note>Martin Schoock, a former student of Voetius who had published a vitriolic attack on Descartes</note>, in which I was being torn apart by various calumnies. After such a response, I thought it impossible that you would have any intention of harassing me, especially since news arrived from various places that my book had been most diligently and frequently read by many—indeed, by many of those who hold Magistracies in the principal cities of these Provinces—and that none of them had observed anything in it that could provide a just handle for Voetius to complain about me, or for you to censure me. Thus, my cause is so universally approved that those who had heard thousands of men discussing it asserted that only two could be found who endeavored to blame me. And these two were openly recognized as the "brokers" <note>original: "proxenetæ," a term implying shady agents or go-betweens</note> of the Voetian faction and his emissaries, as Schoock says, who affirms that he has many such people; a fact which must be very well known to Schoock.

<header>221-223. DEFENSE. <note>original: "APOLOGETICA"</note></header>
<sig>*</sig>

And from this it came about that it was thought your opinion rested on those two main points: and not without merit, if indeed it were such as represented in print in the booklet published without an author’s name under the title *Commenced Proceedings, etc.* <note>original: "Aengevangen proceduren &c."</note>, which Schoockius <note>Martin Schoock, a student of Voetius</note> asserts came from the younger Voetius.

When I learned all this, I thought it my duty to find ways to justify myself and to make the fairness of my cause known to all those who might perhaps think otherwise of it. But regarding the first point, I had no difficulty excusing myself: since I was born in the region where I was, and of the religion I profess, only enemies of France could blame me for friendship with those to whom our Kings usually reveal the inner secrets of their thoughts by choosing them as their Confessors. Such are the Jesuits in France; and specifically | <column-break/> Reverend Father Dinet <note>original: "R. P. Dinetus"</note>, to whom alone it is held against me that I wrote, was chosen as the King's Confessor shortly after the publication of the letter I had addressed to him. And if, notwithstanding this reason, there still remain men so partial and zealous for the Religion that holds sway in these lands <note>Calvinism/the Dutch Reformed Church</note>, that they take offense at all communication with those who profess to oppose it, that should surely seem more shameful in Voetius—who, while wanting to be the glory and ornament of the Belgian Churches <note>original: "Ecclesiarum Belgicarum"</note>, nevertheless writes to Monks whose rule is stricter than the Jesuits', and calls them *Defenders of the Truth* <note>original: "Defensores Veritatis"</note> to worm himself into their favor—than in a Frenchman who openly practices the same sacred rites as his King.

But besides, so that it may be clearly evident to you how much Voetius strives to deceive others, and to persuade those who trust him of things which he himself does not even believe: if you would deign to read the booklet entitled *Seventh Objections, etc.* <note>original: "Septimæ Objectiones &c."</note>, which contains that letter which served as the occasion for the accusation of my friendship with the Jesuits, and for which, as they say, Voetius obtained a condemnation from you; or if at least it pleased you to ask someone who has read it what it is about: you will find that the entire book was written against a certain Jesuit <note>Pierre Bourdin, a Jesuit critic of Descartes</note>, whose friend I now nonetheless boast to be, for my teachers | <column-break/> did not teach me to be irreconcilable. You will know moreover that I then wrote twenty times more against that Jesuit than against Voetius, of whom I spoke only in passing, and with his name hidden. So much so that, when he was the author of the condemnation of that book, he seems to have appointed himself as the representative for the Jesuits, and to have obtained more from you in their favor than they themselves have tried or hoped to obtain from the Magistrates of any of the Cities in which they are said to be most powerful. And certain matters of honesty and courtesy...

...words of courtesy<sup>a</sup>, which I had placed in that book, he seized by the neck <note>original: "rapuit obtorto collo"; a Latin idiom meaning to drag someone into court or to twist an argument by force</note><sup>b</sup>, intending to persuade those who only saw those words without reading the rest that I shared a great intimacy with the Jesuits. This is just as if someone accused me—not in France, certainly, where such frivolous accusations would be held in contempt, but in some jurisdiction where the most severe Inquisition held power—of cultivating a close friendship with Voetius <note>Gisbertus Voetius, the Dutch theologian and chief opponent of Descartes</note>, and proved it by the fact that I call him "Most Celebrated Man" <note>original: "Celeberrimum Virum"</note> in the title of the long Letter which I addressed to him publicly. I do not doubt it will be obvious to those who have read this Letter that the one who accused me in this way delighted in a lie, and that he has turned up his crooked nose <note>original: "naſo ſuſpendiſſe adunco"; to mock or sneer</note> at those to whom he dared to propose such things.

As for the second point, although many witnesses would not have been lacking to refute him if I had wished to name them, I decided nothing would be safer for me than to attack Schoock <note>Martin Schoock, a student and collaborator of Voetius</note> directly, so that he might be punished in place of Voetius if he wished to take the crime upon himself; or, if | he did not possess such extraordinary charity toward the man and preferred to deserve some excuse, he would be bound to reveal the truth of the whole matter.

The prudence, integrity, and generosity of those who administer the Republic in that Province where he lives persuaded me that they would by no means deny justice to one seeking it, even though I had never before had the chance to address any of them, and Schoock had them all as friends and was the Rector of their University when I brought my complaint against him. For justice alone protects Republics and empires; for its sake, the first mortals left the forests and caves to build Cities; it alone is what confers liberty, just as, on the contrary, from the impunity of the guilty and the condemnation of the innocent is born license, which, according to the observation of political thinkers, has always been the ruin of Republics. Thus, I hardly doubted that the most prudent Magistrates, who desire the good of the Republic and are eager to protect their own authority, would solicitously ensure that justice was administered to me where I had sought it.

You later learned what happened as a result, and how the Professors of the University of Groningen <note>original: "Univerſitatis Groninganæ"</note>, whom Schoock requested as his judges, used all the gentleness toward him that he could hope for, | <column-break/> and nonetheless, with singular prudence, gave me all the satisfaction I expected and could legitimately desire. For it is not permitted for private individuals to seek the blood, reputation, or goods of their adversaries; it is enough if their indemnity <note>protection from loss or legal harm</note> is provided for as far as the judge is able; the rest does not concern them, but the public. However, what was of the greatest interest to me in this business was that the falsehood should be uncovered...

He <note>Paulus Voetius, the son of Descartes' rival</note> adds that I did not assert that his father was the author of that book, and on the contrary, that I expressly stated on page 261 of the Latin edition of my book <note>Descartes is referring to his *Letter to Voetius* (1643)</note> that I did not wish to persuade readers of this; but rather that it was produced only with his father's knowledge and consent. By what rule, therefore, does he not only wish to persuade others that I was obliged to prove something other than what I had written, but—what is even more strange—suppose that I was obliged to include enough reasons in my book to prove something that I was not even affirming to be true?

He also fails to add that, in my response to your proclamation of June 13th (which he says was the *lodestar of the judgment* <note>original: "cynosuram judicii"; a guiding principle or "North Star" for the legal proceedings</note> to be established by his Deputies), it was expressly signified that if there were anything of significance in my writings which nevertheless did not seem sufficiently proven, I offered to prove all of it more clearly if I were asked. <meta>This page continues Descartes’ detailed legal defense against the University of Utrecht's authorities. He is arguing that the judgment against him was procedurally flawed, as the authorities treated him as a criminal accuser rather than a defendant, and condemned him without following proper legal standards regarding "calumny" or malicious intent.</meta>

# COMPLAINT <note>original: "QUERELA"; This refers to Descartes' formal legal grievance or remonstrance against the magistrates of Utrecht.</note>
<page-num>300</page-num>

they turned him into the one they condemned, even though he had declared that he did not wish to make himself a plaintiff <note>original: "actorem"; a legal term for the party bringing a lawsuit</note>, nor was he otherwise subject to your jurisdiction. Those who did this did so without forewarning him, and since they did not even want him to know who they were, even though he had offered to provide other proofs than those that had been written, if they were asked of him; they changed the status of the question on which your first proclamation was based, and examined only one matter, which they supposed was written by the accuser, even though he did not write it, which they declared to be false, even though it is true; and which they did not consider as a crime in respect to the one they supposed was accused of it; and finally, not content with acquitting the defendant by judging the accusation to have been false, they furthermore condemned the one whom they themselves had turned into an accuser.

However, I would like it to be observed by you here, that it follows from no laws that an accuser should be condemned simply because the defendant is acquitted, unless it can be proven that the accusation was undertaken with the intent of calumny <term>animo calumniandi: the legal standard of acting with malicious intent to deceive or harm a reputation</term>, and when there was no reason to believe what was being said. This is so much the case that, even if it had been false that Voetius <note>Gijsbert Voetius, the Dutch theologian and Descartes' primary antagonist in Utrecht</note> was the author of the principal slanders in that book (which was, in fact, true); and even if I had accused him of that matter (which I had not); and even if they had judged the author of those slanders to be worthy of punishment (which they did not do); and even if I had been subject to their jurisdiction; and finally, even if they had heard both sides and the witnesses, and had observed all the forms of a legitimate trial <note>original: "legitimi processus"</note>: even then, they would not have had a just cause for condemning me. This is because the presumptions, which were well known to anyone, were sufficient to prove that I had not accused him with a calumnious intent, and that I had a just reason for doing so.

It will perhaps be said that I was not condemned because I accused him regarding this book, but because I wrote many other things about him that would deserve punishment if they were true; and since these were held to be false, the only inquiry made was whether he had produced the book published against me, so that if he were its author, I could be excused by way of recrimination <term>recriminatione: a counter-charge made by an accused person against their accuser</term>, as having been first attacked by him with injuries. But if that were the case, they should have noted at least a few small words from my writings by which he considered himself offended, and forewarned me so that, if I had not yet sufficiently proved everything, I could bring forward other proofs. That, however, was not done; and I can affirm that those two writings which are said to have been condemned by you contain nothing that is not entirely true. Furthermore, even if they were false, they would not suffice to initiate an action for injuries <term>actioni injuriarum: a legal suit regarding personal insults or defamation</term>; with only one exception in the *Letter to the Celebrated Man* <note>original: "Epistola ad Celeberrimum Virum"; Descartes refers to his published letter to Voetius from 1643</note>, page 136, where I called him a slanderer and a liar. But I proved that so clearly in that very place where it was written, that it would not have been very useful for him to initiate a complaint about it. And if | witnesses were to have been provided, they were ready at hand, not just one or two, but—

I could also assert that although the Voetians <note>The followers and family of the theologian Gisbertus Voetius.</note> have released several booklets after my other writing titled *Letter to the Most Celebrated Man, etc.*, in which they try to refute it, they have nevertheless been unable to point out anything distinct in which they claim to have been harmed—except for the fact that I said Gisbertus Voetius was the true author of Schook’s book <note>referring to Martin Schook’s *Admiranda Methodus*, a stinging attack on Descartes that Voetius was suspected of ghostwriting.</note>. Furthermore, in order to persuade those who would only read it in Dutch that there were many insults in the Latin edition which the Dutch translator omitted, they noted in the *Commenced Proceedings* <note>original: "in Aengev. Proced."; a reference to the legal documents of the case.</note> that the scurrilous remarks had not been well rendered as "poetic insults" <note>original: "Poëtiſche ſchimpwoorden"</note>. However, beyond the fact that this was a printer's error—the typesetter put "poetic" <note>original: "poëtiſche"</note> instead of "waggish" or "mocking" <note>original: "poetſighe"</note>—in that specific instance they complain that they were beaten too little rather than too much.

Thus, Most Illustrious Lords, you can observe that they boast of having obtained from you a condemnation of a piece of writing in which even they themselves cannot find any just cause for complaint. And so you may know: when they describe the circumstances of that condemnation—claiming that Gisbertus Voetius neither requested nor procured it, that he was never heard by your Deputies, and that he himself presented the declarations of his witnesses to one of them (witnesses who were also never heard), and more things of that sort—they do not do this for the sake of your honor. Nor do they do it to persuade those who read their writings of their own innocence or my guilt. Indeed, it is clear that I should have been summoned before my legitimate judges <note>As a resident of the Hague and a French subject, Descartes argued Utrecht had no legal jurisdiction over him.</note> if I had been in even the slightest fault; nor would you have lacked the authority to obtain justice from them if you had wished to take up the cause, rather than sending this extraordinary way of proceeding. Instead, they do this to boast of the power they hold over You, and to make themselves as formidable to your subjects as they know they will hereafter be contemptible to the rest of the world once their crimes have become known. Please also take note of this: in the same book in which the younger Voetius writes all these things about you, and again in another titled *The Unjust Tribunal* <note>original: "Tribunal iniquum"</note> which he released later, for no other purpose than to slander the Gentlemen of Groningen for the justice they administered to me, he impudently and without any reason reproaches them with the same things he says were done by you. From this, he takes the opportunity to defame them and attack them with wagonloads of the most hateful insults.

| I will provide two or three examples, taken from that *Unjust Tribunal*.

# COMPLAINT <note>original: "QUERELA"</note>
<page-num>302</page-num>
<header>COMPLAINT</header>

First, it appears in the letter on page 9, where he says:
> *It will be permitted to protest against their unjust*<sup>a</sup> *sentence and judgment, in which there is no judgment at all; indeed, in which there are almost as many nullities as can be committed by those most unskilled in legal matters: such as the incompetence of the judge, the falsehood of allegations, neglected citations of parties, the joinder of issue <term>litis contestatio: the formal stage in a trial where the parties agree on the specific point to be decided</term>, and several other things found in my book.*

Thus, in his view, the sentence is unjust and the judgment is "without judgment," because he supposes the judge was incompetent, the allegations false, the citations of parties neglected, and the joinder of issue omitted. Yet, I showed just a little while ago<sup>b</sup> that all these same things were attributed by him to your own sentence against me. And on page 15 of his book, he pronounces these sentences against them:
> *Whoever justifies the guilty and condemns the innocent, both are an abomination to God; and he is worthy of punishments who, when he ought to have avenged the oppressed, is found to be the oppressor.*

And on pages 31, 32, and 33, he names and describes in particular each of the judges, inventing all the worst things about them, or reciting them solely on the faith of Schoock (who confesses that these depraved and false suspicions regarding his innocent colleagues had been instilled in him by his father long before)<sup>c</sup>, in order to try to make them appear suspect. I do not believe it would be pleasing to any of you or your Deputies to be described in this way, and I would perhaps be tedious to you if I dwelled on this at greater length to show how much it offends you that he wrote all these things.

But I am bound to indicate to you how much he offends the Gentlemen of Groningen <note>The authorities of the city and university where the trial against Schoock took place.</note> by the injustice of his slanders. And first, as for the incompetence | which he reproaches them with, it is devoid of all appearance of probability. For my case was directly referred and recommended by His Excellency the Ambassador to the States of that Province in which Schoock—about whom I was complaining—acts as a Professor; and it was decided by the other Professors who, according to the privileges of their Academy, were his legitimate judges; and who did not act therein as Professors, but as Magistrates. Furthermore, their judgment was reviewed, examined, and confirmed by the Curators of the same Academy, who are from the States of the Province. And yet the younger Voet <note>Paul Voet (1619–1667), son of Gisbertus Voetius.</note> dares to write an entire book against this judgment, even under such a hateful title as *The Unjust Tribunal* <note>original: "Tribunal iniquum"</note>, and he so trusts in your protection that he does not fear to offend the majesty of another entire Province.

He will perhaps also say that I dared to write against the judgment of your Academy. But no comparison can be established between the two:

# DEFENSE <note>original: "APOLOGETICA"</note>
<page-num>303</page-num>
<header>DEFENSE.</header>
<meta>242-244.</meta>

For in that pretended judgment of your Academy, it was a matter of neither civil nor criminal law <gloss>Omitted parenthesis: (*concerning which your Professors also have no power to judge*). See page 242, lines 22-23.</gloss>; but solely of Philosophy, concerning which I am confident many consider me to be an equally competent judge—not to say more so—than your entire Academy. And there is as much difference between the judgment that the younger Voetius attacks and that which I attacked, as there is between true battles fought in war, in which there is a danger to life, and theatrical fights or theoretical disputes held in your Academy, in which no blood is shed, and which are conducted without any anger, provided those who dispute are honorable and upright. It is unheard of for Magistrates to involve themselves in disputes of this kind which arise among the learned concerning Philosophical matters; whereas, on the contrary, I have never heard it said <gloss>Page 243, lines 8-9: *I have never seen, nor heard said.*</gloss> that anyone has ever attacked so insolently and licentiously <gloss>The phrase "And licentiously" is an addition. See page 243, line 10.</gloss>, with evident lies and intolerable slanders, a judgment made by legitimate judges who were friends and allies of those to whom he is subject, without an example being made of him according to the rigor of the law.

Nor can the younger Voetius be excused for the insults with which he tears apart the Gentlemen of Groningen on the grounds that his father is not subject to their jurisdiction <gloss>Omitted: *and that they did not have... with him.* Page 243, lines 17-18.</gloss>. For his father was neither the Plaintiff nor the defendant in that matter; and nothing at all was judged against him; only the depositions of Schoock were admitted, as happens in all criminal proceedings when such depositions can serve to excuse the crime of the one who is accused. For example, if a complaint is brought against someone by a creditor because he passed counterfeit coins to him in payment, and this person says, in his defense, that he did not know the coins were counterfeit, and that they were not minted by him but given to him by another; even if that other person is not under the same jurisdiction, it is not in the power of the judges to summon him and initiate a trial against him; but they cannot, for that reason, refuse to admit the depositions made against him, and they must weigh their truth insofar as it serves to liberate the one whom they must judge; and if they contain such clear proofs (for example, if he produced a letter in the hand of the counterfeiter himself and a written specification of each of those coins which he sent to pay that debt, so that the creditor could no longer complain *that he was his debtor*) <gloss>Parenthesis (*for example, if... his debtor*) added. See page 244, line 5.</gloss>, such that they are bound to acquit him, those proofs must also be communicated to the one who received the counterfeit coins,

He uses a counterfeiting analogy to justify why the Groningen court could use Schoock's testimony against Voetius, even if Voetius was outside their jurisdiction.</summary>

# COMPLAINT <note>original: "QUERELA"</note>
<page-num>304</page-num>
<header>COMPLAINT</header>

...so that he might have his recourse against their craftsman. You might rightly compare those insults and slanders in Schoock's book to counterfeit money; and since I complained about him because of those insults, he said in his own defense that he was not their craftsman, but that it was Gisbert Voetius, and since he did not know me, he did not know they were false. Truly, his judges ought to have considered, before they either condemned or acquitted him, whether he spoke the truth; and he consigned such records to them for that purpose that they could not administer the justice I sought, except by sending those records to me.

Nor can the younger Voetius complain that the lawsuit was not contested for a long time, that I pleaded my case with only a single short letter, without a Proctor or Advocate, and that all those rituals were not observed which <term>vexatious litigation|vitilitigatio; a term for quarrelsome or deceitful legal maneuvering</term> has devised to grant lawsuits immortality. For these formalities are not required except where the law is in doubt; and it is the custom in all Courts that when one of the parties has so bad a case that it is obvious from his own mouth, judgment is rendered <term>summarily|de plano; literally "on level ground," meaning a judgment delivered without a full formal trial</term>, without hearing the other's replies. Thus Schoock was granted as much space and leisure as he requested to deliberate on his business and defend himself: he complains of no injury in this regard; nor can he even say that the scruples of his judges were preoccupied either by the eloquence of my advocates or the subtlety of the proctors: the mere evidence of my right pleaded my case; but the judges were so fair, and my petition so moderate and just, that they granted it to me in its entirety.

Nor is there any more just cause for the younger Voetius to complain about this judgment because it contains one or two little words that are less to his taste, namely "wicked hand" <note>original: "scelerata manus"</note> and "serving the stage" <note>original: "scenæ servire"</note>; or because one of the judges is my friend, and not his father's. For, as for the words that seem harsh to him, upright Judges who detest vices could not have used softer ones to express the crime in question; furthermore, these words are used only to express the deposition of Schoock, who, as is likely, had used many sharper ones regarding Voetius to free himself by accusing him. And surely, to express the wickedness of those who, without his knowledge, had stuffed his book with such slanders—from which he could undergo a dangerous criminal charge—what softer thing could he have said, naming no one, than that they had been inserted into his writing by a "wicked hand"? Thus, therefore, since Gisbert Voetius takes this to himself, he is offended only by his own crime, and not by <margin>those who called a spade a spade <note>original: "ceux qui l'ont nommé"; Latin "scapham scapham dixere"</note></margin>. What also could be softer than to compare it to a comedy through the little words <insert>referring to the trial</insert> "serving the stage," <note>original: "per voculas scenæ servire"</note> not indeed your judgment, as...

<meta>This page continues René Descartes’ response to the accusations made by Paul Voet (the "younger Voetius"). # DEFENSE <note>original: "APOLOGETICA"</note>
<page-num>305</page-num>
<header>DEFENSE</header>

Voetius is attempting to persuade you, aiming to entangle you in his disputes and incite you against the people of Groningen just as he once did against me. But what of the deceptive tactics he used to manufacture false testimony and to carry out everything he felt necessary to extort from you that judgment he is said to have obtained? He acts in such a way that he might later boast that he neither solicited nor procured it.

Regarding the friendship he claims I share with one of the judges, he insults me by suggesting that only one of them is my friend; for I hold all of them in such high regard that there is not one among them whom I do not greatly esteem in return. But our friendship is nothing like the one Gisbert Voetius formed with Schoock, Dematius, Waterlaet, and their like. He gradually entangles these men in his quarrels and binds them to his own defense by making them accomplices in his crimes; he then hunts them down as the most cruel of enemies if they show any sign of being moved by regret. This was clear in the example of Schoock, whom he had summoned to court for that very reason. But after they had mutually threatened to reveal each other's secrets, they seem to have reconciled out of a shared fear that these mysteries might be made public. | Between me and the Gentlemen Professors of Groningen, no such secrets exist. Their goodwill is based neither on self-interest nor even on frequent conversation. Indeed, I have only spoken twice with the man whose friendship is specifically used as a reproach against me; nor did I write to him during this legal matter, because he had signaled long ago <gloss>originally "antea," an addition to the text</gloss> that he did not wish to involve himself in it.

As for the hatred that the younger Voetius claims the judge feels toward his father, it is so justified—and Gisbert Voetius has so thoroughly earned it—that I would not care to deny it. Yet the man whom Voetius takes for an adversary has so often wished to return to his good graces that he has sufficiently shown that he does not hate the person, but rather the vices of Voetius. And I believe all the others burned with that same feeling; none of them failed to detest and turn away from Voetius’s crime once they saw the records produced by Schoock. Indeed, these records were of such a nature that, by the testimony of the son himself (*The Unjust Tribunal*, <note>original: "Tribunalis iniqui," a book by Paul Voet attacking the Groningen judges</note> part 2, preface), many believed after seeing them that neither Voetius himself nor Dematius could any longer be counted among the rank of honorable and upright men. But since this favor toward me and hatred toward him depended solely on a zeal for justice, the greater those feelings were, the more they rendered my cause favorable and the Voetian cause odious to those who came to know them; thus, they further prove the equity of the court's judgment.

Whatever the case may be, it was neither the love nor the hatred of the judges that made Gisbert Voetius and Dematius guilty, but rather their own actions, written in their own hands, and which...

# COMPLAINT <note>original: "QUERELA"</note>
<page-num>306</page-num>
<header>COMPLAINT</header>

Up until now, they have not denied these things, which openly proves that they strove to corrupt Schoock, and indeed did corrupt him, into providing false testimony against me. For, first of all, to make it clear what Voetius wanted Schoock to affirm in court, it is enough to notice that in the primary record of those Acts (which contains the draft of the testimony, written in his own hand, and which he sent to Schoock so that they might follow it), he expressly wanted Schoock to assert that he had written against me and completed his book by his own impulse and of his own accord, partly at Utrecht and partly at Groningen, and indeed entirely alone. He wanted it stated that **neither Mr. Voetius nor anyone else was its author, whether in whole or in part, whether regarding the material, the arrangement, or the style, and thus to deny that Voetius had supplied any material for it.** To this could be added a letter from the same Voetius to Schoock, written on January 21, 1645, which was published at Groningen <gloss>a</gloss> in the *Sacred Offering of Good Faith* <note>original: *Bonæ fidei Sacro*, a pamphlet published during the legal dispute</note>, page 35, which contains these words: *“The sum of the matter comes to this: that you took counsel from the circumstances and decided (namely, to write against me), and that you began and finished that work yourself as to its material, form, method, and style; that no papers or sheets were supplied or sent by me to you, nor any even smallest pre-formed page which you made your own in the writing, etc.”*

Secondly, to prove that these points—which are summarized in two parts: first, that Schoock wrote against me by his own impulse and was not incited by Voetius; and second, that Voetius supplied no material to Schoock for it—are utterly false, it is enough to look at another letter from Voetius, which also appears in the *Sacred Offering of Good Faith*, page 28, written on June 3, 1642. From the very start, it says: *“I will not be reluctant to urge you again to proceed in your disputations against the Sceptics, and indeed as soon as possible, setting aside your other meditations for a while. This will be a most beautiful opportunity to stop the mouth <note>original: "hiatum obstruere," literally 'to block the gap'</note> of that furious and boastful promiser, René Descartes. That Appendix to the Meditations on First Philosophy, published in Amsterdam, especially ought to stimulate you to the outlining of this work. It is so smeared with as many furious and contradictory lies and calumnies against this Academy of ours and especially my own Profession, that it would overcome the iron patience of any readers.”* This is how he speaks of an entirely innocent piece of writing, in which I had said nothing about him that he did not deserve—indeed, he deserved twice as much. This clearly demonstrates that Voetius incited Schoock to write against me: for he even uses the words “to urge” and “to stimulate,” and shows he egged him on more than once; he says—

# APOLOGY <note>original: "APOLOGETICA"</note>

<margin>250-252.</margin> For I urged you again; and I did so on the occasion of the *Appendix* to the *Meditations on First Philosophy*, a writing to which Schoock’s book was indeed opposed. I know well enough that he replies to these points by saying that in this letter he was merely encouraging Schoock to continue his *Theses* <note>In this context, academic arguments or positions defended in public debate</note> against the *Skeptics* and to challenge my opinions within them. But since the title of the book which Schoock later published against me had not yet arrived, he could not have more expressly encouraged Schoock to write it than by goading him to attack me. And although at that time he might have given the name of *Theses* or *Disputations* to that writing which he wanted to be prepared against me—and for which he himself later devised the title, as Schoock declares—it was in truth to be the same book. For the question is not about the name, but about the substance: namely, the slanders about which I complain.

And to explain these things more clearly, I ask you to observe that three different writings were issued on this occasion on behalf of Voetius: namely, the book entitled *The Admirable Method, or the Cartesian Philosophy* <note>original: "Admiranda Methodus sive Philosophia Cartesiana"</note>, which is nothing other than a patchwork <column-break/> of insults against me under the pretext of attacking my opinions; then the *Preface* of the same book with its *Supplements* <note>original: "Paralipomena"</note>, in which the author expressly tries to answer those things I had written about Voetius; and finally the *Historical Narrative* <note>original: "Narratio Historica"</note>, which was published in the name of your University, dealing with the events concerning Mr. Regius <note>Henricus Regius, a disciple of Descartes whose teaching of Cartesian ideas at Utrecht University sparked the conflict with Voetius</note>. It clearly appears from the Letter of June 2nd <note>The French text says "June 3rd"</note> 1642 that Voetius’s plan was to attack me in these three ways. For, besides the first way, to which he encourages Schoock in the words I just cited, look at how he speaks of the two others:

> *Regarding those things that touch our Academy, the Professors will see to it, and they will not allow him to complain that we are in his debt. Regarding the insults he heaps upon me, who do not deserve them, we are even now deliberating on how to blunt them: no one among my colleagues, so far as I know, advises that we should sacrifice to silence [keep quiet]; but by whom, or by what method, a response should be made, **my heart is in great doubt** <note>original Greek: "ἐν δοίῃ μάλα θυμὸς" — a Homeric phrase indicating extreme indecision</note>. There are those who designate me, some who designate my son, and some who designate you; but on this point we are deliberating further <note>term: "ampliamus" — a legal term used when a judge delays a verdict to seek more evidence</note>. Meanwhile, the things pertaining to the truth of the history will be recorded; and they will even be confirmed by testimonies where necessary.*

Thus, even then, he was busy dragging his *Professors* to his side. And as for that which concerned him privately—namely, the very content of the preface to Schoock’s book—he had quite decided not to remain silent:

> *As for sacrificing to silence,* he says, *no one advises it.*

But he was still wavering whether the things he himself was going to write, or procure from others for this purpose, should be sent out <column-break/> under his own name, or his son’s, or Schoock’s:

> *But on this,* he says, *we are deliberating further.*

Which is properly to say that others were indeed persuading him that he himself, or his son, should write, but that he preferred it to be done by Schoock—

<meta>This page continues Descartes’ evidence against the theologian Gisbertus Voetius. On the previous page, Descartes began demonstrating how Martin Schoock’s book was not an independent academic work but a coordinated attack directed by Voetius. # COMPLAINT <note>original: "QUERELA"</note>

And after this, he <note>Schoock</note> wanted to declare in court that he had written of his own motion, and not because he was incited by Voetius!

It is also clear from the same letter that Voetius supplied him with as much material as he possibly could. For a little later, he speaks of my opinions in this way:

> You would do a worthwhile thing if you excerpted all the paradoxes of that sort <note>literally "of that grain"</note> and—having compared them with the monstrous tales <note>original: "teratologiis"; referring to absurd or unnatural ideas</note> of the ancient skeptics and other heretics (found in the works of Augustine and Epiphanius on heresies, and in Gennadius)—refuted them by: 1. Holy Scripture, 2. Reason, both through direct arguments and those leading to absurdity <note>original: "ducentibus ad absurdum"; a logical proof showing a premise is false because it leads to a ridiculous conclusion</note> and driving the man into contradiction, 3. the consensus of the Fathers <note>the early leaders of the Christian Church</note>, 4. the consensus of ancient Philosophers, Scholastics, and recent Theologians and Philosophers^a, so that it might appear to be the common cause of Christianity and of all the Schools. However, it must be noted throughout that he produces nothing new, whether he shows off something sane or something insane, etc.

And indeed, Schoock’s book was forged from these very "pretty" materials.

| That very thing which I have said can, moreover, be understood from another letter by Voetius, written five months later, namely on November 25, 1642, when Schoock’s book was under the printing press; in it, these words appear: |
| :--- |
| > To examine the particular opinions of Descartes <note>original: "Cartesii"</note> is a task for another work and purpose. For now, just return to us neither words nor promises, but those excerpts and papers which you took away from here with you. If there is any gap in the general outline <note>original: "sciographiâ"; a preliminary sketch or architectural draft</note> of this method, we will see to it that we fill it here, unless you have filled it. And these things will be abundantly sufficient for this time. We do not care for particular disputes. |

What then? As Mr. Maresius <note>Samuel Des Marets, a theologian and rival of Voetius</note> ingeniously puts it in *The Last Warning*, page 413: *Mere insults.* And so it is established that the plan for publishing the entire book did not depend on the will of Schoock—who would have preferred to attack my opinions one by one, which would have been far more honorable—but on the judgment of Voetius. Voetius only wanted a general attack written against me, where all the common themes of his own invectives could be deployed to defame me; thus, Voetius is rightly considered its primary author.

If these proofs—which consist of records written in Voetius’s own hand and which he does not deny—are not yet enough to convict him, then not even a thousand witnesses would suffice. But furthermore, Schoock has declared that he still preserves the *Draft* <note>original: "Ideam"</note> of the preface, written in Voetius’s hand; and that preface contains more than 60 pages and is the most injurious portion of the whole book. He declared the same regarding the comparison with Vanini <note>Lucilio Vanini, a philosopher executed for atheism in 1619; a comparison intended to be life-threatening</note>, which is their sole foundation for accusing me of Atheism: namely, because I had written against the Atheists, and because Vanini had also pretended to write against them.

### APOLOGETICA <note>original: "APOLOGETICA"; A formal defense or justification of one's positions</note>

...though [they say] he is an atheist himself; from which they conclude that I secretly teach atheism. In fact, Schoock expressly declared that the words asserting that I "craftily and very secretly rub the poison of atheism onto others" were written by a hand other than his own—that is, by that wicked hand <note>referring to Voetius</note> of which I spoke above^a. But I have complained especially about those words because they contain a most atrocious calumny <note>slander</note> worthy of every punishment. According to the law | a specific crime must be determined for the one who complains in court; one should not wander into uncertainties, as Voetius does when he says he was attacked by my "calumnies," even though he has not yet shown the slightest little word by which I have harmed him contrary to right or law <note>original: "præter jus & fas"</note>.

Furthermore, the *Paralipomena* <note>original: "Paralipomena"; supplements or appendices added to a book</note> added to the preface—the last section of which alone contains almost more bitterness and poison than the rest of the work—were rejected by Schoock from the beginning, but never by Voetius.

My speech would grow to an immense size if I had to gather here all the arguments which prove that the testimony he <note>Voetius</note> suggested or prescribed is false. But, I ask you, observe that all these things I have proposed here are real and do not depend on the report of Schoock; for as to the plan of the preface and other unpublished notes which he says are in his possession, if he did not truly have them, Voetius would have pursued his lawsuit against him more fervently. This shows how | shameless is the calumny of the younger Voetius <note>Paul Voet, the son of Gisbertus Voetius, who defended his father</note>, when he reproaches the Gentlemen of Groningen <note>The magistrates or university officials at Groningen</note> for having judged based on the testimony of a single man (a point he presses most strongly): for even if they had paid no attention to Schoock’s words, they had enough other proofs besides. And yet it is evident that the declaration made at Groningen deserves far more credit than the one he had previously made at Utrecht <note>original: "Ultrajecti"</note>. For in the Utrecht declaration, besides the fact that it had been suggested to him, he testified to nothing other than what he thought was to his advantage—namely, that he was the author of the book to which he had already put his name. He was not before judges, nor did he fear being rebuked, even if what he declared was not true; and he merely presented that written statement to his friend, whom he thought powerful enough to extricate him even if its falsehood became public. But at Groningen, he testified to that which he was ashamed to have known, and which would be most displeasing to his best friends; and he did not testify to it except with some distress of mind^b and before judges. Thus it can be concluded that by the reverence for justice alone and the fear of punishment—lest he lie and take upon himself the burden of another’s crime—he was driven to profess those things which he did profess. Indeed, he declared that he would have confessed the same things at Utrecht if he had been questioned seriously and in court about the whole matter.

...it had been. And it almost always happens, when a defendant or a witness is examined whose interest is in some way to hide the truth, that the deposition he makes in court contradicts those things which he said outside of court; yet no one can, for that reason, take away his credibility.

But it is not enough to have proved that the testimony Voetius prescribed to Schoock was false; Voetius will not believe himself convicted unless it is also proved, furthermore, that he solicited him with great persistence to provide such testimony. Therefore, I would like you to consider not only that he asked this of Schoock, but indeed—what is worse—that he most explicitly commanded it of him. For he placed these words at the end of the formula <note>A "formula" here refers to a draft or template for a legal statement</note> he was prescribing: *“Make the style your own where necessary; meanwhile, let the precision <note>original Greek: ἀκρίβεια (akribeia)</note> of the testimony be preserved everywhere, as much as can be done through Latinity, especially where I have underlined.”* And thus he wanted there to be the "voice of Jacob and the hands of Esau" <note>A biblical reference to Jacob’s deception of his father Isaac, meaning the words sounded like one person but the "touch" or substance belonged to another</note>—the style of Schoock and the lies of Voetius. He commanded the style to be changed, but the sense of everything he prescribed to be exactly retained, especially those words under which he had drawn lines; yet all those things I reported above were underlined. Those who know Voetius are not unaware of how persistent that habit of his is in asking or commanding, especially regarding those he considers inferiors or beholden to him, such as Schoock was. Experience itself proved this, in that Voetius dragged him into court because he did not persist in that testimony.

Furthermore, should not all the goings-about and negotiations of Waterlaet <note>Lambertus van Waterlaet, a follower and agent of Voetius</note> be attributed to Voetius, as well as whatever was done by Dematius <note>Another associate of Voetius</note>, so that Schoock might be gradually induced | to draft his testimony in that formula which had been prescribed to him? For the matter did not concern those two, except insofar as they were friends to Voetius. And yet Schoock affirms that Waterlaet often came to him for that reason, and sent him the draft of the testimony that Voetius desired in Groningen; but he [Schoock] had submitted another more conforming to the truth, since he could not subscribe to that one in good conscience. Indeed, from those things which followed later, it can be known that in the testimony submitted by Schoock, words were omitted which contained the principal lie, namely: *“And indeed alone, so that neither Voetius, nor anyone else was its author, whether in whole or in part, as to the subject matter;”* and certain other things were substituted in their place by him. And as for the “spontaneous action” <note>original Greek/Latin: τὸ motu proprio; doing something of one's own accord</note> and almost all the rest, he [Schoock] had tried to escape through equivocation, by substituting the word "Method" wherever Voetius had placed "book"; so that by "Method" he intended nothing else to be signified than the order of the chapters and the style, of which he wished to be considered the author, and to affirm nothing further regarding the insults and the subject matter, as he later declared. ### DEFENSE

<page-num>258-260. 311</page-num>

...those who would read this testimony would understand by the *Method* <note>Referring to the *Method of Philosophy*, the book at the center of the dispute</note> the entire book. But the rest, in which Schoock <note>Martin Schoock, the titular author of the book attacking Descartes</note> had not insisted on the formula itself, did not seem to have fully satisfied him, and specifically the omission of the phrase *and indeed alone*, etc. For several weeks he pressed that testimony, nor did he use it until, when Schoock came to Utrecht <note>A major university city in the Netherlands</note>, he found a more convenient opportunity to induce him to revise it. Waterlaet <note>Wilhelm Waterlaet, a follower of Voetius</note> was again employed for this purpose, who brought to him this note, written in Dematius’s <note>Matthieu Dematius, a colleague and supporter of Voetius</note> hand:

> *Reverend Sir, I would like certain things to be changed in your testimony; as for what they are, receive them in few words:*
> *In lines 21 & 22, let all things that are underlined be deleted, and let it be written:* **And that I alone completed it.** <note>original: "Meque illum solum absolvisse"</note>
> *In line 30, let only these things be retained:* **I could hardly have sought and learned from friends.**
> *In line 31, let* **To be from another's hand** *be deleted, and let it be written:* **They are by another author, who, when it is necessary, I think, will reveal his name:** *or something similar.*
> *The reasons why I think this should be done, I do not explain here, as I will say them in person. Farewell.*

And the phrase **and that I alone** (namely the book or that *Method*) **completed it** is highly noteworthy here. For that word *alone* ensures that Voetius <note>Gisbertus Voetius, the powerful theologian opposing Descartes</note> would be excluded, which is the foundation of this entire malicious scheme. The other phrase *let only these things be retained, I could hardly have*, etc., could not be so easily understood unless Dematius himself had explained it in the writing with which he wished to defend himself, inserted in the *Unjust Tribunal* <note>original Latin: "Tribunali Iniquo," a polemical work of the time</note>, from pages 117 to 126. But there he informs us that Schoock, in his testimony, had stated that he had learned those particulars which happened at Utrecht partly from Voetius and partly from other friends, as had been prescribed by Voetius; but he, Dematius, believing there were no other friends for Schoock there besides Voetius from whom he could have learned such things, judged that *partly from Mr. Voetius, partly from other friends* should not be put, but that Voetius's name should be removed and only *from friends* should be put; which Dematius playfully defends as if it were done legitimately. "If I have committed any sin here," he says, "the sin should be established in this: that I judged caution must be taken—perhaps with an overabundance of caution, yet harmful to no one, and indeed useful to some (as it would remove the occasion for sinning)—for the innocence of my most dear colleague, to whom the Church of God <note>original Latin: "Ecclesia Dei"</note> <note>a. "of God" [Dei] is an addition. See p. 260, line 10.</note> owes so much." Thus does that holy man call it a "harmless caution" to suborn witnesses who deceive the judges by imagining other friends in place of Voetius, in a matter which he knew had proceeded from Voetius alone,
