### DEFENSE

<page-num>260-262. 312</page-num>

...and thus to procure the condemnation of an innocent man, so that he might be stripped of his honor and goods, and indeed even his life, if it were possible. It cannot be said that this man Dematius—who in this matter surpassed even the diligence of Voetius in deceiving the judges—did not know that Schoock had been induced to write. For since he knew that Schoock had learned what happened at Utrecht <note>A major university city in the Netherlands and the site of the dispute</note> only from Voetius, he could not be ignorant of the rest; nor could he persuade him to put in his testimony that I <note>Schoock</note> alone completed it, without knowing that these words contained a most false lie. Indeed, from the deposition of Schoock, which is reported in *The Sacred Pledge of Good Faith, page 4* <note>original: "Bonæ fidei Sacro"; a book published by Schoock in 1645 to defend his reputation</note>, it is clear that the first plan for that book began at a formal banquet with and in the presence of Dematius himself. These are his words: *“Of course, when in the year 1642, according to his custom, Schoock had traveled to Utrecht during the dog days <note>The hot summer holidays when the university was in recess</note> to visit friends, he was received by Mr. Voetius along with the distinguished Professors of that Academy and several other honorable men at a truly grand and sumptuous banquet. There, after the tables were cleared, Mr. Dematius and others brought up Descartes' Letter to Dinet <note>A 1642 work where Descartes defended his philosophy against Jesuit and Reformed critics</note>, in which Mr. Voetius, his teacher, was thoroughly lashed; Schoock was then asked and invited with urgent encouragement by Mr. Voetius to draw his pen against Descartes on behalf of himself, his teacher.”*

Is it not a monstrous thing that something done so publicly at a feast, before several men who ought to have a care for their conscience and their honor (for I would not like to believe that all who associate with Voetius become like him), and which moreover is so probable in itself that those who judge it only by conjecture do not doubt its truth—namely, that Voetius instigated Schoock to write against me—is it not, I say, portentous that this very thing was chosen by him to be denied before the Judges, to serve as the foundation for the sentence by which he intended to destroy me? Nor can that account by Schoock, made before his own judges, be called into doubt; for his adversaries did not contradict it in their lawsuit against him, into which they sprinkled so many irrelevant and minor matters that they would not have omitted this one, unless they feared they could be convicted by the testimony of those who had been guests together at the time.

But neither is this enough to convict Dematius; | he wants it proved to him that he persistently solicited Schoock to insist on the note he had prescribed; for his entire defense is to say, *“there is no appearance of persistent solicitation here.”* <note>original: "nulla hic importunæ sollicitationis species"</note> As if it were not importunity enough toward someone—after the other had prescribed a testimony for him which he did not wish to admit in its entirety, even though that other person had great power over him—to further send him a note with these words: *“I would like certain things to be changed in your testimony, etc.”*; which is so evidently against good...

...customs and laws, so that even if that paper contained nothing but the truth, the one who sent it would still deserve to be blamed. Or perhaps, after he had done whatever he could on his part, he hoped that the persuasion and authority of many would be more effective than that of one; and it was necessary that Voetius and Dematius—as two very famous old men, and who, I believe, then constituted the entire Theological Faculty of your Academy <note>The University of Utrecht</note>, since a third had died around that time—should join their tricks to overcome the chastity of that Susanna <note>original: "ad castitatem istius Susannæ expugnandam"; a biblical reference to the story of Susanna and the Elders, in which two corrupt old judges conspire to falsely accuse a virtuous woman</note>.

I also do not wish to provoke you against him by saying that he made a mockery of justice when he wanted to take on the role of the defendant without ever being questioned, and to impose on me—I know not how—the role of the Plaintiff <note>original: "Actoris personam"; the legal role of the accuser or prosecutor</note>, and to pretend that I had slandered him by attributing to him a matter which he considers honorable, and finally to procure my condemnation through Deputies whose names I could never know; this deserves nothing less than that he should be made a defendant once and for all so seriously that he has no reason to mock. I also do not wish [to provoke] you against his...

### APOLOGETICA.

<meta>268-270.</meta>

...witness depositions; however, I do not know all the tricks and frauds <note>original: "technas & fraudes"</note> which Gisbert Voetius <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676), a powerful Dutch Reformed theologian and the primary antagonist of Descartes in Utrecht</note> used to obtain the things he achieved; indeed, I do not even know for certain whether he obtained them. I only know this: a man of his character, and one who wields the authority he has held in your city, is capable of achieving much. But since reason dictates and justice demands that, as far as it can be done, we should restore to their original state <note>original: "restituamus in integrum," a legal term meaning to return a person to their previous legal standing</note> those whom we have harmed—whether unknowingly, or even with an intention not so much to harm as to do good—and since it is also the custom of upright men, who care for their own fame and honor as is fitting <gloss>a</gloss>, to solicitously repair the damages they have unknowingly inflicted on others, lest they be believed to have inflicted them by design and with bad intent; just as, on the contrary, it is the mark of the more dull-witted, and of vile souls and men of the lowest sort who have no taste for anything noble, that after a harm is done to someone, even perhaps without the intent to harm, they wish to hurt them further, and hate them for the sole reason that they feel they have earned that person's hatred. It is also characteristic of such men that, once they have stumbled, they think it concerns their honor to defend even what they have done wrongly, although they might secretly disapprove of the deed. In this matter, while they wish to be above men, they sink themselves below the beasts <gloss>b</gloss>, because beasts always do what seems best to them, and there are never men so clever and prudent that they do not occasionally happen to be deceived; and finally, since I consider you second to none in nobility, integrity, and prudence, I do not doubt that—after the frauds and <gloss>c</gloss> falsehoods of my adversaries have been uncovered so that you cannot be ignorant of them—you will be ready to seize the occasion to give me satisfaction in the things I shall ask. Therefore, I would like you to weigh how many burdens you have placed upon me.

First, through your proclamation made on June 13, 1643, you summoned me by the sound of the bell <note>original: "ad sonum campanae," a formal, public summons usually reserved for criminal fugitives</note>, and through those broadsides which were sent everywhere throughout these Provinces with such care, as if I had been a wanderer or a fugitive, and found guilty of some nefarious and most atrocious crime. For although nothing else was mentioned except that I had written against Voetius, nevertheless, because it was hitherto unheard of and supported by no example that someone should be summoned by such an extraordinary ritual for having written against another private individual, and because common people and generally unlettered men do not know the extent of the "sin" that consists in the writing of books: you gave them the occasion to judge that I had committed a great sin and crime in this matter, one which was even without precedent. And this injury was all the greater because it was less...

<meta>270-272.</meta>

...I had deserved: for in truth I had done nothing else but defend myself, far more modestly and moderately than I was required to do, against the most atrocious calumnies <note>false and malicious accusations intended to damage someone's reputation</note> that anyone could devise, and to which it would have been the height of imprudence to hesitate or not oppose myself in a timely manner. For besides what I demonstrated above—that Voetius had long ago formed a plan to persuade everyone that I am an atheist—I have just cause to believe that he also wanted to accuse me of atheism in a court of law, and, as much as lay in his power, to overwhelm and crush an innocent man with false testimonies. For it is no injustice to him to say he is capable of corrupting witnesses; and Schoock <note>Martin Schoock (1614–1669), a Dutch scholar and former student of Voetius who initially attacked Descartes but later confessed to being pressured into it</note> asserts that, since Voetius recommended nothing more to him than to object to my "atheism," ***he promised that such witnesses would eventually come forward (to convict me of that crime), who could indeed be considered regular or first-rate witnesses.*** <note>original: "Nec. & mod. defenſ. pag. 48" refers to a specific legal defense text</note> But since he saw that I was watching over my defense, he could produce none. The second head of grievances with which you have burdened me is that sentence, said to be issued by you, by which, condemning my writings, you gave your Prosecutor the power to proceed against me and, as far as it lay within you, to fine me in reputation and property. I add, as a third point, not only the Decree of <column-break/> June 11, 1645, by which you prohibited printers and booksellers from publishing or selling writings that were in my favor—at which time I received the Judgment of the Gentlemen of Groningen <note>The University and city of Groningen, which eventually cleared Descartes of the charges brought by Voetius</note>, given on April 10 of that same year, which served for my justification—while Voetius took care to have Schoock's letter printed to support his calumnies against me; but also all that protection which for four years you have granted to the insults of that Voetius and the others he incited against me; so much so that for some time none of my friends in your city dared, except by disguising their handwriting and name, to write to me about those things being done there to my prejudice, although they could not legally be done without me being forewarned. And while Schoock indulged Voetius's passions, writing against me to please him with every kind of most atrocious and foul calumny, he was a welcome guest to you and most accepted in your City; and the testimony that had been extorted from him was admitted in court as good and valid, although it was full of contradictions and packed with equivocations, as he later explained; and his book, previously published against me, should have rendered him disqualifiable and suspect. But after he confessed certain truths in my favor, an action for damages was therefore brought against him, <column-break/> and although he proved them so evidently that the Gentlemen of Groningen could not doubt them, he still could not be acquitted by you. So much so that you seem, for four years, to have applied all your effort to putting handcuffs on me so that I might not defend myself while I was being beaten by the adversary.

<summary>Descartes accuses the Utrecht magistrates of bias, claiming they protected his rival Voetius and suppressed his own defense by banning the sale of his books while allowing libelous works to flourish. He highlights the shifting testimony of Martin Schoock as evidence of Voetius's attempts to frame him for atheism.</summary>

# APOLOGETICA
<note>original: "APOLOGETICA" — Works written in defense of one's positions or reputation.</note>

<meta>272-273.</meta>

...my adversary <note>the OCR reads "fario," likely a truncation of "adversario"; Descartes is referring to Martin Schoock</note>, and he poured out all his rage and fury upon me. But among the reasons for which I expect satisfaction <note>legal redress or an official acknowledgment of wrongdoing</note> from you, let me also include this one, if you please: namely, that I did not wish to break those bonds by which you held me, although it would have been very easy; and that I patiently endured all the injuries I have received since then from the Voetians <note>the followers or family of Gisbert Voetius, Descartes' primary academic and theological rival</note>, attempting nothing for my own vindication, because I saw you protecting them with your whole body in such a way that they could not be struck by me without you also being hit; nor did I wish to offend you. I earnestly and humbly beg that you be willing to attend to all these things, so that I may obtain the satisfaction I expect from you. 

But if it is not granted to obtain any other, deign at least to grant me what is not usually denied even to those guilty of the most serious crimes: namely, that I might know through you what sentence they say has been passed against me, by which judges it was passed, what fundamental cause they had for passing it, and what were the main points of both the accusations and the evidence upon which they condemned me. Concerning these matters, I pray to God that He might deign to inspire in you those counsels which will better serve to promote His glory, and from which you may derive greater praise and renown among all those who value virtue, and so that I myself may have a just reason for declaring myself,

->Most Noble and Ample Lords,<-

->DES CARTES.<-

The same work by G. Voet <note>Gijsbert Voetius (1589–1676), a Dutch Calvinist theologian and the chief academic rival of Descartes</note>, *Selectarum Disputationum Pars Prima* (First Part of Selected Disputations, 1648), provides the following passage regarding the 4th thesis *De Atheismo* (On Atheism), defended on July 13, 1639. The passage was clearly revised and expanded in 1647 for publication:

> “Even to this very day, many among the Belgians, especially the Dutch, being too eager for novelty, admire Libertinism <note>original: "Libertiniſmo (*sic*)"; a term used then to describe freethinkers who rejected traditional religious constraints</note> with too much patience and stupidity. They kindly tolerate all sorts of fanatics arising and emerging here, or Libertines, neutrals, and atheists flocking here from elsewhere on account of the freedom or license allowed to sects. They converse familiarly with them and, primarily out of their usual kindness toward foreigners and travelers, hold them in high regard. For they are delighted either by their civility of manners, or by their urbanity and skill in wit and jokes, or by the readiness or at least the display of some talent, or by some degree of either their eloquence or talkativeness, or by their poetic ability, or by some art and wonders <note>original: "thaumaturgiis"; referring to marvelous effects or 'magic'</note> and mathematical and mechanical inventions, or by some exercise in mere arithmetic and practical geometry. These and other things are commonly preferred over solid wisdom and piety, which are too peevish and bothersome to overly refined and fickle men. This is the honor given to piety! Hence the fertile harvest, fury, and insolence of atheists, libertines, followers of Lucian <note>original: "Lucianorum"; likely referring to the ancient Greek satirist Lucian of Samosata, often associated by theologians with mockery of religion</note>, and neutrals among us. Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous humanist scholar</note> says in a cited letter that he knew many who denied God; and in that same place, he was dealing with a friend from Berchem, a man of letters—but this man remained in the Popish [Catholic] Netherlands. In Holland, there was recently a certain Torrentius <note>Johannes Torrentius (1589–1644), a Dutch painter who was prosecuted for his alleged blasphemy and ties to the Rosicrucians</note>, unlearned and a <term>ἰδιωτικὸς</term> <note>original: "ἰδιωτικὸς" [idiotikos]; a Greek term meaning a private person or a layman, used here to mean someone without professional or academic training</note>, a painter by trade and art. What he could not expect from his brush, he sought through his chatter, by which he drew cautious and pleasure-seeking women and other insane men into the Epicurean profession <note>The philosophy of Epicurus, frequently misrepresented in this era as mere hedonism and pursuit of physical pleasure</note> (toward which they were already inclined) and at the same time swindled them out of their money, so that some went bankrupt. The sum of his atheism seemed to be this: that hell is to live miserably here, but heaven is to live well here and enjoy good things. The Senate of Haarlem, having gathered testimonies and on the advice of seven most excellent jurists, held an inquiry concerning him; but...

On the relations between Descartes and Desmarets <note>Samuel Desmarets (1599–1673), also known as Maresius, a French Protestant theologian who taught in the Netherlands</note>, here is the testimony of the latter in his work *Ultimate Patience finally Overcome, etc.* <note>original: "Ultima patientia tandem expugnata etc."</note> (Groningen, 1644), the last chapter of which has precisely this title: *In which those matters regarding the Noble Mr. Descartes are weighed*, p. 397-423:

Nor do most of the more discerning doubt that the writer of the infamous Narrative was driven by no other wedge than to come to the aid of Mr. Voetius's suffering reputation, using those things that had transpired in our Academic Senate: by diminishing, if he could, the credibility of the Acts through the things he released against my own reputation. And Mr. Voetius himself is conscious that he has scattered here and there his complaints about the illustrious Mr. Schoock being led astray by me; which was also the reason why I was called a "simple Villain" and he a "double Villain" by him. And to create greater envy against me here, it is vehemently exaggerated that Descartes is a Papist <note>original: "Pontificius"</note> and a disciple of the Jesuits, whom I have armed and whose patronage I have undertaken against a Reformed Theologian... »

# CLARIFICATIONS

> » Regarding Mr. Voetius <note>Gijsbert Voetius, the influential and conservative Dutch theologian at Utrecht University</note>, I would not have had to resort to evasions and equivocations if I had been legally required to respond to the demand he wished the Illustrious Mr. Schoock to make of me: *Whether anyone had shared the Acts of the Synod of The Hague with Descartes?* I would not have been ashamed to deny it, had I done so, since I could have done it without fault: for I had ceased to be a member of that Synod, and I did not receive its Acts under the seal of confession... » (Page 401.)

> « As for the claim that I seduced the Illustrious Master Schoock <note>Martin Schoock, a former student of Voetius who initially attacked Descartes but later turned against his teacher</note> into revealing Mr. Voetius’s "Eleusinian Mysteries" <note>A reference to the ancient Greek mystery cult at Eleusis, used here metaphorically to mean Voetius's "dark secrets" or hidden orchestrations</note> during the legal proceedings, it contains just as much truth: for it is certain, and clear from the public Records, that the Illustrious Mr. Schoock, of his own accord and out of a duty of conscience, declared all those things when summoned to court by the Noble Descartes. Indeed, how far I was from "stirring this Camarina" <note>A Latin proverb meaning to disturb an existing nuisance and make it worse, based on a Sicilian marsh that caused a plague when drained</note> is evident from the following. First, when Mr. Descartes himself asked me<sup>a</sup> to offer certain copies of his *Letter against Mr. Voetius, written in opposition to the "Admirable Method of Cartesian Philosophy,"* <note>The *Admiranda Methodus* was a scathing attack on Descartes, published under Schoock's name but largely authored by Voetius</note> in his name to the most Noble Curators of our Academy at the time: I refused to do so, lest I should seem to seek out trouble, but left it to the bookseller to whom they had been sent to handle it. Second, when on November 7, 1643, the Noble Descartes wrote to me<sup>b</sup> that it was his intention to drag the Illustrious Mr. Schoock into court and proceed seriously against him, unless he voluntarily declared that he had written with Voetius as his instigator and author—asking if I would either attempt to secure this latter admission (of which he already had evidence from elsewhere) or at least advise him on how he should approach the matter here—I discouraged him from all litigation<sup>c</sup>. I indicated that it did not seem likely to me that the Illustrious Mr. Schoock, who was said to have voluntarily burdened himself to relieve another, would do anything contrary to that; I advised him to either take revenge on the people of Utrecht <note>original: "Ultrajectinis"</note> with a generous contempt, or to defend himself with his own weapons—namely, with some writing. I asked that, if he decided to attempt anything, he would allow me to be entirely outside of the factions and seek someone else whose help he might use: for Mr. Schoock was the head of our Academy (he was then Rector Magnificus <term>The traditional title for the head of a university</term>), and peace flourished among colleagues, which I did not wish to see disturbed. I indeed congratulated myself that he had judged the cause I had defended as fit for his own advancement, but since our plans were different, it would not be without envy if I were to participate in his. To which that most Noble Man agreed, in a letter written December 12, 1643<sup>d</sup>, even praising my candor, declaring that he no longer wished the matter to be handled as he had first requested; that he had now pursued other matters of greater importance and would proceed by another path; and that he would remain a friend to me, even if all correspondence between us was broken off. And indeed, from that time, I neither wrote to him, nor he to me; and what plans he was agitating, I did not know. » (Pages 402-403.)

> « Perhaps the business would have remained buried in deep silence, had not Mr. Voetius’s "Lover of Truth" <note>Dutch: *Lief-hebber der Waerheyt*, a pseudonym used in a pamphlet supporting Voetius</note>—last year, in his little book titled *Procedures Begun at Utrecht, etc.*<sup>a</sup>—"stirred the fire with a sword" <note>Latin: *ignem gladio fodicaſſet*, an ancient proverb meaning to provoke an already heated situation</note> and reported (what was scarcely known) how the complaint of Descartes had been sent by the French Ambassador to the Illustrious and Powerful Lords of the States of this Province. This complaint I had not yet seen when that book was published in Utrecht. [That author] had scoffingly translated <note>original: *ſcopticè traduxiſſet*</note> the letter and the intervention of his Excellence the Ambassador's sacred person; he had shifted the entire blame for the Cartesian Philosophy and the atrocious insults which were contained in abundance therein onto Mr. Schoock alone; he had publicly affirmed that Voetius had nothing in common with Schoock’s book, about which Descartes was already complaining at Groningen even against Schoock himself; finally, he asserted that Schoock, whose style was sufficiently apparent in that book, was ready to profess it as his own and defend it. For, I ask, what was this but to incite the friends of Mr. Descartes to urge or resume the business? What was it but to insult our Illustrious and Powerful States, as if they had refused to administer justice to a learned and noble man for whom the Ambassador of the Most Christian King <note>A title for the King of France</note> so expressly intervened, and had cast aside his letters among the waste paper; and what was it but to compel the Distinguished Mr. Schoock to cast off this hatred once and for all, for the sake of both honor and conscience? What wonder is it, then, if the Noble Descartes, returned from France<sup>b</sup>, through himself and his friends frequently traveling to The Hague<sup>c</sup> to meet our Leaders, insisted, expostulated, and complained about the neglect of the Ambassador’s recommendation? What wonder if he approached the Academic Senate, under whose jurisdiction the defendant he sought was subject? What wonder if the Distinguished Mr. Schoock gladly seized this opportunity to clear his conscience and to wash away the complaint deposited against him with the Illustrious and Powerful Lords of the States, which was so hateful and heavy to him? » (Pages 403-404.)

> « But concerning myself, I truly profess that I did not know—as I have always been little curious about matters not concerning me—before the Letters of the Noble Mr. Descartes were delivered to our Academic Senate<sup>d</sup>, what was being agitated | in that matter; how the Distinguished Mr. Schoock, with his letters full of complaints, denounced to Mr. Voetius that he would finally reveal all these things to Voetius's own infamy; how he proposed to Mr. Voetius the questions that might be put to him if the matter came to judgment; how Voetius suggested they be eluded through shameful malicious litigation <note>original: *vitilitigationes*, a term for carping or dishonest legal maneuvering</note> and equivocations; how he tried to persuade Mr. Schoock that Descartes would not dare to move anything here against him; how he spread the word that he would come here to ensure Descartes was thrown into chains, so that the latter might be deterred from instituting his action against Mr. Schoock; how he supplied Schoock with thonged spears <note>original: *haſtas amentatas*, a metaphor for prepared or sharpened arguments</note> with which he might defend the more difficult points of the Cartesian Philosophy, sometimes not...

> » ...without the appearance of Blasphemy <note>original Latin: *fine specie Blaſphemiæ*</note>: such as this specifically, that Descartes could be metaphorically and without insult called "Cain the wanderer" <note>original Latin: *Caïnum vagum*; a biblical reference to Cain being cursed to wander the earth after killing Abel</note>, because even God, he said, is compared in Scripture to a lion, a wolf, a thief, etc. We have here many letters from Mr. Voetius himself, from which the truth of what I say has become fully known, not only to me, but to my Reverend and Distinguished Colleagues. » (Pages 404-405.)

> « Since I was therefore ignorant of all these things before the Noble Descartes had instituted his legal action against the Distinguished Mr. Schoock, that matter happened to me far more unexpectedly than to even the defendant himself, or to Mr. Voetius, who at least now discovers that the highest cunning is to lack cunning <note>original: *summam eſſe aſtutiam carere aſtutiâ*</note>, and that nothing is safer, no way more direct, than to act sincerely. Hidden schemes, contrary to virtue and truth, finally come to light and cover their authors in shame... » (Page 405.)

This citation reveals to us the existence, and gives us a summary of a private correspondence between Descartes and Desmarets, which had escaped our investigations. Five new letters must be intercalated into the general correspondence at the following dates:

1. Descartes to Desmarets, May–June 1643.
2. Response from Desmarets, June 1643.
3. Descartes to Desmarets, 7 Nov. 1643.
4. Response from Desmarets, Nov. or Dec. 1643.
5. Descartes to Desmarets, 12 Dec. 1643.

To these five letters are added at least two others which are earlier: one (now lost) from Desmarets to Descartes, and the latter's response, which is our letter CCXCI, vol. III, p. 605-607. We can even date this last one more exactly: Descartes speaks there, indeed, of the "three first sheets" (vol. III, p. 606, l. 6) that he received from Voetius's book against Desmarets; now we know, from Desmarets himself, that these three first sheets were known toward the end of September 1642:

> « Now, toward the end of September of the year 1642, the first three leaves of his *Specimen* <note>The *Specimen philosophiae Cartesianae*, a critique of Descartes's philosophy</note> (i.e., Voetius's) had been seen by some, »

(*Ultima patientia* etc., p. 318), and Descartes had them in his hands for some time already (vol. III, p. 606, l. 12-13). Furthermore, Descartes is waiting for the end of the printing, and already knows that the work will have "about twenty sheets" (l. 29); (it has exactly a bit more than 21, being 511 pages <term>in-12</term> <note>A book size where each sheet is folded into 12 leaves, creating 24 pages per sheet</note>). Therefore the publication is near, and Desmarets informs us that it occurred at the beginning of March 1643:

> « around the beginning of March of the year 1643, although the first page of the book gave the year 1642 (which was also mysterious <note>original Greek: *μυστηριωδὲς*</note>), the *Specimen* appeared. »

(*Ultima patientia*, p. 326.) Descartes's letter would therefore be, not from January 1643, but rather February, and undoubtedly from the same date—February 18 or 19—as letter CCXCV, where it was found inserted (vol. III, p. 617).

### III

#### PAGE 280, NOTE *a*.

These twelve pages (p. 253-264) form a parenthesis of a historical nature within the large work—otherwise entirely dogmatic—by Paul Voet <note>Paul Voet (1619–1667) was the son of Descartes' great rival, Gijsbert Voetius</note>, *REFORMED NATURAL THEOLOGY* <note>original Latin: *THEOLOGIA NATURALIS REFORMATA*</note>. Here they are *in full* <note>original Latin: *in extenso*</note>:

> « ... Blame falls upon the triumvirs <note>original Latin: *triumviri*; referring to the three main opponents: Descartes, Desmarets, and Schoock</note> (would that the necessity of making this public did not constrain me!): Descartes, Mareſius <note>Samuel Desmarets</note>, and Schoockius <note>Martin Schoock</note>. They joined their efforts here to present an innocent Father (Gisbert Voetius) as infamous and heterodox to the entire world. What did he do in return? Nothing, except that—by denying those things to be true which they freely, liberally, and with impunity throw at him without proof or even attempting to prove—he decided to possess his soul in silence and patience. Lest they should continue to run riot with impunity in the future, I thought something should be replied to them here, without hatred or bias, by which at least their arrows launched against my father might be blunted. Before I do this, I will briefly narrate the occasion for the hatred conceived against my Father. »
> « Descartes was instigated by his own Philosophy, which was condemned and proscribed in the University of Utrecht <note>original Latin: *Academiâ Ultrajectinâ*</note> by the judgment of the Professors, with the approval of the Noble and Distinguished City Senate. Because this was done at the time when my Reverend Father was serving as Rector Magnificus <note>the head of the university</note>, Descartes—as if it had been done by his procurement—published a most virulent booklet entitled *Letter to Dinet* <note>original Latin: *Epiſtola ad Dinetum*; a letter Descartes wrote to the head of the Jesuits in France to defend his philosophy</note>, as well as another, *Letter to a Most Famous Man* <note>original Latin: *Epiſtola ad celeberrimum Virum*</note>. Mr. Mareſius was embittered (I will not recall other matters here, as I am writing a blameless defense) because he was defeated and condemned in the controversy over the *Brotherhood of Mary* <note>original Latin: *Marianæ Fraternitatis*; a theological dispute involving a lay religious group</note>, which he had initiated against my Father, by the judgment of the Theological Faculties of all the Universities in the Netherlands, as well as the illustrious Schools—except for Groningen, where he was teaching at the time—and also by the opinion of the supreme theologian André Rivet <note>original Latin: *Andreæ Riveti*</note>. Mr. Schoock was given cause to renounce his friendship with my Father because he believed himself to have been slighted by my Reverend Father (wrongly, in truth) because he had never been recommended for the Theological Professorship at Utrecht. As if that could have been done by my Father's care alone, and not by the order of the City Senate, to whose authority all matters are committed. »
> « I must deal first with Descartes; who, since he has caused harm even after death through his surviving and reprinted booklets, must be repelled in them as one dead among the living. And although I neither can nor wish to harm the deceased, I will be able to heal my Father, who was harmed while he lived. Not indeed with insults for insults, or... »

# RECTOR AND PROFESSORS
## *Of the University of Utrecht*
### TO THE CANDID READER, GREETINGS.

In what manner the Reverend and Renowned Mr. Gisbert Voetius, our most dear Colleague, was defamed by the author of the *Letter to Dinet* <note>René Descartes published this letter in 1642, attacking Voetius</note>, is not hidden from you, kind Reader. We had already then decided to assert the reputation of this excellent man by public testimony; but for certain reasons the matter was delayed until this day. But since the aforementioned author has set neither end nor limit for himself, but has added to the prior letter another much more bitter one <note>referring to Descartes' *Letter to Voetius* (1643)</note>, and as it has been translated into the vernacular <note>Dutch</note> by malevolent men so that our Colleague might suffer an even greater loss of reputation among all people, we thought we must no longer delay. By the mandate and authority of the Most Honorable City Senate, we have judged that this present Testimony, together with the Historical Narrative of those things which were done and conducted among us so that the old Philosophy <note>Traditional Aristotelian Scholasticism, which the university sought to protect from Descartes’ innovations</note> might be retained in possession, should be published: not that we might harm anyone's fame or reputation, but that the innocence of a man who has deserved most excellently of our University might become more and more known to all.
Farewell.
->Given at Utrecht on the Rhine,<-
->September 28, 1643.<- <note>original Latin: *IV Kal. Octob. CIƆIƆC XLIII*. The 4th day before the Kalends of October.</note>

# TESTIMONY
## *Of the University of Utrecht.*
### THE RECTOR AND PROFESSORS OF THE UNIVERSITY OF UTRECHT
#### To the Reader, Greetings.

Although virtue and integrity of life do not need the votes of others, such at times is the wickedness of men that those who carry with them living witnesses of their innocence are forced to flee to testimonies. This has been experienced by...

<meta>This page continues the official defense of the University of Utrecht against René Descartes, following the introduction provided by Paul Voet. The text is part of a formal testimony vindicating Gisbert Voetius and his colleagues from accusations made in Descartes' "Letter to Dinet."</meta>

<meta>catchword: One</meta>

...several of our Colleagues, most distinguished men: who, since they conduct their lives, morals, and studies in such a way that they are approved by all—serving as an example to individuals and an ornament to the entire Academy—have nevertheless been shamefully torn apart by insults and outrages in the letter of René Descartes to Dinet <note>René Descartes wrote an open letter to Father Pierre Dinet, a Jesuit provincial, in 1642, which contained sharp criticisms of the Utrecht professors</note>. And although they did not fear that their reputation among good men and those familiar with the affairs of our Academy would be endangered by the aforementioned letter; yet, because they noticed that a certain heterodox person <note>Likely referring to Henricus Regius (Henri Le Roy), a former protégé of Descartes turned rival</note> recently transferred some slanders from that letter into his own pamphlet; and lest other unskillful people should do the same, or the gullible believe that these lies and slanders are based on historical truth: they judged that their innocence should be protected by this Academic testimony. 

We, therefore, yielding to their most just request, testify that it is false what the author of the letter writes (page 175), *that certain colleagues, seeing a Physician <note>original Latin: *Medicum*; referring to Henricus Regius, Professor of Medicine</note> preferred over themselves, were manifesty envious of him, and very often contended with the Magistrate so that the new method of teaching <note>A reference to Cartesian philosophy</note> might be prohibited.* For besides the fact that there was no cause for envy, the leading role in petitioning the Magistrate did not belong to them, but to others who were moved by the common danger to the Academy: since the situation itself cried out that the old way of philosophizing <note>The traditional Aristotelian or Scholastic method</note> could not be changed without great detriment to the Academy. And even these men did not petition the Magistrate "very often," but only once: not by their own whim, but by the counsel and delegation of the Academic Senate. 

Furthermore, it is far from the truth that those who are said to have been envious labored *throughout a whole three-year period so that the new Philosophy might be forbidden to the Physician; or that a new province, as if for a reward for work well done, was given to the Physician by the Magistrate: so that within three years, he obtained a problematic profession through the special recommendation of that Theologian <note>Gisbert Voetius</note> whose side is now attacked by slander:* nor was any controversy moved against him before his disputation on the circulation of the blood <note>original Latin: *circulatione sanguinis*; Henricus Regius was one of the early defenders of William Harvey’s discovery of blood circulation, which traditionalists often viewed with suspicion</note> had been released.

Moreover, it is a wicked speculation by which the author of the letter (page 179) *seems to want to blame the foot-stamping of the scholarly youth on certain Colleagues, we know not which;* for until now there has been no disputation in any faculty, however somewhat fervent, in which the audience did not punish the immodesty of the disputants with noise and the stamping of feet <note>original Latin: *supplosione pedum*; a common form of student protest or heckling in 17th-century universities</note>. As for the fact that during one disputation, contrary to custom, the Presiding Professor himself seemed to be hissed out, whereas otherwise that storm is feared only by those opposing or defending, we admit that this was a wrongful act; indeed, it is a grief to us that those who gathered for the sake of learning should take it upon themselves to act as judges; but it was neither in our power to turn that evil away from the President, nor was it done by the trickery or counsel of any of us.

Furthermore, it is a manifest slander by which the author of the letter (page 187) *attempts to attribute the decree of the Academic Senate, concerning the retention of the Old Philosophy in teaching, to the Rector alone; while he writes that some who disagreed were overcome by the number of votes, and feigns that others, being peaceful men, did not wish to contradict their Rector, whom they knew to be biting.* For the fact that everyone agreed to the decree is abundantly proved by the petition presented to the Most Noble City Senate and signed by everyone; and it is false that any of us were forced by the "bitingness" of a most mild man <note>A defensive reference to Voetius, portraying him as gentle rather than aggressive</note> to say one thing and feel another.

...was at least one of the Colleagues who did not oppose the decree, but rather felt it should be recorded in the Academy's official records instead of being published in print.

Furthermore, regarding the "power" of the Theologian <note>Referring to Gisbert Voetius, a leading Dutch Calvinist theologian and fierce opponent of Descartes</note>, which the author hatefully exaggerates in the said letter (pages 177 and 185), we recognize no such thing in this college. Here, the freedom to judge and dissent is equal for all—unless, perhaps, one considers "power" to be the respect and authority earned through great service to the University and the Church. We also admit that this same Theologian, while serving as Rector—whose duty it was to ensure the University suffered no harm—called the Senate together and presented a report. However, we flatly deny that he acted as both accuser and judge in his own personal grievance. In fact, he publicly declared that he would handle personal insults himself, and that he was bringing only the collective interests of the University before the Senate.

Finally, we protest the significant injustice done to the aforementioned Theologian by the author of the letter, who labels him a *turbulent and seditious Rector* (pages 188 and 211). In truth, he did nothing in a disorderly or rebellious manner during his entire year in office. On the contrary, we credit his particular vigilance and skill for calming the unrest and restoring the University's original peace.

To make these matters even clearer, we provide a Historical Narrative of the events that took place here. We ask the reader—unlike the author of that letter—to trust the public testimony of the University rather than listening to the secret lies of gossips. Issued at Utrecht, March 1, 1643. (*In the previously mentioned pamphlet, these two documents are followed by the Historical Narrative, which makes up the largest part of the work.*)

### COPY OF A TRANSLATED EXTRACT FROM THE ACTS OF THE CONSISTORY OF UTRECHT.
<note>original Latin: *Synedrii*; refers to the governing body of the local Reformed Church</note>

The President presented certain records concerning the Reverend Consistory, which read word-for-word as follows:

Since Mr. Voetius is being weighed down by various slanders, insults, and defamations—specifically through public writings published under the name of René Descartes—he felt it necessary for this Reverend Consistory to provide testimony regarding his preaching, his life, and his conduct. He asks whether he is not a great defender of the true Reformed Religion against all idolatry, superstition, sects, and opinions contrary to the truth of the Word of God, according to the requirements of his office.

After reading these records and considering their contents, the Reverend Consistory reached a decision and sent the following decree to the Honorable Lords on August 7, 1643:

At the request of the Honorable Senators of the City of Utrecht, asking that a truthful testimony be provided for Professor Gisbert Voetius regarding his duties, life, actions, and conduct: the Reverend Consistory of the Reformed Church of Utrecht finds no reason why it should not, in every way, grant such a petition...

...should grant this, especially since everyone is bound to bear witness to the truth, particularly if they have been asked to do so.

We therefore testify, certify, and declare, according to the sincere truth, before each and every person to whom these documents shall be shown: that the aforementioned **Master Gisbert Voetius**, minister of the Gospel at Utrecht, is pure and sound in the doctrine which accords with piety; that he is exceptionally vigilant in his ecclesiastical duties, daily producing great and hoped-for fruits through his edifying sermons; and that he is highly esteemed by us all and by the Church of God. Regarding his life, deeds, and conduct, he has behaved—and continues to behave—among us in such a way that we know nothing else to testify except that he is honorable, endowed with virtue, and upright. He has shown himself to be modest and peace-loving in his interactions, both among his colleagues and within the church at large. Therefore, we all, individually and from our hearts, desire and even pray to God that we may be permitted to enjoy his ministry in the Church of Utrecht for a long time to come, for the glory of God and the edification of the Church.

### EXPLANATIONS.
<page-num>329</page-num>

...indeed we had hoped) by their learning, piety, and diligence, they have been useful beyond measure to the Academy, and still are, and this not without the full satisfaction of the Magistrate and all honorable men; among whom **Master Gisbert Voetius**, <note>Voetius (1589–1676) was a powerful Dutch Calvinist theologian and a fierce opponent of Descartes’s philosophy.</note> Doctor and Professor of Sacred Theology, as well as pastor of the Church, is not to be counted among the last, being as he is solid in teaching, dogmatic in sermons, subtle in disputes, detesting and fighting against *Atheism*, *Libertinism* <note>In the 17th century, "libertinism" referred to freethinking or a lack of religious restraint rather than just moral loose living.</note> and any heretical opinions contrary to the Holy Scriptures, leading many who had wandered back to the true religion by his doctrine and the example of a pious life, and eradicating superstition from the hearts of simple men: so that, in a Professor and Doctor of Theology, nothing more could be wished for or desired. And just as all these gifts make him pleasing and acceptable to all honorable and pious people, so too do they excite bitter hatred and envy among the enemies of truth, as has appeared in many ways, especially from two letters published under the name of the aforementioned *Descartes*, one of which was sent to a Jesuit named *Dinet*, the other distinguished by the title: *Letter of René Descartes to the Most Celebrated Man, etc.* <note>The "Most Celebrated Man" refers to Voetius himself; the title was sarcastic.</note> In which that *Descartes* accuses the aforementioned **Master Voetius** of many crimes, impieties, and vices—namely, that he abused sermons for lies, scurrilous insults, a passion for contention and sedition, the defamation of various people, and the disordered rebuke of powerful men, showing contempt for superior powers; that he was a hypocrite, defiant, quick to anger, usurping authority over his colleagues and affecting the same over all men; that he had been a seditious *Rector of the Academy*, and still remains so in the Republic, along with other things of this kind; and therefore (namely, *Descartes*) warning the rulers of this city to attend to these matters and punish him (namely, *Voetius*) on that account, although *Descartes* himself also marks or taxes those same rulers with censure because they had prohibited the sale in their city of the defense of *Regius* <note>Hendrik de Roy (Regius) was a disciple of Descartes whose theses caused a major academic scandal in Utrecht.</note> regarding certain *Theses*, even though it was known to the whole world that this defense was modest and fair. After all these things had become known to the Lords of the Senate, they themselves, on the most recent *June 13* (although the innocence of **Master Voetius** was known to every person who knew him well), by a proclamation made after the ringing of the bell, had signaled to the aforementioned *Descartes* that he would be permitted to present himself in this city within the space of the next three weeks, enjoying immunity in coming and going, so that he might confirm the contents of the two aforementioned letters in such a way as he himself judged useful to his intention. Regarding which publication, the often-mentioned *Descartes*, in his letter given on the following July 6, *New Style*, <note>New Style refers to the Gregorian calendar, which was used in some parts of Europe while others still used the older Julian calendar.</note> had written to the aforementioned Lords of the Senate <note>original: "see this letter, vol. IV, p. 8-13"</note>, among other things, that the recently published letter, the inscription of which was: *Letter of René Descartes to the Most Celebrated Man, etc.*, was written in such a way that the proofs, which served for the verification of all those things he had written about that man, were found added everywhere, insofar as they could reasonably be demanded of him; and that for this reason he had specifically omitted many of that man's actions | known to him, so that he would not be bound to produce witnesses for their proof; saying also in that same letter, among other things, that the Senate, if it inspected what he had written regarding those matters, would notice that he had intended this above all, beyond the just defense of his own honor.

### EXPLANATIONS.
<page-num>330</page-num>

...had worked so that he might consult the interests of the Republic and the aforementioned City, as well as the reputation of the Academy on both sides. When the aforementioned Lord Senators had thoroughly read and examined the previously mentioned Letter, as well as the two others mentioned in the said publication, the Senators took care to have them inspected and examined by their Commissioners and others established outside of any partisan interest, as was proper. From their report, they understood that the aforementioned *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> complains unjustly that he has been excessively harmed by **Master Voetius**, since he does not bring forward even the smallest proof, but only draws consequences from false presuppositions, relying on uncertain conjectures and bad presumptions. From these, he falsely attributes to **Master Voetius** that he is the author, promoter, editor, or co-creator of various booklets by which the oft-mentioned *Descartes* thinks himself injured. Furthermore, it was clear to the Senators that all these things were falsely fabricated and contrary to the truth. 

Thus, the aforementioned *Descartes* had no cause at all to so enormously damage the good name and reputation of **Master Voetius**; instead, this behavior rather smacked of the spirit of the **Jesuits** <note>The Jesuits were the influential Catholic religious order where Descartes was educated. Voetius, a staunch Calvinist, used this connection to imply Descartes was a secret agent of Catholic interests.</note>, of whom he confesses to have been a disciple and whom he professes to have held in high regard throughout his life. Moreover, he brings no other proof for his bitter and wicked defamations and accusations than from rumor and the false reports of most lying men, enemies of this republic and the Academy, as well as of the Reformed Religion. 

And since the innocence of the again-named **Master Voetius** is sufficiently established to the Senate—and even though it was not necessary, this same innocence was demonstrated by the testimonies of certain private individuals as well as many respectable colleges—the Senate therefore declares the two aforementioned letters to be defamatory writings and infamous libels <note>original: "famososque libellos"</note>. By these, not only is the good name and reputation of **Master Voetius** enormously damaged, but also the interests of the Academy, the specific reputation of the Professors, and the government of this City are brought into contempt. Therefore, it [the Senate] commands all and each that they do not presume to print, import, sell, or distribute the aforementioned *Letters*, in whatever language they may be, within this City or its jurisdiction, whether directly or indirectly, secretly or openly. This is under penalty of discretionary punishment, as the matter arises, with the right of legal action reserved for the Lord Praetor <note>The chief judicial officer of the city.</note> of this City against the aforementioned *Descartes* in the name of the aforementioned parties.

And it was signed:

->*Agreed in my presence*<-

->C. D. RIDDER.<-

> I turn now to **Master Samuel Maresius** <note>Samuel Des Marets (1599–1673), a theologian who was a contemporary rival to both Descartes and Voetius at different times.</note>, who, since he borrowed most of his points against the *Reverend Father* [Voetius] from the writings of *Descartes*, will find himself refuted once Descartes is refuted, and his own ideas outlawed. However, because in some matters he resorts to the *acts of the Academic Senate of Groningen*, I will only reply this: the *Groningen acts* were maliciously fabricated by a very few Professors—three or four, no more—while the others disagreed. He hardly dares to call it a judgment, but points to it as the testimony or declaration of **Schoock** <note>Martin Schoock, a student of Voetius who authored a fierce attack on Descartes's philosophy, leading to a legal battle.</note> for the Reverend Father...

» [The judgment] regarding the illustrious De Maets <note>original: "de Matio"; Carolus De Maets was a colleague of Voetius</note> cannot cause prejudice. Having seen and duly examined everything contained in the letters given by order of the most noble Academic Senate of Groningen to the most Noble and Renowned **Master René Descartes** on the 16th of the Calends of 1645, and all that was conducted in the same Senate on April 10th of the same year, and which is found annexed to the same: We, the undersigned Professors of the Law Faculty at the University of **Leiden** <note>original: "Lugduno-Batavâ"</note>, having been asked concerning the law and the effect of these acts, respond that the sentence passed by the aforementioned Senate seems to us to be null and void due to various defects and causes, and does not deserve the name of a "definitive sentence"; and that by it, neither the rights, nor the fame and reputation of the Reverend **Master Gisbert Voetius** and others can, should, or ought to be harmed or diminished.

### EXPLANATIONS.
<page-num>332</page-num>

*The Defendant from Groningen <note>Martin Schoock</note>, having been arrested and summoned in a case of injuries <note>original: "injuriarum"; in a legal sense, this refers to defamation or libel</note> by the other party. The aforementioned court, all things having been maturely weighed, including the "saving clause" <note>original: "clausulâ salutari"; a legal formula allowing the court to grant any relief deemed just</note> with which the petition is equipped, and doing justice with the advice of practicing legal experts: condemns the Defendant to declare—before the Sheriff <note>original: "Prætore"</note> and two Aldermen <note>original: "Scabinis"</note> here in the registry, for a more precise elucidation and supplementation of those things which he said and wrote in his papers and personal responses during the trial here and elsewhere—that the draft of the testimony <note>original: "formula attestationis"</note> sent to him by the Plaintiff <note>Gisbertus Voetius</note> for the purpose of the Defendant providing it, and the correction by the Associate <note>Carolus De Maets</note> on the small note that was presented (both of which are mentioned at length in the trial), were not false. And further, that it was never his intention to declare before the Academic Senate of Groningen that the Plaintiff or the Associate solicited the Defendant, or arranged to have him solicited, to testify or attest to anything false, or that such a thing was extorted from him by importunity. He must also declare that he attributes no falsehood or dishonesty to the Plaintiff and the Associate, nor presumes any such thing of them. He shall further desire that whatever the Defendant himself—out of zeal for his own honor and to avoid all infamy—may have said or written somewhat harshly, which might perhaps be taken or twisted into another sense, be so understood, and if necessary, corrected, so that all falsehood and dishonesty be removed from the Plaintiff and the Associate; and that he shall leave an instrument of such a declaration in proper form for the Plaintiff and the Associate. And the court judges that the Defendant is not to be held further, nor is his honor and reputation harmed or diminished by the aforementioned declaration; denying the Plaintiff and the Associate their petition and conclusion instituted for another purpose regarding honorable and useful amendment, balancing the costs of the trial for these reasons.*

*Thus done and pronounced at Utrecht, 31 May 1649.*

<page-type>preface</page-type>

->ŒUVRES. III.<-

# | TO THE READER <gloss>a</gloss>

From the time that the philosophy of the noble man **RENÉ DESCARTES** first saw the light of day, it has been received by many, but not in one single way; indeed, it has experienced various fortunes, depending on whose hands and temperaments it fell into. There are those who raised serious objections to it, to which that heroic man <note>Descartes is often referred to in 17th-century texts with epithets like "hero" of philosophy.</note> responded seriously, both in Latin and in French. Others, when they could do nothing else, wished nonetheless to gnaw at and bite it; regarding whom—as the Philosopher himself predicted in the Preface to the *Meditations on First Philosophy* <note>original: *Medit. Metaph.*</note>—not caring to understand the sequence and connection of his arguments, their only aim was to quibble over individual clauses. Therefore, although they found many opportunities for mockery, they objected to nothing of substance or worthy of a response <gloss>b</gloss>. Of this same sort is a certain shadowy and light-shunning character <note>original: *Tenebrio quidam ac Lucifuga*—a stinging insult for an anonymous critic who hides from the "light" of truth.</note>, who calls himself now Theophilus, now Mercury the Cosmopolite, in a pair of pamphlets published a few years ago <gloss>c</gloss>; and a recent theologian in his *Theological Consideration of the Cartesian Method*...

---

a. This Preface is not by Descartes, who did not even approve of it; see Vol. V, p. 114, l. 8. The *first edition* <note>original: *édition princeps*</note>, which we follow here, only provides page numbers starting from the poem *To René Descartes* etc., p. 10. Nevertheless, it took the preface into account, pp. 3-9. We will reproduce this pagination at the top of the pages in the present edition.
b. See Vol. VII, p. 9, l. 29, to p. 10, l. 5.
c. One of them bore this title: "*Notes on Cartesian First Philosophy, by Theophilus Cosmopolita.*" A pamphlet printed in 16mo during the summer of that year (1643), without a printer's name, based on a copy that was pretended to have been first printed at The Hague. Imposture and calumny reigned throughout, from the title to the conclusion of the pamphlet. The extravagance of the style and the coarseness of the insults with which it was filled so strongly resembled those that Mr. Regius attributed to Voetius <note>Gisbertus Voetius was a powerful Dutch theologian and a fierce opponent of Descartes.</note> in his lectures and conversations, that one can reasonably presume that, of everything that might belong to Voetius, only his name was hidden in this entire pamphlet, and his spirit was manifest everywhere. <margin>Manuscript Letters 23, 24, from Regius to Descartes.</margin> Voetius hardly behaved otherwise in the defamatory writings he took care to spread against Mr. Descartes, often under a borrowed name and sometimes under a fake one. (A. BAILLET, *The Life of Mr. Descartes*, Vol. II, pp. 204-205.)

Others have risen up against Cartesian philosophy in theses usually proposed for debate in Paris, Utrecht, Groningen, Franeker, and Leiden. They have either attacked its Author in open warfare, or rushed upon him secretly under the general title of "New Philosophers," or altogether concealed his name. Specimens of both of these latter types occurred very recently in the oldest and newest Academies of the United Netherlands. In the Academy of Leiden, a primary philosopher <sup>d</sup>—a man who, as Mr. Descartes judges, is not bad, and simple rather than prudent—was carried away by some passion or other and attributed such fatuous, inept, and tasteless opinions to certain "New Philosophers" that he made himself a laughingstock to many, a joke and a source of ridicule to others, and a source of pity to many more. And although in the act of disputing he did not pronounce this four-syllable name, **DESCARTES**, and when publicly challenged to produce the name of any "New Philosopher" holding such foolish opinions, he failed shamefully here; nevertheless, he behaved and turned himself in every direction so that it was easily established to any of his listeners that no one other than Mr. Descartes was being designated. ### IN THE PROGRAM ###

<meta>(8-9)</meta>

...wrote a certain dissertation on *Leucophlegmatic Cachexia* <note>A medical term of the era referring to a pale, bloated physical condition caused by an excess of phlegm; here, it served as the formal subject of a medical thesis.</note>, to which he added several Corollaries <note>Additional propositions or consequences attached to the main argument.</note> intended to demolish the principles of Descartes's *Metaphysical Meditations*. When the formal debate was halted, these were sent out on an open sheet <note>A broadside or placard intended for public display.</note> through various cities of Holland, as a sign of either triumph or a challenge to start a fight over them. Even though the most noble Mr. Descartes looked down on these assaults and "barkings" of the Theses and Considerations with a great soul and never wished to reply <sup>a</sup>, he finally allowed himself to issue some Response to that Broadside of Corollaries. This response did not seem unworthy of the light of publication to the Friend to whom he sent it and gave power over it <sup>b</sup>; by which perhaps the Author of the Broadside might be brought back to a better mind, and because it might seem to some that there is something in it worthy of a defender. For Mr. Descartes has never failed, nor does he fail, his reputation or his supporters in responding, if anything worthy of a response has been produced against his Philosophy. But as for calumnies and trifling nonsense—things that do not strike at his own opinions or responses, but merely run into objections he himself devised or others brought forward to find the truth, or which pluck a small part here and there from his writings—these he ignores. Truly, "The eagle does not catch flies" <note>original: *Aquila non captat muscas*; a Latin proverb meaning that a great person does not concern themselves with trivial matters.</note> <sup>c</sup>. But enough of Prefaces; it will be worthwhile to read and weigh the examination and Notes of the Broadside itself.

Mr. Descartes, having received it in this second form, immediately recognized the Author by the style and by common rumor..." (A. BAILLET, *The Life of Mr. Descartes*, vol. II, p. 334-335.) <meta>This page follows a description of the public disputes between Descartes and his critics at the University of Utrecht. It serves as a transition from the prose accounts of these academic battles to a celebratory poem in honor of Descartes's philosophical achievements, likely intended to bolster his reputation against his detractors.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>

# | TO RENÉ DESCARTES,
## Restorer of Philosophy,
### Ornament of the Age.

->Not bound to swear by the words of any Master,<- <note>This is an allusion to the Roman poet Horace: "Nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri." It signifies Descartes's rejection of scholastic authority (like Aristotle) in favor of independent reason.</note>
While you, *René*, drink truth from the very fountain of truth,
And you restore to the Mind its rightful laws, and take from the Senses
That excessive faith which the gullible crowd bestows:
Doubting in some unknown way, you sweep away all doubts,
And from things uncertain, you read all that is certain.
Surely the Atheist falls by his own weapons: and poorly does Sextus, <note>A reference to Sextus Empiricus, the ancient proponent of Skepticism. The poem argues that Descartes uses skeptical doubt to eventually defeat the skeptics.</note>
Withholding his assent, find himself conquered by his own art.
Now that Mind and God have been found, nothing can stand in the way;
Behold, matter itself is subjected to your genius.
Which, split by Motion into various and a thousand shapes,
Causes the noble work of so vast a world to rise.
From this, the seeds of Heaven, Earth, Sea, and nourishing Air
Flow, poured through this great void.
What is the nature of Fire? What makes the ruddy Sun
To shine? From whence is Color added to mixed things?
Whence comes the trembling of the Earth, by what force do the white seas swell, <note>Refers to earthquakes and the tides.</note>
Why does hexagonal Snow, or the round drop of rain, fall?
Do you wish to know why Iron enters the Magnet? This is the work
Of René alone, from whom no path remains hidden,
By whose genius both the Ancients and the Moderns rise,
Nor do all the ages claim to have seen his equal.
Whoever enviously refuses to lower the rods of office to him, <note>original: "submittere fasces." In ancient Rome, lowering the *fasces* (bundles of rods representing authority) was a gesture of submission or respect to a higher power.</note>
Violating Nature, shall be an adulterer to his Mother.
And seeking to strike his tooth against a fragile thing, he shall strike
Something solid. It would have been better not to have touched it at all.
Since the first principles so respond to the final ends, who would believe
He could reveal these sacred things without God? ª

---

ª <margin>Who wrote these verses? In a letter to Princess Elisabeth dated January 31, 1648, Descartes indicates the author's name by the first letters only. (See vol. V, p. 114, l. 14.) <margin>10</margin> A few days ago, I received two small books <note>original: "libellos"; these were likely pamphlets or short polemical works common in 17th-century intellectual debates.</note>, in one of which I am openly and directly attacked<gloss>a</gloss>, while in the other, I am targeted only covertly and indirectly. Regarding the first, I am not at all bothered; indeed, I am grateful to its author, because, since he has collected nothing but futile quibbles and <term>calumnies</term> <note>Slanderous or false accusations intended to damage a reputation.</note> that no one could believe,
<margin>15</margin> despite his wicked labor, he has by this very act testified that he could find nothing in my writings that could be justly criticized. Thus, he has confirmed their truth more effectively than if he had praised them, and he has done so at the expense of his own reputation. However, the other pamphlet moves me more deeply; for although it contains nothing openly about me, and it comes forth
<margin>20</margin> [under another's name]...

And indeed there is no doubt that concerning <term>contingent things</term> <note>Things that are not necessary and could be otherwise, like whether a person is sitting or standing.</note> it can be said that the nature of things allows them to be in one way or another: for example, that I write now, or that I do not write. And it no more belongs to the nature of a mountain that it is not without a valley, than to the nature of the human mind that it be what it is: namely, that it be a <term>substance</term> <note>A thing that exists by itself, rather than existing as a quality of something else.</note>, if <margin>10</margin> it is a substance, or certainly that it be a <term>mode</term> <note>A quality, state, or "way of being" of a substance.</note> of a corporeal thing, if indeed it is such a mode. This is what our author <note>Descartes refers here to Henricus Regius, his former disciple.</note> attempts to persuade us of here, and to prove it he adds these words: *or if we follow some other philosophers* ᵃ, etc., where by *other philosophers* he clearly points to me; <margin>15</margin> for I am the first who considered <term>thought</term> <note>original: "cogitationem"</note> as the principal <term>attribute</term> <note>An essential quality that constitutes the nature of a substance.</note> of an incorporeal substance, and <term>extension</term> <note>original: "extensionem"; the property of taking up space.</note> as the principal attribute of a corporeal one. But I did not say that those attributes are in them as if in subjects distinct from themselves; and we must take care that we do not understand "attribute" <margin>20</margin> here to mean nothing other than a "mode": for whatever we recognize as being attributed to something by nature—whether it be a mode that can be changed, or the entirely immutable essence of that thing itself—that we call its attribute. Thus in God there are many attributes, but no modes. Thus <margin>25</margin> one of the attributes of any substance is that it subsists through itself. Thus the extension of some body can indeed admit various modes within itself: for its mode is one way if that body is spherical, and another if it is square; but extension itself, which is the subject of those <margin>30</margin> modes, considered in itself, is not [a mode] of a corporeal substance <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("substantiæ cor-"), likely intending to say "corporeal substance's mode."</note>...

-># NOTES<-

...it can be [granted] that those things which are different, and of which neither is contained in the concept of the other, belong to one and the same subject; for it is the same as if it were said that one and the same subject has two different natures. This <margin>5</margin> implies a contradiction, at least when the question concerns a **simple and non-composite subject** <note>A "simple" subject is a single, unified thing that cannot be broken down into parts or divided.</note>, just as it does in this case.

But three things must be noted here; if this writer <note>Descartes refers to Henricus Regius, his former disciple turned critic.</note> had understood them well, <margin>10</margin> he would never have fallen into such obvious errors.

<column-break/>

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **First** | It belongs to the nature of a **mode** <note>A "mode" is a specific state or quality of a substance, such as "shape" is a mode of a physical body; it cannot exist without the body.</note> that, while we can easily understand a **substance** <note>A "substance" is a thing that exists independently, requiring nothing else but God for its existence.</note> without it, we cannot conversely clearly understand a mode unless we simultaneously conceive of the substance to which it belongs. As I explained in <margin>15</margin> *Part 1 of the Principles, Article 61* <margin>a</margin>, and all **Philosophers** <note>Descartes refers here to the "Scholastics," the academic thinkers who followed the traditions of Aristotle.</note> agree on this. It is manifest from his fifth article that our opponent has not paid attention to this rule: for there he admits, *we can doubt the existence of the body, while meanwhile we do not doubt the <margin>20</margin> existence of the mind* <margin>b</margin>. From this it follows that the mind can be understood by us without the body, and therefore is not a mode of the body. |
| **Second** | What I wish to be noted here is the difference between **simple and composite beings**. Indeed, a **composite** being is one in which two or more **attributes** <note>A fundamental property that constitutes the essence of a substance, like "extension" for matter or "thought" for mind.</note> are found, <margin>25</margin> each of which can be understood distinctly without the other. |

<column-break/>

For from the fact that one is understood without the other, we know it is not a mode, but a thing or an attribute of a thing which can exist without the other. However, a **simple being** is one in which such attributes are not found.

->## ON THE PROGRAM<-

<margin>28-30</margin>
<note>original: "IN PROGRAMMA" — This refers to the "Programma" or broadsheet published by Henricus Regius in 1647, which challenged Descartes's views on the nature of the soul.</note>

From this it is clear that the subject in which we understand only <term>extension</term> <note>The property of taking up physical space; the essence of matter.</note> along with the various <term>modes</term> of extension is a **simple entity**; just as is the subject in which we recognize only <term>thought</term> <note>Mental activity; the essence of the mind.</note> with its various modes of thinking. <margin>5</margin> However, that subject in which we consider extension and thought together is a **composite entity**: namely, the human being, consisting of soul and body. It appears that *our author* <note>Regius</note> has here taken the human being to be the body alone, of which the mind would merely be a mode.

<margin>10</margin> Finally, it must be noted here that in subjects composed of several <term>substances</term> <note>Independent things that require nothing else but God to exist.</note>, one is often the primary one, which is considered by us in such a way that whatever we add to it from the others is seen as nothing other than a mode. For example, a clothed man <margin>15</margin> can be considered as something composed of a man and clothes; but "being clothed" is, in respect to the man, only a mode, even though the clothes themselves are substances. In the same way, *our author* could, in the case of a human being who is composed of soul and body, consider the body as the primary thing; by reason of <margin>20</margin> which, "being animated" or "having thought" is seen as nothing other than a mode. However, it is foolish to infer from this that the soul itself—or that by which the body thinks—is not a substance distinct from the body.

Moreover, he attempts to confirm his statements with this <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is reached from two linked premises.</note>: <margin>25</margin> *Whatever we can conceive, that can exist:* <note>original: "Quicquid possumus concipere, id potest esse"</note> *But that the mind is one of these (namely, a substance, or a mode of bodily substance), can be conceived: for neither of these implies a contradiction: Therefore, etc.ᵃ* <margin>30</margin> Here it must be noted that this rule—*whatever we can conceive can exist*—although it is mine, and true, as often as...

I also do not wish to examine what is contained in *article four*<insert>a</insert> regarding the Holy Scriptures, lest I seem to arrogate to myself the right to inquire into another man’s religion. But I will say only this: three types of questions must be distinguished here. <margin>5</margin> First, some things are believed by faith alone, such as the mystery of the **Incarnation**, the **Trinity**, and similar matters. Second, others, although they pertain to faith, can also be investigated by <term>natural reason</term> <note>Descartes refers to "natural light" (*lumen naturale*), the innate human capacity to discover truths through logic and intellect without divine revelation.</note>; among these, the **existence of God** and the **distinction of the human soul from the body** are usually listed by orthodox <margin>10</margin> theologians. And finally, there are others which in no way pertain to faith, but look only to human reasoning, such as the **squaring of the circle**, the making of gold through the <term>chemical art</term> <note>original: "auro arte Chymicâ faciendo"; Descartes is likely referring to alchemy, which was still a serious pursuit of the era.</note>, and the like.

Just as those people misuse the words of Sacred Scripture who, by explaining them poorly, think they can extract these <margin>15</margin> latter [scientific] questions from them, so too do those detract from its authority who suspect that the former [purely theological] matters ought to be demonstrated by arguments sought from Philosophy alone. Nevertheless, all theologians maintain that it must be shown that these mysteries are not contrary to the natural light of reason, and they <margin>20</margin> place their chief study in this.

As for the middle category—the existence of God and the soul—theologians judge that they are not only not contrary to the natural light, but they even encourage philosophers to demonstrate them by human reasons to the best of their ability. Moreover, I have never seen anyone who affirmed <margin>25</margin> that the nature of things allows for a matter to be otherwise than as the Holy Scripture teaches, unless they intended to show indirectly that they had no faith in that Scripture. For since we were born as human beings before we were made Christians, it is not credible that anyone seriously embraces those opinions <margin>30</margin> which they think are contrary to the **right reason** that constitutes a human being, so as to [embrace] the faith through which they are a Christian...

I observed that there were certain thoughts in me which did not proceed from external objects, nor from the determination of my will, but from the faculty of thinking alone which is in me. <margin>5</margin>
certain diseases, like gout or stones <note>original: "podagram, vel calculum"; kidney or bladder stones.</note>, are innate. This is not because the infants of those families suffer from these diseases while still in 
<margin>10</margin>
their mother's womb, but because they are born with a certain disposition or faculty for contracting them.

Indeed, in *Article 13*^a, he draws a truly remarkable conclusion from the preceding one. He says (implying that the mind does not need innate ideas, but that the faculty of thinking alone 
<margin>15</margin>
suffices for it), "*all common notions, engraved on the mind, take their origin from the observation of things or from tradition:*". It is as if the faculty of thinking could achieve nothing by itself, and never perceives or thinks anything except what it 
<margin>20</margin>
receives from the observation of things or from tradition—that is, from the senses. <margin>25</margin>
not shown to us by the senses. Indeed, there is nothing in our ideas that was not innate to the mind, or the faculty of thinking, with the sole exception of those circumstances which relate to experience: namely, that we judge that these or
<margin>30</margin>
those ideas, which we now have present to our thought, refer to certain things placed outside of us.
