[The idea] of God, which is within us, does not come from our faculty of thinking—as if it were innate to it—but from divine revelation, or tradition, or the observation of things. <note>Descartes is quoting the argument of his opponent, Henricus Regius, who claimed that the idea of God is learned from the outside world rather than being a fundamental part of the human mind's structure.</note> We will more easily recognize the error of this assertion if we consider that something can be said to come from another either because that other is its <term>proximate cause</term> <note>original: "causa proxima"; in Aristotelian and Cartesian logic, the immediate, direct cause that produces an effect.</note> 
<margin>5</margin> 
and primary cause, without which it cannot exist; or because it is merely a <term>remote and accidental cause</term> <note>original: "remota & accidentaria"; a secondary factor that triggers a process but doesn't actually create the result itself.</note>, which namely gives the occasion for the primary cause to produce its effect at one time rather than another. <margin>10</margin> 
for them to do it, are accidental and remote causes, because perhaps they would not have done it unless ordered. There is no doubt, however, that tradition or the observation of things is often a remote cause, inviting us to attend to the idea of God that we are capable of having, 
<margin>15</margin>

<margin>20</margin> 
figure is shown to us by painters to represent God. <margin>25</margin> 
if through hearing, nothing except words and voices; if indeed through the other senses, nothing is contained in it that can be related to God. And indeed, it is manifest to everyone that sight, properly and of itself, shows nothing except pictures, nor hearing anything except voices or sounds:

This means they are always existing within us **potentially** <note>original: "potentiâ"; a philosophical term meaning the capacity for something to exist or happen, even if it isn't happening right now.</note>; for 
<margin>5</margin> to be in some faculty is not to be in **actuality** <note>original: "actu"; the state of being currently active or fully realized.</note>, but only in **potentiality**, because the very name "faculty" designates nothing other than a potentiality. <margin>24</margin> contingent <note>original: "contingens"; something that might or might not be true, or might or might not exist.</note> existence, as in the ideas of all other things, but altogether **necessary and actual** existence—is contained within his concept. <summary>Descartes defends his concept of "innate ideas," explaining they are natural capacities for thought rather than pre-formed knowledge, while mocking his critic Revius for attacking the idea that fetuses have conscious knowledge of God.</summary>

--- Page 765 ---
<meta>This page continues Descartes’s defense against the theological faculty at Leiden, specifically responding to the "Programma" (a published broadsheet) by his critics. Descartes is addressing the charge that his method of "universal doubt" makes him a temporary atheist or a skeptic, arguing that his doubt was merely a tool used to eventually reach more certain proofs of God’s existence.</meta>

<page-num>367</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>IN THE PROGRAM.</header>
<meta>58-59.</meta>

...that one must doubt, or that all trust in the senses must be revoked, or that sleep is not to be distinguished from wakefulness, or similar things which have occasionally been thrown at me by ignorant slanderers; but that I have rejected all these things in the clearest words, and <margin>5</margin> refuted them with the strongest arguments—indeed, I might even venture to add, more strongly than they have been refuted by anyone before me. 

In order to perform this more conveniently and effectively, I proposed, at the beginning of my *Meditations* <note>original: "Meditationum"</note>, all those points as being doubtful; they were not first <margin>10</margin> discovered by me, but were long ago repeated by the Sceptics <note>A school of ancient philosophy that argued humans cannot achieve certain knowledge. Descartes used their own weapons against them to find a truth that could not be doubted.</note>. What, then, is more unjust than to attribute to a writer opinions which he only recounts for the purpose of refuting them? What is more foolish than to imagine that those false opinions are being taught, at least during that time when they are proposed and not yet <margin>15</margin> refuted; and therefore that he who relates the arguments of atheists is a *temporary Atheist* <note>original: "Atheum temporarium". This was a specific charge from the theologian Jacobus Revius, suggesting that even if Descartes found God later, he was an atheist while he was "doubting" during the first chapters of his book.</note>? What is more childish than to say that if he should die in the meantime, before he has written or found his hoped-for demonstration, he would die an Atheist, and that he has taught a pernicious doctrine in advance—and <margin>20</margin> not rather that *evil must not be done so that good may come* <note>original: "esse facienda mala, ut eveniant bona". A reference to a common moral and biblical principle that one cannot justify a sinful means (like doubt) for a holy end (like proof of God).</note>, and such things? 

Someone will perhaps say that I did not report those false opinions as belonging to others, but as my own. But what does this matter? Since in the same book in which I reported them, I refuted <margin>25</margin> them all; and from the very title of the book it could be understood that I am completely far from believing them, since in it demonstrations of the existence of God <note>original: "existentiâ Dei"</note> are promised. Is anyone so dull-witted as to think that someone who composes such a book is ignorant, while [writing] its first pages...

---

a. Volume VII, p. 17-23.
b. *Ibid.*, p. p. xix, xxi, xxiij.

<summary>Descartes refutes the accusation that his method of starting with doubt makes him a "temporary atheist." He argues that he only raised skeptical arguments to ultimately prove God’s existence more effectively.</summary>
<keywords>Methodical Doubt, Meditations, Scepticism, Temporary Atheist, existence of God, Revius, theological controversy</keywords>

--- Page 766 ---
<meta>This page continues Descartes’s defense against his critics, specifically responding to the "Programma" (a broadsheet) published by theologians at Leiden. Descartes is explaining why he used a first-person, meditative style to present skeptical arguments, comparing his method to the way the Bible records the words of the impious before correcting them.</meta>

<page-num>368</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>### NOTES</header>
<meta>59-62.</meta>

...written down, what he has undertaken to demonstrate in the following pages? Moreover, I proposed the objections as if they were my own, because the style of the *Meditations* <note>original: "meditationum"</note> required this, which I judged to be the most suitable style for explaining reasons. If this 
<margin>5</margin> reasoning does not satisfy our censors, I would like to know what they say about the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "Sacris Literis"</note>, with which no human writings are to be compared, when they see in them several things that cannot be correctly understood unless they are assumed to have been spoken by the impious, or at least by others than the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Spiritu Sancto"</note> or the 
<margin>10</margin> Prophets. Such as, in Ecclesiastes <note>original: "Eccl."</note> chapter 2, these words: *Is it not better to eat and drink, and to show one's soul the good of one's labors? And this is from the hand of God. Who will devour and abound in delights as I?* And in the following chapter: *I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God might prove*
<margin>15</margin> *them and show that they are like beasts. Therefore, the death of man and of cattle is one, and the condition of both is equal: as man dies, so also let them die; all breathe alike, and man has nothing more than the beast, etc.* Do they believe that the Holy Spirit is teaching us there that the
<margin>20</margin> belly is to be indulged, that we should abound in delights, and that our souls are no more immortal than those of cattle? I do not think they are so insane. But neither should they slander me because, while writing, I did not use those precautions which were never observed by any other writers, nor even by the 
<margin>25</margin> Holy Spirit himself.

Third and finally, I warn the author of those pamphlets <note>This refers to the anonymous "Programma" and related tracts attacking Descartes's philosophy.</note> that I never wrote that *God ought to be called the efficient cause <term>efficient cause: the primary agent or force that produces an effect; in this context, the cause of one's own existence</term> of himself, not only negatively but also positively,* as 
<margin>30</margin> he very thoughtlessly affirms on page 8 of his second pamphlet. Let him search, read, and turn over my writings: nothing [anywhere]...

<summary>Descartes defends his use of skeptical arguments by comparing his "Meditations" to Ecclesiastes, arguing that recording false or impious ideas for the purpose of refutation is a standard practice even in the Bible. He also denies claiming that God is his own "positive efficient cause," a point of theological contention.</summary>
<keywords>Meditations, Holy Spirit, Ecclesiastes, skepticism, efficient cause, theology, Leiden controversy</keywords>

--- Page 767 ---
<meta>This page concludes Descartes’s response to his critics, specifically those who misrepresented his views in a public "Programma." He mocks the futility of their slanders and notes that his actual writings contradict their accusations. The page ends with the place and date of composition: Egmond, December 1647.</meta>

<page-num>369</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>### ON THE PROGRAM.</header>

...will find nothing similar in them, but rather the complete opposite. That I am as far removed as possible from such monstrous opinions is well known to all who have read my writings, have some knowledge of me, or at least do not think me entirely foolish. And for that reason, I wonder greatly what the aim of those <term>Slanderers</term> <note>original: "Calumniatorum"; Descartes refers to the theologians, likely including Revius and Trigland, who accused him of atheism and Pelagianism.</note> is: for if they wish to persuade people that I have written things that are the direct opposite of what is found in my works, they ought first to see to it that everything I have published is suppressed, and also erased from the memory of those who have already read them; for as long as they do not do this, they harm themselves more than me. I also wonder why they attack me with such bitterness and such zeal—me, who never provoked them and did them no harm, though perhaps I could harm them if they provoke me—while meanwhile they do nothing against many others who have refuted their doctrine in entire books and mocked them as <term>Simplicities</term> <note>original: "Simplicios"; likely a play on the character "Simplicio" from Galileo’s dialogues, representing the traditional Aristotelian view, as well as a general term for simpletons.</note> and <term>Andabatae</term> <note>original: "Andabatas"; ancient gladiators who fought in helmets without eye-holes, thus fighting blindly. Descartes uses this to describe critics who strike out without understanding their target.</note><sup>a</sup>. I do not wish to add anything here to call them away from their project of attacking me in their pamphlets: I am pleased to see myself held in such high regard by them; but meanwhile, I pray for their sanity.

*These things were written at Egmond in Holland, around the end of*
*December, in the year 1647.*

->THE END.<-

a. See above, p. 168, note *b*. See <term>ERASMUS</term> <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Dutch Renaissance humanist.</note>, Adages <note>original: "Adagia"</note>: Chilias II.
Centuria III. Proverb 33: *Andabatae* <note>Blindfolded gladiators.</note>.

<summary>Descartes concludes his defense by highlighting the absurdity of his critics' slanders, noting that his published works clearly refute their claims, and he mockingly prays for their sanity.</summary>
<keywords>Descartes, slanders, Andabatae, Egmond, Erasmus, polemics, 17th-century philosophy, Holland</keywords>

<meta>This page provides a bibliographical clarification following the conclusion of Descartes’s "Notae in Programma" (Notes on a Program). It lists the subsequent publications by Henricus Regius and the defenses of Descartes written by his followers like Tobias Andreae and Johannes Clauberg against critics such as Revius and Lentulus.</meta>

<page-num>369</page-num>

# CLARIFICATION

Regius <note>Henricus Regius (1598–1679), a Dutch physician who was once Descartes's protégé but became a bitter rival after publishing views on the mind that Descartes found materialistic and dangerous.</note> did not consider himself beaten after Descartes's response to his broadside of 1647. He returned to the attack twice, in 1648 and in 1657:
1° *Explanation of the Human Mind, etc., against Descartes.* <note>original Latin: "Explicatio Mentis humanæ &c. contra Cartesium"</note> (Utrecht, 1648, quarto.)
2° *A brief explanation of the Human Mind, or the rational Soul, previously submitted for public examination, and then somewhat clarified by the efforts of H. Regius of Utrecht, and defended against the notes of Descartes. Final edition...* <note>original Latin: "Brevis explicatio Mentis humanæ. sive Animæ rationalis, antea publico examini proposita, & deinde operâ H. Regii Ultraj. nonnihil dilucidata, & à notis Cartesii vindicata. Editio postrema..."</note> (Utrecht, printed by Th. ab Ackersdijck and G. à Zijll, year 1657, quarto, 36 pp.)

In the meantime, a friend of Descartes, Tobias Andreae <note>Tobias Andreae (1604–1676) was a professor at Groningen and a staunch defender of Cartesian philosophy in the Netherlands.</note>, had published a response to Regius in 1653:
*A Brief Replication offered in place of the Brief Explanation of the Human Mind, or the Rational Soul, of Mr. Henricus Regius, Physician and Philosopher of Utrecht, to strengthen the notes of Descartes on the Broadside concerning the same subject, and to better illustrate the truth. By* **Tobias Andreae**, *Master of Liberal Arts, Ordinary Professor of History and Greek Literature in the esteemed Academy of Groningen and Omland.* <note>original Latin: "Brevis Replicatio reposita Brevi Explicationi Mentis humanæ... A Tobia Andree..."</note> (Amsterdam, printed by Lodewijk Elzevir <note>The Elzevirs were a famous family of Dutch booksellers and printers active in the 17th century, known for their high-quality editions of scholarly works.</note>, 1653. Printer's mark: *the Minerva*. Small duodecimo, 6 preliminary leaves, 320 pp., 1 leaf of errata, 1 blank leaf.)

On the other hand, Revius <note>Jacobus Revius (1586–1658) was a Dutch theologian and poet who fiercely opposed Cartesianism on the grounds that it led to atheism.</note> had just published: *Theological consideration of the Cartesian Method*. <note>original Latin: "Methodi Cartesianæ consideratio theologica"</note> (Leiden, 1648, duodecimo.) This work prompted a response in favor of Descartes after the philosopher's death:
**Johannes Clauberg's**, *professor in the public Gymnasium of Duisburg-on-the-Rhine, Cartesian Defense against Jacobus Revius, theologian of Leiden, and Cyriacus Lentulus, professor at Herborn: first exoteric part, in which René Descartes's Discourse on Method is defended, while at the same time illustrious examples of Cartesian logic and philosophy are presented.* <note>original Latin: "Joh. Claubergii... Defensio Cartesiana, adversus Iacobum Revium..."</note> (Amsterdam, published by Lodewijk Elzevir, 1652, small duodecimo, 6 preliminary leaves, 631 pp.) Finally, Cyriacus Lentulus, professor at Herborn, had published against Descartes: *The New Wisdom of René Descartes, revealed by a method easier than before*. <note>original Latin: "Nova Ren. Des Cartes sapientia, faciliori quàm antehac methodo detecta"</note> (Herborn, 1651, duodecimo.)

<summary>This page lists the primary bibliographical sources involved in the intellectual conflict between Descartes and his former disciple Regius, as well as various theological attacks and defenses of Cartesianism following Descartes's death.</summary>

<keywords>Henricus Regius, Tobias Andreae, Jacobus Revius, Johannes Clauberg, Cyriacus Lentulus, Cartesianism, Dutch philosophy, Elzevir press, 17th-century bibliography</keywords>

# INDEX.

**TELESIO** (Bernardino): 26. <note>original: "TELESIUS." Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588) was an Italian philosopher whose work "On the Nature of Things" helped shift focus from Aristotelian metaphysics to sensory experience and naturalism.</note>
**Tertullus**: 75-6, 77, 95. <note>An orator in the New Testament (Acts 24) who prosecuted the Apostle Paul; the name is often used in polemics to imply a smooth-talking but malicious accuser.</note>
**Theophilus**: 337. <note>The person to whom the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles are addressed; the name means "friend of God."</note>
**THERSITES**: 63, 95, 147, 149, 166-7, 171. <note>A character from Homer's "Iliad" known for his insolence and vulgarity; used here as an archetype for a crude or slanderous critic.</note>
**THIENEN**: 66, 72.
**THOMAS** (Saint): 176. <note>original: "THOMAS (Stus)." St. Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century Scholastic theologian whose synthesis of faith and reason remained central to Catholic and even some Protestant thought.</note>
**THRASO**: 39. <note>A character from the play "The Eunuch" by Terence; a archetype of the boastful soldier or "braggart."</note>
**THUILLERIE** (G. DE LA): 217, 242, 291, 302, 322. <note>Gaspard de la Thuillerie, a French diplomat who served as ambassador to the Netherlands during the height of these intellectual controversies.</note>
**TIMON**: 142. <note>Timon of Athens, the legendary misanthrope who retreated from human society.</note>
**TOBIE D'ANDRÉ**: 370.
**TORRENTIUS**: 23, 140-1, 318. <note>Laevinus Torrentius (1525–1595), a Dutch humanist, poet, and Bishop of Antwerp.</note>
**TRIGLANDIUS**: 106. <note>Jacobus Trigland (1583–1654), a key Dutch Reformed theologian and a staunch defender of orthodoxy against the Remonstrants.</note>
**TULLEKENS**: 66.
**TULLIUS** (M.): 36, 83. <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman whose works on ethics and rhetoric were foundational to early modern education.</note>

**UDEMANS**: 69, 96. <note>Godefridus Udemans (1581–1649), a Dutch minister influential in the "Further Reformation" and author of practical guides on Christian life.</note>
**UTENBOGARDUS**: 87. <note>Also spelled Wtenbogaert; a leading figure of the Remonstrants who advocated for religious tolerance in the Dutch Republic.</note>

<column-break/>

**VALENCIA** (GREGORY DE): 176. <note>original: "VALENTIA (GREG. DE)." Gregorio de Valencia (1550–1603), a Spanish Jesuit who taught in Germany and was a major defender of Catholic orthodoxy.</note>
**VALLE** (G. DE): 22. <note>Possibly a pseudonym for the philosopher Vanini, or a reference to Giulio Cesare della Valle.</note>
**VANINI** (J.-C.): 5, 22, 142, 160, 174-6, 179, 181-2, 207, 210, 254, 286-7, 308. <note>Lucilio (Julius Caesar) Vanini, an Italian philosopher executed in 1619 for "atheism" and "blasphemy." He was a frequent "boogeyman" in 17th-century theological debates.</note>
**VINNIUS** (A.): 331. <note>Arnoldus Vinnius (1588–1657), one of the most famous legal scholars of the 17th century at the University of Leiden.</note>
**VIRGIL**: 31. <note>original: "VIRGILE." The Roman poet of the Augustan age, author of the "Aeneid."</note>
**VORSTIUS**: 196. <note>Conrad Vorstius (1569–1622), a Remonstrant theologian whose appointment at Leiden triggered a massive international religious and political crisis.</note>

**WAESBERGE** (Joh. van): 5, 6, 56, 136, 204, 234. <note>Johannes van Waesberge, a member of a prominent family of Dutch printers and publishers active in Utrecht and Amsterdam.</note>
**WATERLAET** (Lambert van): 70, 161, 234, 246, 253-4, 257-9, 298, 305, 310-311. <note>Lambertus van Waterlaet, a schoolmaster in Utrecht who engaged in fierce polemics against Descartes and his local followers.</note>
**WEEDE** (Joh. van): 214. <note>Johan van Weede, a prominent member of the Utrecht city council and a patron of various intellectual causes.</note>
**WTENBOGARDUS**: *See* UTENBOGARDUS.

**ZANCHIUS**: 105. <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), an Italian Protestant Reformer and an influential teacher of Reformed Scholasticism.</note>
**ZONST** (L. van): 66.
**ZUERIUS**: *See* SUERIUS. <note>Likely referring to Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn (1612–1653), a professor at Leiden known for his work in history and linguistics.</note>

->[Decorative Endpaper]<-

This page features a full-bleed decorative pattern, a traditional element of fine bookbinding. The design consists of a dense, repeating organic motif printed in vibrant red ink against a pale tan or beige background.

The pattern resembles branching coral, seaweed, or <term>dendritic</term> <note>From the Greek "dendron" (tree); describing a branched form resembling a tree, moss, or crystal growth.</note> formations. It is characterized by irregular, spiky offshoots and occasional circular nodes or clusters interspersed within the branches.
